Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Where next for Moses Itauma? Filip Hrgovic's savage verdict has shattered the Mike Tyson hype as Britain's fallen prodigy begins his long road back, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
The most alarming contribution to the inquest into the slaying of Moses came from the national hero of Croatia who was the real story of a Saturday night at the O2 which was dark for British boxing but dazzling to behold.

Filip Hrgovic said of our young Itauma: ‘No, I didn’t feel his power.’

That will be as devastating to the lad previously hailed as the next Mike Tyson as James Bond being told he is no longer attractive to women.

It will hurt even more than the punches which sent him reeling from domination to defeat and hospital on the evening he was supposed to become the second youngest world heavyweight champion of all time.

Power has been Moses Itauma’s middle name since he began felling giants like saplings. Suddenly, at 21, he is being likened to Samson who lost his mythological strength when he had a haircut.

Were there clues in how Hrgovic survived the first eight rounds of this IBF world title fight and countless punches, every one of which looked as if it would have knocked out a horse?

Moses Itauma saw his hope of becoming the second youngest heavyweight world champion ended by Filip Hrgovic

Hrgovic, right, declared afterwards that he 'didn't feel his power' in another blow to Itauma

To suggest as much would be to downplay the superhuman heart and phenomenal resilience of chin with which Hrgovic realised his own lifelong ambition of global glory. Just in time at 34.

Nevertheless, Itauma could not finish him off. Which brings other factors into issue. It is concerning, also, that Britain’s young lion should gas out on the first time in his career he was required to go beyond six rounds. Trainer Ben Davison finds himself under inquisition as to whether presumption of another early KO left Moses short on stamina build-up. Or did he simply punch himself out?

Whatever the reason, it was worrying to see one so young that exhausted as he staggered to extinction as early as the ninth round. Certainly Hrgovic put into words what many of us felt. That he was beaten in a large part by experience. The new champion who had vowed to ‘smash the kid’s face and send him back to high school’ had this to say after he had done just that: ‘He is a tremendous talent but he boxed like an amateur and must learn to fight like a professional.

‘With more experience he would have known he was winning every round and what he should have done was box out the fight to a points decision behind his jab. Not keep trying to knock me out. Although I did know he would tire the longer the fight went.’

But no power in his punches? Of being dropped once, a flash knock-down in the second round, Hrgovic said: ‘I didn’t feel it. He is very fast and caught me off balance with a punch I didn’t see.’

And so it would come to pass that in the battle of their ages it was from the kid’s corner that the white towel came fluttering in. By then not to great surprise. As early as the fifth round Itauma was beginning to grimace at the physical demands being made of him and the heavy hits he, too, was taking. In the eighth he launched a desperate assault which Hrgovic not only rode out but also inflicted damage of his own.

To his credit Itauma prodded out some punches at the start of the ninth but looked more like a fish floundering out of water. Hrgovic speared him with what he called ‘strength which came from Jesus Christ’.

So what next for he who was hailed as the next Mike Tyson? Hrgovic’s advice: ‘Several easier fights to gain more experience and rebuild his confidence. And I do think that with his speed of hand he will become a world champion one day.’

Hrgovic highlighted how he had used his experience to see off the challenge of Itauma

Hrgovic showed phenomenal resilience to achieve his lifelong dream at the age of 34

Hrgovic advised Itauma to take some easier fights to rebuild his confidence after the defeat

Promoter Frank Warren sympathised: ‘A first defeat does take away that aura of invincibility and we will give Moses the time it takes to recover from that. He is still a very special talent.’

Meanwhile, heavyweight life goes on. Warren has announced October 17 at the O2 for a lip-smacking WBO world-title rematch of the thunderous Battle of Britain between champion Daniel Dubois and white-collar graduate Fabio Wardley. Hrgovic will make his first championship defence against Cuba’s mandatory challenger Frank Sanchez and makes a prediction when he says: ‘I want to go on to a title unification fight against Daniel.’

And may it please the lords of the ring that Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury get their act together in November, whether it be in London or New York.

It will be some while before Itauma rejoins the fray, from the back of the queue. He went home from hospital the morning after his downfall to begin recuperation from the battering and also a leg injured as he reeled against the ropes.

The psychological wounds will take much longer to heal. Though it is not impossible. Muhammad Ali, Joe Louis, Joe Frazier, George Foreman and Lennox Lewis – to name but a few – all lost more than one fight and came back as champions.

But Moses Itauma the next Mike Tyson? Even as Filip Hrgovic goes home to a much-deserved hero’s welcome in Zagreb, one thing we do know for sure is that if the original Iron Mike had landed just one of the punches he took on Saturday night, he would have been knocked out.

Sports.title: Boxing legend Tony Mundine dies aged 75 - as his ex-NRL star son Anthony Mundine flies back to Australia from the Middle East
Sports.content:
Boxing legend Tony Mundine dies aged 75 - as his ex-NRL star son Anthony Mundine flies back to Australia from the Middle East

Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died.

The 75-year-old is understood to have suffered a heart attack on Sunday.

His son Anthony Mundine – a former NRL star who followed in his father's footsteps and forged a successful boxing career after leaving the game – is reportedly flying back from the Middle East, Code Sports reported.

Mundine senior made history as the only Australian boxer to fight professionally across four weight divisions, in which he held the Australian titles for middleweight, light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight classes.

He also fought for the World Boxing Association (WBA) middleweight title in 1974.

His impressive record from 96 fights is 80 wins, 64 of those being KO victories.

When Anthony took to the ring in 2000 following a successful rugby league career, his father served as his primary trainer.

Under his guidance, Anthony rose to the top of the sport, twice winning the WBA super-middleweight title in 2003 and 2008, the IBO middleweight title in 2009, and the WBA interim super-welterweight title in 2011.

Tony Mundine (left) has died, with his son Anthony (right) on his way back to Australia

Tony was inducted into the Australian boxing hall of fame in 2005 (pictured in his boxing days)

He became his son's trainer during his highly successful boxing career

Tony was born in the town of Baryulgil in north-eastern NSW, on the lands of the Bundjalung people.

He played for Grafton Rugby league club before being offered a place at the Redfern All Blacks in the South Sydney Junior Rugby League.

Between seasons, he trained at a gym run by Ern McQuillan, who took him on in a fighter-trainer contract.

In later life, he resided in Redfern where he ran the Redfern Gym.

He was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1986 for service to sport and to Aboriginal youth.

In 2005, he was inducted into the Australian Boxing Hall of Fame.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma LOSES IBF world heavyweight title clash in huge upset: British star leaves arena on a stretcher after being stopped by Filip Hrgovic in ninth round
Sports.content:
Moses Itauma LOSES IBF world heavyweight title clash in huge upset: British star leaves arena on a stretcher after being stopped by Filip Hrgovic in ninth round

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Moses rose to the mountain summit and was left there as a brother Christian climbed over him and walked on to the promised land.

There was a hugely significant difference from his biblical namesake.

Itauma was flattened in a fight against Filip Hrgovic the Croatian Iron Man of such astonishing violence that it was frightening.

A fight so brutal that the most trumpeted UK boxing prodigy for decades had to be carried out of the ring on a stretcher - make that his shield - and on to hospital.

The other promise - that of becoming the second youngest world heavyweight champion of all time behind Mike Tyson - went unfulfilled.

Hopefully not for good.

Moses Itauma has suffered his first pro defeat at the hands of Croatian star Filip Hrgovic

Itauma, 21, was taken away from the ring on a stretcher after a brutal contest

But not the prediction of a fight across their ages to remember for years to come.

Twenty-one played 34 and the kid lost - after flooring and pounding Hrgovic for eight rounds.

By his own admission Hrgovic did ‘not know where I found the strength and energy to beat him to the ground in the ninth.

But he did venture to add: ‘ I knew he would tire at some point.'

As Itauma was submerged by a torrent of punches the towel fluttered in from his corner.

He lived to fight. Maybe only just.

Prior to the showdown, questions had hung over London’s 02.

Was Moses too young to fulfil all the prophesies?

Was Fil the Croat too late in life to seize the Holy Grail?

Hrgovic claimed the vacant IBF world heavyweight title after surviving plenty of heavy punches - and dealing his own

Had Itauma lost his cool at the very last with that schoolboy shove at the weigh-in. Or had he been asked to help sell the last few tickets somewhat surprisingly still for sale on Friday evening?

Had Hrgovic — who was fighting a British boxer for the fifth consecutive time — eventually succeeded in getting under the skin of the lad whose face he threatened to smash?

Would we be treated to the promised slugfest and brutal knockout? Which of them might be launched to stardom?

As they say, anything can happen in heavyweight boxing — and Itauma was to find that out to his cost later.

Among those who were looking most keenly for answers were potential future opponents for Itauma. Daniel Dubois, another big-hitting English heavyweight prodigy who already wears the WBO world championship belt, and white collar puncher Fabio Wardley.

Those two meet this October in a rematch of their midsummer slugfest in which Dubois prevailed by brute force and willpower in the 11th round — and the pair squared up to each other in the ring before the main event, which was scheduled for 12 rounds.

That will all have to wait for now. Itauma, who was born in Kezmarok, Slovakia, but raised in Kent after moving at eight years old, stormed out of the blocks.

Both had pledged to go for a quick kill in the fervent 02. Itauma was as good as his word. His first five big shots won the first but Hrgovic’s chin proved resilient.

Itauma is the most trumpeted British heavyweight prodigy for decades, but this is a setback

Moses tested it to better effect at the onset of the second and scored a flash knockdown. But the Croat rallied and slowly came into the fight, shaking Itauma three times in the third.

In the fourth, there were worrying signs for the man from Zagreb as a cut appeared above his right eye. Itauma kept examining the Hrgovic chin but he could not land the early finish.

To his credit, Hrgovic was giving as good as he got as he traded blows with Itauma in the fifth during some brutal exchanges.

It was pretty much the same story in an astonishing sixth that tested the resilience of both to the limit as they tried to land a killer blow. By now, both fighters appeared to be struggling as the gas tank appeared to empty.

It was new ground for Itauma in the seventh as he had never gone beyond six rounds.

In his impatience, some of his swings became wild. But not all. By the end of the round, Hrgovic was being treated for a swelling above his left eye.

It looked all over in the eighth as Itauma unleashed a flurry of big shots. But Hrgovic refused to down tools and found a second wind in the ninth as he put paid to Itauma’s hopes of a historic victory.

Other men were brave beyond the call. But the most rousing salute of all must go Croatia's first world heavyweight champion.

Filip Hrgovic. What a man.

Sports.title: Filip Hrgovic insists he knew Moses Itauma would 'gas out' in world heavyweight title fight - but backs the beaten British star as 'the future'
Sports.content:
Filip Hrgovic declared he knew that Moses Itauma would 'gas out' after handing the Briton a shock defeat in their heavyweight world title fight.

Itauma had been the heavy favourite heading into the showdown at the O2 Arena and was bidding to become the second youngest heavyweight world champion in history after Mike Tyson.

The 21-year-old, who had won all 14 of his previous fights, looked on course for victory after knocking down Hrgovic in the second round and continued to control the fight.

Hrgovic, however, remained resilient and held off Itauma with the British star looking exhausted by the end of the eighth round.

The Croatian seized his chance in the ninth and pinned a struggling Itauma back, with the towel eventually thrown in to end the contest.

Hrgovic, who became Croatia's first heavyweight world champion, insisted he knew early on in the fight that Itauma would tire and despite 'losing every round' would be able to take advantage of his rivals' conditioning late on.

Filip Hrgovic has insisted he knew Moses Itauma would 'gas out' in their world title fight

Itauma controlled much of the fight but the contest was stopped in the ninth round after the visibly exhausted British fighter struggled against Hrgovic

'You're going to be sending Moses back to high school. Let me ask my young friend something. Is chin important? Is chin important?' Hrgovic said.

'He didn't seem to think so, but I think he may have answered that question. Look, chin is important.

'He's an amazing fighter. I want to thank him for accepting this fight, to give me a chance to become a new superstar in the heavyweight division.

'I'm the present, and he's definitely the future. He's an amazing fighter. He's one of a kind. He's the best I've been in the ring with, but he needs more experience.

'From the first round, I saw him gassing out. He started fast. I knew he was going to gas out.

'I knew when my chance came, I needed to push. That is what I did.'

Itauma, who left the ring on a stretcher and went to hospital for checks, has been backed to bounce back from the defeat.

'Filip done amazing to ride through the storm! I’ll say this now! Moses Itauma will be world champion! He will learn so much from tonight,' Bellew wrote on X.

Hrgovic insisted Itauma is still 'the future' with several stars backing Itauma to learn and bounce back from the first defeat of his career

'The biggest thing I’ll take from tonight is just how brave and tough Moses was.

'We knew Filip was super tough. Tonight we learned Moses is also tough, Once he learns to pace a 12 round bout he’s gonna rule for a while!

'Filip Hrgovic’s chin needs to studied…'

Eubank Jr added: 'Not sure what happened tonight. Moses was fighting well & then gassed out it seems… at his young age this should simply not be happening.

'Time to rethink his training camp moving forward I think. Congratulations to Filip Hrgović becoming the new heavyweight champ.'

Sports.title: Quiet, Bible-reading Moses Itauma boasts near-decapitating punching power and is on the cusp of greatness as he looks to emulate Mike Tyson - but here's why Filip Hrgovic will NOT be a walkover, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
Quiet, Bible-reading Moses Itauma boasts near-decapitating punching power and is on the cusp of greatness as he looks to emulate Mike Tyson - but here's why Filip Hrgovic will NOT be a walkover, writes JEFF POWELL

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

I’m going to punch your nose bone into your brain.

So Mike Tyson spoke from the dark depths of his New York upbringing in the crack cocaine quarter of Brownsville by way of petrifying his opponents.

No weapon against you shall prosper. Every tongue which rises against you in judgement you shall condemn.

So Moses Itauma quotes biblically from Isaiah 54:17 before entering the ring.

As Itauma stands on the brink of becoming the second youngest world heavyweight champion in boxing history, so comparisons with the legend who still holds that distinction multiply.

Teddy Atlas, one-time trainer of Iron Mike whose motivational tools included a loaded gun pointed at Tyson in a changing room, is taken by a likeness in their near-decapitating power.

Moses Itauma will look to bring his huge punching power to bear against Croatia's Filip Hrgovic in their IBF world title fight on Saturday

Itauma tries to bring his huge punching to bear against Croatian hard-man Filip Hrgovic in this Saturday night’s fight at London’s O2 for the vacant IBF world title. He does so grateful for the compliment, while stressing the variance in their personalities.

‘I’m flattered to hear that from such a respected figure in boxing,’ he says. ‘Of course I like being compared with the great Mike Tyson as a fighter. But we are different people. I’m not braggadocious. I don’t threaten or bad-mouth people. I respect all my opponents.’ Of whom all 14 have been beaten out of sight, 12 of them by knock-out, none lasting longer than six rounds.

By Itauma standards that is a lengthy statement. Mostly when asked questions about his growing reputation, his own potential for greatness, his thrilling impact on this business, the skills as well as the punching, his stock reply is: ’Honestly I don’t see myself that way.’ He usually adds: ‘I know I’m a young man, still learning.’

So young that if he defeats Hrgovic he will have come within two months of Tyson’s record as the youngest heavyweight champion. ‘I did have an ambition to be that man,’ he says. ‘But honestly it was only in the back of my mind. More important is how I develop.’

In this hard old game which is wearying of the faux-murderous ranting, table throwing and foul language – followed by brotherly love at the final bell – he is a quiet breath of fresh air. It is the pace at which Itauma is developing, at 21, which is the cause for real concern among the heavyweight fraternity.

Atlas speaks to his all-round abilities: ‘It’s not only the southpaw KO punch but the fast combinations, the balance, the reading of an opponent which gets him into position for maximum effect.’

Itauma’s trainer has no need of a pistol to encourage hard work on those qualities. He convinces by persuasion and reports: ‘Moses is a fast and eager learner.’

The young man himself attributes his professionalism and determination to his parents and how they brought him as a three-year-old from the small town of Kezmarok in Slovakia to the British naval port of Chatham. He credits his Nigerian father for his physical strength and his Slovak mother for his will-power. That blend exposed them to the Eastern European racism which obliged them to immigrate to the UK. Moses was the last of them to make the journey, waiting with an aunt while his parents scouted the land on England’s south coast and then sent for him to join them and his two brothers.

The pair clashed on the eve of a fight that could see Itauma become the second youngest heavyweight world champion

The gratitude of the family is to be seen by the Union Jack hung on the walls of their home. In return, the UK has acquired a working family and a potential world heavyweight champion. Perhaps even the undisputed heir to Oleksandr Usyk, more of whose vacated alpha-belts will come into Itauma’s sights if all goes well at the O2.

Not that Hrgovic should be taken at all lightly. At 34 the man from Zagreb is in his prime and until Moses came along was the most avoided heavyweight on the planet. He has frequently been passed over for deserved world title shots, while being fobbed off with ‘final eliminators.’

To their credit several of our heavies have risen to the challenge of the most highly rated fighter in Croatian ring history. He has mopped up Joe Joyce and cult figure Dave Allen.

The only defeat of his 21 fight career was inflicted by Daniel Dubois in one of those elimination bouts but he was ahead on points when he suffered the deep cuts which forced the eighth round stoppage. Notably, as it comes to Itauma, he has withstood the big punching of both Dubois and Joyce. As well as the renowned KO power of Chinese giant Zhilei Zhang.

Itauma, who has not come close to losing in his first 14 professional fights, knows Hrgovic will not roll over easily and declares himself ‘prepared for this one to go as long as it takes.’ But he does add: ‘I know that people don’t come to see heavyweights box to points decisions.’

The humorous Croatian has tweaked the Moses nerves by saying: ‘It will be good for his boxing soul when I give him the experience of a first defeat.’ Itauma’s unruffled answer: ‘Mike Tyson used that to rattle his opponents but it didn’t do them much good.’

Since 15 of Hrgovic’s 20 victories have been knock-outs the blood lust will be rising in a packed O2 in anticipation of a slugfest. As well as expectancy of confirmation that this Moses is on a journey to the undisputed crown.

That would require him making a successful first title defence against Cuban slugger Frank Sanchez, who was paid to step aside from his mandatory right to be in one of the corners this Saturday.

After that, fans, how about a good old-fashioned British barn-burner against the winner of the Dubois-Fabio Wardley rematch for the WBO belt? With whichever gladiator still standing going on to mop up the other two titles vacated by Usyk. The WBC and WBA held respectively by Germany’s Agit Kabayel and Russia’s Murat Gassiev.

Promoter Frank Warren may switch the order by saving his two youngest prodigies from fighting each other until they have bagged all the alpha belts between them. Which would keep them apart until late next year.

The prospect of Itauma coming out top of that pile would have seemed premature until he obliterated America’s Jermaine Franklin inside five rounds this March. Now the bookies quote him as the favourite against all-comers.

Hrgovic should not be taken lightly with the Croatian having been the most avoided heavyweight on the planet, who has deserved more shots at world titles

By the time all that is done and dusted, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua might have settled finally their longstanding differences so that one or other could provide a cross generational Wembley extravaganza. For which Itauma might still be just 22.

Teddy Atlas would expect nothing less than Itauma crushing AJ or The Gipsy King. Albeit by way of a variation on the Tyson theme. He explains: ‘Moses brings other dimensions. Movement. Positioning. Patience when needed if he doesn’t stop ‘em in the first round. And his KOs usually come from combinations. When he sees an opening he throws a lot of leather. He is a more complete boxer. But Mike is still boxing’s most pure one-hit knock out puncher.’

Hrgovic will provide the most severe test yet of Itauma’s finishing power and his punch resistance. If he passes, we may well be witnessing the start of something very big indeed.

Might even Oleksandr The Greatest of his generation have seen Moses coming when he dropped all those belts?

*Itauma v Hrgovic will be televised live on DAZN pay-per-view

Sports.title: PRINCE NASEEM HAMED: New British boxing heavyweight star Moses Itauma could be as big as Michael Jordan or Tiger Woods... and even better than me!
Sports.content:
Naseem Hamed is late.

It is not, as you might expect, because the former world champion has travelled halfway across the country to meet. He lives 10 minutes down the road from the Fairmont Windsor Park, one of his favourite hotels.

'I'm only late because I live so close,' he jokes. 'What can I say, you know me, I like making an entrance.'

Hamed strolls into the library room in a black T-shirt and black shorts, grabs a cup of tea in a rather more elegant china mug than most people would settle for, and drops into his chair.

There is still a presence about him. A big energy. The kind that made him one of British boxing's biggest stars long before social media existed.

We are here to talk about Moses Itauma, who this weekend will attempt to become the youngest British heavyweight champion in history when he faces Filip Hrgovic for the vacant IBF title.

Daily Mail Sport sat down with Prince Naseem Hamed to speak about Moses Itauma

Hamed was full of praise for young British superstar Itauma, who is fighting Filip Hrgovic

The pair are facing off for the vacant IBF heavyweight title at London's O2 Arena this weekend

And Hamed has barely settled in before he delivers a verdict that would have been unthinkable for the man who once called himself The Prince.

'I'm going to say something I've never said before. I think Moses is better than me. I haven't said that about many fighters. Actually, I haven't said that about any fighters. But, I think Moses has a very bright future. He is going to be the best that's ever lived.

'Listen, I can't just put him right there in front of every greatest fighter that's ever lived right now. He has to face some challenges and everybody needs a dancing partner in boxing. You know, Muhammad Ali had Joe Frazier, and Thomas 'Hitman' Hearns had Roberto Duran and Sugar Ray Leonard. But, Moses has got the ability to go all the way and beyond.'

And Hamed is talking about more than just boxing. He sees the makings of a sporting star in the mould of the biggest names in the world.

'I've seen Moses has become the face of Nike. Let me tell you something about Nike: they don't really get it wrong too much. They pick the right guys. When they picked Michael Jordan, they chose right. When they chose Tiger Woods, they chose right. They've got Moses now and they've chosen right.'

Think about that for a moment. The Prince Naseem Hamed, a man whose entire persona was built around the certainty that he was the most talented fighter in history, has just volunteered another man for the throne.

He is not saying it because he has been pressed into a comparison or because he is trying to be generous to a young protege. He is saying it because, having watched Itauma, he genuinely believes it.

'I've always waited for somebody to come along that I could say is going to be better than me,' he says. 'And I can honestly look at Moses and just think, yeah, this guy's the one. There is no one else I could even think about saying that about.'

So why Itauma?

Hamed points to something beyond the knockouts.

'He's more of a correct and complete fighter compared to what I was. Mine was a natural force of ability. It was all ad-lib. You didn't know what was going to happen, it was one of a kind and although Moses has that too, I think he's more calculated. More correct. His speed is blinding for somebody who's six foot four. He's so light on his feet, can move and has got blistering speed. Then there is the power. That's why it's going to be really hard for anybody in the sport of boxing today to get anywhere near him.'

Now Itauma has the chance to show the world why Hamed is so convinced.

At 21 years and seven months, he is only fractionally older than Hamed was when he challenged Steve Robinson for the WBO featherweight title. Hamed went into that fight 19-0 with 17 knockouts, having boxed 68 professional rounds.

Itauma is 14-0 with 12 knockouts and has boxed just 31 rounds.

It is an extraordinary lack of experience for a man about to fight for a world heavyweight title, particularly against Hrgovic.

The Croatian is 34, has won 20 of his 21 fights and stopped 15 opponents. His only defeat came against Daniel Dubois. He is bigger, older and vastly more experienced than most of the men Itauma has faced.

And there is a question hanging over the unbeaten Brit: what happens when somebody finally makes him uncomfortable?

Hamed had to answer it himself against Kevin Kelley in New York.

It was Hamed's US debut, with HBO heavily promoting his arrival and plastering his face across Times Square. But instead of the quick finish he had expected, Kelley dropped him three times - only for the Brit to rise each time and win.

Itauma has never faced that kind of adversity. He has not boxed beyond the sixth round and, after stopping his last two opponents inside five rounds, has spent barely sixteen minutes in the ring over his last two outings.

Hamed knows there is no way of predicting how someone will react when they are finally forced into that territory but believes Itauma is equipped to handle it.

'I've always said you don't know how somebody is going to react until they get hit with a huge shot.

'Everybody talks about Moses not having enough rounds, but I didn't have loads of rounds either. We both didn't have that learning phase in the same way a lot of fighters do.

'With the Kelley fight, it was the first time I found myself in that sort of situation really and I dealt with it. I got knocked down, I got back up and I won the fight. That's experience in itself.

'Of course I'd love Moses to have more experience. I'd love him to go through those hard rounds and learn what fighters normally learn. But boxing is about levels.

'And when you're already on the level Moses is on, you don't necessarily need to go through everything everybody else has gone through to get where you're going.'

Hamed (pictured in 1999) finished his career with a record of 36 wins and one defeat

Hamed believes Itauma is better than he was and argued the young Brit could become as big a sporting star as the likes of Michael Jordan and Tiger Woods

Hamed points to Itauma's demolition of Dillian Whyte as evidence.

Whyte was 36 and well past his best when they met, but he was still a former world title challenger with years of heavyweight experience and a record that included fights with Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury.

Itauma took him apart in just a few minutes.

'Who would have thought that the fight with Dillian Whyte, with all his experience and with the trouble that he gave AJ and everything else, was going to be such a one-sided fight over in, I don't know, minutes?'

There is another part of Itauma that Hamed keeps returning to.

His humility.

'I love the fact of how humble he is,' Hamed says. 'His parents must have brought him up to be the man that he is today, because it shows. And he's a breath of fresh air in boxing.'

That matters because the attention around Itauma is already enormous.

Frank Warren, Hamed's old promoter, has called him the most talented boxer he has worked with at that age - even more talented than Hamed - and the nation are already crowning him the next face of British boxing.

Hamed knows what it is like to be placed under that kind of spotlight, so I ask him whether the expectations ever weighed on him. His answer is characteristically Hamed.

'I didn't know what pressure meant. I never felt pressure. I didn't understand pressure. I couldn't even spell it.

'So, I never felt that I was that type of guy to let things like that get under my skin, or be nervous, or feel pressure in any way.

'And we always say pressure makes diamonds, so I don't think that's going to happen with Moses.'

It was a different time in British boxing, but Hamed was not alone in carrying the weight of expectation. Ricky Hatton, who was on the undercard against Kelley that night in New York, would go on to become one of the biggest names in the sport alongside Hamed.

'I loved everything about Ricky. Ricky was a people's person. I never, ever saw support for a fighter in this country the way they loved Ricky. The amount of people that used to come out to Vegas to watch him fight, there was too many people! He just took over everything.

'When he'd fight in Manchester, there'd be over, I don't know, 50,000. We never saw crowds come out like that for any fighter in the history of boxing in the UK. Ricky had something special in regards to the love in people's hearts, how he made people feel and how he was just one of the boys, and just how genuine he was. He'd say what he felt, similar to myself.

'But he was an exceptionally good fighter. He was an amazing body puncher, and he did unbelievable in his career. He's one of the fighters that we can all say will go down in history as one of the best fighters this country has ever produced.

'It was just so sad to find out when we did about him. God bless him and his family. His family, I can't even imagine what they've been through and what they're going through. He's sadly missed. He'll never be forgotten, and he lit up Manchester in a way that nobody did.'

Itauma (right) is 14-0 with 12 knockouts and has boxed just 31 rounds in his career (pictured in action against Ilja Mezencev in May 2024)

Itauma will hope to prove Hamed right when he takes on Hrgovic in the much anticipated bout

For all the memories, the conversation brings Hamed back to the present and to his frustration that two of Britain's biggest current stars have chosen to take their long-awaited showdown away from the fans who helped make them.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury look set to meet at Madison Square Garden on November 20, but Hamed thinks the fight belongs somewhere else.

'I think that's a UK fight. I think that's a big UK fight, and I think it should sell out Wembley. Madison Square Garden is an amazing place, and it's history, isn't it? And it will always be history in the making for any big fight.

'But I would prefer to watch that fight on our own soil, in London, and I think the British public deserve that to be in this country. You've got great British fighters that had a huge name in boxing a little bit before now, but in my eyes, that fight's better to be in London than in the States and in New York.'

As for who wins, even Hamed refuses to make a definitive call.

'That's a good question. I think any of them can win. For me, if Tyson Fury fights like he did against Wilder the first or the second time, it's going to be hard for AJ to beat that kind of guy.

'But we don't know who we have today in regards to Tyson Fury and where he's really at, and we don't know which AJ we have, especially after his last fight and everything he's been through.

'Look, it's going to be a big fight. Is it around about three, four, maybe five years too late. But regardless, I think the British public still want to see it.'

And that, ultimately, is why Hamed's excitement about Itauma feels so significant. He remembers what it was like when British boxing had fighters who could command the attention of an entire country. He believes Itauma could be the next one.

There is only one thing left for Itauma to do: prove him right.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic weigh-in descends into chaos as British star PUSHES rival off stage - before being SLAPPED
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic had to be pulled apart by security after their heavyweight weigh-in descended into chaos when Hrgovic was pushed off the stage before slapping his British rival.

The two heavyweights exchanged heated words during their face-off before lining up for one final set of photographs.

But when Hrgovic stepped in front of Itauma, the Brit shoved him forward, sending his opponent tumbling off the stage.

A furious Hrgovic immediately climbed back up and slapped Itauma, who then went berserk as both men attempted to fight before security rushed in to drag them apart.

The extraordinary scenes came just 24 hours before Itauma's first shot at becoming heavyweight world champion.

It was a notable change from the 21-year-old, who has remained largely calm throughout the build-up despite Hrgovic's repeated attempts to get under his skin.

Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic had to be pulled apart by security after their heavyweight weigh-in descended into chaos

Itauma started the chaos when he pushed Hrgovic off stage before his rival slapped him

Itauma had previously dismissed his rival's insults as 'schoolground banter', while Hrgovic has tried to provoke him at almost every opportunity during fight week.

The British heavyweight had even told his manager not to nibble at Hrgovic during Thursday's press conference, seemingly determined not to be drawn into any of the mind games.

But after keeping his composure throughout the week, it was Itauma himself who finally snapped at the weigh-in.

And while it offered a side to the unbeaten heavyweight that few have seen before, those watching appeared to love it.

Hrgovic was still furious when he spoke after the confrontation and vowed to 'smash' Itauma when the pair meet in the ring tomorrow night.

Itauma, meanwhile, admitted that he had been unable to resist the temptation to react.

'I had a scratch to itch and I had to do that today,' he said.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury at risk of COLLAPSE: AJ faces 10-day deadline to agree terms on New York super-fight or see it cancelled
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury at risk of COLLAPSE: AJ faces 10-day deadline to agree terms on New York super-fight or see it cancelled

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Anthony Joshua has 10 days to agree terms or the richest fight in British boxing history will fall by the wayside.

Tyson Fury is already in full training in Miami and his promoter Frank Warren warns: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

Joshua and his promoter Eddie Hearn's heated opposition to this Battle of Britain being moved from Wembley to New York delayed further this spectacle which the public have been demanding through two decades.

Hearn has led the heated demands for even more millions to compensate Joshua for waiving his first-contract right to the fight taking place in England.

Netflix and the Saudi Arabians, who are the nine-figure paymasters, insist that the event goes to Madison Square Garden to maximise broadcast revenue from the vast American market.

Anthony Joshua, pictured on holiday in Oman this week, faces a Tyson Fury fight deadline

Tyson Fury's promoter Frank Warren says Joshua must sign terms by the end of next week

Warren says: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Of the argument that the British public need to see the fight between two of their own for which they've waited so long Warren says: 'There's nothing new about this. Some fans travel to the fight and the majority watch on TV.

'Our Joe Bugner fought Muhammad Ali in Kuala Lumpur. Two of Muhammad Ali's greatest fights were against fellow Americans Joe Frazier and George Foreman in Manila and Zaire. It's always about who's paying the money.'

'In the end you just have to get it on. Or not.'

November 20 in the Garden is the working date and venue and Warren says: 'I'm still confident it will go ahead in November.

'Tyson certainly wants it and will be ready to fight. If not AJ then someone else.'

Sports.title: The underlying upgrade that boosted McLaren's performance jump
Sports.content:
McLaren’s win in Zandvoort, their second in a row after Budapest, highlighted a key point: the updates introduced on either side of the summer break did more than restore the aerodynamic load the car had been missing. They also enabled the team to take a decisive step forward.

At the Barcelona Grand Prix, for instance, McLaren’s strengths had already begun to emerge, and the same was true at Spa, where the car appeared in its most convincing form. The faster and longer the corner, because absolute speed alone is not the sole factor, the more competitive the car becomes. The latest upgrades delivered the extra downforce required to turn the car into the benchmark through those sections.

The effectiveness of these developments surprised even McLaren, as the performance shown in the high‑speed sections exceeded internal expectations.

Yet another factor behind the Zandvoort victory went somewhat under the radar: the debut of the new front wheel rims, a detail that McLaren technical director of engineering Neil Houldey had already hinted at ahead of the weekend.

McLaren wheel cover comparison Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“We introduced a small change to the rear section of the floor to generate a bit of extra load, along with some minor tweaks to the rear brake ducts. We also have new front wheel rims, which will help us build more temperature in the tyres. These updates are not significant in terms of lap time, but they do make us slightly more competitive”, Houldey said.

Why is this detail so interesting? After the race, team principal Andrea Stella noted that both Budapest and Zandvoort were high-downforce circuits that naturally suited the car's characteristics better than other tracks. However, looking back at Monaco, where the team hoped to fight at the front and repeat previous successes of last year, McLaren and struggled ended outside the podium positions.

The reason for those struggles went beyond cornering speeds and circuit characteristics. While Monte Carlo gives teams greater set-up freedom with fewer compromises, the car suffered from a lack of downforce and from difficulty generating temperature in the front tyres, which reduced overall grip. This limitation had already emerged earlier in the season, most notably in Australia and China, where the car experienced pronounced graining, while in Japan, where graining was not an issue and the new asphalt improved the overall grip, the MCL40 gained its first podium of the season.

One of the concerns heading into the Zandvoort weekend was the possibility of front‑axle graining, although it ultimately proved to be minimal for everyone. The real challenge was getting the tyres into the right temperature window, even over a single lap. That became clear in the final Q3 attempt on Saturday, when Lando Norris secured pole position, while other teams, struggled to bring the tyres up to temperature and needed an additional lap.

Aston Martin 2026 wheel comparison demonstrates a difference between the front and rear to manage temperatures Photo by: Gianluca D'Alessandro

This is where the topic connects with the updates introduced in the Netherlands. With wheel rim development open once again this season as part of the rule changes, teams have gained a powerful tool for managing tyre temperatures and operating pressures. The internal cavities of a custom rim design, that some teams call “pockets”, allow engineers to passively control air exchange and thermal transfer to the tyre.

At Zandvoort, McLaren focused specifically on this area to retain higher temperatures within the rim structure and, in turn, transfer that heat more effectively to the tyre. This is why only the front rim, manufactured by long‑standing partner Enkei, was updated, accompanied by a more closed wheel cover designed to limit the cooling effect of ambient airflow as it strikes the assembly and to reduce drag.

The rear rim remained unchanged because rear‑tyre degradation was already a key factor throughout the weekend, as seen during the sprint and the race. In that area of the car, the priority was to keep temperatures under control in the traction phases and the high‑speed sections rather than adding more heat. Strong gusts caused the cars to slide through the high‑speed corners, where additional downforce becomes critical, as well as through the key traction zones on the exit of the slower corners.

Sports.title: "How can you allow this?" – Wolff shares Lauda story behind Hamilton's iconic F1 pole
Sports.content:
When Toto Wolff held his annual media session with a select group of Dutch journalists at Zandvoort, one of the topics that came up was how a Formula 1 team can get the maximum out of a driver and, related to that, how much freedom a team principal should give a star driver.

The most recent example is Max Verstappen and the considerable freedom he is given at Red Bull, for instance with his own racing team and endurance adventures such as the Nürburgring 24 Hours.

As is well known, the Dutchman does that with a Mercedes-AMG GT3, although the question remains whether another F1 team – Mercedes, for example – would ever give a driver like Verstappen just as much freedom.

When Wolff is asked that question, he gives an almost philosophical answer, explaining that a team principal must always analyse the best approach to getting the maximum performance out of a particular driver – and must therefore try to understand his personality.

"I think every team is different, but I think what I am trying to do is to identify what it is that makes the driver fast within our structure," Wolff said.

"What kind of framework do we need to provide to extract the best performance of the driver, and part of that is obviously the well-being. And that is something that I am very keen on as well.

"I have never put drivers in a box and have never said this is how you need to be."

Max Verstappen, Mercedes-AMG GT3 Photo by: Miguel Reis / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"Toto, how on earth can you allow this?"

With Verstappen, that freedom involves competing in other racing series, but Wolff’s thoughts immediately go back to the most telling example from his own career as an F1 team boss: Hamilton’s passion for fashion, particularly in the build-up to the 2018 Singapore Grand Prix.

"I remember Lewis Hamilton with his fashion collection back in the day and there was this Singapore race. I remember it was 2018 or 2019, when he launched his Tommy Hilfiger collection," Wolff recounted.

"He had a fashion show in Shanghai where he FaceTimed us. He was grateful that Mercedes changed from Boss to Hilfiger to allow him to have his own collection. He showed everything and said, look at this, this is my catwalk, this is my collection. I can't believe it!"

The fashion show in Shanghai took place on 4 September, but Hamilton did not immediately head to Singapore afterwards. In between, he still had New York Fashion Week on his schedule to present his collection in the US.

"And then he flew from Shanghai to LA or New York, and did it there," Wolff recalls. "Niki Lauda said to me back in the day, I cannot comprehend why you allow this. We are racing in Singapore next weekend, so how is this even possible?"

The criticism intensified when Hamilton’s journey to Singapore was delayed and he was set to arrive late for the first engineering meeting.

Hamilton arrived late in Singapore after the fashion shows, but Wolff defended his driver against criticism Photo by: Glenn Dunbar / Motorsport Images

"Lewis said that he needed to do another stopover in London or so, I don’t even remember. He calls me on Wednesday and says that it will be touch and go, arriving on Thursday for the first engineering meeting.

"I replied, do me a favour, because I'm already getting lots of shit here for you doing a 360 around the world in funky clothes!

"But then he called me again and said, I'm late, the flight has been delayed. So Niki says to me, I really can't believe how you can allow that."

"Lewis, please don’t let me down this weekend"

What followed, however, was telling in two respects: firstly, in Wolff’s willingness to protect his drivers and give them freedom, and secondly, in how Hamilton then repaid that trust on track.

"When he arrived, I said, 'Lewis, do me a favour. I'll take it from you here, I'll take all the criticism from everyone, but just don't let me down this weekend.'

"Understood, he said, and this is when he had this unbelievable pole position. There was that sensational lap and then he won the race, disappearing in the distance.

Hamilton repaid Wolff’s trust in Singapore and went on to clinch his fifth world title just over a month later Photo by: Jerry Andre / Motorsport Images

"After the race he came back to me and said, that was a good deal, no?"

Wolff concludes with a laugh that from that moment on, even Lauda was fine with what Hamilton did away from the track, as long as it did not negatively affect his performance on it.

"Niki said to me afterwards, 'I'm never going to criticise it anymore, even if he flies to the moon before a race!'"

Hamilton took pole in Singapore by more than three tenths of a second over Verstappen and six tenths over title rival Sebastian Vettel. The Mercedes driver won Sunday’s race by almost nine seconds from Verstappen and would secure his fifth world title just over a month later in Mexico.

Sports.title: Haas completes latest TPC test as focus on 2027 F1 driver line-up decision grows
Sports.content:
Haas has completed its latest Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) run with Ryo Hirakawa, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara in action, as focus on its 2027 Formula 1 driver line-up increases.

With the 2027 F1 silly season picking up speed since the end of the summer break, Haas is one of the few teams to officially decide its driver line-up for next season.

While Oliver Bearman looks assured of retaining his place at the team for 2027, attention has turned to Esteban Ocon’s position, with Haas making no secret of its intention to assess all of its options.

The American team has just completed a three-day TPC test at Portimao, where reserve driver Hirakawa was in action alongside 2025 Formula 2 champion and McLaren development driver Fornaroli and current F2 title contender and Ferrari junior Camara. Each driver completed laps in the VF-25 – Haas’ 2025 F1 car – at the Portuguese venue from 26-28 August.

It follows a similar TPC test Haas ran last month, when it gave an opportunity to Toyota-backed drivers Sho Tsuboi and Nirei Fukuzumi at Fuji.

While no further information has been revealed about the Portimao TPC test, it was made clear it was part of the wider plan by Haas to evaluate all interested drivers before making a final decision on its 2027 line-up.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I think it's really good that other people are actually interested in us,” Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said ahead of the Dutch GP last weekend.

“At the moment, we're not performing so well. We cannot challenge for points, but I think it's nice that other people can see the potential in us. Within the constraint how we're fighting and we're trying to improve the team. We just take it as a compliment that other drivers are interested.”

Komatsu has stressed his immediate focus is on the short term to maximise performance from both the car and its drivers in 2026, indicating Haas will take its time to decide its future driver pairing.

In Haas’ short history in F1, it has often been one of the last teams to announce its driver line-up for the following season – so a similar timeline isn’t unrealistic given the relatively stable driver line-ups elsewhere on the grid for 2027.

“We’re not in any rush,” Komatsu said at Zandvoort. “We’re focused on our two drivers, Ollie and Esteban, trying to get the best out of them. They’ve got the tough challenge, right? You know what they are capable of.

“Ollie has showed it repeatedly, Esteban, when he is happy with the car, you know what he can do. So we need to really just focus on providing them with the best possible car, best set-up adaptation, and get the best out of them. And then both of our drivers are fully focused. So at the moment, we’re focused on that.”

Sports.title: What Norris' contract extension means for McLaren and Piastri
Sports.content:
With what is undoubtedly coming with a salary befitting a world champion, Lando Norris has put pen to paper to a deal tying him to the Woking-based team until 2030, with options for multiple additional years after that, taking Norris into his 30s.

Imagining Norris wearing a different-coloured race suit has always felt like a mind-bending exercise. Now, the 26-year-old's bumper McLaren contract has definitively taken one of F1's leading stars out of the driver market for years to come, turning Norris into a bona fide franchise driver for the team.

Read Also: Formula 1 Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030

Norris started his McLaren career a decade ago, when he was picked up by Zak Brown and supported through the single-seater ranks with Carlin, replacing Stoffel Vandoorne as a grand prix driver in 2019 as part of a new wave of Britain-born talent including George Russell and Alex Albon.

Turning from a fast but raw and insecure talent into a championship-winning superstar, last season was undoubtedly Norris' coming-of-age year, overcoming driving style struggles, mechanical failures and a formidable team-mate in Oscar Piastri to take his first world championship.

That triumph seems to have changed something within Norris. From hoping he could one day achieve his dreams, he finally gained the confidence to know that he could. Seeing is believing.

"Lando is driving and operating at the level of a world champion," team boss Andrea Stella said after Norris' Zandvoort win. "What I like the most about his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving. And I think especially after the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but is a way of working with Lando and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular. And I think this approach has led Lando to continuous improvements."

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Search for stability underpins quiet 2027 silly season

It's exactly the type of steady presence, then, that McLaren was keen to tie down for the foreseeable future, willing to fork out an undisclosed but no doubt significant chunk of cash to do so.

Aged 26, Norris is only just entering his prime, so securing its most successful driver since Lewis Hamilton provides McLaren with additional stability as it aims to overcome a slow-ish start to the 2026 season. Norris' brace of wins either side of the summer break are a sign the team is starting to get there.

One look at a particularly quiet transfer market further reinforces the idea that stability is a prized quality to have right now. Teams have been stretched to their limits with the complex 2026 power unit regulations, so they are keen to remove as many unknowns off the board elsewhere, as long as their drivers are performing.

When Max Verstappen, as ever the silly season's dominant domino, decided to stay put at Red Bull, the 2027 starting grid was inevitably going to look very similar to this year's. Alongside Verstappen's decade-long tenure at the Milton Keynes team, Charles Leclerc has also reinforced his commitment to Ferrari, and Mercedes will no doubt want to achieve the same longevity with its drivers, especially Kimi Antonelli.

Speaking to Motorsport.com, Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur explained the value of Leclerc's long-term relationship with Maranello: "Having this kind of continuity is always positive. For me it's also much easier to work with drivers that I have known for ages. Sometimes you don't need to discuss [something] when you have known someone for 10, 15 or 20 years, when the first feeling is the good one, and you know what he's thinking."

It is clear that mutual trust and understanding also exists between Norris and McLaren, to the benefit of both parties.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Pauline Ballet / LAT Images via Getty Images

What about Piastri?

It will be intriguing to see how Piastri and his camp look at this high-profile deal for his team-mate. The Australian extended his deal to 2028 at the start of the 2025 championship, which looked like his to lose until a combination of a decline in performance, driver mistakes, team errors and bad luck saw him finish behind both Norris and Verstappen.

It was a huge blow to Piastri, and unease over team orders and the team's rules of engagement at points through the 2025 campaign, such as a controversial position swap at the Italian Grand Prix or contact between the two team-mates in Singapore and Austin, may well replay on his or his management's mind when digesting the implications of Norris' long-term big money deal. Those who believe McLaren is and always will be Norris' team certainly won't see his contract extension as anything other than a confirmation of that idea.

But right now, Piastri has more pressing concerns. Compared to his ironclad first half of the 2025 season, the 25-year-old has suffered an extended slump in performance with the 2026 generation of cars, seemingly going through similar driving style struggles that he faced last year on low-grip circuits like Austin and Mexico.

Team principal Stella said Piastri's issues are "purely technical" rather than anything mental, whether related to how 2025 finished or 2026 started, as he reaches a full calendar year without a grand prix win on Monday.

McLaren's solution isn't too dissimilar to how it fixed Norris last year, working with Piastri behind the scenes to make adaptations both from a car and driving style point of view. If it succeeds, it has its two aces back for what is shaping up to be a closely-fought second half of 2026, and a potential title challenge next year.

McLaren's end goal is still for both drivers to be fighting each other for wins and titles, which would involve Piastri following a similar trajectory towards a long-term contract extension. It is up to the Australian's camp to decide whether that's in his interest, or whether it might be time to explore new horizons. In any case, Piastri's current deal until the end of 2028 means time is on his side. The same can be said for McLaren.

In the meantime, McLaren has its reigning world champion tied up for the entirety of the current rules cycle. It's one less puzzle piece on the board as the Woking squad aims to retain and even reinforce its title-winning team.

Sports.title: Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030
Sports.content:
Lando Norris and McLaren have agreed to a long-term contract extension, keeping the world champion at the Formula 1 team until at least 2030.

On Saturday morning McLaren announced it had tied Norris to the team until 2030, with multi-year options to further extend the 26-year-old's stay. Norris personally announced the news to the Woking factory staff during the team's annual family and friends open day.

"McLaren is my home, and I’m very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," Norris said. "When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships.

"We’ve achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we’re capable of achieving it. I can’t wait to get back in the car in Monza and I’m very excited about what the future holds for us, both over the rest of this season, and in the coming years.”

Norris' previous deal ran until the end of 2027, effectively increasing the Briton's stay at Woking for at least four more years. Team-mate Oscar Piastri is still under contract until the end of 2028 after extending his deal at the start of last year.

Salaries are rarely revealed in F1, but it stands to reason Norris is in line for a bumper pay rise off the back of his world title and his all-round progress as a driver, which has carried through into a strong first half of 2026. Norris capitalised on McLaren's car upgrades to win the last two grands prix in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Pauline Ballet - Formula 1

In addition to the new contract extension, Norris was also gifted with his championship-winning 2025 car, the MCL39.

Team principal Andrea Stella was "delighted" to continue working with Norris for the foreseeable future. "He is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team," Stella said.

"Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together. With him and Oscar, we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1."

Norris started his McLaren journey as a junior driver in 2017, before being promoted to a race seat in 2019. He has since exclusively raced for the papaya squad and amassed 13 grand prix wins, 18 poles, and 48 podiums.

The team's CEO Zak Brown, who has played an integral role in bringing Norris through the ranks, said: “His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves.

"Together with Andrea, Oscar and the wider team, Lando has helped drive McLaren into a new papaya era of success, helping us go from the back of the grid, to double consecutive constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and our first drivers’ championship in 17 years.

"We are extremely excited about what lies ahead and remain fully focused on continuing to compete for wins and championships.”

Sports.title: Mercedes still searching for answers on why it was “rubbish” through high-speed corners in Dutch GP
Sports.content:
Mercedes trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin rated the team’s pace through Zandvoort’s high-speed corners as “rubbish” and is looking for answers on its inconsistency between both stints and drivers in the Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix.

After a strong start to the Zandvoort weekend, with George Russell taking pole and victory in the sprint race, Mercedes dropped behind McLaren’s Lando Norris, who secured pole and victory in the grand prix.

While Mercedes still took 2-3 in qualifying and the race, with Kimi Antonelli getting the better of team-mate Russell in the race to extend his championship lead to 59 points, the team was at a loss on why its early pace didn’t carry through the weekend relative to its main competition.

“We've got a few things on the performance side to try and dig into,” Shovlin said on Mercedes’ Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show. “We're going to be getting on with that this week and see what we learn.

“But there were a few corners where we were pretty rubbish, like that combination of [Turns] 7, 8, 9. You could see [it in] the faster-speed [curves]. And it also gives the tyres on the left-hand side of the car a tough time. And we don't really understand yet fully what's causing that.

“We've got some ideas, but that's not a problem that we've suffered with so far this year. And there's plenty of circuits that have got kind of continued corners in one direction.

“We were a bit off the pace in the fastest of those [turns]. And then our problems kind of grew a bit as we went through. All the other corners look solid.”

James Allison, Mercedes, Andrew Shovlin, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

What added to Mercedes’ confusion was that minimal changes were made to the cars between the sprint race and grand prix, as well as during the race itself. While Shovlin accepts a level of expected pace deviation per tyre compounds and life, seeing each driver suffer at different times during the grand prix left Mercedes uncertain about the cause.

“We didn't change the car. We obviously had different compounds at different stages. But again, we need to understand a bit,” he said.

“George's first stint was a bit lacklustre compared to his later ones. And then with Kimi, first stint was good, and then dropped a bit on the second, dropped a bit more on the third, a bit came back on the third. It wasn't like we were playing around with electronic settings or up and down on flap angles. And for him, the balance of the car was quite different stint on stint.

“The two drivers, normally they report similar things with a car at the end of the race. Both of them, their perception of the balance, and probably the reality is George had a more understeery car, Kimi had a more oversteery car. If we look at how they were set up, we don't yet know quite why we got such a big difference.

Read Also:

“So, though, really good to have a strong point-scoring weekend when we weren't at our best in terms of performance. It was actually good fun, sat on the pitwall and having to make decisions in a hurry. I think the whole team enjoyed that and rose to the occasion. And it was definitely a good result, given where we were.

“But yeah, a bit of head-scratching to do over the next few days.”

As Shovlin pointed out, Mercedes still picked up its second-highest points score as a team this season – 46 points, only behind the 55 points it notched up at the Chinese GP – granted both were sprint race weekends with more points on offer.

Sports.title: Ferrari to deliver upgraded F1 engine at Italian GP
Sports.content:
Ferrari will use its ADUO-permitted upgrade on its engine for the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix, while also bringing aerodynamic updates and track-specific parts for its home round.

Following reliability checks and the announcement of Ferrari being over 4% behind on the Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) benchmark – and therefore permitted to two upgrades this season – the Italian squad has moved to immediately update its power unit.

Ferrari’s engineers, led by Enrico Gualtieri, have given the green light to introduce the new power unit, which features a revised combustion chamber and turbocharger, with the forecasted increase of 15 horsepower expected to halve the deficit to the Mercedes unit, which is considered to be the best all-round package. A performance boost is also set to come from new fuel developed by Shell.

The 067/7 engine permitted under ADUO has reached the reliability threshold in repeated bench tests: Ferrari, therefore, is aiming for a strong result in front of an expectant home crowd at Monza, with engineers targeting peak power and a different torque delivery to ensure a better distribution of electrical energy.

Ferrari will also roll out a new and more aerodynamically-efficient version of the Macarena rear wing, not used in previous events, along with the blown exhaust, which may be tweaked if a further reduction in drag is needed at Monza.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Foto di: Marcel van Dorst / EYE4images / NurPhoto via Getty Images

The Scuderia, which will also run a livery to celebrate Michael Schumacher’s success at Ferrari, is targeting the Italian GP as the place to kickstart its title charge after failing to reach the podium in the last two rounds.

Ferrari has been handed a boost via Mercedes, which has already confirmed Kimi Antonelli will serve a back-of-the-grid penalty for a full power unit change, following reliability woes earlier in the season which have moved the Italian through his permitted allocation.

Mercedes team-mate George Russell is not set to serve a penalty, with Baku considered a possibility due to similar track characteristics to Monza, as the team aims to dent Ferrari’s charge with one driver at the front.

Monza hasn’t been a happy hunting ground for Ferrari in recent years, with just three wins in the last 19 Italian GPs, but Ferrari is aware it must strike back, having been outscored by McLaren in the last two rounds and slipped to 87 points behind Mercedes in the F1 world constructors’ championship.

Sports.title: Ukraine files complaint to FIA ethics committee after Russian ban lift
Sports.content:
Ukraine has lodged a formal complaint to the FIA ethics committee following the lift to the ban on Russian competitors in international motorsport.

The Ukrainian Automobile Federation (FAU) requested an urgent investigation into the Russian Automobile Federation (RAF) on Thursday, stating it is in breach of FIA rules over national sporting authorities.

The FAU has alleged that the RAF has opened and operates offices in Crimea, Sevastopol, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Oblasts regions, which are recognised as Ukrainian territory by the United Nations.

In its complaint it pointed to the breach of “Article 3.3 of the FIA Statutes and Article 1.4.1 of the International Sporting Code, both of which provide that only one ASN [national body] may be recognised per country, with authority extending over that country's entire national territory.” Therefore, the FAU argues that by operating in Ukrainian territory, the Russian federation is breaking FIA rules.

The complaint also highlights the leaders of the RAF – including president Boris Rotenberg – are under international sanctions by the United States, United Kingdom and European Union for aggression against Ukraine.

The FAU has requested an immediate investigation and that the RAF must close its offices.

The Russian flag Photo by: Mark Sutton / Motorsport Images

“This is a clear breach of the FIA Statutes by the Russian Automobile Federation, which, as an FIA member organisation, is bound to comply with them,” Oleksandr Feldman, FAU president, said. “We urge the FIA President to take urgent action to have these offices closed, and for the Russian Automobile Federation to be sanctioned for its actions.”

Earlier this month the FIA reversed its restrictions on Russian and Belarusian drivers, who are now able to compete under their national flag, having been previously denied following the outbreak of war in Ukraine in 2022.

The changes do not extend to holding international events in Russia or Belarus, and these continue to be part of the restrictions. The FIA cancelled its contract for the Russian Grand Prix in 2022, set to be the final race for the Sochi Autodrom as the Igora Drive circuit was planned to take over in 2023.

In that period Russian drivers have tended to switch to a different national body to continue competing: Robert Shwartzman raced under an Israeli flag, while the likes of Daniil Kvyat and Nikita Bedrin have Italian racing licences. Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have also been represented by Russian drivers across the junior categories.

Sports.title: Formula 1 fan’s video reveals the strange sound of super-clipping | Brief
Sports.content:
Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has repeatedly claimed fans of the sport either don’t know ‘clipping’ exists or don’t understand it.

Under the series’ current technical regulations, cars are so short of energy ay many tracks they are forced to slow significantly as they approach high-speed corners. This robs drivers of the challenge of attacking the championship’s most spectacular corners at full speed and denies fans the thrill of watching them.

One fan highlighted the problem during the British Grand Prix weekend. Silverstone is one of the quickest tracks on the calendar and Max Verstappen admitted he laughed when he first saw how poor the cars would perform at the circuit.

The result is exactly the kind of footage F1 is at pains to avoid showing in its broadcasts this year. Instead of attacking Silverstone’s fastest corners at full speed with the engines howling, the cars coast through quietly, with none of their former drama:

Sports.title: Palou clinches fifth IndyCar championship title in seven years | IndyCar
Sports.content:
Alex Palou continued his domination of the IndyCar series by clinching his fifth title on Sunday.

The 29-year-old has won the championship in all bar two of the seven seasons he has contested it. He debuted in the series at Dale Coyne in 2020 before moving to Ganassi the following year. He has delivered the title for his current team every season except 2022, when Penske’s Will Power won the championship.

Palou claimed his latest title with one round remaining. He has claimed six victories so far this season – two fewer than last year. He took pole position for the series’ blue riband race, the Indianapolis 500, but was unable to repeat his 2025 victory.

His latest championship triumph came in unusual circumstances during the series’ double-header race weekend at the Milwaukee Mile oval. Saturday’s first race was halted due to rain, and not resumed until after the completion of Sunday’s second race.

Andretti’s Kyle Kirkwood was Palou’s closest threat heading into last weekend, but finished behind him in both races. Palou clinched the title with a 100-point lead over McLaren’s Christian Lundgaard by the end of the weekend.

McLaren’s Pato O’Ward took back-to-back victories, moving him into the thick of a close fight for the runner-up spot behind Palou. Lundgaard, Kirkwood and O’Ward are separated by just four points.

Palou will defend his latest championship title next year as the most senior driver in Ganassi’s line-up. His team mate, six-times champion Scott Dixon, who scored his last victory over a year ago at Mid-Ohio, will join O’Ward at McLaren.
