Maduro releases his first images from the Brooklyn jail, taken two months ago

30th Sunday, August 2026 - 23:54 UTC Full article

Former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro released on Sunday, through his X account, the first known photographs since he entered the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York, where he has been held since January. The images show him in sportswear making a victory sign.

“I am sending these photos as a small gift to all my grandchildren, to the children, and to all the good people who love us,” he wrote in the accompanying message. “I want you to know that we stand firm, with our hearts full of your love.”

The photographs are not recent. According to sources close to him, they were taken on June 25, during Father's Day week; Maduro himself saw them on July 13 and they reached his circle by post this week. There is no confirmation from the Federal Bureau of Prisons regarding their authenticity or date.

Pequeño regalo de amor y esperanza



Envío estas fotos como un pequeño regalo a todos mis nietos y nietas, a los niños y niñas, y a toda la gente noble que nos ama. pic.twitter.com/Z6u3130arn — Nicolás Maduro (@NicolasMaduro) August 30, 2026

Maduro was captured in Caracas on January 3 by US forces and transferred to New York along with his wife, Cilia Flores. Both pleaded not guilty to the four narcoterrorism-related charges brought against them. “I am innocent. I am not guilty. I am a decent man. I remain president of my country,” he said at his first appearance, at which he also argued he had been “kidnapped.” His lawyer described the operation as “a military kidnapping.” There is no conviction against him.

Federal judge Alvin Hellerstein set the trial to begin in June 2027, following a joint request from prosecutors and the defence in July. Before that, a hearing on November 17 will determine whether Maduro enjoys immunity as a head of state, an argument with which his defence seeks to challenge the entire proceeding.

Little has emerged about his conditions in detention. According to his son, Nicolás Maduro Guerra, he spent the first months in an isolation cell and now shares space with other inmates. He has 510 minutes a month for calls to the outside world, with a limit of sixteen minutes per conversation, which he uses daily to speak with Caracas.

The release of the images comes two days after the government of acting president Delcy Rodríguez, formerly his vice-president, announced alongside the US administration an agreement granting Washington majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan reserves, around 21% of the country's total. The arrangement is structured through a joint venture with 100-year concessions over seventeen fields.

World.title: ‘A Child of My Own’: 4 reasons the Netflix film breaks the true-crime mold
World.content:
Why would a woman decide to fake a pregnancy and see it through to its ultimate consequences?

This is the central question that Chilean director Maite Alberdi — an Oscar nominee for “The Mole Agent” and “The Eternal Memory” — sets out to answer in “Un Hijo Propio,” or “A Child of My Own,” a Chilean-Mexican coproduction and Alberdi’s first project shot outside her home country.

Recently released on Netflix, “A Child of My Own” chronicles real events that took place in Mexico City in 2009.

The story follows Eleonor Alejandra Marín Mendoza, a young woman who pretends to be pregnant for months and ultimately kidnaps a newborn baby to sustain her lie. It is a crime that still shocks Mexico, and for which Marín served more than 13 years in the Santa Martha Acatitla prison.

Unlike conventional true crime, which often revels in sensationalism, this 96-minute documentary takes a more human and intimate approach. Through a structure that combines reenactments and real testimonies, the film chooses to explore the sociological and psychological causes of the event.

Or, as Alberdi said in an interview with Marie Claire, “I was never interested in making a film focused solely on what happened, but rather in trying to understand the ‘whys’: what personal, family, and social context lies behind their decisions.”

Widely acclaimed by international critics, “A Child of My Own” is already emerging as a strong favorite to represent Mexico at the upcoming Goya and Oscar awards.

If you haven’t added it to your streaming list yet, here are four compelling reasons not to miss it.

A Child of My Own | Official Trailer | Netflix

Watch this video on YouTube

1. A documentary that surpasses any fiction

The first reason to get hooked on this documentary is its plot: a true story that captivates with its almost unbelievable scope.

The film traces the married life of Eleonor Alejandra Marín Mendoza also known as Ale, with a sensitive performance by Ana Celeste Montalvo in the dramatized segments, and portrays a young woman whose identity has been completely reduced to her reproductive role. Somewhere between the absurd and the tragic, we witness a farce that defies all logic.

Like many Mexican women, Alejandra always dreamed of a traditional home and a family full of children. With that goal in mind, she marries Arturo Calderón Gamiño (played by Armando Espitia) at a young age, but her plans are thwarted when she suffers several miscarriages.

As if that weren’t enough, she is forced to cope with an increasingly hostile environment, especially since her husband blames her for the losses and rejects the idea of adoption.

Under pressure from her suffocating family and her own desire, Alejandra hides her miscarriage and pretends she’s still expecting a baby. To keep up the charade, she drastically changes her routine: she gains weight to simulate a growing belly, obtains fake ultrasound images at her workplace and organizes her own baby shower.

Against all odds, her scheme seems to finally come to fruition when she meets a pregnant woman willing to give up her newborn, and they reach an informal agreement. But, as is often the case with lies, the situation eventually spirals out of control, and the documentary takes a surprising turn.

Revealing exactly what happens would spoil the key plot twists. What we can tell you is that Alberdi dissects the anatomy of the farce, showing how a lie and a mental health crisis escalate into a serious crime.

One of the documentary’s more striking moments comes from Alejandra, who sums up her tragedy: “I was afraid that [Arturo] would leave me because I hadn’t been able to become a mother, and that I would be singled out and judged. In the end, I was judged for something much worse.”

2. A narrative structure that breaks the mold

Another reason to watch “A Child of My Own” is its narrative structure: a bold blend of dramatizations and real-life testimonies. Overall, this project differs from Alberdi’s previous works in that it is divided into two distinct sections that play with the viewer’s expectations.

The film begins with the casting call to select the actress who will play Alejandra. From there, the first half unfolds as a traditional fictional drama. Through the use of professional actors and meticulous staging, this section reconstructs the events from the protagonist’s perspective. It’s a practical tool for understanding how social pressure and the trauma of failed pregnancies led her to mental dissociation and the creation of a parallel reality in front of her family.

Among them are Alejandra herself, her husband Arturo, Judge Taissia Cruz Parcero, and Mayra Navarro, the mother of the abducted child. The film’s hybrid nature requires the viewer to confront a woman in crisis before unpacking the structural causes of the problem.

3. Alberdi’s judicious direction

The third reason to watch this documentary is Alberdi’s judicious direction, as she intelligently distances herself from the sensationalism that often plagues the true crime genre. Instead of seeking visual impact or exploiting the scandal, the Chilean filmmaker’s camerawork stands out for its maturity, compassion and respect.

Alberdi masterfully walks a fine line: she films her subject with profound humanity, yet without ever justifying the crime or glossing over the gravity of the theft. The director delivers a well-rounded work that trusts the viewer, demonstrating that documentary film is not meant to condemn, but to help us understand the most complex dimensions of the human condition.

4. An important social commentary on motherhood

Historically, Latin American society — and especially Mexico — has demanded that women fulfill the maternal role. When a woman does not have children, it is common for those around her to judge her and make her feel incomplete or dysfunctional.

“A Child of My Own” shows the consequences that this cultural mandate can entail. Without resorting to simplistic judgments, the documentary analyzes the reproductive expectations placed on women.

Rather than simply recounting the kidnapping, the film strives to shed light on the cultural forces and the familial and institutional negligence, such as the lack of psychological support following pregnancy loss, that contributed to the crime.

In this case, Alejandra resorts to lying to protect herself from the constant rejection of those around her and from her own sense of failure as a woman and a wife.

“Of course, Alejandra committed a crime; of course, sheNew had to go to prison. But at the same time, she is a victim of the system. She is a victim of her family,” Alberdi told the BBC in an interview.

Undoubtedly, one of the greatest strengths of this film lies in its ability to shake the viewer with pressing questions: Why is a woman’s worth still reduced to her reproductive capacity? And, above all, what are we doing to change this collective reality?

World.title: Charrería: How a plant and an emperor shaped Mexico’s sport
World.content:
Charrería, Mexico’s national sport, is a unique competitive equestrian tradition deeply associated with Mexican identity. Mexico was home to the first cowboys, and the charro suit, since adopted by mariachis, remains one of the most iconic symbols by which Mexico is recognized around the globe.

Unlike popular traditions like Day of the Dead, which have deep roots in Indigenous heritage, charrería is a product of cultural syncretism. It emerged from the combination of European influences and native traditions. However, it also blended European fashion, ranching practices and local ingenuity, creating something distinctly Mexican.

Of all these influences, two stand out. The fashion preferences of Emperor Maximilian of Habsburg and the strong fibers of a plant known as henequén. While seemingly unrelated, these two elements shaped the ranching lifestyle of charrería and the competitive spirit that followed, producing a lasting legacy.

Let’s explore how a plant and an Emperor influenced one of Mexico’s most cherished traditions.

Henequén in Yucatán

“Perhaps the most important single local contribution to charrería is the henequén rope,” Chuy Mora, a third-generation charro in Guadalajara and founder of Entre Charros cultural experiences, told me. “Without henequén ropes, we wouldn’t have charrería as we have it today.”

Henequén is a strong, natural fiber extracted from the leaves of an agave plant native to the Yucatán Peninsula. Known as “ki” in the Mayan language, the native communities used henequén fibers to produce ropes and twine, among other goods.

The ropes used by the natives were stronger and lighter than those traditionally used in Europe, which were mostly made from local plant fibers like hemp and flax. While strong and flexible, they would break easily.

“Although rope had always existed, the materials were very weak, and the result was a weak and thin rope which was very difficult to wield,” Mora said.

When the Spanish conquistadores arrived in Mexico and discovered the benefits of henequén, they established a large agro-industry around it. During the 19th and 20th centuries, it was exported in large quantities from Yucatán to the United States and Europe, to support commercial goods like sacks, bags and rugs — in addition to cords and ropes.

The effect of henequén on cattle ranching

Just as henequén ropes held ships steady on the high seas and tied down crops in the fields, they also supported the evolution of charrería. The cattle sector, in particular, not only benefited from henequén ropes but changed dramatically because of them.

“Henequén revolutionized cattle management because the rope wouldn’t break when roping an animal,” Mora pointed out. “It also revolutionized the saddle. From being made of straw or leather, they had to add a wooden frame that could withstand the rope tie. It revolutionized livestock farming worldwide.”

The suertes (“chances” or “luck”) charros perform in today’s charrería competitions, which replicate the techniques ranchers traditionally use to manage their cattle, were made possible by henequén. Without it, the skills charros use today to wield ropes wouldn’t exist.

“Thanks to henequén, ranchers developed new skills in handling the rope that were not possible before,” Mora said.

The popularity of henequén eventually decreased after synthetic fibers were invented in the 20th century. But its long-lasting impacts cannot be overstated.

Maximilian’s influence on the charro suit

Over a century and a half ago, Mexico was ruled by Austrian Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg and his wife Carlota, during a period known as the Second Mexican Empire. Although they reigned for only a short period of time (1864-1867), Maximilian and Carlota left a lasting impact on Mexico’s culture. One of these influences was the charro outfit, significantly shaped by Maximilian’s fashion preferences.

“Maximilian didn’t want to impose European fashion in Mexico,” Mora said. “Rather, he wanted to reach out to the people and project an image of a popular emperor.”

Instead of wearing rigid European uniforms when he toured the country, Maximilian adopted and promoted the dress of Mexican hacendados (landowners), which blended Spanish and local elements.

Until then, the charro attire was practical and more closely tied to the countryside and ranch life. It was the dress workers would wear during fieldwork. Under Maximilian and Carlota, the suit became a prestigious fashion item. So much so that the upper classes began wearing it, too. Thus it soon acquired an air of aristocratic elegance at receptions, parties and parades.

Nearly a century later, during Mexico’s Golden Age of Cinema, the image of the charro was deeply cemented in the collective imagination through legendary figures like Jorge Negrete and Pedro Infante. Their performances, often wearing the charro dress inspired by Maximilian, turned charros into a cultural icon. These movie stars embodied a proud, romantic, and distinctly masculine ideal of Mexican identity.

The cultural legacy of mariachis

This ideal traveled the world thanks to the mariachi, who adopted the charro suit early in the 20th century.

Coplas (Remasterizado) - Jorge Negrete y Pedro Infante Full HD

Watch this video on YouTube

“The mariachi of Justo Villa, made up of four musicians, was originally from Cocula, Jalisco. When Porfirio Díaz visited the hacienda of La Sauceda, he heard them play and took them with him to Mexico City,” Mora explained. “From there, they were sent to a fair in Chicago, and they sent them dressed in charro suits. This was the beginning of their international fame.”

The charro suit remains Mexico’s most emblematic dress. It is made up of a short jacket, fitted trousers with silver buttons, a white cotton shirt, a bow tie, a wide-brimmed sombrero and ankle boots. Depending on the occasion, a charro can choose from three versions. There’s the work suit, the half-gala suit, and the gala suit. However, mariachis always wear the gala suit.

Gabriela Solis is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: El Jalapeño: US asks Mexico to keep its citizens from even looking at the border
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

WASHINGTON, District of Columbia — Following high-level security talks in Washington on Thursday, U.S. officials formally requested that the Mexican government enact a nationwide buffer zone preventing its own citizens from coming within line-of-sight distance of the international boundary, foreign ministry sources confirmed.

The request, presented by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to Mexican Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco, would require an estimated 12 million residents of border communities to either relocate inland or close their eyes whenever facing north.

According to delegates familiar with the private meeting, U.S. negotiators expressed concern that the mere physical presence of Mexican citizens on Mexican soil creates an operational hazard for illegal immigration.

“The fundamental issue is proximity,” said a senior U.S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic protocol. “When a Mexican citizen stands on a sidewalk in Ciudad Juárez and looks across the river, it creates an atmosphere of potential movement. We are simply asking Mexico to manage its geography in a way that aligns with our political preferences.”

Under the proposed bilateral security framework, Mexican authorities would establish a 15-kilometer “Visual Exclusion Zone” along the northern frontier. Municipal planners in Tijuana are reportedly evaluating giant canvas curtains to obscure views of San Diego, while residents of Nogales may soon be required to submit weekly affidavits certifying they have no immediate plans to walk in a northerly direction.

Ministry officials reportedly countered by offering to install topes on northern-pointing footpaths, noting that bilateral cooperation has already yielded historic reductions in cross-border foot traffic.

The diplomatic friction comes despite public statements from both governments praising recent progress on counter-narcotics and security integration. In a post on X following the bilateral summit, Velasco noted that existing security cooperation schemes have “yielded the best results in the region,” though he did not clarify whether those results included the eventual depopulation of northern Mexico.

U.S. officials remain hopeful that a compromise can be reached before the upcoming fiscal quarter, proposing that Mexican citizens wishing to live near the border apply for a special domestic presence permit certifying that their proximity is entirely coincidental.

World.title: Cenote hunters’ love for exploring the Yucatán Peninsula inspires new guidebook
World.content:
For Canadian forester David Palmer, a deep dive into the history and majesty of Mexico’s crystal-blue cenotes has been a decades-long fascination. Palmer and his wife, Doris Demers, are cenote hunters.

Sometimes, this involves visiting two or three per day, during a month-long visit to the country. Palmer says this challenge has been nothing short of awe-inspiring.

“I’ve never seen a cenote I didn’t like,” Palmer says. “Our aim was to cover the whole [Yucatán Peninsula], physically and geographically, taking in as many cenotes as we could. We’re at about 140.”

Scattered throughout the Mexican states of Yucatán and Quintana Roo, there are believed to be around 10,000 cenotes. However, only around 250 can be visited. That’s because many of these cenotes are buried underground.

The Yucatán has very few permanent surface-level rivers; many of them are subterranean. Rainwater infiltrates the porous limestone landscapes and makes its way into these cenotes and caves.

The name for the natural sinkholes scattered throughout the Yucatán Peninsula comes from the Maya word tsʼonoʼot, meaning accessible groundwater. They have been regular water supplies and also used for sacrificial purposes throughout Mesoamerican history. Without them, the National Institute of Anthropology and History notes, the growth of Maya civilization would have been very difficult.

A guidebook to Mexico’s cenotes

For Palmer and Demers, their great endeavor to hunt down as many cenotes as they could spawned an idea for an English-language guidebook.

On a chance encounter with a fellow Canadian couple who owned a bookstore in Puerto Morelos, Quintana Roo, Palmer said he knew there was an opportunity. The owners told Palmer that, despite growing demand and questions from visitors about an English-language guidebook, they did not have one available for the region’s iconic natural wonders.

“Now that piqued my interest,” Palmer said. “Since we were going around looking at them anyway, we started to keep an account.”

He set out to capture their majesty and beauty, one sinkhole at a time. The new book, “A Guide to the Cenotes of the Yucatán Peninsula,” is expected to be published in the coming weeks.

“The caverns may remain hidden for centuries until a probing tree root pokes an opening into the ceiling of the cavern, revealing the wondrous world below,” the book reads. “Sometimes, in sinkhole fashion, an entire section of the surface will collapse into this watery underworld.”

Scientists have established that the Sistema Ox Bel Ha, covering vast stretches of the Yucatán Peninsula, is the longest underwater cave system in the world and the second-longest general cave system ever explored, behind the 686-km-long Mammoth Cave National Park system in Kentucky in the U.S.

Their special place in Mexico’s landscape and cultural identity has been brought into focus over the years through investigations into wastewater management and increased urbanization.

Where are the best cenotes?

Nestled between Calle 37 and Calle 39 in the city of Valladolid, you will find Cenote Zaci.



“It’s 50 meters across and 80 meters deep,” Palmer says. “I thought it was gorgeous, absolutely stunning.”

However, when a local hardware store owner heard those comments, she told him that Zaci was nothing when compared to the magnificent Dzitnup.

“(It’s) 10,000 times better,” the owner told Palmer.

Palmer said some locals took their entrance fees and pointed towards the direction of the cenote. The concerning part for Palmer and Demers was that the entrance was a small hole in the ground.

“Down we went, a little bit warily. We’d never been in an underground one before,” Palmer says.

According to the forthcoming guidebook, “A shaft of light from the hole in the ceiling plays over the shimmering mystical water and some of the most spectacular limestone formations in the region are on display. [It’s] the cenote that made cenotes famous in 1995 when National Geographic featured it on its cover.”

Forget your worries at X’Batun and X’ooch

As you snake your way down the 20-meter stone staircase towards Cenote X’Batun, its glassy water has an alluring quality. Located a stone’s throw from San Antonio Mulix and 50 kilometers south of Mérida, there’s a good reason it featured prominently on Palmer’s list.

“It is an open, low-walled oasis where the jungle comes right down to the gorgeous turquoise water, and so does the bird life,” he said.

Within the guidebook, visitors to this cenote are told to keep their eyes peeled for several bird species, including colorful kiskadees, orioles and motmot.

However, Palmer said people need to take care when approaching the water, as there are slippery steps that require attention.

“Once in the water, it is heavenly,” Palmer said.

Meanwhile, Cenote Xooch’s image is one that has been made world-famous through travel magazines and nature photography. The cascading Alamo tree roots fall into the shimmering blue cenote. It’s an image that continues to go viral through travel influencers. Snorkeling is also very popular at this vast circular cenote due to the clarity and depth.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: The mystery of the missing beeswax in Diego Rivera’s ‘La Creación’
World.content:
Ten years ago, a team of researchers began investigating the presence of beeswax in Diego Rivera’s famous mural, “La Creación.”

The ingredient was an essential component in an ancient Greek painting technique that Rivera claimed to have brought back to Mexico.

Now, a decade later, the conclusion is all but final: There is no wax in “La Creación.”

According to one of the project’s lead researchers, Sandra Zetina Ocaña, the scientific finding is further supported by contemporaneous accounts.

“It’s in the books,” Zetina Ocaña, an art historian specializing in materials and techniques at UNAM’s Instituto de Investigaciones Estéticas, tells me. “I’m not the one saying it; his own colleagues from that time are saying that he lied to them.”

But the story of “La Creación” is much larger than some lie Rivera allegedly peddled to the public.

It is a testament to the exploration of the meaning of materials in Mexican muralism and a reminder of how art and science can work together to reveal new dimensions of the creative process.

The controversial beginning of Diego’s ‘La Creación’

In the early 1920s, Rivera returned to post-revolutionary Mexico after a decade spent living in Paris.

At the time, Mexico’s secretary of public education, José Vasconcelos, was grappling with the high level of illiteracy among the country’s populace. Eager to galvanize the education of the masses, he hired Rivera to paint a mural in the Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso.

The mural, “La Creación,” depicts the birth of humankind with Adam and Eve, as told in the Biblical story of “Genesis,” while also paying tribute to ancient Greek mythology. The four cardinal virtues and the nine muses who inspire creativity are symbolized with Latin American features, hinting at the cosmovision of Vasconcelos’ “Cosmic Race.”

As models for the muses, Rivera used women emancipated during the cultural movement of post-revolutionary Mexico. “All the women portrayed are fascinating,” Zetina Ocaña says, adding that they “changed what it meant to be a woman.”

Critics at the time praised Rivera’s playful use of proportions, claiming he “revives monumental painting not only in Mexico, but throughout the world.” Jean Charlot, a French painter who later worked in the U.S. and Mexico, said that Rivera successfully bridged Cubism and large-scale mural painting.

Today, “La Creación” is widely considered the starting point of Mexican muralism.

However, despite the positive reviews, Vasconcelos disliked the mural, arguing that Rivera failed to capture the Mexican spirit.

Rivera himself later conceded that, “despite the effort to express genuine Mexican beauty in the characters, it still resists in its execution and even in its internal meaning, because of overly strong European influences.”

Occidental influence and encaustic painting

Rivera’s decade-long stay in Europe was not only reflected in the mural’s Byzantine iconography and Cubist style. It extended into his painting technique as well.

Encaustic painting involves mixing beeswax with resin and pigments, and then applying heat to layer it onto a surface. It was developed by the ancient Greeks and rediscovered during the Renaissance.

Leonardo Da Vinci reportedly tried applying the technique to a wall painting of “The Battle of Anghiari” but ultimately failed and never finished the work.

In a conversation with his fellow artist Juan O’Gorman, later published by the Colegio Nacional, Rivera discussed his use of encaustic painting in “La Creación.”

“It can truly be said that [with La Creación] true encaustic painting was restored for the first time since the Greco-Roman period,” Rivera told O’Gorman.

Going one step further, Rivera claimed that he had innovated an encaustic technique unique to Mexico by incorporating resin from the copal tree as a binding material.

Technique as an inseparable part of the image

For the next century, Rivera’s claims about the use of encaustic painting in “La Creación” went largely unchallenged.

That is, until a group of art historians and chemists at UNAM decided to look a bit deeper and perform a forensic study of the mural, hoping to identify its material aspect. To understand why, for more than a decade, a team of researchers investigated traces of beeswax in Rivera’s mural, one must understand the importance of materials in the artistic process.

David Alfaro Siqueiros, considered one of the “three greats of muralism,” wrote in “How to Paint a Mural” that “It must not be forgotten that the materials and tools of production in the visual arts have a generative and determining value, both formally and aesthetically.”

Zetina Ocaña similarly explained that what she finds so compelling about Mexican art in the early- to mid-20th century is its focus on thematic and material reinvention.

Siqueiros, for example, incorporated nitrocellulose paints, originally an industrial lacquer for cars, into his murals. Besides enabling him to paint dynamic colors quickly, the use of industrial materials carried an ideological meaning as well: breaking with elitist artistic traditions and reflecting the technological progress of the time.

Similarly, Pablo Aguilar-Rodríguez, a chemist at UNAM and the driving force behind the forensic investigation of “La Creación,” points to the work of Mexican painter and Rivera’s son-in-law, Rafael Coronel.

According to a chemical analysis, Coronel used a type of dental filling as a binding material in his mural “Paisaje Abstracto.”

“It is a material that was completely unrelated to that purpose, and at the time the mural was painted, it represented a major technical innovation,” Aguilar-Rodríguez says. “Understanding it from this chemical perspective tells me that Coronel innovated not only in his content, but also in his materials. Being able to understand art from that perspective seems very, very special to me. I don’t think Coronel’s intention could have been understood without this analysis.”

The forensic analysis: Where is the beeswax?

To test Rivera’s claims about the use of beeswax and copal in his mural, the research team employed an elaborate process.

Through optical, digital and electron microscopy, Zetina Ocaña meticulously examined the mural to determine which areas were best suited for further chemical analysis. Once samples were selected, they went through chromatographic analysis and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

Although all the samples showed traces of copal, none revealed the presence of beeswax.

While pursuing his doctorate, Aguilar-Rodríguez had developed a technique in which spectroscopy and microscopy are combined to create chemical maps of paintings, identifying polymers such as acrylics and nitrocellulose or beeswax.

“I was able to identify beeswax very clearly in another work by Diego Rivera, ‘El Matemático,’ so I could use the samples that had already been taken from ‘La Creación’ and analyze them again using this same methodology,” Aguilar-Rodríguez says.

But when analyzing the samples that Zetina Ocaña had sourced from “La Creación,” he, too, failed to back up Rivera’s claims.

‘As an art historian, I wanted to die’

The researchers hypothesized that the application of heat during the encaustic procedure might have eliminated any traces of beeswax. To test this, they burned beeswax samples to different degrees. But no matter how much heat they applied to the material, it was always detected in further testing.

Next, they wanted to determine whether the beeswax had potentially degraded and been lost to time. However, after analyzing samples from other encaustic murals of Diego’s time, including those by Siqueiros and Charlot, they successfully confirmed the presence of beeswax, leaving little doubt about the truth behind “La Creación.”

“No, there isn’t any beeswax,” Aguilar-Rodríguez says. “There never was. It didn’t degrade. It simply wasn’t added in the first place.”

Zetina Ocaña says that every time she met with her team, she left with a headache.

“They would tell me, ‘There’s no wax. There’s no wax.’ And I’d say, ‘Really?’ They would look at me and say, ‘There’s no wax, Sandra,’” Zetina Ocaña says. “We would have liked to spoon-feed it a little, put a little wax in there, but no. As an art historian, I wanted to die.”

Beyond the truth: Cultural heritage and the synergy of art and science

The question of whether Rivera used an ancient painting technique goes beyond the question of truth and the meaning of materials in the artistic process.

It is part of a broader dialogue that centers the future of Mexico’s cultural heritage.

Cultural heritage is the conglomerate of artifacts, belief systems and traditions that define a nation’s identity and history. Mexico is particularly rich in its cultural heritage, earning the ninth spot on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.

But time takes its toll on physical artifacts, and their conservation is becoming increasingly important.

In another study led by Aguilar-Rodríguez, Frida Kahlo’s painting “Dos Fridas” was analyzed to understand the inherent degradation process when frequently transporting the artwork for exhibition.

The white regions painted with zinc oxide proved especially concerning, while lactic acid was found to be a significant culprit behind the artwork’s degradation. The researchers also concluded that cleaning the artwork with water might accelerate the chemical breakdown of the organic compounds.

Likewise, to understand the conservation challenges of Coronel’s “Paisaje Abstracto” and develop a proper treatment, his unknown binding material had to be identified. The dental filing material uncovered during forensic analysis paved the way for an effective conservation strategy.

‘A historian’s dream’

Dr. María de las Mercedes Sierra Kehoe, an art historian and postgraduate faculty member at UNAM, highlighted the beauty of bridging art and science.

Mercedes Sierra Kehoe is part of a multidisciplinary research team that includes art historians, conservation specialists and scientists working within the National Laboratory for Research and Conservation of Cultural Heritage (LANCIC).

She and her colleagues analyzed Rivera’s “Sueño de una tarde dominical en la Alameda Central” using various techniques like X-ray fluorescence, infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy and reflectance spectroscopy to identify the pigments and materials that make up the mural’s color palette.

“Bringing the humanities and science together has allowed us to discover and recognize elements, processes and projects that would not have been possible to uncover without these instruments,” Mercedes Sierra Kehoe tells me. “It is a historian’s dream.”

Without practical applications, though, scientific discoveries risk losing their salience.

“I always praise the work of my colleagues in conservation,” Mercedes Sierra Kehoe says. “They are heroes without capes, because ultimately they are responsible for ensuring that our historical heritage endures.”

Deliberate deception or something more innocent?

Despite the recent scientific revelations behind “La Creación,” one question remains: Why would Diego Rivera misrepresent the techniques he used in its composition?

“He is a very talented artist, but he is a very erudite artist — an artist who studied a lot, who practiced a lot, who researched a lot,” Zetina Ocaña says. “What is true is that he had painted with wax, because we have a beautiful painting which he presented at an Autumn Salon as an encaustic wax painting.”

According to Zetina Ocaña, Rivera may not have been trying to intentionally dupe the public at all. Rather, it might’ve been a case of timing and the painter merely getting ahead of himself.

“He hadn’t even started painting yet, and they were already publishing an article about him in the newspaper,” Zetina Ocaña explains. “And that’s where he says he’s going to use wax, the encaustic technique.”

Mercedes Sierra Kehoe offers another explanation.

“A very important part of Diego Rivera is that we have to understand that he was a great painter who understood the art market — he knew how to sell himself, he knew how to work the media,” she explains. “So it’s not that the artist lied, right? At that moment it was his own reality, and that’s how he wrote it.”

Or, maybe, he was simply lying.

Much like a chef who doesn’t want to reveal his secret recipe, or an inventor working on a patent, Zetina Ocaña explains, Rivera was known to have lied about his painting techniques, a deliberate deception to hide his artistic process and “a particular way of making something that is very personal.”

Whatever the reason, Zetina Ocaña says that 10 years on, she’s left with more questions than answers.

“I think that when you ask a research question that is successful as a question, it generates more questions, right?”

She goes on to say, “It became an even greater mystery,” adding, “It is also like a good novel, a good poem — something always remains.” Zetina Ocaña invokes Argentinian author Jorge Luis Borges, who likened the “aesthetic moment” to being left in a conversation that doesn’t end.

“And that is what I feel with this mural: That it is a conversation that opened up, and that we continue to have, and that I believe will give rise to other conversations.”

World.title: From the archive: Learning Spanish? Don’t be shy or afraid of making mistakes
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article, for example — originally published in November 2019 — explores the leap of faith required when learning Mexican Spanish.

When I first arrived in Mexico, I had two years of college-level Spanish under my belt. While I was an enthusiastic learner, I was also a very self-conscious speaker, terrified of making embarrassing mistakes and generally sounding like a 2-year-old.

I did, in fact, sound like a 2-year-old at first, as there’s simply no way around being a “baby” when one is first learning. Happily, I survived that stage and now speak at least as well as a know-it-all 13-year-old.

Part of my apprehension with the language was the sense that Mexico’s love-hate relationship with the United States would lead to some situations in which I’d be mocked for my accent or mistakes that I would inevitably make.

After all, most people here know very well how Latinos are treated by certain segments of the U.S. population when they’re on the other side of the border, so I’d imagined that the temptation to dish some out to us collectively would be at least a little irresistible.

For the most part, that didn’t happen. It’s also possible that I simply didn’t realize it was happening, but I think most of us humans have a pretty good sense of when others are laughing at us.

Once in a while someone will have a longish conversation with me (in Spanish) and then say something like, “So, you don’t speak Spanish, eh?” or they’ll point out that they “could tell right away that I was American because of my accent” which always makes me bristle, as I’m pretty sure my accent is, while definitely existent, not obviously American.

(My Mexican friends may disagree with me on that one; I’d ask them, but the answer might be too painful for me to hear.)

There’s some sting in it, but I do my best to chalk up any unflattering comments about my Spanish to cosmic justice and not take it too personally.

In the part of Mexico where I live, English is not considered an essential skill the same way it is in the north or in tourist areas. Because of this, most foreigners in my area do their best with the language: they take classes, they practice, they work hard to get better.

Learning a language is sign of respect

They understand, above all, that learning the language of your hosts, if you are able, is a matter of respect.

When I traveled to Los Cabos recently to visit a friend, I saw how different things were in a town that depends on tourism from their English-speaking neighbors: I was addressed in English at all times, and if I answered in Spanish it almost seemed to startle people, as if they’d come into contact with a dog that had learned to produce human sounds.

For the most part, Mexicans are charmed when we non-native speakers at least try. They’re patient and encouraging, and try their best to be helpful. Mexico really is an ideal place to learn Spanish, as I can’t imagine another place in which more impromptu and consistent support among the general population would be given.

That said, I know many of my compatriots are shy about learning — and especially about using — the Spanish that they know already. I completely understand: there’s nothing that makes us feel quite as vulnerable as not being able to “prove” that we are smart, complex, discerning individuals.

There’s no way around sounding like a simpleton when we’re on that long uphill trajectory, and simply put, it can be a humiliating experience.

But again: at least attempting to learn the local language, if one is able, is a matter of respect. “Well then, what about all the people in the U.S. that haven’t bothered to learn English? I bet you don’t go around preaching to them about respect, do you?”

The short answer is that no, indeed I do not. Because here’s the difference: most people who go to the U.S. without already speaking English are in survival mode, just trying to make it from one day to the next, often working a dizzying number of hours both to both survive, and likely to send money back home.

Most Americans and Canadians, however, come to Mexico either in vacation or retirement mode. Some, sadly, come because their spouses or loved ones have been deported and they want to keep the family together.

If one is on vacation, of course, learning the language won’t be expected. But if you settle here, an effort must be made.

Find a school, or find a teacher. Find someone to sit and help you practice. Spend time just listening to people with no intention of adding to the conversation. One of the best pieces of advice I’ve ever received for learning a language is literally to pretend to be a baby: listen to the sounds, watch people, let whole social situations piece themselves together and come into focus slowly.

Babies, after all, spend at least a couple of years listening and observing before they try to string together a sentence with more than four words in it.

On my first plane ride into Mexico, my nervousness increased with each sentence given in Spanish by the flight attendants: the more they spoke, the more I realized I wasn’t catching anything at all that they were saying.

Since then, I’ve made about a million mistakes, linguistically embarrassed myself in every way imaginable, and surely sounded much less sophisticated than I imagine myself to be.

But I’ve gained the ability to talk to most people on this side of the world and have developed some of the closest relationships of my lifetime in this language.

Hands down, totally worth it.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: A governor takes a U-turn, CJNG loses more ground and business booms
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 24 in Mexico began on awkward footing following a Morena party faux pas in Sinaloa. Rubén Rocha Moya, currently under investigation in the United States for alleged collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel, briefly reclaimed the Sinaloa governorship after months on leave, only to retreat again two days later. Meanwhile, several storm systems dumped rain on most of the country, and an investigation into fuel theft in Tamaulipas turned up a startling menagerie of exotic animals.

Also this week, President Sheinbaum revealed new reforms and a US $6M windfall for Guerrero schools as she prepares to soon give her second annual report to the nation.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum weighs in on Rocha’s status in Sinaloa

President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the week fielding questions about the fallout from Rocha Moya’s brief return to the Sinaloa governorship from Aug. 21–23 and the future of Sinaloa’s leadership.

At Monday’s mañanera, as Sonora’s cattle trade with the U.S. reopened, she addressed the episode directly for the first time, saying she learned of Rocha’s Friday return through his social media post and had no prior knowledge of his plans. “I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” she said, later calling the decision “imprudent.” She credited Rocha’s renewed leave request — approved unanimously by Sinaloa’s Congress that Sunday — as “the best thing for Sinaloa,” and dismissed rumors that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador had encouraged Rocha’s return as “political fiction.”

Sheinbaum extended the same standard to other Morena officials swept up in the same U.S. indictment. Asked on Tuesday about Senator Enrique Inzunza — one of 10 Sinaloa-linked officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking ties, who had signaled he might return to the Senate — she said the same principle applied. “Yesterday I gave my opinion on the case of the governor of Sinaloa, who is now on leave. I feel the same way about all 10 cases under investigation by the Attorney General’s Office,” she said. Inzunza subsequently separated from Morena’s Senate caucus on Wednesday, though he remains in office as senator.

Multiple CJNG busts across three states

Security forces delivered a string of blows against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) this week. A coordinated operation across Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán from Aug. 21–23 resulted in 20 arrests and the seizure of weapons, drugs and exotic animals tied to the cartel, with authorities raiding 36 properties and confiscating firearms, fentanyl, methamphetamine, 113 vehicles and a drone jammer.

That action followed a separate military-led operation in Michoacán targeting alleged CJNG leader Heraclio “El Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez last week, which produced roughly a dozen more arrests, including relatives of the suspect. Combined, the two operations brought the week’s tally of alleged CJNG detentions to 32, part of what Security Minister Omar García Harfuch described as an effort to systematically dismantle the group’s operational and financial capacity rather than simply rack up arrests.

Confusion and concern in Mexicali

A U.S. security alert warning of a possible “August 25 threat” in Mexicali created a tense but ultimately murky standoff between caution and normalcy. The alert prompted the U.S. Mission to suspend official travel and activity in the border city, reportedly linked to fears that the crime gang Los Rusos might retaliate after a 120-kilogram fentanyl seizure — roughly 4 million doses — from a property connected to the group.

Mexican officials responded by increasing patrols around public buildings, but as Tuesday came and went without a major incident, the federal security cabinet said it had found no evidence of a specific or imminent threat to the public. Residents described a largely normal day, and the Mexicali-Calexico border crossing remained open throughout, leaving the alert’s basis and its practical necessity still unclear.

Economic data: Record highs alongside warning signs

Revised GDP figures showed the economy grew in the second quarter but contracted in June, with the primary sector contributing the steadiest growth. Foreign direct investment in Mexico yielded US $34.968 billion in FDI in the first half of 2026, its highest semester total ever recorded, up 2.1% year over year, even though the second quarter alone saw a 3.5% annual decline. Manufacturing captured 38.6% of that investment, and the United States remained the dominant source at $16.871 billion.

Trade data added to the good news: July exports hit a record US $81.4 billion, up 43.7% annually, driven by a 134% surge in electrical and electronic equipment shipments tied to U.S. demand for AI and data-center infrastructure inputs. At her Wednesday press conference, Sheinbaum cheered the numbers as proof of a “strong” economy, pointing to record FDI, 60 million people employed and a firm peso, and argued that years of minimum-wage increases had not triggered the inflation or capital flight critics once predicted.

That optimism gained further support when Mexico placed among the OECD’s fastest-growing economies, ranking sixth with 1.4% quarterly growth against an OECD average of 0.5%. But the jobs report complicated the picture: Mexico posted its best monthly job gain of 2026 in July, yet the increase was driven entirely by informal employment, with more than 1.08 million informal jobs added while over 412,000 formal positions vanished. Informality climbed to 56.2%, its highest level since December 2021 — a reminder that headline growth figures can mask deteriorating job quality.

This week’s investment announcements

Schneider Electric announced a major expansion of its operations in Querétaro, reinforcing the state’s role as an industrial and technology hub. Danish firms unveiled a US $510 million renewables project set to boost Campeche’s clean energy supply, adding to the country’s growing green energy portfolio. And Jalisco is set to host Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant, a facility in Ciudad Guzmán capable of recovering up to 95% of materials from the roughly 1.6 million panels already installed statewide.

A fresh framework for environmental protection

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena presented a bill to put environmental justice at the center of Mexican law, proposing reforms to the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection. The initiative would require more forward-looking assessment of major projects, close loopholes that let developers split projects to dodge full environmental review, strengthen restoration and remediation requirements and add specific protections for environmental defenders and Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, rural and urban communities.

Foreign Minister strengthens ties in South Korea and Washington

Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco kept a packed international schedule this week. In Seoul, he met with South Korean officials and executives from Samsung, Hyundai, LG and Posco to promote investment in technology, semiconductors and education, part of groundwork for a 2026–30 bilateral action plan ahead of a planned visit by South Korea’s president. He then traveled to Washington, where he held his first face-to-face meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both sides publicly stressed cooperation against drug and arms trafficking, Bloomberg reported that Washington privately pressed Mexico to do more to stop its own citizens from crossing into the U.S.

Aura farming battles debut in Mexico

A new social-media-driven trend reached Mexican public squares this week: aura farming battles, in which participants strike poses, dance and reference memes to project confidence and style while crowds judge who accumulates the most “aura.” Events popped up at Mexico City landmarks as well as in Xalapa and Torreón, though at least one Veracruz municipality banned the contests in public parks on administrative grounds.

Sheinbaum proposes dual-citizenship ban

Sheinbaum also unveiled a constitutional amendment that would bar dual nationals from running for president, governor or Mexico City mayor unless they renounce their other citizenship before registering as candidates. The government argues current constitutional language contains a loophole and that the country’s highest offices should be held only by people with unambiguous national allegiance — a proposal likely to draw scrutiny over its impact on Mexican-born citizens with binational ties.

Mexican athletes shine internationally

Cyclist Isaac del Toro won the Tour of Germany, becoming the first Latin American rider to capture the race, finishing 53 seconds ahead of France’s Louis Barré.

Mexico won two gold medals and a bronze at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam: Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez took gold in women’s lightweight double sculls, Kenia Lechuga won gold in lightweight single sculls, and Alexis López earned bronze in men’s lightweight single sculls.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test whether this week’s political and security cracks widen further. In Sinaloa, the ongoing conflict between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos remains unresolved, complicating the search for a permanent successor. Pressure is also unlikely to ease on other Morena-aligned officials named in the same U.S. indictment, amid broader questions about the party’s exposure to organized crime in states beyond Sinaloa. With Sheinbaum’s second annual report to the nation approaching, how she navigates these overlapping crises could shape both her security narrative and her party’s credibility heading into the fall.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexico Marches for Its Disappeared in 16 States as a Car Bomb Hits Zacatecas
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts —The marches: Families of the disappeared marched across Mexico on Sunday, with protests reported in 16 states. —The bomb: A car bomb exploded outside the municipal police station in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas, on Sunday night. —The toll: At least six civilians and one police officer were wounded; 11 private vehicles and two patrol cars were damaged. —The backdrop: More than 100,000 people are registered as disappeared in Mexico. —The catch: The government’s answer is financial; it says it has frozen 24,622 accounts linked to criminal money. —Also today: State oil company Pemex cut its debt only because the government transferred capital to it.

The Mexico disappearances crisis filled the streets of 16 states on Sunday, the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances. The same evening, a car bomb exploded outside a police station in Zacatecas and wounded seven people.

A country marching for its missing

Sunday 30 August is the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances. In Mexico it belongs to the buscadoras, the searching mothers who dig for their children.

Marches were reported in at least 16 of Mexico’s 32 states, according to organisers’ tallies. Many marchers carried the shovels and pickaxes they use in the field.

Guanajuato, one of the most violent states, saw protests in León, Celaya, Irapuato, Salamanca and beyond. In León, searchers read out the names of the disappeared as they walked.

The fresh numbers explain the anger. Celaya’s disappearance cases jumped from 534 in 2025 to 834 in 2026, a rise of 56 percent, Latinus reported.

León follows with 628 cases and Irapuato with 601. The searchers say the state protects them too little; one collective in León reported being threatened while posting search notices.

A mother named Amalia told reporters she has looked for her son Néstor for five years. “The authorities cannot tell me anything,” she said. “There is no trace of him.”

The Zacatecas car bomb

While the marches went on, Zacatecas delivered the weekend’s darker headline. At around 8 p.m. on Sunday, a car bomb detonated outside the municipal police station of Ojocaliente.

At least six civilians and one police officer were wounded. The blast damaged 11 private vehicles, two patrol cars and nearby homes.

Videos shared on social media showed a family with children fleeing the burning scene. The wounded are receiving medical care, said Rodrigo Reyes, Zacatecas’ secretary general of government.

The explosive was placed in a private car, Reyes said, and a security operation was deployed. No arrests had been announced by Monday morning.

Car bombs remain rare in Mexico, and each one raises the fear of escalation. Zacatecas has been contested by cartels for years, and July brought a ten-victim massacre in the state.

The state’s answer: follow the money

The federal government wants the Mexico disappearances crisis answered with finance as much as force. It says it has now frozen 24,622 bank accounts in its campaign against criminal money.

The figure comes from the security cabinet’s campaign reporting. It covers accounts linked to extortion, fuel theft and cartel finances.

The strategy leans on the Financial Intelligence Unit, known as the UIF. That is the same agency now working with Pemex against fuel theft along the Gulf corridor.

For the marching families, account freezes are an abstract comfort. Their demand on Sunday was simpler: search protocols, protection for searchers and answers.

Pemex’s debt: smaller, but not healthier

A separate Monday storyline matters more to bondholders. Pemex reported a lower debt load, but the reduction came from capital transferred by the federal government.

In plain terms, the state oil company did not earn its way to a smaller balance sheet. The treasury paid down the debt for it.

That distinction matters for anyone holding Mexican sovereign risk. Pemex’s obligations are, in practice, the government’s obligations.

The pattern has run for years, and markets have learned to price it. What changes each quarter is only the size of the transfer.

What expats and investors should take from the weekend

For foreign residents, the marches are a window into the country’s deepest open wound. The Mexico disappearances crisis touches daily life far beyond the headline cities.

The Ojocaliente bomb does not change the security map for expat hubs. It does confirm that cartel tactics in contested states keep hardening.

For investors, the two threads to watch are financial. The account-freezing campaign shows enforcement capacity, while Pemex shows fiscal cost.

Both stories return quickly. Prosecutors in Zacatecas must name suspects, and Pemex must show whether the next quarter brings operations or another transfer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why were there marches across Mexico on 30 August 2026? Families of the disappeared marched for the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances. Protests were reported in at least 16 states, including Guanajuato and Zacatecas. What happened in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas? A car bomb exploded outside the municipal police station at around 8 p.m. on Sunday. At least six civilians and one police officer were wounded, and no arrests had been announced. How deep is the Mexico disappearances crisis? More than 100,000 people are registered as disappeared in Mexico. In Celaya, Guanajuato, cases rose 56 percent in a year, from 534 in 2025 to 834 in 2026. What is the government doing about criminal finances? The government says it has frozen 24,622 bank accounts linked to criminal money. The campaign is led by the Financial Intelligence Unit, the UIF. Did Pemex really reduce its debt? Pemex reported lower debt, but the reduction came from capital transferred by the federal government. The company did not generate the improvement from its own operations.

Connected Coverage Zacatecas was already in our pages after July’s ten-victim massacre and the troop deployment. The money trail runs through the UIF–Pemex pact against fuel theft and Mexico’s war on huachicol. World.title: Vaca Muerta Exports Push Argentina Toward a Record Year
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

ARGENTINA · ENERGY

Key Facts —What happened: Argentina is heading for record exports of US$103.2 billion in 2026, the exporters’ chamber projects. —How big: January to July sales hit US$58.365 billion, up 22.9 percent and the best start to a year on record. —The real story: Crude oil was Argentina’s top export in the last two months, above corn and soy for the first time. —The catch: Ten products still generate 44 percent of all exports, so the record rests on a narrow base. —Where it shifts: Neuquén, San Juan and Santa Cruz are gaining weight, carried by shale, metals and lithium. —What comes next: Italy’s ENI and partners move the Argentina LNG project toward a November investment decision.

Argentina’s exporters’ chamber now projects a record US$103.2 billion of sales abroad in 2026, with Vaca Muerta exports of crude oil displacing corn and soy at the top of the table.

A record year, projected and half-delivered

The projection comes from CERA, the Argentine exporters’ chamber, in its August trade monitor. It puts 2026 exports at US$103.2 billion, well past the US$88.446 billion record of 2022.

The first seven months already back the call. Exports reached US$58.365 billion between January and July, up 22.9 percent on the same period of 2025.

July alone brought in US$8.854 billion, the fourth-highest monthly figure in Argentine history. The trade surplus for the seven months reached US$16.080 billion, up 338 percent year on year.

Imports, notably, fell 3.5 percent to US$42.286 billion over the period. The surplus is being earned abroad, not just saved at home.

Oil takes the top spot

The symbolic shift is at the top of the table. Crude oil exports reached US$5.722 billion in the first seven months, up 59 percent, driven mainly by higher volumes.

In each of the last two months, crude was Argentina’s single biggest export product. It finished above corn and soy, the crops that have defined the country’s trade for a century.

Fuels and energy, the category riding on Vaca Muerta exports, reached US$9.151 billion, up 50 percent. Vaca Muerta, the shale formation in Neuquén province, now produces about 70 percent of national oil output.

The caution sits in the concentration. The ten fastest-growing products supplied 44 percent of everything Argentina sold abroad, or US$25.591 billion.

The map of exports is moving south and west

The consultancy Abeceb, quoted in the chamber’s report, reads the record as a geographic reordering. Neuquén, San Juan and Santa Cruz are gaining weight in foreign trade.

Neuquén rides Vaca Muerta exports, San Juan and the Andean provinces ride metals and lithium. Gold brought in US$3.211 billion, up 44 percent, and lithium carbonate US$1.169 billion, up 187 percent.

The mining chamber expects the sector to reach US$9 billion in exports this year. That would be 50 percent above 2025.

Agro-industry still pays the biggest bill. Farm-based manufactures exported US$18.911 billion in seven months, up 13 percent, helped by a record harvest.

Italy’s door into Vaca Muerta exports

The European angle runs through Rome. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s alliance with President Javier Milei has warmed the pipeline for Italian capital, and the vehicle is already chosen.

Italy’s ENI is a partner with state-controlled YPF and the Emirates’ XRG in Argentina LNG, the flagship liquefied-gas export project. The consortium presented it under the RIGI investment regime in June.

Studies cited by industry media put Argentine LNG projects at close to US$30 billion of investment toward 2030. Export capacity could reach 28 million tonnes a year by the end of the decade.

Longer term, the central bank projects total goods exports of US$143.8 billion by 2030. Its projected goods surplus for that year is US$41.8 billion.

Why it matters beyond the pampas

Every export dollar lands in a central bank that is rebuilding reserves. The trade surplus is the raw material of the government’s whole financial programme.

The main buyers remain Brazil, the United States and China, in that order. Sales to the European Union have grown almost 20 percent this year on the back of the Mercosur agreement.

For investors, Vaca Muerta exports are no longer a promise but a line item. The open question is whether pipelines, LNG ships and rigs can be built fast enough to keep Vaca Muerta exports growing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will Argentina export in 2026? The exporters’ chamber CERA projects US$103.2 billion, a record. Sales from January to July reached US$58.365 billion, up 22.9 percent on the same months of 2025. What is Argentina’s biggest export now? Crude oil. It earned US$5.722 billion in the first seven months, up 59 percent, and led the monthly ranking in the last two months, above corn and soy. What role does Vaca Muerta play? The shale formation produces about 70 percent of Argentina’s oil and anchors the energy surge. Fuels and energy exports grew 50 percent to US$9.151 billion in seven months. How are Italian companies involved? Italy’s ENI partners with YPF and XRG in Argentina LNG, presented under the RIGI regime in June. Industry studies see close to US$30 billion of LNG investment toward 2030. How big is Argentina’s trade surplus? The surplus reached US$16.080 billion from January to July 2026, up 338 percent year on year. July’s surplus alone was US$2.115 billion.

World.title: Brazil’s Congressional Earmarks Quadruple in a Decade as State Firms Sink
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: Brazil’s congressional earmarks reached R$47.1 billion (US$9.1 billion) in 2025, up 315% in eleven years. —Who counted: The figures come from a study series by Ipea, the federal government’s own economic research institute. —The real story: Nearly half the Health Ministry’s discretionary money now arrives via earmarks, so lawmakers decide spending that ministries once planned. —The catch: Most earmark money now funds running costs, not investments, and nothing guarantees the same funds return next year. —The other drain: Federal state-owned companies are running a deficit of R$8.3 billion (US$1.6 billion) in 2026 so far. —The symbol: Correios, the postal service, is heading for the worst annual result in its history, its own minister concedes.

A study by Brazil’s own research institute shows congressional earmarks more than quadrupling in a decade, while state-owned companies post record deficits and the postal service heads for the worst year in its history.

What the Ipea study found

Brazil’s congressional earmarks are budget amendments that let each deputy and senator direct part of the federal budget. The money pays for things like ambulances, health clinics or street paving in their home districts.

The volume formally committed jumped from R$11.3 billion (US$2.2 billion) in 2014 to R$47.1 billion (US$9.1 billion) in 2025. Adjusted for inflation, that is growth of 315% in eleven years.

The study was produced by Ipea, the Institute of Applied Economic Research, at the request of Deputy Eduardo Bandeira de Mello. Estadão published its findings on Monday.

The turning point was 2015. A constitutional amendment made individual earmarks mandatory, so the executive must now pay what each lawmaker designates.

Ipea’s researchers call the result “budgetary parliamentarism”. In plain English: Congress, not the government, increasingly decides where federal money goes.

Where the money goes now

Social policies absorbed R$35 billion (US$6.8 billion) of the 2025 total, up 282% in real terms. That is about three quarters of all earmark spending, and the constitution reserves half of individual earmarks for health.

Health spending via earmarks rose from R$5.1 billion (US$1 billion) in 2014 to R$24.8 billion (US$4.8 billion) in 2024. Earmarks now fund 45.4% of the Health Ministry’s discretionary budget, up from 18.6%.

Here is the catch the headline hides. In 2024, 91.7% of health earmark money paid for running costs like maintenance and supplies, not new investments.

Those costs repeat every year, but earmarks have no guarantee of continuity. A clinic funded this way can lose its money the following year, which makes planning nearly impossible.

The Supreme Court has spent two years forcing transparency onto the system. Justice Flávio Dino now requires work plans, dedicated bank accounts and public reporting for the loosest category, known as Pix amendments.

The state companies bleeding at the other end

While Congress directs more money, the companies the state owns are losing more of it. Federal state-owned enterprises are running a deficit of R$8.3 billion (US$1.6 billion) in 2026, according to central bank data reported in the Brazilian press.

That figure excludes Petrobras and the public banks, which finance themselves in markets. It measures the weaker companies that may one day need taxpayer money, which is why economists watch it.

The deficit surpassed the whole of 2025 by May and is the worst in the central bank’s series since 2002. High interest rates and financial expenses explain part of it; management problems explain the rest.

Correios, the symbol of the problem

The postal service Correios is the single largest source of the red ink. Management Minister Esther Dweck has conceded the company will post the worst annual result in its history in 2026.

Correios lost R$3.2 billion (US$618 million) in the first quarter alone, after losing R$8.5 billion (US$1.6 billion) in 2025. A Treasury-guaranteed loan of R$12 billion (US$2.3 billion) keeps the operation running.

The government blames structural decline in mail and fierce private competition in parcels. Critics point to political appointments after the state companies law was loosened in 2023.

Both readings agree on the direction. The taxpayer guarantee means a failed restructuring lands in the budget, alongside the earmarks Congress is not giving up.

What to watch from here

The first test is the Supreme Court. Stricter transparency rules on Pix amendments could still shrink the least traceable part of the congressional earmarks machine.

The second is the Correios restructuring plan, which assumes the company returns to healthy indicators after 2026. The voluntary layoff programme has so far fallen short of targets.

The third is the election. Neither congressional earmarks nor state companies will be reformed before October, because both are how incumbents deliver visible benefits to voters.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Brazil’s congressional earmarks? They are budget amendments that let each deputy and senator direct part of the federal budget to chosen projects. Since a 2015 constitutional change, payment of individual earmarks is mandatory for the government. How much do the earmarks total? Committed earmarks reached R$47.1 billion (US$9.1 billion) in 2025, up from R$11.3 billion (US$2.2 billion) in 2014. That is real growth of 315% in eleven years, per the Ipea study. Why do critics say earmarks hurt planning? Most earmark money now pays running costs that repeat every year, but nothing guarantees the funds return. Health earmarks alone fund 45.4% of the ministry’s discretionary budget, tying its hands. How big is the state companies’ deficit? Federal state-owned enterprises are running a deficit of R$8.3 billion (US$1.6 billion) in 2026 so far, per central bank data. The figure excludes Petrobras and the public banks. What is happening at Correios? The postal service is heading for the worst annual result in its history, its own minister says. It lost R$3.2 billion (US$618 million) in the first quarter and survives on a Treasury-guaranteed loan of R$12 billion (US$2.3 billion).

World.title: Brazil: Judicial Debt Collection Hits Record 1.2 Million Cases in 2025
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts —The record: Brazilian courts received 1,239,537 new judicial debt collection cases in 2025, up about 60 percent on 2020. —What it covers: Court enforcement of private debts proven by documents, from loans and rent to cheques. Tax debts are excluded. —The backdrop: A record 80.4 percent of households were in debt in March 2026, and defaulters total 82.8 million adults. —The payout: Creditors recover only 6.1 percent in São Paulo bankruptcy cases, which run more than 16 years on average. —The response: Brasília is betting on the Desenrola Brasil renegotiation programme and new guarantee-fund-backed payroll credit. —The catch: The justice council changed its statistics panel in June, so the 2026 comparison stops at March.

A record 1.24 million Brazilians and companies were sued over unpaid private debts in 2025, as judicial debt collection rose 60 percent in five years and household over-indebtedness set new highs.

The numbers behind the record

The data come from the National Council of Justice, known by its Portuguese initials CNJ, which oversees Brazil’s judiciary. Its statistics panel tracks extrajudicial non-fiscal enforcement, the court-driven collection of private debts.

New filings rose every year of the series: 772,645 in 2020, 838,701 in 2021, 994,098 in 2022 and 1,131,730 in 2023. The count reached 1,194,184 in 2024 and a record 1,239,537 in 2025.

The category covers debts proven by documents: bank loans, vehicle and property financing, rent, cheques and commercial invoices. It excludes tax enforcement and captures consumers and companies alike.

The first quarter of 2026 brought 295,541 new cases, according to a G1 news portal survey of the CNJ panel. A panel redesign in June broke the series, so a full-year comparison is no longer possible.

Why judicial debt collection is exploding

Household indebtedness reached 80.4 percent in March 2026, the highest since the National Confederation of Commerce began its survey. A year earlier the figure was 77.1 percent.

The Central Bank estimates that debt service consumes about 30 percent of monthly income. Total household debt equals half of a full year’s earnings.

Credit bureau Serasa counted 82.8 million defaulters in March 2026, or 50.5 percent of the adult population. The average debt was R$6,728.51 (US$1,299), with the total near R$557 billion (US$107.5 billion).

The worst delinquency rates in May 2026 were in Amapá, the Federal District, Amazonas, Mato Grosso do Sul and Rio de Janeiro. Serasa’s map shows the strain is national, not metropolitan.

Judge Káren Rick Danilevicz Bertoncello, of the Rio Grande do Sul state court, sees no culture of renegotiation among borrowers. She singles out online betting as a growing driver of new defaults.

The last resort that pays back six cents

Fernando Corrêa, a jurimetrics specialist at the Brazilian Jurimetrics Association, says enforcement is a creditor’s last resort. Suing typically pays off only after about a year of arrears, within the five-year legal limit.

The recovery math is brutal. The Insolvency Observatory of the jurimetrics association and PUC-SP, a São Paulo university, finds creditors recover 6.1 percent in the city’s bankruptcy cases.

Those cases run more than 16 years on average. Creditors themselves file 91.9 percent of bankruptcy requests, and about a third of them are financial and insurance firms.

In effect, the courts have become the collection department of last instance. That clogs dockets while returning cents on the real to the plaintiffs.

The over-indebtedness law and the court project

Brazil’s 2021 over-indebtedness law, known as the Lei do Superendividamento, places duties on creditors to lend responsibly. It also gives consumers a path to restructure their debts through the courts.

The Rio Grande do Sul court’s over-indebtedness project has handled 31,075 cases, more than 20,000 of them still active. It has produced 6,273 agreements, and 13,657 of the people served are elderly.

The model shows what judicial debt collection could look like when settlement replaces seizure. It remains a pilot in a system drowning in new filings.

What to watch from here

The first marker is the CNJ panel itself, and how its new methodology reports judicial debt collection from June onward. A comparable 2026 total may not exist until next year.

The second is Desenrola Brasil, the federal renegotiation programme. Its reach decides how many disputes ever arrive before a judge.

The third is the 2026 payroll-credit expansion, which lets private-sector workers borrow against their FGTS severance-fund balances. Cheaper credit could ease defaults, or simply add to the pile.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is judicial debt collection in Brazil? It is the court enforcement of private debts proven by documents, such as loans, financing contracts, rent and cheques. The National Council of Justice counted a record 1,239,537 new cases in 2025. How much did judicial debt collection grow? New cases rose about 60 percent between 2020 and 2025, from 772,645 to 1,239,537. Filings increased in every year of the series. Why are so many Brazilians being sued over debt? Household indebtedness hit a record 80.4 percent in March 2026, and debt service consumes about 30 percent of monthly income. Credit bureau Serasa counted 82.8 million defaulters, half of all adults. Do creditors actually recover money in court? Rarely. In São Paulo bankruptcy cases, creditors recover 6.1 percent on average after proceedings lasting more than 16 years, according to the Insolvency Observatory of the Brazilian Jurimetrics Association and PUC-SP. What is the government doing about over-indebtedness? Brasília runs the Desenrola Brasil renegotiation programme and expanded payroll-deducted credit backed by the FGTS severance fund in 2026. The 2021 over-indebtedness law also places responsible-lending duties on creditors.

Sources: G1 survey of the National Council of Justice statistics panel; National Confederation of Commerce Peic survey; Central Bank of Brazil; Serasa; Insolvency Observatory of the Brazilian Jurimetrics Association and PUC-SP; Rio Grande do Sul Court of Justice.

World.title: Argentina Household Debt: Church Warning Ahead of Papal Visit
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

ARGENTINA · SOCIETY

Key Facts —What happened: Argentina’s top bishop warned the government about record Argentina household debt ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s November visit. —The numbers: Bank delinquency among families hit 12.8 percent in June, and 30.1 percent at virtual wallets. —The real story: Families are borrowing through phone apps to cover food and basics, not to consume. —The catch: The 30.1 percent wallet delinquency rate is worse than the pandemic peak of 27.1 percent in May 2020. —Who is hit: Some 5.91 million Argentines are behind on payments, out of 20.96 million people holding debt. —What comes next: The Church wants rules on how much of a salary can be pledged to debt before the Pope arrives.

The head of Argentina’s bishops’ conference warned the Milei government not to take a superficial view of household debt, as delinquency at virtual wallets runs above the worst level of the pandemic.
