What the bishop said

Monsignor Marcelo Colombo, president of the Argentine Episcopal Conference, chose a weekend radio interview to press the issue. He spoke to Radio Mitre Mendoza on Sunday.

His message to the government was blunt. “What you cannot do is take a superficial view, let alone say: we are not interested, let them sort it out,” he said.

Colombo asked for clear criteria on access to credit. He suggested a public discussion about how much of a person’s salary can legitimately be committed to debt payments.

He drew a line between two kinds of borrowing. Some loans are, in his words, clearly abusive the moment they are signed; others drip month by month until the borrower is trapped.

The numbers behind the warning

The figures come from the Centre for Argentine Political Economy, known as CEPA, working from central bank debtor records. They show how fast Argentina household debt has turned sour.

Bank delinquency among families reached 12.8 percent in June 2026. At the virtual wallets, the phone-app lenders that dominate small loans, the rate hit 30.1 percent.

That wallet figure passed the pandemic record of 27.1 percent set in May 2020. In total, 5.91 million people are in an irregular situation out of 20.96 million debtors.

The Argentina household debt burden is measurable in pay packets. In April, monthly debt service absorbed 24.1 percent of the country’s wage mass, and personal loans plus credit cards made up 73 percent of the irregular balance in May.

Borrowing to eat, not to spend

Colombo compared the moment to the Church’s earlier campaign against online gambling. Then, families fell into debt through addiction to betting.

Now, he said, the debt trap is different, and it is Argentina household debt built on phone apps. People borrow through virtual wallets to cover essential expenses, and the debt accumulates quietly until it cannot be repaid.

That framing cuts against the official optimism. The government has presented the credit boom as proof that confidence is back and consumption is recovering.

The politics of a papal visit

The timing is not accidental. A Vatican delegation arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday to prepare Pope Leo XIV’s visit, scheduled for 8 to 11 November.

City officials expect between 600,000 and 800,000 people at the main events. The Pope’s social teaching on debt and poverty will hang over every homily.

For President Javier Milei, the warning lands in a sensitive week. His economy minister, Luis Caputo, has just relaunched mortgage credit and is counting on mattress dollars returning to the banks.

Colombo’s critique does not reject credit itself. It asks who carries the risk when a family borrows at wallet rates to buy food.

What it means for readers abroad

For investors, Argentina household debt is the soft underside of the recovery story. A consumer rebound financed at 30 percent delinquency rates is not a rebound that lasts.

For expats, the practical note is simpler. The credit offers flooding phones and social media carry costs that Argentine consumer law does little to cap.

Watch whether the government answers before November. A regulation on salary-attached lending, or even a debt-relief gesture, would read as a pre-papal concession.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Argentine Church say about household debt? Bishops’ conference president Marcelo Colombo warned the government not to take a superficial view of record household delinquency. He asked for clear criteria on credit access, especially for loans covering basic needs. How bad is Argentina household debt delinquency? Bank delinquency among families reached 12.8 percent in June 2026, and virtual-wallet delinquency hit 30.1 percent, above the pandemic peak. Some 5.91 million people are behind on payments. Why is the warning linked to the Pope’s visit? A Vatican delegation arrived in Buenos Aires on 30 August to prepare Pope Leo XIV’s visit on 8 to 11 November. The Church is putting social debt on the agenda before he arrives. What did Colombo propose? He proposed criteria for taking on debt and a debate on how much of a salary can be committed to repayments. He distinguished abusive loans from debts that accumulate month by month. How much of wages goes to debt service in Argentina? In April 2026, monthly debt payments absorbed 24.1 percent of the household wage mass, according to CEPA. Personal loans and credit cards were 73 percent of the irregular balance in May.

World.title: Peru Faces El Niño With Savings at a 25-Year Low, Ex-Finance Minister Warns
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

PERU · ECONOMY

Key Facts —The warning: Former finance minister Alonso Segura says El Niño finds Peru with savings at a 25-year low. —The comparison: In 2017 Peru’s emergency buffers exceeded 4 percent of GDP; today they are largely consumed. —Market exposure: Analysts name cement maker Pacasmayo, food group Alicorp and power utility Engie as most exposed. —The budget: The draft 2027 budget rises 3.5 percent to over S/266.5 billion (US$79.5 billion). —The catch: Peru still has access to markets, but past savings were spent despite record commodity prices. —What comes next: The government weighs three measures against tax breaks costing S/27.7 billion (US$8.3 billion) in 2027.

Peru faces a potentially severe El Niño with its fiscal savings at their lowest point in almost 25 years. The Peru El Niño warning comes from Alonso Segura, the former finance minister who now heads the country’s fiscal watchdog.

Segura’s warning: the piggy bank is empty

Alonso Segura is not just any critic. He ran the finance ministry between 2014 and 2016 and now presides over the Consejo Fiscal, Peru’s official fiscal watchdog.

His message in Gestíón on Monday was stark. El Niño, he said, finds Peru with financial-asset savings at their lowest point in around 25 years.

Every Peru El Niño event tests the state’s coffers. This one arrives at the weakest fiscal position in a generation, and the stock market is already pricing the storm.

He offered a comparison that should worry investors. When the last big El Niño hit in 2017, Peru’s stabilisation fund, liquidity reserve and contingent credit lines stood at a historic peak above 4 percent of GDP.

Those buffers were then consumed, first by that El Niño and then by the pandemic. What pains him most is that the drain continued through record after record in commodity prices.

Peru still has access to international markets, Segura conceded. The question is whether the government will “throw the house out the window” when it revises the fiscal rules.

The new macro framework and its risks

The backdrop is the Multiannual Macroeconomic Framework for 2027–2030, just published. It is the first such plan of President Keiko Fujimori’s government.

Segura welcomed that the framework admits the deterioration of Peru’s public finances. But he warned it builds in consensus growth forecasts that carry extra risk.

The economy ministry wants to raise the ceilings on the fiscal deficit to fund the El Niño response. The Consejo Fiscal says any such adjustment demands concrete measures to protect sustainability.

His watchdog’s central complaint is about permanence. Much of the spending locked in over recent years, he said, cannot simply be switched off.

That is the quiet story of the draft 2027 budget, which rises 3.5 percent to more than S/266,506 million (US$79.5 billion). Payroll and pension commitments grow by law, while investment is what gets squeezed.

The listed companies in the storm’s path

Gestíón asked Lima’s brokerages which stocks a stronger Peru El Niño would hit hardest. Three names came back: Cementos Pacasmayo, Alicorp and Engie Energía Perú.

César Huiman, senior analyst at Renta4 SAB, said climate uncertainty raises the risk premium and compresses valuations. Prices fall before earnings are even touched.

His history lesson is sobering. In the severe 2015–2016 event, the four stocks he tracks fell 17 percent on average, though copper prices and US rate cycles shared the blame.

In the 2023–2024 event the same names corrected 6 percent on average. The broader Peru Select Index slipped just 0.8 percent over that period.

Pacasmayo carries direct exposure to Peru’s northern coast, where El Niño usually bites hardest. Marco Contreras of Kallpa SAB noted that reconstruction can later turn cement demand positive.

Engie’s risk sits in its hydroelectric assets and scarcer water. Lower rainfall is already pushing generation toward costlier gas and diesel plants, Contreras said.

For food group Alicorp, the weak point is its agricultural business. Its diversification and Peru’s resilient mass consumption should cushion the blow.

The banks are not immune either. Credicorp reports about 9 percent of its loan book in farming and fishing; BBVA in Peru reports 8 percent.

Three measures against S/28 billion of tax breaks

The second fiscal thread runs through tax expenditure. That is the money the state chooses not to collect through exemptions, exclusions, refunds and deductions.

The new macro framework puts this year’s bill at S/26,350 million (US$7.9 billion). For 2027 it projects S/27,697 million (US$8.3 billion), above 2.1 percent of GDP and 12 percent of expected tax revenue.

Exemptions made up 53 percent of tax expenditure between 2021 and 2026. Nearly one sol in three went to exclusions from whole tax categories.

The sales tax, known as the IGV, accounts for almost S/20,800 million (US$6.2 billion) of the 2027 cost. The exemption for farm products alone costs nearly S/4,500 million (US$1.3 billion), and the Amazon region’s exemption nearly S/4,000 million (US$1.2 billion).

The government’s answer has three parts. It promises not to expand tax breaks, to let expiring ones die on schedule, and to tighten the rest.

Thirteen benefits expire this year, worth S/848 million (US$253 million). The biggest are the income-tax exemption for non-profit foundations, at almost S/500 million (US$149 million) a year, and the exemption for bank deposit interest, at S/268 million (US$80 million).

Experts quoted by Gestíón want the knife to go further. Carlos Gallardo of the Peruvian Institute of Economics named breaks for restaurants, hotels and hair salons as the obvious first cut.

Former tax chief Sandro Fuentes urged a full review of the Amazon regime instead. He also warned that the tax agency Sunat needs operating tools, not just legal ones.

What this means for expats and investors

For a foreign resident, the Peru El Niño story is about practical things. Expect pressure on food prices, road closures in the north and east, and a busier state.

For an investor, it is about credibility. Peru’s crown jewel has always been macroeconomic stability, and Segura is warning that the jewel is being pawned.

The dates to watch are close. Congress will debate the budget and the fiscal-rule changes through the spring, while the first heavy El Niño rains are expected toward year-end.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Alonso Segura warn about El Niño? He said El Niño finds Peru with financial-asset savings at their lowest point in around 25 years. In 2017 the country’s emergency buffers exceeded 4 percent of GDP. Which Peruvian stocks are most exposed to El Niño? Renta4 analyst César Huiman named Cementos Pacasmayo, Alicorp and Engie Energía Perú. In the severe 2015–2016 event, the stocks he tracks fell 17 percent on average. How much do Peru’s tax breaks cost? The government projects S/27,697 million (US$8.3 billion) in foregone revenue for 2027. That is above 2.1 percent of GDP and 12 percent of expected tax collection. What three measures is the government examining? It promises not to expand tax benefits, to let expiring ones lapse on schedule and to tighten the rest. Thirteen benefits worth S/848 million (US$253 million) expire this year. Who is Alonso Segura? Segura was Peru’s finance minister from 2014 to 2016. He now presides over the Consejo Fiscal, the country’s official fiscal watchdog.

The growth side of the story is in Peru’s US$10 billion mining pitch. World.title: Medellín Mayor Hands the FBI Corruption Evidence as the Nicolás Petro Case Gets a New Prosecutor
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

COLOMBIA · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Medellín mayor Federico Gutiérrez flew to the United States to hand US agencies a dossier on alleged corruption under his predecessor. —The allegation: City funds under Daniel Quintero were allegedly moved through Panama and the United States to appear legal. —The names: The dossier covers Quintero, his brother Miguel and four allies; Miguel was indicted in Medellín on the same day. —The catch: The evidence is the mayor’s own investigation, and no US authority has confirmed opening a case. —The politics: Gutiérrez answered President De La Espriella’s anti-corruption call and says the Quintero case dovetails with the Petro case. —Also on Monday: Prosecutor Juan Martín Parada took over the case against Nicolás Petro, the former president’s son.

Medellín’s mayor Federico Gutiérrez has taken a Medellín corruption dossier to the FBI and US homeland security detectives, alleging that public money was laundered abroad under his predecessor, as a new prosecutor took over the case against Nicolás Petro.

What Gutiérrez took to the FBI

The mayor travelled to the United States on Tuesday 25 August carrying what the news magazine Semana described as a package of evidence. He delivered it to detectives of Homeland Security Investigations, known as HSI, and to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the FBI.

The hypothesis in the files is that Medellín’s public resources were moved to Panama and the United States during the Quintero administration. The aim, witnesses told judicial authorities, was to give the money an appearance of legality.

The dossier names six people: former mayor Daniel Quintero, his brother Miguel Quintero, Sebastián Ortega, William Ortega, Johny Jaramillo and Edison López, known as “Chano”. A well-known international precious-metals trader also appears in the city’s files, Semana reported.

Which investigations the mayor means

The Medellín corruption push is not abstract. On the day Gutiérrez flew out, prosecutors in Medellín indicted Miguel Quintero over irregularities at the Metropolitan Area of the Aburrá Valley, the regional planning authority.

Witness testimony says the former mayor’s brother led contracting processes and collected bribes without holding public office. A judge is due to issue the first conviction in that case.

Gutiérrez has also said he will cooperate with President Abelardo De La Espriella’s new anti-corruption bloc. In his telling, the Medellín corruption case would connect with the cases around the Petro family.

The hope in Medellín is that the Trump administration will collaborate in clarifying what happened to the city’s money. Whether US agencies open a formal case is their decision, not the mayor’s.

A new prosecutor for the Nicolás Petro case

The second piece of Monday’s judicial news came from Barranquilla. Prosecutor Juan Martín Parada has taken over the case against Nicolás Petro Burgos, the eldest son of former president Gustavo Petro.

The case dates to July 2023, when the younger Petro was arrested on charges of money laundering and illicit enrichment. Prosecutors say he bought around US$400,000 in real estate with money that did not match his declared income as a regional legislator.

Part of that money allegedly came from figures with drug-trafficking pasts and was meant for his father’s 2022 campaign. A cooperation agreement with prosecutors later collapsed over missed deadlines, a saga we covered when the new allegations surfaced and when prosecutors denied political pressure.

Why these two stories belong together

De La Espriella won the presidency on an anti-corruption platform, and his first month has put that theme everywhere. The Medellín corruption dossier and the Petro prosecution are its two most visible tests.

Both cases carry the same risk. If they advance on evidence, they strengthen the judiciary; if they stall or look selective, they feed the old Colombian suspicion that corruption cases are campaign tools.

For foreign residents and investors in Medellín, the practical question is narrower. A credible clean-up of city contracting would be good news for anyone doing business with the district.

What to watch from here

The first marker is any confirmation from HSI or the FBI that the Medellín corruption material has become a formal investigation. The second is the first Metropolitan Area conviction, expected shortly.

In Barranquilla, watch how Parada handles the Petro file. A new prosecutor can speed a case up, slow it down, or reopen the question of a cooperation deal.

Frequently Asked Questions

What evidence did Medellín’s mayor give to the FBI? Federico Gutiérrez delivered a dossier alleging that public funds under former mayor Daniel Quintero were moved through Panama and the United States to appear legal. The files name Quintero, his brother Miguel and four allies. Has the FBI opened a Medellín corruption investigation? No US authority has confirmed a formal case. The dossier is the Medellín mayor’s own investigation, and Gutiérrez says he hopes the Trump administration will collaborate. Who is the new prosecutor in the Nicolás Petro case? Juan Martín Parada has taken over the money-laundering and illicit-enrichment case against the former president’s son, which dates from July 2023. What is Nicolás Petro accused of? Prosecutors say he bought around US$400,000 in real estate with unexplained money, part of it allegedly from figures with drug-trafficking pasts and intended for his father’s 2022 campaign. He has denied the charges.

World.title: Brazil Gross Debt Hits 82.5% of GDP in July, Highest Since 2021
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

BRAZIL · PUBLIC FINANCE

Key Facts —What happened: Brazil’s gross public debt rose to 82.5 percent of GDP in July, the highest since April 2021. —How big: The debt reached R$10.9 trillion (US$2.1 trillion), up from 81.9 percent of GDP in June. —The real story: Interest cost R$98.963 billion (US$19.1 billion) in July alone, driving a R$97.6 billion nominal deficit. —The catch: The primary balance was in surplus, so July’s entire deficit is interest, not new spending. —Who it covers: The figures span the federal government, social security, states and municipalities, excluding Petrobras. —What comes next: The twelve-month deficit of 9.34 percent of GDP keeps pressure on the 2027 budget fight.

Brazil gross debt climbed to 82.5 percent of gross domestic product in July, the highest in five years, the central bank reported on Monday. The public sector stayed in primary surplus, yet interest alone produced a nominal deficit of R$97.6 billion (US$18.8 billion).

What the central bank reported

Gross general government debt reached 82.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in July. In money terms, that is R$10.9 trillion (US$2.1 trillion), up from 81.9 percent in June.

The Brazil gross debt figure is the highest since April 2021, when the country was still spending its way through the pandemic. The data come from the Banco Central, Brazil’s central bank, released on 31 August.

The measure is broad. It covers the federal government, the INSS social security system, and state and municipal governments.

Two things sit outside it. Companies in the Petrobras group and the state-owned banks are excluded, because the statistics track the non-financial public sector.

A surplus that still leaves a deficit

The primary balance, which measures revenue minus spending before interest, was positive in July. The consolidated public sector ran a surplus of R$1.361 billion (US$263 million).

A year earlier, July produced a primary deficit of R$66.6 billion (US$12.9 billion). So on this measure, the accounts improved sharply.

Then comes the interest. July’s interest bill was R$98.963 billion (US$19.1 billion), swallowing the surplus many times over.

The nominal result, which includes interest, was therefore a deficit of R$97.602 billion (US$18.8 billion). A year earlier the nominal hole was even deeper, at R$175.576 billion (US$33.9 billion).

What is pushing the debt up

The central bank breaks the monthly rise in Brazil gross debt into parts. Interest added 0.75 percentage points to the debt ratio, and currency effects added 0.19 points.

Nominal GDP growth pulled the ratio down by 0.38 points, and the primary surplus trimmed 0.01. In other words, growth helped, but not enough.

The net picture moved the same way. Public sector net debt rose to 69.1 percent of GDP, or R$9.165 trillion (US$1.77 trillion), from 68.5 percent in June.

The twelve-month picture

Over the twelve months to July, the nominal deficit totals R$1.240 trillion (US$239.4 billion). That equals 9.34 percent of GDP, an improvement from 9.99 percent in June.

Interest explains almost all of it. The twelve-month interest bill stands at R$1.150 trillion, or 8.67 percent of GDP.

Brazil gross debt keeps climbing precisely because of that arithmetic. High interest rates mean the state must run large primary surpluses just to stand still.

July’s surplus was far too small for that job. The debt ratio rose 0.6 points in a single month.

The politics around the numbers

The data land in the middle of an election-year argument about Brazil’s finances. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent last week courting bankers and congressional leaders over dinner at the Alvorada palace.

His allies dismiss talk of a fiscal crisis and point to the primary surplus as proof of control. Investors tend to watch the other number, the one that includes interest.

The 2027 budget bill, filed with an “effective” surplus below the official target, is now before Congress. Monday’s Brazil gross debt print gives the opposition fresh ammunition for that debate.

For foreign readers, the takeaway is mechanical. Until interest stops growing faster than the economy, each monthly surplus buys less calm than the last.

Frequently Asked Questions

How high is Brazil’s gross public debt? Brazil gross debt reached 82.5 percent of GDP in July 2026, or R$10.9 trillion (US$2.1 trillion). It is the highest level since April 2021. Did Brazil run a deficit in July 2026? Yes and no. The primary balance showed a surplus of R$1.361 billion (US$263 million), but interest of R$98.963 billion produced a nominal deficit of R$97.602 billion (US$18.8 billion). What is the difference between primary and nominal balance? The primary balance measures revenue minus spending before interest on debt. The nominal balance includes interest, so it shows the full financing need. How much interest does Brazil pay? July’s interest bill was R$98.963 billion (US$19.1 billion). Over twelve months, interest totals R$1.150 trillion, equivalent to 8.67 percent of GDP. Who is included in Brazil’s debt figures? The gross debt covers the federal government, the INSS social security system, and states and municipalities. Petrobras-group companies and state banks are excluded.

Sources: Banco Central do Brasil, Valor Econômico, CNN Brasil, Poder360, SBT News.

World.title: Benque Viejo Town Council thanks Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing for Mollejon road upgrades
World.content:
Benque Viejo Town Council thanks Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing for Mollejon road upgrades

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Benque Viejo Town Council announced that following lobbying on behalf of the farmers, residents and road users who rely on the Mollejon Road leading to Mollejon Dam and Arenal Village, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH) team began road works today.

The Benque Viejo Town Council noted that the works will commence at the exit of Benque Viejo Town where the pavement ends and continue toward the Mollejon Dam.

“These much needed road works will greatly benefit the many farmers and residents in the area by improving accessibility and making travel safer and more reliable. The road improvement will also benefit the taxi operators and residents traveling to Arenal Village.

We want to thank the Julius Espat and his MIDH Team for their valuable assistance and commitment to the people of Cayo West,” the council expressed.

The Benque Viejo Town Council says that it remains dedicated to advocating for the needs of communities and working toward meaningful improvements that directly benefit residents.

World.title: International News: Colombia captures suspected Tren de Aragua leader as US security cooperation deepens
World.content:
International News: Colombia captures suspected Tren de Aragua leader as US security cooperation deepens

By Zoila Palma: Colombian security forces have captured a suspected senior leader of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, in an operation praised by the U.S. Southern Command as a sign of deepening security cooperation between the two countries.

Luis Saúl Pérez Nieto, also known by the aliases “Páez” and “Nairobi,” was captured Thursday, with Colombian authorities accusing him of coordinating weapons and drug-trafficking networks across the region.

Colombian police said the operation also involved the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

Authorities accuse Pérez Nieto of helping expand Tren de Aragua’s operations in Peru while coordinating drug and arms trafficking across the continent, AP reports.

The gang, which originated as a prison gang in Venezuela, has expanded into a transnational criminal organization with operations across parts of Latin America.

The arrest comes as Colombia’s new conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella moves to strengthen security cooperation with Washington and intensify the fight against organized crime.

The U.S. Southern Command welcomed the capture, stating that “Narco-terrorists have no safe haven in our hemisphere,” while DEA Administrator Terry Cole congratulated Colombian authorities on the arrest of a senior Tren de Aragua leader.

Colombian and Peruvian authorities said the United States had requested Pérez Nieto’s arrest and extradition on allegations including terrorism, money laundering, drug trafficking and criminal conspiracy.

Colombian police also said he escaped Venezuela’s Tocorón prison in 2023 alongside Tren de Aragua leader Héctor “Niño Guerrero” Guerrero Flores, who was killed in a U.S. military strike earlier this year.

The arrest comes amid broader efforts by the United States, Colombia and other countries in the region to target organized crime and drug trafficking networks.

World.title: 53 Belize City traffic wardens complete enforcement training; sworn in as Special Constables
World.content:
53 Belize City traffic wardens complete enforcement training; sworn in as Special Constables

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department, through the National Police Training Academy (NPTA), has successfully completed a one-month Enforcement Training Programme for 53 Belize City Council Traffic Wardens. The programme was delivered in two separate two-week cohorts and was designed to prepare the participants for expanded enforcement responsibilities.

The training focused on strengthening the wardens’ legal knowledge, professionalism and operational skills, while helping them better understand their responsibilities when interacting with members of the public.

Participants took part in classroom instruction, practical exercises and scenario-based learning to prepare them for real-world enforcement situations.

The programme concluded with a closing ceremony attended by representatives of the Belize Police Department, NPTA, Belize City Council, instructors and the participating traffic wardens.

In his remarks, Commissioner of Police Rosado highlighted the significance of the powers and responsibilities being entrusted to the participants as they transition into their new roles as Special Constables.

Commissioner Rosado reminded the participants that “with great power comes greater responsibility,” stressing that their authority must be exercised with integrity, discipline, professionalism, accountability and respect for the rights of the public. He encouraged them to recognize the trust placed in them and to ensure their conduct reflects positively on the Belize Police Department, Belize City Council and the wider law enforcement community.

The training was facilitated by members of the NPTA, including Assistant Superintendent Jermaine Hyde, Sergeant 1270 Leon Ferguson and Corporal Maurice Martinez, along with other instructors and personnel.

World.title: Crop tops, tank tops out: Schools enforce dress codes for parents
World.content:
Crop tops, tank tops out: Schools enforce dress codes for parents

By Zoila Palma: A growing number of primary and secondary schools across Belize are implementing dress codes for parents and other adults entering their campuses, asking visitors to dress appropriately while on school grounds.

The guidelines vary by school, but commonly discourage attire such as crop tops, tank tops, very short pants or shorts, and ripped or cut-up jeans.

Parents are instead being encouraged to wear more modest and appropriate clothing when visiting schools for meetings, dropping off or picking up children, attending activities, or conducting school business.

School administrators say the guidelines are intended to promote a respectful and appropriate environment on campus.

As more schools introduce or reinforce these expectations, parents are being encouraged to familiarize themselves with their respective school’s dress code before entering the campus.

World.title: International News: Ontario Premier warns US-Canada trade war would be “devastating” for both countries
World.content:
International News: Ontario Premier warns US-Canada trade war would be “devastating” for both countries

By Zoila Palma: Ontario Premier Doug Ford is warning that an escalating trade war between the United States and Canada could have devastating consequences for both countries, as tensions continue to rise over tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ford strongly criticized the tariffs and said they could ultimately hurt the American economy, ABC reports.

“Everyone’s feeling bullied by President Trump, and this is the worst thing you could do for the American economy,” Ford said. “I just don’t see the purpose. It’s absolutely backwards.”

The United States recently announced plans to impose an additional 50% tariff on many Canadian goods after trade negotiations broke down, while Canada is set to respond with retaliatory tariffs beginning September 8.

Ford also pointed to the importance of Canada’s role in supplying crude oil to the United States, saying Washington must decide whether it wants to rely on Canada or pursue alternatives such as Venezuela. “Well, you know something? That’s going to be up to President Trump. Who do you want to deal with? An unstable government like Venezuela, or do you want to deal with your No. 1 trading partner, your No. 1 ally?” Ford said.

Trump has also threatened to double auto tariffs on Canadian vehicles beginning January 1, 2027.

Ford said such a move would be “devastating” for both countries, particularly because Canada is a major purchaser of U.S.-made vehicles.

World.title: International News: Road blockades spread across Petén, disrupting border crossings including Melchor de Mencos
World.content:
International News: Road blockades spread across Petén, disrupting border crossings including Melchor de Mencos

By Zoila Palma: Protests over rising fuel and basic food prices have intensified in Guatemala’s Petén department, with taxi drivers, truckers and other motorists blocking roads.

The demonstrations that began on Friday, August 28 continue today, Monday August 31, disrupting transportation and access at several key locations across the department.

This morning, motorists maintained road blockades in multiple areas of Petén. Access to the central area of Petén was blocked in front of Mundo Maya International Airport in Santa Elena, while the ferry service in Sayaxché was also suspended, halting transportation across the Pasión River.

Guatemalan Journalist Cesar Soler noted that the protests are being concentrated at several strategic locations, including the Ferry de la Pasión, El Rosario National Park, Las Pozas and La Ceiba in Sayaxché. In La Libertad, demonstrators are positioned at the borders with Mexico at the El Ceibo and El Naranjo crossings, as well as at the La Esperanza crossing.

Other affected areas include Melchor de Mencos on the Belize border, San Benito along the road leading to San Francisco, San Andrés at the crossing toward Sacpuy, Poptún at the Machaquilá Bridge, Santa Ana at La Potra crossing, and Santa Elena near Mundo Maya Airport and at Kilometer 8 near Turicentro.

The disruptions are raising concerns for travelers and commercial traffic moving between Guatemala and Belize, particularly through the Melchor de Mencos border area.

Motorists and travelers heading through Petén are being urged to exercise caution, monitor developments and be prepared for possible delays or changes in road access as the protests continue.

World.title: Crackdown on care
World.content:
TUFTON...people must play their part...or they make way for someone else to do itPhoto: Garfield Robinson

SPURRED by more than 1,000 patient complaints in the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect report, portfolio Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent medical professionals accountable will intensify.

The move comes as the ministry prepares to publish its accountability data in September, which Tufton says highlighted various client complaints of poor communication, professional conduct, and overall patient experience.

“We’re looking to transform the health workforce. We are taking an inward look, recognising that a highly qualified health system cannot exist without sound governance, and that transformation requires effective leadership, which will be essential to managing the critical components of health.

“So when we speak about an accountability framework, it’s about delivering service with compassion, with empathy and, of course, ensuring that every patient is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness at every point of care,” said the minister as he delivered the keynote address at the Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston in St Andrew last Friday.

According to him, the report’s data aims to isolate departments and individuals responsible for poor patient experiences rather than allowing the failures of some to tarnish the reputation of the wider health-care system.

“Where there is a problem, we need to identify the institution, the department, and who is in charge. You have to start with all the names, because you can’t allow one bad apple to spoil the whole lot…Tell me where the worst experience takes place, the bad experience; tell me which department, and tell me who is in charge.

“And what leadership ought now to do is to address the specifics of a problem. Stop generalising the problem, because we’re letting down people who make sacrifices every day to do the work, and that’s a new modus operandi…People must play their part, and we must emphasise and insist on it, or they make way for someone else to do it,” charged Tufton.

The minister’s push for greater accountability comes amid heightened public scrutiny of the health-care system after the death of 33-year-old Kenise Dunn gained widespread media traction. The eight-month pregnant mother of three passed away at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days post-delivery.

When asked if his call for accountability extended to the contentious incident, Tufton told the Jamaica Observer that he cannot comment conclusively while the investigation is ongoing. Still, he emphasised that health-care professionals are always bound by a duty of care. “What I’ve heard, preliminary, is that, clinically, there was a diagnosis of the problem, but it appears, based on some of the feedback — including from persons who are on the ward — that maybe the management of the customer care and the empathy to the patient may have been less than desired. Now, I don’t have the final report, so I prefer not to conclude on that,” he said. “But the truth is drawn from what I said about the complaints report, the 1,000, which I spoke to, it’s quite clear that while we have excellent health workers, we have to work harder at delivering service with compassion and with empathy. And it’s not good enough to just have technical competence. If you treat people badly, if you don’t listen to them, if you don’t respond to them, if you don’t give them a sense of comfort when they’re in distress, then it hampers the healing process,” said the minister. In the meantime, Tufton urged the 141 recipients of the Barry Wint medical grant, valued at over $190 million, to be the difference once they enter their respective fields of practice. “I say this at the risk of offending some, that money is not the primary issue in health care, currently public health; the primary issue is how we conduct ourselves within the system. People who are in the system only for a pay cheque are not sufficiently willing to give the commitment and show care. You cannot afford to be like that. You have to show a better way, and that’s what Barry Wint is investing in. Not just in your capacity as a technical and competent person, but in moving the process forward,” the minister said. Pointing to what he identified as the major weaknesses of the system, Tufton noted that health care in Jamaica lacks a sufficient number of practitioners — specifically specialised individuals — and professionals with the capacity to show empathy to patients. He reiterated that that was not the type of behaviour that he expected from recipients of the Barry Wint scholarship, and challenged them to become “a catalyst for change”. “If you just want to be a nurse, a doctor, a biotech engineer because at the end of the month you’re going to get a fat pay cheque, and that’s the only driving motivation to apply and to pretty up the application for this money, do not accept it. There are too many people in the profession who see the profession only in financial terms, and not enough as a passion and commitment to enhance service delivery for those who need it, Jamaicans who are in distress,” he said firmly.

World.title: Jamaicans loud and proud!
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago’s High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix shares her admiration for the manner in which Jamaicans display pride in their country while speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. Photo: Naphtali Junior

FROM schoolchildren in the country’s colours to packed cultural events, Trinidad and Tobago’s new High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix says the unapologetic pride Jamaicans display in their identity is one of the things that has impressed her most since taking up her post.

Having lived in several Caribbean countries, Thomas-Felix said Jamaica’s expression of national pride stands out to her because of how openly it is displayed in everyday life, from the workplace to sporting and cultural events.

She was particularly struck by the way Jamaicans embrace national occasions, including Jamaica Day, when people turn out in the country’s colours, adding that the celebration of national identity extends beyond the traditional observances of Independence and Emancipation.

“You all have a national day — schoolchildren, big people going to work in Jamaica colours. I was so struck by that when I experienced it… Don’t get me wrong, because Trinidad and Tobago has a deep sense of pride and love, but it’s the way, the open way in which it’s displayed in Jamaica,” she expressed during the a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters last Friday.

For Thomas-Felix, the pride is also visible in how Jamaica celebrates its culture, with Reggae Month — commemorated in February — providing an entire month of activities centred on one of the country’s most recognisable cultural exports.

She said that visible enthusiasm has helped her better understand Jamaicans in the Diaspora.

“Everywhere you go within the country, they say, ‘Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica,’ and I think that is so encouraging, and it gives me a better understanding of the Jamaicans I know who don’t live in Jamaica,” she said.

Thomas-Felix, whose parents are Grenadians and who has lived in St Vincent, Barbados, and Trinidad and Tobago, stressed that she was not suggesting that Trinbagonians lack national pride, but said she was particularly impressed by how visibly Jamaicans express theirs.

“There’s this open display of pride, and I think you all should keep that. I think that is just an excellent way to let [future] generations inherit that and continue with that, because I really, really like that,” she said.

Her comments come as Thomas-Felix seeks to strengthen ties between Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago across areas including trade, culture, and people-to-people relations.

She said the relationship between the two countries extends well beyond governments, pointing to Trinidadians who have built lives and careers in Jamaica and Jamaicans who have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago.

For Thomas-Felix, those personal connections are part of the Caribbean relationship that she wants to strengthen during her tenure.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds,” she said.

World.title: Slow movement on Spring Mount road repairs
World.content:
Residents of Spring Mount listen keenly as manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw (left) provides an update on plans to rehabilitate collapsed roads in the area.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — A soil test is among the items to be done before the State-run National Works Agency (NWA) can finalise a design to rebuild Spring Mount road in south St James. Last October’s Hurricane Melissa caused two major breakaways on the heavily trafficked route, leaving commuters with the choice of engaging in risky road use or a much longer, more costly journey.

With schools about to reopen, residents of Spring Mount and neighbouring areas have become increasingly anxious for an update on what is being done to fix the road. They were given the clearest signal, Thursday evening, that the road will likely be rebuilt in the same location; but there was no timeline on when work will start.

“We are looking to build back the road. We have looked at different possibilities and I can tell you straight up, one of the things that we are looking at is to take down the hillside and acquire [those] two houses on top of the hill,” manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw told residents during a meeting held at Spring Mount Basic School.

He said the goal is to rehabilitate the roadway as soon as possible, restoring the vital connection between the north and south of the parish. The damage has made safe passage by vehicular traffic impossible just beyond Spring Mount Police Station. Residents have established a pedestrian path which is sometimes utilised by motorcyclists.

Shaw made it clear that there will be challenges in executing the project, given its scope and magnitude.

“It is not the normal run of the mill [approach of] looking at it as a breakaway, put up a wall, backfill it, and move on. No. We are going to have to do what are called bore hole tests,” he warned, adding that this falls outside the technical capabilities of the NWA and a private sector firm would have to be engaged.

These tests, he explained, will provide laboratory-based information on the soil in the area that will guide the designs on which work has already started.

“That testing of the material beneath there will inform us as to what else, if required, needs to be done to ensure that… when we build up that road, you have it longer than all of us inside here will live,” Shaw told the audience.

“Based on the survey that was executed, a design is being worked on but that design will not be finalised until the boreholes are done,” he added.

He explained the importance of the soil tests.

“A crucial factor in this area is the springs. It’s called Spring Mount for a reason. We have to design with that in mind to ensure that we don’t see a situation where we build a big wall, costing a lot of money… and then, [as seen in other locations] rain came, and the entire retaining wall just moved like… it was plastic,” Shaw outlined.

“We have that kind of experience and historical knowledge on which to build or not to build. We are not taking anything lightly in ensuring that the design solutions that we come up with, they are adequate, they are appropriate, are sufficient, and necessary for the particular areas that we are going to be working,” he added.

Responding to residents’ questions about timelines, the NWA representative said he was unable to provide one as it depends on the soil testing which is being done outside of the agency. He did, however, promise to explore ways in which alternate routes — such as the journey through Kempshot, up the treacherous Charlie Mount — may be improved.

Councillor Uvel Graham (Jamaica Labour Party, Spring Mount Division) was at the meeting and while he acknowledged that the project is complex he expressed frustration that it is moving too slowly.

“To be honest, I was looking for more of a timeline and that these tests would be done already and people would be hearing that the next two to three months, the work would start,” he told the

Jamaica Observer after the meeting.

World.title: ‘I’ve run my leg’
World.content:
GREENE...I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AFTER a brief but impactful two-year term as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Health and Wellness, Errol Greene is ready to pass the baton, proud of his legacy but acknowledging that critical work remains.

“As we gather to award students pursuing courses in public health, I am filled with mixed emotions. I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness,” said Greene, as he formally announced his retirement from the role — which takes effect Monday, August 31 — while delivering greetings at the Dr Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston last Friday.

Under the scholarship, named in honour of the former chief medical officer, recipients are awarded up to $1 million annually for health care-related studies in priority fields such as nursing, biomedical engineering, and medicine.

For this year’s staging, 141 awardees were selected from more than 700 applicants to benefit from over $190 million in scholarships, with the Government having spent approximately $900 million towards the initiative to date.

“While there’s a sense of nostalgia, there’s also a sense of tremendous pride and optimism as I look out at this room filled with talented, ambitious, enthusiastic, and determined persons who represent the future of health care in Jamaica,” said Greene, who noted that he would continue to watch their progress as professionals in the health field from the sidelines.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer if his retirement signalled a complete departure from public service, Greene offered a cryptic, “We’ll see how it goes.” However, he maintained that he is ready to hand over the reins to a capable professional who can drive the remaining work forward.

“We have done well, and we can do better. I certainly want to be a part of the journey because I know my minister is passionate about health, he’s passionate about service delivery, and I would have run my leg of the race and I have handed over the baton, so I’ll just go in the pavilion and watch the race finish,” he said.

Before his two-year stint as permanent secretary, Greene led a career spanning decades. His life as a public servant began when he assumed the role of town clerk of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) and also served at the St Thomas Municipal Corporation.

He then pivoted to begin service in the health sector, serving as regional director of the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), which oversees health services in Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, and St Catherine.

He was also a former regional director of Western Regional Health Authority and a former chief executive officer of the Kingston Public Hospital.

Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton, who delivered the keynote address at the scholarship event, used the opportunity to acknowledge Greene’s contributions and bid him farewell.

“Our permanent secretary, who is not riding off in the sunset, but is closing one chapter to start another, Mr Errol Greene…give him a round of applause, please. I believe he has done 50 years, thereabout. I don’t want to tell his age, because he is still young,” joked Tufton. “But he has done a whole heap of years, whole heap of decades to public service, and I just want to recognise him and thank him for his services.”

World.title: UWI Freshers’ Series delivers a hit, energises campus
World.content:
DJ Breeze in full flight at Freshers’ Fete.

Jermaine Francis, vice-president of properties and special initiatives at The University of the West Indies, Mona Guild of Students, has described this year’s Freshers’ Series as one of the most successful in the past five years, attracting one of the largest turnouts seen during that period.

The Freshers’ Series took place from August 26-28.

According to Francis, the strong participation and vibrant atmosphere throughout the week signals that “the vibes on campus are back.” He noted that the enthusiasm and engagement displayed by students demonstrates the immense value and potential of the university market.

“UWI, Mona provides corporate entities with a unique opportunity to connect with the next generation of leaders and consumers. The energy is back, the students are engaged, and the platform is growing. I am urging corporate Jamaica to tap in and become part of these experiences,” Francis told the Jamaica Observer on the weekend.

Francis is therefore encouraging corporate Jamaica to take greater interest in and tap into this unique and dynamic student market. With major events such as UWI Integration Thursday and UWI Carnival on the horizon, he believes there are significant opportunities for brands to engage directly with thousands of young, influential, and emerging consumers.

The first event in the Freshers’ Series was the Freshers’ Concert, which took place inside Students’ Union on the campus. Representatives from the various halls performed talented pieces including singing, drama and poetry.

“The idea behind the Freshers’ Concert is really to give our new students a proper welcome to UWI and allow them to experience the university beyond the classroom. We wanted each hall to come together, showcase their creativity and talents, and give the freshers an opportunity to build friendships and create memories from the very start of their university journey. We also ensured that the freshers got the opportunity to interact with their guild councillors.

The George Alleyne Hall emerged winner, with Mary Seacole Hall, Elsa Rynie Towers, Irvine Hall, and Taylor Hall finishing in second, third, fourth and fifth places, respectively.

“The halls showcased a range of talents, including singing, dancing, drama and other creative performances. What stood out to me was how each hall found its own way to tell a story and represent their identity through their performance. The Freshers’ Concert also gives the freshers an opportunity to get involved and feel like they are part of The UWI community from early. University is not only about academics; it is also about the relationships you build and the experiences you have along the way,” said Francis.

On Thursday, August 27, Freshers’ Cocktail took place under the theme “Port of Paradise”.

“The Freshers’ Cocktail, themed Port of Paradise, was a premium and elegant experience designed to give incoming students an opportunity to dress up, socialise, and enjoy an evening of entertainment, fine cuisine, and networking. The event created a sophisticated atmosphere within the Freshers’ Series, combining elements of Caribbean culture with exceptional food, performances, and meaningful social interaction. The objective was to create a welcoming environment where freshers could connect with one another outside of the traditional orientation setting. We wanted students from different faculties, halls of residence, and backgrounds to interact, build friendships, and develop a genuine sense of belonging within The UWI, Mona community,” Francis explained.

On Friday, August 28, Freshers’ Fete, under the theme “Island Fever”, closed the week in a major way, with popular university DJs playing hits that saw students partying until early Saturday morning.

“Freshers’ Fete was the perfect climax to an exciting and memorable week of activities. The energy was unmatched, the turnout was strong, and students came together to celebrate the beginning of their university journey in an atmosphere of unity, entertainment, and celebration. The experience was premium and exceptionally well supported. We would like to extend special recognition to our valued sponsors, including CPJ, which provided Str8 Vybz Rum and Angostura Chill, as well as Red Bull, Reggae Jammin’, JN Bank, LASCO Food Drink, and Wisynco, through brands such as Wata and Mpowa. We are also grateful to all the other sponsors and partners who came on board and contributed to making the Freshers’ Series a success,” said Francis.

DJs including Carlos A-Team, DJ Jubba and Breeze, and Kurt Riley provided the musical vibrations.

World.title: Young scholar rises above Riverton roots to pursue dreams
World.content:
Recipient of the Open Tertiary Male Bursary award Javon Gentles (left) embraces his sister Kadeen Fyffe at the Burger King National Scholarship Programme Awards held last Tuesday at AC Hotel Kingston. Photo: Naphtali Junior

BORN and raised in one of Kingston’s inner-city communities, Javon Gentles knows what it is like to lose opportunities due to his Riverton City address rather than his credentials. But when he took the stage at the Burger King National Scholarship Awards last Tuesday, he showed up as a testament to perseverance and being able to rise above the limitations placed on him.

“I grew up in a community where potential is everywhere, but opportunities are often scarce. Growing up there taught me resilience and resourcefulness. It also taught me the hard truth: Sometimes people will see your address before they see your character, your abilities, or your potential.

“But I learned that I could not control the assumptions others made. What I could control was what I believed, the opportunities that were brought to me, and the place in which I wanted to go — the direction in which I wanted to choose to take. And I choose greatness,” declared Gentles, as he spoke on behalf of the 2026 cohort of scholars at the AC Hotel Kingston.

The scholarships — valued at more than $14 million and awarded to 34 high achievers and are granted by Restaurant Associates Limited, franchise operator of Burger King in Jamaica — provide funding to students who sat the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) exam and are entering secondary schools, as well as students heading into accredited local universities.

Standing proudly as the recipient of the ‘Open Tertiary Male Bursary’ award, Gentles shared that he learnt from an early age that success did not happen by chance, but by sacrifice, determination, and resilience.

On his quest for greatness, Gentles did not squander his time as a student at St George’s College, serving in various leadership roles and amassing 10 grade ones at the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) level, and four distinctions across both units of the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE).

Yet, even with an exemplary academic record, his dreams of advancing to the tertiary education level remained uncertain.

“A dream that I have carried for years, [is] becoming a neurosurgeon. But, of course, with my background, eventually my dream, you know, it’s a difficult reality. I had the hope, I had the motivation, I had the grace and the feeling of experience, yet the financial reality of pursuing my career at The UWI [University of the West Indies] forced me to ask a difficult question: Can I actually afford to become a doctor? I had to consider whether to place the burden [of me getting higher education] on my family or to enter the workforce sooner, you know, choosing a path that might offer faster financial security, but not the fulfilment I was seeking,” said Gentles, adding that it was the hardest decision he ever had to make.

But, as he faced his darkest hour, navigating derailed dreams, Gentles shared that his reality changed instantly when he became one of the recipients of the Burger King scholarship and bursaries awards.

“To the Burger King family, thank you. Thank you not only for the financial support that makes this opportunity possible, but for believing in the potential of young Jamaicans and choosing to invest into our futures. This award is more than financial. It is an opportunity. It is motivation. It is a powerful reminder that the path we have chosen, no matter how difficult, is worth continuing,” he said triumphantly.

In an invigorating message to his fellow awardees, Gentles encouraged the scholars to make the most of the opportunity by tackling the future with confidence and a responsibility to become the best version of themselves.

“Fellow scholars, the trail ahead will not always be easy. There will be challenges, uncertainty and moments of doubt. But, we are prepared. So let us move with courage, let us work with discipline, and let us lead with integrity and let us serve with purpose. And when we reach the places we are working toward, let us turn around and make the trail wider, brighter for those coming behind us, because our success should become a bridge for those who are coming after us. The trail is before us, my dear scholars. Let us go and set it ablaze,” he charged.

Watching after her brother with sheer pride as he commanded the stage, Kadeen Fyffe told the Jamaica Observer that Gentles had always been exceptional.

“I’m very much delighted and happy for him. He’s been doing well academically, so this is well deserved. But this [scholarship] wasn’t expected because we tried other places for scholarships before, but Burger King came through. So we big up Burger King for giving the youth hope to pursue their dreams, and we thank God for giving us this grace and the privilege to watch him reach as far as he has…we thank our mother, Juliette Sital, who is the backbone for both of us. So, as he starts this new journey, we’ll continue to trust God,” said Fyffe.

For her part, minister of state in the Ministry of Education Rhoda Moy Crawford highlighted the ceremony’s theme, ‘Blazing a trail to success’, encouraging the scholars to continue on their path of excellence and to rise again when faced with challenges.

“To blaze a trail is to create a path where there may have been none before. It means pursuing your goals, even when the road is unclear. It means being brave enough to explore your abilities, to challenge yourself, and sometimes to go further than where anyone else in your family has gone before. Use this opportunity to develop the knowledge, skills, character, and confidence to make the most of your journey,” charged Crawford.

World.title: GIVE US A HAND!
World.content:
Justin Greaves (second right) celebrates with teammates after dismissing Australia’s Alex Carey during the day/night third Test at Sabina Park in Kingston, Jamaica, on July 12, 2025. Photo: Naphtali Junior

With India and England set to tour the Caribbean next year, Jamaica Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says the Government must make a serious effort to ensure the two cricketing powerhouses play at Sabina Park.

Although not officially announced by the ICC or the respective cricket boards, the West Indies are expected to host the Indians next June where they will play two tests, three One-Day Internationals (ODIs) and five T20s. England are scheduled to arrive next December to battle the Caribbean men in five T20s in preparation of the 2028 Twenty20 (T20) World Cup.

India’s last visit to the region was in the summer of 2023 while England last toured in the final quarter of 2024.

Bennett, who also serves as a CWI board director, told the Jamaica Observer that unlike other touring nations, territories have to make official bids to CWI to host the Indians and the English because of the significant commercial value the two teams bring.

“The bid documents should be out in another four weeks. I’ve already written to the Ministry of Sports outlining and sensitising them to the fact that England and India will be here next year,” he said. “As soon as that document comes out then we’re going to have to engage the Ministry of Sports, and probably the Ministry of Tourism too, in a serious way to ensure that we do bid for those games because they do have serious economic impact.”

Bennett says he’s optimistic the Government will follow through and see the value of the tours, particularly with India.

“Jamaica is just three hours away from the eastern seaboard of the United States and about three million Indians and cricket-loving or cricket-crazy people live on the eastern seaboard of the US so it can be a huge tourism opportunity,” he said. “So we’ll have to sit down with the Government and engage them and see how we go. The initial response that I’ve had is that there is a deep interest [within] the Government in these tours so, like I said before, we will see how it goes.”

Over the last two years, Sabina Park has seen an uptick in international matches, hosting South Africa, Bangladesh, Australia, and most recently Sri Lanka in June.

The steady turnout for those matches caught the eye of CWI President Dr Kishore Shallow who, according to reports, was impressed with Jamaica’s recent hosting stints.

However, Bennett says the Government will have to be more proactive this time around, given the number of bids CWI is expected to receive from around the region.

“There are other countries that have tourism as their main industry and they’re going to be wanting the tours too, and they’re going to be competitive too,” he said. “So we have to be on the ball and to do what we’re doing, and not only do what we should do, but we need to do it on a timely basis. We need to get in there as early as possible to see what we can get from those tours.”

Bennett, though, says Jamaica should gain an added advantage after the crowd support witnessed during the Sabina Park leg of the Caribbean Premier League earlier this month.

“It must be a factor because it’s not about just allocating to territories based on a wide basis. Cricket West Indies is not going to allocate matches just because you’re a territory and you haven’t had a game for one season or a game should go here and a game should go there. Clearly, there must be a consideration for crowd support, crowd support is an economic thing,” he said.

“The West Indies is out there to make money also and if territories support the game and come out in large numbers, clearly, we’ll have an advantage as far as the allocation of the game is concerned. I asked the cricket-loving public in Jamaica to come out and strengthen my hand and they certainly did. We can look forward to the India and the English tour with some sort of positivity. I’m sure that the crowd has put us into a place where we can barter and express our desire in a more forceful way.”

Bennett also hasn’t ruled out the possibility of hosting matches when visitors Afghanistan take on the Windies in February in both a red-ball and white-ball series.

However, the series could be postponed due to the Windies’ participation in the 50 over World Cup Qualifier which also starts in February.

World.title: Hundreds benefit from dental health fair in Mandeville
World.content:
Dental students McKenna Doyle (left) and Brianna Lopez (right) pose for a photo with 10-year-old Davere Lawrence after his dental procedure on Friday in Mandeville. Kasey Williams

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Hundreds of children and their parents benefited from free dental services during a back-to-school health fair dubbed 1000 Smiles, thanks to a partnership between overseas mission group Great Shape! Inc and businesses here.

The one-week fair, hosted at the Mandeville Baptist Church and supported by Golf View Hotel, Garden Hotel, Lial Global, QVC Financial Solutions, Allied Real Estate, Manchester Chamber of Commerce, and Ultimate Dining, attracted people from south-central Jamaica and as far north as Trelawny.

Dr Harvey Arnce, a board member of Great Shape! Inc, said 20 volunteers — including a mixed group of final-year dental students and retired doctors — participated in the mission.

“I have been doing this with the team for 22 years across the Caribbean. I have been to most of the islands. We also partnered with the Sandals Foundation,” he said in reference to missions, including a recently concluded health fair in St Ann.

Students from five dental schools participated in the health fair in Mandeville.

“The University of Western Ontario, Mid-Western University Illinois, Mid-Western University in Phoenix, University of the Pacific in San Francisco, and University of Southern California; the students typically come on these missions when they are not in school, so that is in August/September,” Dr Arnce told the Jamaica Observer last Friday.

Among the dental services offered were teeth filling, cleaning and extractions

“We have to limit the volume of what we do on each patient, because 500 people who showed up for this week’s treatment and if we did a full mouth’s restoration, 400 [would] get to be seen. We are trying to just do a quadrant on each person,” said Dr Arnce.

He is encouraging Jamaicans to pay greater attention to their dental health.

“The diet here has high carbs and people get tooth decay. They don’t have check-ups on a regular basis. The decay gets bigger from inside the tooth and by the time it hurts, it is already too late for that tooth to be fixed and they end up with extractions. You almost have to be serviced on a yearly basis to fix a problem while it is in the early stages.

“If not, you would require a root canal treatment or an expensive crown. People would rather have it out, it is an economic and cultural issue as well as an availability issue of help. We are trying to solve the availability and affordability issue,” he added.

The Great Shape! Inc team will now turn its focus to the western end in Negril, to continue its mission.

“We typically do about two weeks in each location and then we move. In each location we [stay] at a hotel and we go out to say two or three clinics,” explained Dr Arnce.

Among the beneficiaries of the dental clinic was Lorrimers, Trelawny resident Daegia Isaacs and her four children — ages 10, 16, 12, and five.

“I was scrolling through

TikTok and I saw someone talking about it and I did some checks and found that it was legitimate. I travelled all the way from Trelawny to be here, it is a huge help, especially that all four of my children [benefited]. I saved over $100,000 for all four of them and I was able to utilise the service for myself. Being that my children are not on any health insurance right now, this is a huge help,” said Isaacs.

General manager at Golf View Hotel Keitho Nembhard lauded the sponsors of the fair.

“We are in the centre of the island with small hotels. We don’t have a lot of rooms, so we partnered with Garden Hotel and they were able to accommodate the team and we gave up a lot of our rooms as well to accommodate the team. Meals were provided through the hotels and Ultimate Dining. QVC Financial Solutions was our transportation provider for the team. Allied Real Estate provided logistics and support… The Mandeville Baptist Church hall was used and the church was more than happy to accommodate the dental clinic,” said Nembhard.

World.title: Germany’s far right eyes small eastern state as springboard to national power
World.content:
“Every single one of you is making history right now!” Ulrich Siegmund, the charismatic face of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt set to become state premier should the party win big in a vote on Sept. 6, told a cheering crowd of thousands of supporters at an AfD campaign event in the former industrial town of Merseburg. “Someday, in 20 or 30 years, you’ll look in the history books and say: ‘It began here. It began in 2026 in Saxony-Anhalt!’”

Should the AfD win an absolute parliamentary majority in the state — current polls show them a few seats away from that goal — the party’s strategy for governing strikes a delicate balance: pursuing radical change that distinguishes the party from the establishment — delivering the political revolution it has long promised — without going so far as to alienate ordinary Bürger, middle-of-the-road citizens who don’t want the boat rocked too hard.

The personification of that strategy is Siegmund, a former perfumes and fragrances salesman with a quick smile who across large swaths of eastern Germany receives adoring crowds posing for selfies with him. His celebrity-like appeal obscures the party’s extreme edge. Domestic intelligence authorities have designated the AfD Saxony-Anhalt branch as an extremist organization that includes former members of a banned group modeled on the Hitler Youth.

Ulrich Siegmund’s voters wearing campaign merch at an event in Querfurt on August 21, 2026. | Nette Nöstlinger/POLITICO

To strike the balance the party seeks, the AfD in the state, for instance, intends to set up a “deportation task force” made up of key state ministers and police while seeking to avoid the scenes of chaos and violence evident in the U.S. when the Trump administration imposed similar measures. The party wants to blend extreme proposals — like redoing school history classes to teach less about Nazi crimes and slash funding for art deemed “anti-German” —with mundane policies that few would protest: like increasing funding for fire departments with response areas that include highways.

“We have to legitimize AfD policies through a practical example. That is our task,” said Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the brainchild of the AfD’s program for governing in Saxony-Anhalt, at a regional party conference in Magdeburg in July.

To pull it off, the party has identified up to 200 positions in the state’s civil service that are to be filled with a cadre of party loyalists, some of whom have been pre-selected throughout Germany or specifically trained by the party in Berlin — an unprecedented move in postwar Germany, where the civil service is meant to be apolitical —to speed the execution of the AfD’s agenda while keeping things running smoothly. They’ve also come prepared with concrete plans to thwart expected efforts by mainstream opposition parties to block their agenda in courts.

World.title: French MEP Raphaël Glucksmann’s path to the Elysée faces surprise hurdle
World.content:
Influential left-leaning businessman and media mogul Mathieu Pigasse, tapped by the United States to restructure Venezuela’s debt, is also mulling a primary run, according to a person close to him who, like others in this piece, was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the state of the race.

But Faure, who has led the Socialists for more than eight years, is the most likely to offer Glucksmann a run for his money.

One Socialist lawmaker said it’ll now be a close contest. Another one of the party’s MPs said Faure can sometimes appear immortal, “kind of like Highlander.”

Glucksmann is already facing attacks for his brand of centrist-leaning politics and an elitist image bolstered by his relationship with a top French TV anchor and his childhood as the son of a famous philosopher.

In an interview Monday, Royal referred to Glucksmann as “the media’s darling child.” MP Philippe Brun, who is running in the primary, last week called Glucksmann the French equivalent of a coastal elite.

Whoever wins the primary will face the specter of François Hollande’s imposing shadow. The former president is eyeing a comeback — but has decided to forgo the primary.

World.title: L’UE soumet ChatGPT, Reddit et Roblox à ses règles les plus strictes en matière de plateformes
World.content:
Les services en ligne comptant plus de 45 millions d’utilisateurs dans l’UE sont soumis à ce régime plus strict, qui concerne désormais 28 plateformes et moteurs de recherche.

La classification éventuelle de ChatGPT fait l’objet d’une attention particulière depuis que la société a annoncé l’année dernière compter 120 millions d’utilisateurs. Mais l’exécutif européen a eu du mal à déterminer si l’outil d’OpenAI relevait de la catégorie des moteurs de recherche ou de celle des plateformes. Ce chatbot très populaire, considéré comme l’un des précurseurs de la révolution actuelle de l’intelligence artificielle, fait déjà l’objet d’une réglementation stricte à Bruxelles en vertu de l’AI Act, le règlement européen sur l’intelligence artificielle.

Reddit, un forum de discussion fondé en 2005, a déclaré dénombrer 57,2 millions d’utilisateurs en juillet, tandis que la plateforme de jeux Roblox en a revendiqué 46,6 millions dans l’Union européenne.

Joost Hagesteijn, directeur général de Roblox pour l’Europe, a déclaré dans un communiqué : “Nous sommes fiers d’être la première plateforme de jeux vidéo à franchir cette étape importante au sein de l’UE”, ajoutant que “la sécurité est au cœur de toutes nos activités et nous nous réjouissons de poursuivre notre collaboration constructive avec la Commission européenne”.

OpenAI et Reddit n’ont pas immédiatement répondu à une demande de commentaires.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

World.title: Czech MEP and Babiš ally guilty of EU subsidy fraud, court rules
World.content:
Jana Nagyová in the European Parliament an institution of the European Union in Brussels in Belgium the 13th of May 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas via AFP

Jana Nagyová will file an appeal to Czechia’s supreme court, her lawyer said.

European lawmaker Jana Nagyová is guilty of EU subsidy fraud in a €2 million case related to Agrofert, the agriculture conglomerate linked to Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, Prague's High Court confirmed Monday in an appeal ruling.

The court sentenced Nagyová, a Patriots for Europe MEP and a former adviser to Babiš, to a suspended three-year prison term, with a five-year probation period, and a fine of about €20,000 for subsidy fraud and damaging the financial interests of the EU. The decision upheld a lower court ruling from May.

Nagyová has repeatedly denied the charges against her and will appeal to Czechia's Supreme Court, her lawyer said. She was stripped of her immunity by the European Parliament in April.

World.title: Belgium to US ambassador: Stop attacking our officials online
World.content:
Maxime Prévot during a plenary session of the Chamber at the Federal Parliament in Brussels, on July 9, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images

“Any further provocation” could trigger “an unnecessary escalation in our relations,” Brussels said.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot urged U.S. Ambassador Bill White on Monday to stop targeting government officials in his social media tirades, as further provocation could strain bilateral ties.

Prévot told White in a meeting that public comments “personally targeting Belgian officials … cannot be tolerated,” and “any further provocation would be counterproductive and could lead to an unnecessary escalation in our relations,” according to a statement from his spokesperson sent to POLITICO.

“The role of an ambassador is governed by well-established diplomatic rules and practices, including mutual respect and non-interference in internal affairs,” the written remarks continued.

World.title: Sánchez takes rare swipe at Spain’s king over Ceuta crisis
World.content:
“A lot of people think I’ve been governing for a long time, but I’ve only been in power for eight years,” said Sánchez, who has visited Ceuta four times since becoming prime minister. “The king has reigned for 20 years. How many times has he gone to Ceuta and Melilla? Not once.”

Sánchez’s statement was technically incorrect: Felipe VI has only been on the throne since 2014. The prime minister appeared to be referring to former King Juan Carlos I’s five-hour visit to Ceuta in 2007 — the last time a Spanish head of state visited the city.

The only other Spanish heads of state known to have visited were King Alfonso XIII, who traveled there in 1927, and President of the Second Republic Niceto Alcalá-Zamora, who visited Ceuta in 1933.

While declining to “share the content of the conversations I have with the head of state,” Sánchez emphasized he had recommended the king travel to the city. He said a royal visit would happen but declined to say when, noting it depended on “there being the conditions for it to happen.”

In the past, Spain’s kings have played an important role in the country’s interactions with Morocco. Juan Carlos I had a deep personal friendship with the late King Hassan II of Morocco, and was frequently called upon to handle back-channel negotiations when Madrid and Rabat clashed.

But Felipe VI is not known to have a similarly close relationship with Morocco’s current monarch, Mohammed VI. According to the Sánchez government, Spain’s king was asked to call his counterpart in Rabat in the immediate aftermath of the crisis but declined to do so.

World.title: Israel, Greece seal €3B ‘Achilles Shield’ defense deal
World.content:
Greece put the deal’s total value at €3.035 billion, adding that 19 Greek companies are already involved, accounting for more than €750 million of the program, with plans to build a domestic production base capable of exporting equipment. Defense Minister Nikos Dendias said Greece would become “the first country in the European Union to adopt a similar system.”

The deal caps a fast-deepening security partnership between the two countries.

In January, Greece and Israel agreed to expand cooperation on drone and underwater-vehicle swarms, cyber threats, military exercises and defense technology. The push feeds into Greece’s “Agenda 2030,” a sweeping military overhaul aimed at modernizing the armed forces and building more weapons at home.
