Athens is going further than some other European buyers of Israeli air defenses. Germany bought the Arrow 3 system in 2023 and Finland acquired David’s Sling in 2024. Greece says it will be the first EU country to stitch several Israeli platforms together into a single national shield against ballistic missiles, aircraft and drones.

World.title: France, Germany make pitch to overhaul EU foreign policy
World.content:
The new paper from France and Germany is an attempt to boost Kallas’s role while recognizing that much of the real power to conduct foreign policy lies with the Commission.

The proposals also foresee weakening the EEAS somewhat by moving some of its 5,000 staff and functions into the Commission amid pressure to slash the EU’s long-term budget, according to three diplomats who spoke to POLITICO.

The Franco-German paper will be in focus as EU foreign ministers gather Tuesday in Wicklow, Ireland.

Not everyone is pleased: “A big institutional change right now is not realistic,” a EU diplomat said, ruling out any major reforms before the end of von der Leyen’s second term in 2029.

“Let’s face it … EU foreign policy only works if Member States want it,” an EU official, granted anonymity to speak freely, told Brussels Playbook. “Shifting some teams from the EEAS to the Commission won’t fix the Middle East or stop Russia’s war.”

“The EU would have more leverage globally if we’d better align the tools we have — from diplomacy to visa policies, trade, aid and EU missions — in pursuit of European interests. The HRVP [Kallas] can provide that strategic direction, given her link to the Council,” the official said.

World.title: Why the Baltics are pushing back against new fears of a Russian attack
World.content:
Nearly a week after CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow fuelled fears that Russia could be preparing to test NATO, European officials are pushing back against suggestions that a conventional attack might be imminent.

 

From Finland and Romania to the Baltic states, governments say there is no evidence Moscow is preparing for a direct confrontation with NATO – even as they continue strengthening their defences and warn of a growing Russian threat.

Officials across NATO’s eastern flank argue that preparing for Russian aggression is not the same as expecting it.

John Hardie, deputy director of the Russia Program at the US-based Foundation for Defence of Democracies, told Euronews that Ratcliffe may have been delivering several messages in Moscow.

“My own view is that a conventional Russian military attack against a NATO member remains highly unlikely, especially while the Ukraine war continues,” Hardie said. "However, even while that scenario remains unlikely overall, there are reasons to see the risk ticking up a bit."

“The Iran war has reduced US readiness, while the Trump administration has sowed doubt regarding US political will to defend Europe. In recent months, we've seen intrusions into NATO airspace that could have been intended to probe our response.”

Hardie also said US officials may also be worried about what Putin could do if he feels “frustrated or cornered” in Ukraine, although he saw a second round of Russian mobilisation as a more likely response.

No imminent attack, but better be ready

Hardie’s assessment broadly mirrors what European leaders are saying publicly.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb dismissed predictions that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO country within the next few years.

“If anyone has a crystal ball like that – that’s great. I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” Stubb told Germany’s Bild newspaper over the weekend, adding that the intelligence available to him supported his assessment.

“It makes no sense for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance.”

Nonetheless, Finland is strengthening its defences along its 1,340-kilometre border with Russia, while Sweden has granted a request from Helsinki to send Gripen fighter jets and a naval vessel to support Finland’s territorial surveillance along the border.

Finnish officials see no contradiction: greater military preparedness is intended to deter Russia and guard against drones, airspace violations and other forms of escalation, not brace for an impending attack.

Romania has offered a similar assessment. Defence Minister Radu Miruță told Romanian broadcaster Digi24 on Sunday that Bucharest and its allies were constantly sharing intelligence, with “no indication” that Russia intended to attack a NATO member.

“I don’t think Russia has any intention to attack a NATO member country,” Miruță said.

Romania shares a 614-kilometre border with Ukraine and has repeatedly seen Russian drones cross into its territory.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was more explicit still, saying in a statement on X that the country's military threat level had not changed and the risk of a direct Russian invasion remained low.

Latvia nevertheless remains on heightened alert for cyber attacks, sabotage, provocations and drones, while strengthening its eastern border alongside NATO allies.

“Readiness for a possible threat is not the same as an immediate threat,” Kulbergs said. “These two things must not be confused.”

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia are among NATO’s biggest military spenders relative to the size of their economies.

When ‘hybrid’ warfare is already war

Poland has struck a more cautious tone.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said after a briefing from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte this weekend that “the escalation from Russia’s side is progressing”.

“We cannot rule out provocations from Russia against one of NATO’s members,” Tusk said. “The next six months will be decisive, and we must be prepared as Poland and NATO for various scenarios.”

His warning points to another dimension of Europe’s threat assessment: while a conventional attack may not be imminent, Russian aggression is already taking other forms.

European governments have accused Moscow of cyber attacks, sabotage and other hostile operations across the continent, while Russian aircraft and drones have repeatedly violated NATO airspace.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna argued on X that calling activities like these “hybrid warfare” understates the threat.

Responding to comments by Estonia’s foreign intelligence chief Kaupo Rosin, Tsahkna wrote: “Enough with the euphemisms. Putin’s campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe is not ‘hybrid warfare’. It is state-sponsored terrorism. Call it what it is.”

Hardie also said such Russian actions were already taking place.

“As for aggressive acts below the threshold of open war, such as arson against European defence plants, those are already occurring and have been for years now, but to limited strategic effect,” he told Euronews.

“Moscow does have options to escalate in this area, but doing so is unlikely to achieve much greater impact and could perversely produce blowback.”

World.title: YouTube's new 'exposure-based' model counts hovering over video as a view
World.content:
YouTube is about to make every video on the platform look far more popular overnight, and it will not cost the company a cent.

 

The platform is shifting to what it calls an "exposure-based model" for views, applied across every format, including shorts, long-form videos, podcasts and live streams.

Under the new system, a "view" counts the moment the first frame plays, even if someone is just hovering over a thumbnail.

The upshot is simple — the big number under every video is about to go up, probably fast, and it will be counted the same way everywhere on the platform.

The change kicks in for any video uploaded after 24 August, which will show the new first-frame count from the outset.

Videos already on the platform keep their existing tally until then, after which future views get counted under the new rules.

YouTube frames this as a tidying-up exercise, more "consistency" across the platform, no content slipping through uncounted and less confusion about what a view actually represents.

But there is a useful precedent for what "consistency" actually means in practice.

YouTube already ran this experiment when it switched its short videos over to first-frame counting back in March last year, and the results were immediate: view counts on Shorts jumped by roughly 70%, according to YouTube's own figures. Seventeen months later, the company is rolling the same trick out everywhere else.

It is also just catching up. Instagram and TikTok have counted views this way for years, and creators who post across all three platforms have long watched their YouTube numbers look comparatively anemic by contrast.

This closes that gap, on paper if nothing else.

Here is the catch: none of it will put an extra cent in creators' pockets, since YouTube is not changing how it calculates ad payouts. It will keep a separate metric, now branded as "engaged views" or someone watching for several seconds, the old standard, specifically for that purpose.

Inflated headline numbers will largely be show while the money still flows according to the old method.

YouTube says the shift came from creator feedback that the tangle of different view metrics made it hard to gauge true exposure.

That claim is plausible, though the timing also works in YouTube's favour.

Most creators do not primarily earn through YouTube ad revenue: according to marketing platform IdeaEquity, up to 70% of creator income comes instead from brand deals and sponsorships, where view counts function as a bargaining chip rather than a direct source of payment.

Which is the real function of this change.

Bigger numbers give creators more leverage to walk into brand negotiations, but none of that leverage comes out of YouTube's pocket.

The platform gets to hand out a popularity boost that costs it nothing and hands the bill for actually paying creators more, if there is one, to advertisers and brands instead.

World.title: New AI models pose growing threat to the global economy, Bailey warns
World.content:
Emerging AI models pose a growing threat to financial stability and economic growth, Financial Stability Board (FSB) Chair and Governor of the Bank of England Andrew Bailey has warned.

 

The letter was sent on 28 August to G20 finance ministers and central bankers ahead of their meeting on Monday and Tuesday in Asheville, North Carolina, US.

Bailey wrote that the FSB will remain "focused on identifying emerging vulnerabilities, strengthening resilience and ensuring that innovation is consistent with financial stability," as many jurisdictions do not have sufficient protocols in place.

His warning comes amid a period of profound global instability and uncertainty that is heightening market volatility.

Conflict in the Middle East is driving up energy prices and fuelling inflation, while large-scale AI investments in the United States are adding further inflationary pressure. At the same time, unprecedented trade decisions by US President Donald Trump are contributing to an increasingly unpredictable economic environment.

In this scenario, a new generation of sophisticated AI models is emerging. These systems are capable of identifying and exploiting digital vulnerabilities in complex systems – such as banking infrastructure and other sensitive servers – with potentially catastrophic consequences for the economy.

One notorious example is Mythos, a model developed by Anthropic, which has advanced autonomous coding and cybersecurity capabilities. Unveiled in April 2026, the model is not available for public use due to the significant potential risks it poses.

"Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers," Bailey wrote.

"Taking appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis should in my view be a priority and would benefit all sectors of the economy, including by supporting financial stability and economic growth."

Bailey also noted that "AI will not respect national borders", meaning that while governments can legislate and enforce regulations at national level, an AI disruption with financial stability implications can have a global impact wherever it begins.

"Differences in legal frameworks, cyber capability, resilience and recovery capacity across jurisdictions could therefore have consequences well beyond the jurisdiction in which an incident originates and may themselves become a source of vulnerability," Bailey wrote.

The FSB chair exhorted firms and authorities to prepare for "a threat environment characterised by a higher volume of vulnerabilities and a faster pace of patching" and to adapt safety systems.

The next G20 meeting will occur in Miami, Florida on 14-15 December.

World.title: 'I remain deeply sorry': John Galliano calls off Met Gala retropective show over racism row
World.content:
Legendary British fashion designer John Galliano and New York's Metropolitian Museum of Art have decided to call off a planned exhibition set to launch next year's Met Gala.

 

The show was meant to celebrate and portray the highlights of the pioneering creator's career but the plans were immediately deried after they were announced last month because of Galliano's antiSemitic and racist tirade which forced him into the fashion wilderness.

On Monday, the museum said 'John Galliano: Horizons' would be replaced by an as yet unnamed show.

"Following thought discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition," Max Hollein director and CEO of the museum announced in a statement.

Galliano also published the statement on Instagram adding "After much reflection and discussion with The Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time.

"I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it."

Meltdown in public

Galliano's meteoric rise was matched by his dramatic fall from grace. He was talk of the town throughout the 1990s and became head design honcho at French luxury fashion house Givenchy thanks to his innovative and bold creations. Within two years, he was promoted by LVHM to run Dior and further success followed as he cemeted his status across luxury goods and pop culture.

But shortly before presenting at the 2011 autumn/winter Paris Fashion Week, he was caught on video hurling a series of racist and antisemitic marks at a couple at a Paris café. At one point, he was recorded saying: “I love Hitler.”

He was fired by Dior and later convicted of public insults based on origin, religious affiliation, race or ethnicity – remarks that the state prosecutor called “pitiful and dreadful”. The court fined him €6,000, rejecting his argument that he was in a fragile emotional state following the death of a close friend.

By 2013, however, his image was already being rehabilitated. Then Vogue editor Anna Wintour helped secure him a temporary residency at Dominican designer Oscar de la Renta’s studio before the autumn 2013 New York Fashion Week. The collaboration earned praise, with critics highlighting Galliano’s signature theatricality in de la Renta’s ready-to-wear collection.

Now 65, Galliano, has apologised often for his outburst, claiming he had suffered from alcoholism and drug addiction. Many Jewish leaders have accepted his contrition as genuine, too.

World.title: Germany and France float plan to bring Kallas under von der Leyen's supervision
World.content:
Germany and France have floated a joint plan to bring High Representative Kaja Kallas under the direct supervision of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as part of an overhaul of the European Union's foreign policy.

 

The plan is set to be discussed on Wednesday during an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland. Kallas will chair the session.

The Franco-German project aims to address one of the bloc’s most persistent weaknesses in external action: institutional cacophony.

Under the complex design of the Treaty of Lisbon, the High Representative leads the European External Action Service (EEAS) and designs, coordinates and implements foreign policy on behalf of the 27 member states.

She simultaneously serves as one of the European Commission's vice-presidents.

However, the hefty portfolios that set the pace of international politics, such as trade, energy, climate and migration, largely fall within the Commission's remit, depriving the EEAS of material leverage to bring to the table. Enlargement, another field with a marked geopolitical dimension, is also firmly in the Commission's hands.

This division of powers has allowed Ursula von der Leyen to significantly expand her foreign policy role, as demonstrated by her response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. She has also travelled extensively to sign a variety of headline-making deals.

Von der Leyen's expansive clout has raised eyebrows across capitals, prompting occasional rebukes of "overreach" and "power grab", even though she has often been encouraged by EU leaders to take the lead on global crises.

The German-Franco plan envisions giving Kallas a hands-on role in the coordination of foreign-related areas operated by the Commission's director generals (DGs), such as development aid (DG INTPA), humanitarian relief (DG ECHO), defence industry (DG DEFIS) and relations with neighbouring countries, which are split between DG ENEST (Eastern Europe) and DG MENA (the Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf).

Trade, a high-stakes portfolio, could also be considered.

A department dedicated to foreign policy would be formed to reinforce the new structure. The Commission used to operate a DG for external relations (DG RELEX) until it was absorbed into the EEAS in 2010.

The European Commission in Brussels. European Union, 2026.

In practice, Kallas would have broader hands-on responsibilities inside the Commission.

But the upgrade would ultimately benefit von der Leyen because she would remain the highest authority as Commission president, mirroring the hierarchical arrangement between a prime minister and a foreign minister at the national level.

The EEAS, which Kallas currently leads independently of von der Leyen, would be weakened to reduce the risk of an institutional clash.

At the same time, the German-Franco proposal seeks to strengthen the voice of member states in setting up foreign policy.

The reform would require amending the 2010 decision that established the EEAS, rather than the Treaty of Lisbon. A unanimous agreement would be needed.

The plan comes at a time of global turbulence that has laid bare the vulnerabilities of the bloc's foreign policy. Although member states agree that a comprehensive reform is in order, they are yet to agree on a common path forward.

In June, a French paper pitched three options to overhaul the role of the High Representative: expand her powers, shift them to the Commission or shift them to the member states. The last two options would effectively hollow out the position.

The document forced Kallas to send a message of reassurance to the EEAS staff. She then called on capitals to present ideas on how to improve the external action.

World.title: South African airline Airlink defends dramatic stadium flyover
World.content:
A South African airline has defended a low-level flying stunt over a packed-out rugby stadium in Cape Town on the weekend.

 

Two Airlink-operated jets soared just above city's DHL Stadium ahead of a test match between South Africa and New Zealand, prompting cheers from the reported crowd of more than 50,000 below.

According to flight-tracking firm Flightradar24, the lead aircraft flew roughly just 41 to 46 feet above the roof of the stadium.

Dramatic footage of the flyover quickly began circulating on social media, prompting mixed reactions as some expressed concerns over safety.

In a statement on Sunday, Airlink defended the manoeuvre.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” the carrier said.

“The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby,” it added.

The airline also shared footage and images of the move in a post on X, writing: "Planning. Precision. Performance."

Gayton McKenzie, South Africa's Minister for Sports, Arts and Culture, hailed the stunt as "spectacular."

"It’s a well known fact that we have the best pilots in the world, that was spectacular, next time I will ask the pilots to land on the field, prepare to be amazed further," he said.

For Scottish pilot Scott Bateman, however, the stunt left him "aghast."

"The lead aircraft reportedly cleared the stadium roof by around 40–50 feet," he wrote in a post on social media. "Hundreds of professional aviators around the world have looked at those images and expressed concern. That deserves more than 'nothing to see here'".

He added that aviation did not "become one of the safest forms of transport by defending everything that worked."

"It became safe by relentlessly examining the things that nearly didn’t".

World.title: New finds in the Bernese Jura: meteorite treasure reaches record size
World.content:
In the canton of Bern, above Lake Biel, on Twannberg and Mont Sujet, lies one of Europe's most important meteorite strewn fields. Fragments of an extraordinary celestial body have been unearthed there time and again for decades.

 

The number of known finds has now risen to more than 2,200. This means the extent of the meteorite fall is significantly greater than initially assumed.

The Twannberg meteorite did not hit the Earth as a single large block, but exploded as it entered the atmosphere. Its debris was scattered over an area of around six kilometres in what is now the Bernese Jura.

Scientists estimate that the celestial body struck the Earth around 175,000 years ago. Originally it is thought to have measured between four and 20 metres across and to have weighed at least 250 tonnes.

First discovery in 1984

The story of the meteorite find began on 9 May 1984. At the time, a Swiss farmer discovered an unusual block weighing around 15 kilograms in a field. At first it was unclear what it was. Subsequent analysis showed that the find consisted of iron and did indeed come from outer space.

In the decades that followed, further fragments were discovered. It was above all the systematic use of metal detectors that led to a sharp increase in the number of known pieces.

New finds from 2026: decades after the first discovery, fragments of the meteorite are still being recovered. ZVG/NMBE

"Ten years ago there were 400 fragments, now there are more than 2,200," explained geologist Beda Hofmann from Bern's Natural History Museum to Swiss broadcaster SRF.

Extremely rare meteorite

The Twannberg meteorite belongs to the group of iron meteorites and is classified as a member of the extremely rare IIG group. It is so far the only known IIG iron meteorite in Europe. This type of meteorite is characterised, among other things, by an unusually low nickel content and a high phosphorus content. Only a handful of specimens of this class are known worldwide.

For science, the fragments are particularly valuable: they can provide clues to the composition and evolution of celestial bodies and offer a glimpse into the early history of our solar system.

Glaciers helped to distribute the fragments

The finds are also of interest for research into the history of the Swiss landscape.

According to experts, some of the newly discovered fragments were transported by glaciers. Around 175,000 years ago, huge glaciers covered large parts of the Swiss Plateau – in places the ice sheet was more than a kilometre thick. Because the new finds have been discovered at higher altitudes than previous fragments, they can offer fresh insights into the vast masses of ice during the penultimate ice age.

In this sense, the finds are witnesses to two eras: they originally came from outer space, but later became part of Earth's history and were shaped by ice-age landscape processes.

Search continues

The search on Twannberg and Mont Sujet is far from over; researchers and meteorite hunters are continuing to comb the area with metal detectors for new remains.

That is, however, more difficult than it sounds, as the soil also contains metal objects that have nothing to do with a meteorite, such as aluminium foil or nails. Anyone wishing to search also needs a permit from the appropriate archaeological service.

The discoveries highlight the untapped potential of Switzerland's meteorite field: with every additional fragment, researchers learn more about the original celestial body and the story of its impact.

World.title: Estonia moves to protect youth’s mental health in the digital age
World.content:
On Monday, Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal tasked national experts with finding ways to reduce the negative impact of social media and gaming environments on youth’s mental health, as countries in Europe are stepping up social media control.

 

The advisory board of ten experts – ranging from a vice-chairman of the Estonian National Youth Council to a neuroscientist and a clinical psychologist – has until next year to come up with proposals and recommendations for the state, parents and young people related to both social media and video game environments.

The aim is to develop solutions that recognise the important role digital environments play in young people’s everyday lives, while also addressing and reducing the risks associated with their use.

The work will focus on identifying potential risks to young people’s mental health, preventing problematic digital use, raising awareness among children and parents, and exploring ways to create a safer digital environment that better protects young people’s rights, health and well-being.

"Anxiety and mental health problems among young people are a serious and growing concern,” Estonia’s Prime Minister said in a press release.

Several countries have imposed or are discussing restrictions on social media for young people, including Belgium (Flanders), Bulgaria, Denmark, Spain and other European Union countries.

Michal believes that “more important than bans is to find solutions that would actually help our young people.”

“That is why I have convened an advisory board consisting of Estonia's leading experts to find effective ways to reduce the negative effects of social media in cooperation with researchers, youth work specialists and youth representatives," he said.

At the first meeting, Andra Siibak, professor of media studies at the University of Tartu, was elected chair. "We will start looking for and discussing these solutions in the Advisory Board in cooperation with young people to reach recommendations that would be not only science-based but also applicable in the opinion of the target group itself," said Siibak.

Estonia’s prime minister tasked national experts with finding ways to reduce the negative impact of social media and gaming environments on youth’s mental health. Carl-Robert Kagge/Estonia's Government

Rising concerns

Recent Estonian research points to growing concerns about young people's experiences online.

According to the University of Tartu's 2025 EU Kids Online Estonia study, students are increasingly encountering disturbing online content, sexually explicit messages and excessive internet use. The research also found a link between children's mental well-being, online bullying and exposure to harmful content.

Data from the National Institute for Health Development's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study also points to an increase in problematic digital use. In 2022, 8% of 11- to 15-year-olds reported symptoms associated with social media addiction, up from 6% in 2018. The figure was 10% among girls and 7% among boys, with 13-year-old girls identified as a particularly vulnerable group.

The study found that 63% of girls and 47% of boys spent at least two hours a day on social networks, with usage increasing with age.

Longer use of electronic media for communication was associated with lower life satisfaction, shorter sleep, poorer academic performance and more frequent depressive episodes.

There has been a growing global movement aimed at controlling youth’s social media usage. Just last week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms: Meta's Instagram and Facebook will soon lock kids out at midnight and cap their scrolling at two hours a day, part of an $18bn (€15.4bn) settlement with 48 US states.

World.title: Argentine superstar footballer Lionel Messi announces international retirement
World.content:
The Argentine legend announced that he will not play for the national team again, ending an illustrious international career.

Argentina legend Lionel Messi announced his international retirement.

39-year-old Messi, widely considered the greatest football player of all time, won the 2022 World Cup in Qatar with Argentina, bringing the title back to the country for the first time since 1986.

The 2026 World Cup, Messi's last appearance in the world's most well-known footballing competition, ended with disappointment for Argentina after its loss to Spain in the final.

The Argentine is his country's most capped player with 207 appearances, in which he scored 125, another all-time record.

With Messi as captain, Argentina also won the Copa America in 2021 and 2024.

His club career will continue at current club Inter Miami, to which he moved in 2023 from PSG and after a 15-year career with Spanish giants Barcelona, with whom he won the UEFA Champions League four times and the Spanish title ten times.

More to come...

World.title: Court says India must uphold Pakistan water treaty
World.content:
An international tribunal has ordered India to "observe its obligations" under a water-treaty with Pakistan.

The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague has ordered India to uphold a water-sharing treaty with Pakistan which has led to a recent increase in tensions between the two neighbors.

The PCA said New Delhi must "observe its obligations" under the treaty with on the sharing of the Indus and other rivers, which the Indian government this year sought to suspend.

In a statement, the court found unanimously found that "none of the grounds" put forward by India were justified and "concluded that the Treaty [...] remains fully in force."

The court noted that India "remains bound by the obligations incumbent upon it," particularly regarding the design and operation of "hydroelectric projects on the western rivers."

It said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty.

A Pakistani government spokesman said Islamabad "welcomed" the PCA order.

India threatens to dry out Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is the India-Pakistan water treaty?

The 1960 Indus Water Treaty governs the use of water from six rivers which originate in India but flow into Pakistan as part of the Indus basin — a resource relied on by hundreds of millions of people.

The Indus river cuts through ultra-sensitive demarcation lines between India and Pakistan in Kashmir, the Himalayan territory both countries claim.

India said in May 2025 that it was suspending its membership of the treaty after accusing Islamabad of backing a deadly attack on tourists on the Indian side of Kashmir.

India's Water Minister CR Patil said earlier this year that the government would ensure that "not a single drop of water" will flow into Pakistan.

Pakistan denies backing the Kashmir attack and has accused India of seeking to "weaponize" the precious water resource.

Islamabad has previously said it would consider any attempt to change the flow of cross-border waterways as an "act of war."

World.title: How China buried Tibet flood images after Nepal disaster
World.content:
A flood has devastated communities along the China-Nepal border, but in Tibet the disaster was followed by a digital crackdown. Censors erased viral footage while state media flooded platforms with official content.

When a catastrophic flash flood swept through the rugged China-Nepal border on August 26, the physical devastation was immediate.

In Nepal, a black torrent of mud and rock tore through communities, leaving hundreds dead and thousands more missing along the borderlands.

But across the frontier in Tibet, an autonomous region of China, the physical disaster was almost instantly mirrored by a digital one: the rapid, high-tech erasure of the catastrophe's visual evidence.

As survivors tried to upload raw footage of the deluge, China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action, executing a sophisticated, precision operation to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truths.

The contrasting realities — a tragic humanitarian crisis in Nepal and a tightly sanitized, triumphant rescue narrative in China — reveal the evolving mechanics of Beijing's modern censorship machine.

Rather than imposing a blunt, blanket blackout, authorities deployed advanced image-recognition technology and "saturated information" tactics to drown out domestic scrutiny while deflecting diplomatic friction abroad.

The fall of the 'National Gate'

In the immediate aftermath of the flood-triggered mudslide, local residents captured dramatic footage of the torrent engulfing Gyirong Port, a critical overland trade hub between China and Nepal.

The most striking video showed a black wall of water and debris crashing into and destroying the border crossing's massive "National Gate."

In an article titled "An Unrecorded Mudslide Rushes into Gyirong Port" on WeChat, a universal app that combines messaging with payment options and social media functions, local blogger "Matou Qingnian" described the chaotic scene.

"The most terrifying moment happened at the Gyirong Port," the author wrote, describing video footage of crowds, including children, fleeing in panic before a pitch-black torrent swallowed the camera's view.

Within hours, both the article and the raw video footage vanished from Chinese social media.

According to China Digital Times (CDT) , an independent watchdog that tracks Chinese internet censorship, the video of the collapsing "National Gate" was systematically blocked from being shared on WeChat, even in private messages.

"The footage itself contained no graphic violence, no protests, and no political slogans," explained Mira, a CDT editor who specializes in tracking sensitive keywords and media. "The target of the censorship was the symbol itself: the National Gate."

Digital analysts note that this censorship highlights a significant upgrade in China's internet policing tools. Instead of merely filtering text-based keywords, platforms now rely heavily on video fingerprinting, image hashing, and machine-learning models to recognize specific visual scenes.

Once a visual sequence is blacklisted, it is intercepted before it can ever be posted.

Satiety as a shield: the art of 'saturated' censorship

The suppression of the Gyirong Port disaster reflects a broader shift in Beijing's strategy: from mass deletion to "precision surgery" and narrative flooding.

A search for "Tibet mudslide" on Xiaohongshu — China's popular lifestyle and search platform — reveals the mechanics of this "saturated information environment."

Rather than showing an empty search page, the platform's algorithm feeds users a carefully curated stream of state-media reports from China's state broadcaster CCTV and news agency Xinhua.

The visual landscape is dominated by high-resolution, sterile graphics: "before-and-after" comparisons, maps of high-altitude glacial collapses — the official scientific cause of the disaster — and state-approved aerial drone footage.

The raw, chaotic cellphone videos recorded by eyewitnesses at the border are entirely absent.

By filling the digital space with a high volume of "safe" and visually appealing official content, the state satisfies the public's immediate curiosity while preemptively suffocating independent reporting or organic discussions, ananysts note.

Rescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port Image: Lhasa Fire and Rescue Mobile Detachment/Handout/Xinhua/picture alliance

On Weibo, China's microblogging giant, the narrative arc was similarly managed. While "Tibet mudslide" briefly trended on August 26, the domestic casualty figures were quickly frozen the next morning at three dead and 558 missing.

Almost immediately, the platform's trending topics were redirected toward the government's swift response.

Two heavily publicized, lengthy official reports dominated the news cycle: Chinese President Xi Jinping convening a Central Politburo meeting to coordinate rescue and relief efforts, and Premier Li Qiang arriving in Gyirong to personally direct operations on the ground.

These headlines effectively turned a major human tragedy into a highly orchestrated exhibition of state competence.

The dangerous 'half-year' question

Beneath the veneer of efficient state rescue efforts lies a deeper, systemic vulnerability that Beijing was desperate to hide: a history of structural negligence.

On August 27, a hashtag briefly slipped through the censors and trended on Weibo: "Gyirong Port Reopened Only Half a Year Ago." It amassed over 347,000 views in less than an hour before it was abruptly deleted. The hashtag pointed to a damning timeline of infrastructure failures.

In July 2025, Gyirong Port was completely shut down after being devastated by another severe flash flood. It took nearly six months to rebuild and reopen the port on January 1, 2026. Eight months later, the port has been destroyed again.

As the deleted "Matou Qingnian" article noted, Gyirong Port has now suffered mudslides during the flood seasons of 2024, 2025, and now 2026. In 2025, several Chinese personnel went missing or were killed.

By erasing the "half-year" trend, censors blocked an inevitable and dangerous train of public inquiry.

If the state-of-the-art border facility was destroyed twice in 14 months, it raises critical questions about site selection, shoddy infrastructure construction, and the complete failure of glacial lake monitoring and early-warning systems in Tibet.

These questions are especially sensitive in Tibet, a region under intense security and political control since the 1950s. Foreign journalists are strictly barred from entering the region outside of highly choreographed government-led tours.

According to human rights groups, local Tibetans who attempt to speak with foreign journalists or share independent accounts online face immediate detention or arrest.

High-altitude friction

The informational firewall does not stop at China's borders; it has also created a diplomatic rift with neighboring Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the disaster's human toll.

In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Parshuram Kaphle, a prominent Nepalese foreign policy journalist, publicly accused Beijing on X (formerly Twitter) of failing to share critical trans-boundary data.

"Nepal has been addressing the legitimate security concerns of our neighbors," Kaphle wrote in a post that has since been deleted. "However, it must be said with sadness that our northern neighbor has significantly undermined us. By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life."

He further wrote , "We have continually faced crises originating from their territory, while we continue to address all their concerns, necessary or unnecessary. Why must Nepal alone pay the price of one-sided love?"

The Chinese government has rejected any accountability. On August 27, the Chinese Embassy in Nepal issued a statement on Facebook, dismissing accusations of failing to issue warnings or causing the disaster through upstream dam failures as "fake news."

"Accusation helps nothing," the embassy statement read. "Cooperation saves lives."

But for families searching for more than 3,000 missing loved ones along the muddy banks of the Himalayan border, cooperation remains as obscured as the truth behind the digital firewall.

This article was originally published in Chinese.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Politics take center stage at Venice Film Festival
World.content:
With works about Gaza, Ukraine and Elon Musk, political cinema is in the spotlight at the 2026 Venice Film Festival.

The Venice Film Festival used to be the place where the awards season put on its best tuxedo. This year, it looks more like a war room, as politics and political cinema are set to dominate the red carpet.

The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2 with Danny Boyle's "Ink," a drama about Rupert Murdoch's 1969 takeover of Britain's The Sun tabloid — the origin story of the Murdoch right-wing media empire.

Over 11 days on the Lido, audiences will get films about Israel and Gaza, Russia's war on Ukraine, the CIA-backed coup in Pinochet's Chile, ICE raids in Minneapolis and a tell-all documentary on the world's richest man.

Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera has called it Venice's "most political" edition ever.

'NAZA,' a documentary by 'No Other Land' directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, runs in the official competition Image: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

Venice goes political

This year's competition includes "NAZA," a documentary from "No Other Land" Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examining Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

US-Russian director Julia Loktev chronicles Vladimir Putin's crackdown on independent journalism in "My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile," a sequel to her 2024 doc.

DW co-production 'Letters From the Silenced Country' portrays life under repression in Belarus Image: DW/ZDF/Arte

Andrei Kutsila's "Letters From the Silenced Country" a DW, ZDF/Arte and TVP co-production, about repression in Kutsila's native Belarus, will have its world premiere in Venice.

As will Alex Gibney's four-hour Elon Musk documentary "Musk," a film the richest man in the world has already denounced, sight unseen, as a "hit piece."

And Laura Poitras, the Oscar-winning director of "Citizenfour," will screen what she describes as a "short horror film," the documentary "They're Here," co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller and built from previously undisclosed footage of ICE's operation in Minneapolis.

Laura Poitras also won the Golden Lion award in 2022 for best film for 'All the Beauty and the Bloodshed' Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance

This is a new look for Venice.

Under Barbera, the festival had until recently cultivated a reputation as a place for movie stars and Oscar campaigns. You go to Venice to watch Timothee Chalamet on the red carpet, or George Clooney and Brad Pitt yucking it up at a press conference.

Venice let the other big European festivals — Berlin, and to a lesser degree Cannes — be the homes of political movies and the polemical debates that accompany them.

Berlin's political backlash

But Berlin's reputation as a festival for activist cinema has taken a major hit. The past three years have seen political debate, primarily over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, overwhelm discussions of cinema at the Berlinale, to the point where the future of the festival looks in doubt.

At this year's Berlinale, jury president Wim Wenders was lambasted online for saying filmmakers "have to stay out of politics." At the awards ceremony, when Syrian-Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib called out the German government for being "partners in the genocide in Gaza by Israel," the backlash nearly cost Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle her job.

Venice, by contrast, has spent the past two years leaning into political cinema.

How will she react to political questions? Actor Maggie Gyllenhaal is the president of the international jury this year Image: Federico Vespignani/AA/picture alliance

Venice leans into controversy

Last year saw the world premiere of Kaouther Ben Hania's "The Voice of Hind Rajab." The harrowing docudrama, which recreates the killing, by Israeli forces, of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl and her family in Gaza City, received a 22-minute standing ovation, a Lido record. The Israeli military has recently announced an official investigation into Hind Rajab's death.

Just days before, thousands marched on the Lido in protest of the war in Gaza. Filmmakers called on Barbera to label Israel's campaign "a genocide." He didn't go that far, speaking instead of his "huge sadness" over the suffering in Gaza and Palestine.

But the Venice boss didn't flinch, then or now, from programming films that address, head-on, the most controversial topics of the day.

Danny Boyle's Rupert Murdoch drama 'INK' opens the festival Image: StudioCanal/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ukraine objects to 'Dau'

Russian films selected by the festival are also sparking protest.

Ukraine's foreign ministry, culture ministry and its embassy in Italy issued a formal complaint over Barbera's decision to include Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU," an art house drama about life under Soviet rule in Ukraine, in official competition. Ukraine objects to the film's Russian connections.

Khrzhanovsky is Russian-born, though he renounced his Russian citizenship and now lives in exile in Berlin. The film's lead, Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, still lives and works in Russia and has never publicly condemned Russia's war on Ukraine.

Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who stars in 'DAU,' has remained silent on Putin's invasion of Ukraine Image: Getty Images/AFP/S. de Sakutin

In a statement, the Ukrainian ministries said programming the film "sends a deeply worrying signal" given the war.

Barbera is not backing down. He called the criticism a "smear campaign" from people who haven't seen the film.

Khrzhanovsky took to social media with his rebuttal: "'DAU' is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy," he wrote. "It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil."

The stars are still coming

Venice hasn't completely abandoned its Hollywood stars.

Robert Pattinson, of "Batman" and "Twilight" fame, will hit the Lido this year with "Primetime," playing a controversial US reality TV producer.

Robert Pattinson is among the stars expected on the red carpet Image: Luca Carlino/NurPhoto/picture alliance

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents in Chile on the eve of the Pinochet coup in "Wild Horse Nine" from director Martin McDonagh ("Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri").

Real-life couple Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz star as husband and wife in Florian Zeller's "Bunker," about an architect commissioned to build a nuclear shelter for a billionaire.

George Clooney and 93-year-old acting legend Ellen Burstyn will swing by to collect Golden Lion awards for lifetime achievement.

A Venice regular: George Clooney will attend this year to receive an honorary Golden Lion Image: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

Venice also hasn't abandoned its role as a gathering place for cinema's elder statesmen — several of them German.

Wim Wenders, fresh off the Berlinale storm, brings an altogether gentler work to the Lido, a 3D documentary on the work of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

Werner Herzog, the last wild man of '70s German cinema, returns to narrative filmmaking for the first time in seven years in Venice with "Bucking Fastard," starring real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara.

And for those who just want to forget about the world for a moment and just kick back and sing, pop stars Liam and Noel Gallagher are expected on the Lido for the premiere of the Oasis reunion documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Deceived and deployed: How young Cameroonians end up fighting in Russia's war in Ukraine
World.content:
Analysts say economic desperation and fraudulent recruitment schemes are funneling Cameroonian youth into the Russian military — with deadly consequences. Does the Cameroonian government need to act more decisively?

Cameroon has emerged as one of the leading sources of African recruits for the Russian military, with young men lured by false promises of jobs and fast-tracked Russian citizenship, only to find themselves on the front lines of the war in Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials say that nearly 3,000 citizens from various African countries are known to have fought — or were still fighting — for Russia as of May this year; Cameroon, Ghana, Egypt, Kenya and Uganda were identified as major source countries.

In April, the Cameroonian government confirmed that Russia had reported the deaths of 16 Cameroonian nationals, seven of whom died in military action in Ukraine.

Charles Ojiambo Mutoka, 72, shows a picture of his son Oscar, who he learned was killed in August while fighting for Russia in Ukraine Image: Tony Karumba/AFP

Poverty driving youths into Russia's duplicitous schemes

The actual death toll is likely higher, according to DW correspondent Dorcas Ekupe, reporting from Bamenda in northwestern Cameroon.

"When you look at other publications and see what is happening — even seeing families who are grieving their loved ones — the number is really much higher than what the government had earlier said," Ekupe told DW's AfricaLink program.

She described two forces causing this worrying phenomenon: economic desperation and deliberate deception.

Many recruits, she said, travel to Russia believing they have secured jobs in construction or as security guards, or that they are participating in study programs.

"Once in Russia, they then end up on the battlefield," Ekupe said.

African recruits fighting in Ukraine: Where's the AU? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia's perceived appeal meanwhile is also being amplified by highly structured influence campaigns:

Banjo Herman, a lecturer and political analyst at the University of Bamenda, pointed to the key role of the the Russian paramilitary Wagner Group as well as its successor, the Africa Corps, as Moscow's primary instrument for expanding its presence and reputation across Africa.

Military recruitment dressed up as 'cultural' outreach

He also cited Russian government programs such as the "African Initiative" and "Alabuga," which present themselves as cultural or educational exchange schemes but have been linked to military recruitment.

"On the surface, sometimes it looks like cultural outreach," Banjo said. "Sometimes Cameroonians are lured thinking it is for work, not necessarily knowing what is beneath the surface," adding that offers of Russian nationality within six months are also a particularly powerful draw.

France has previously described the African Initiative as a front administered by Russian intelligence services, designed to spread propaganda.

Why young men continue to risk their lives

Banjo stresses, however, that the economic situation of the recruits is typically the main motivator.

"Imagine that you are a carpenter in Cameroon who cannot even earn 100,000 CFA francs (€150; $175) a month, but somebody is promising you 3 million CFA francs to come and work," he explains. "It is very attractive."

Meanwhile, he also highlighted the fact that not all Cameroonians in Russia are the victims of deception: Some have lived there for years, were absorbed into the military over time, and are, by all accounts, doing reasonably well.

Yet the promise of financial reward combined with the prospect of gaining Russian citizenship explains why even people aware of the risks continue to accept recruitment offers to fight in Ukraine, he believes.

Ekupe corroborated this, noting a prevailing attitude of fatalism among some youth: "Sometimes people say, 'If I die, I die,'" and agree to join Russian forces.

Africans pay high human cost fighting for Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Those left behind often suffer the most

Families left behind meanwhile are forced to bear the cost in silence: Ekupe described cases in which mothers only learned of their sons' deaths years after the fact — in one instance, when a fellow soldier called home to report that a 35-year-old Cameroonian had been killed in combat.

She added that many families have received no financial compensation from the Cameroonian government, and that some of the men who died had left behind their pregnant wives as well as their children.

Contact between recruits and their families is often severed abruptly.

"When they get there and discover it was not as promised, it is really difficult to inform their family," Ekupe said. "Sometimes they have to take time to adjust to the new environment and the situation, in which they find themselves."

According to the Kenyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, more than 200 of its nationals had crossed into Russia bz January 2026, but only 18 have returned Image: Minako Sasako/AP Photo/picture alliance

Russia ducking from responsibilty

On the question of legal responsibility, Banjo noted that international law does not, in principle, prohibit a foreign national from voluntarily enlisting in another state's armed forces.

Legal liability arises, however, when recruitment involves fraud, coercion, trafficking or mercenary activity.

Banjo cited Article 47 of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which defines a mercenary as someone who agrees to take direct part in hostilities with private financial gain as their main motivation.

Under current frameworks, the responsibility for the death of a foreign fighter in another country's war rests largely with the individual and their family, not the recruiting state.

Cameroon: insufficient campaigns to fight recruitement

Cameroon's government has stated publicly that it does not deploy troops abroad outside international mandates, and has warned citizens against joining foreign conflicts.

Analysts are nevertheless calling on the Cameroonian government, and African governments more broadly, to pursue a three-pronged response to stop more people from risking their lives in Russia.

This approach would include economic reforms to create opportunities and reduce the conditions that make deceptive recruitment attractive; direct diplomatic engagement with Russia to hold recruitment networks accountable; and a public awareness campaign that issues clear, proactive public warnings to citizens about the dangers of following such schemes.

Relatives of Kenyan nationals conscripted by the Russian army demand urgent government action to repatriate their kin Image: Tony Karumba/AFP

Ghana meanwhile has already formally raised the issue with Russia, demanding an end to the recruitment of its nationals.

However in Cameroon's case, there might be another major hurdle in the country's longstanding military ties with Russia, which President Paul Biya moved to renew in 2014 and 2015.

Banjo also said the absence of an official Cameroonian policy response to date reflects, at least in part, the government's awareness that the recruitment is carried out by private actors — limiting the state's formal grounds and opportunities for intervention.

"For the government to stop this," Banjo said, "it has to go back to its governance policy and have a policy that is inclusive, transparent, and in which people can find opportunities within the system."

World.title: Tariffs spat: Carney bets Canada can defy Trump
World.content:
Canada is facing new US import penalties after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China. Other countries are watching as the Trump trade clash turns into a fight over economic sovereignty.

Canada has been quietly praised for refusing to fold under pressure from US President Donald Trump in the long-running fight over trade tariffs.

The latest talks between the North American neighbors collapsed on August 21. Until the 11th hour, both sides were talking as if a deal was within reach.

The United States then put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of Canadian goods, while Ottawa pledged to match those duties on US imports.

Until the talks folded, Canada's approach was to cut a deal that would reduce the tariffs and keep cross-border supply chains functioning, particularly in the automotive and steel sectors.

Threat of all-out trade war between US, Canada looms To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US negotiators were, however, accused of changing the terms at the last minute, which the Canadian side said would have forced them to match US tariffs on China.

According to Ottawa, Washington wanted a say on future trade deals with other nations and to prevent Chinese goods being routed through Canada to evade US duties.

Trade spat becomes sovereignty issue

Dan Ciuriak, a senior fellow at the Canada-based Center for International Governance Innovation, described Trump's tariff-matching plan as "fortress North America," which he said was now a sovereignty issue for Ottawa.

"Canada is a trading nation," Ciuriak told DW. "If we align perfectly with the Americans — primarily about China — we then end up sacrificing our trade policy."

There is a recent precedent. When the US imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles last year, Canada followed suit. Beijing retaliated with 100% tariffs against one of Canada's biggest exports — canola.

Canada's $4.9 billion exports of canola oil, meal and seed to China were cut in half last year, according to data from the Canada-China Business Council.

"The smaller country is the one that bears the brunt in this kind of game. So that’s one very good reason for Canada to have an independent trade policy," said Ciuriak.

As the US-Canada talks collapsed, Ottawa also complained that Washington had sought relief from rules on French-language movies and shows. Canada said this amounted to interference in its language and culture.

Canadians back the walkaway

Despite the uncertainty and higher cost to business from walking away, the Canadian prime minister's approach to negotiations with the US has broad public support.

A survey conducted by the Angus Reid Institute found that three-in-four Canadians backed the more hardline move, despite concerns over the impact on the domestic economy.

Ciuriak noted how Trump's barbs of turning Canada into the 51st US state and threats to turn Lake Ontario into Lake America have emboldened ordinary Canadians to boycott US travel and products.

"Travel by Canadians to the United States has plummeted," said. "There has been a popular consumer backlash against buying American products."

New government data show Canadians made nearly 500,000 fewer trips to the US in the first three months of 2026 and spent about $800 million less on those visits.

A survey last month by the Angus Reid Institute found that 40% of Canadian grocery shoppers were checking product origins, and that most of those shoppers avoided US goods when they could.

Although the two economies are tightly bound together, the new US duties apply to only about 5% of the $382 billion in goods that Canada exports to its southern neighbor.

The Royal Bank of Canada warned that a no-deal would impact 0.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) and jobs, while University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimated it could cost as many as 90,000 jobs.

Trump has ordered US officials to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America Image: Al Drago/UPI Photo/IMAGO

Canada's stance closely watched globally

Other governments are also watching to see how standing up to Trump plays out.

During their own negotiations, the European Union, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea and dozens of smaller partners all agreed to lower tariffs in return for market access, investment pledges or alignment with US policy.

Only China has so far met Trump's tariff threat head-on, matching tariffs with tariffs and negotiating as a fellow superpower, rather than taking the first deal on offer.

Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January that middle powers must act together, warning that if they were "not at the table," they would be "on the menu."

For now, Carney is holding the line largely on his own. New Canadian tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods — including steel, aluminum, dairy, electronics and farm equipment — take effect on September 8. They are likely to be met with US retaliation.

While matching US tariffs dollar-for-dollar sounds aggressive, Ciuriak thinks they need not "punish" the Canadian economy.

"Canada's tariffs ... apply to products Canada both buys from and sells to the US. As American tariffs cut off Canadian sales south of the border, the Canadian measures create space at home for that production."

Trump has threatened higher tariffs on Canadian automakers from January Image: Dax Melmer/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

New Trump pressure on Canadian autos

From January, Trump has threatened to raise duties on Canadian autos, trucks, parts and steel unless production moves to the US.

He also refused to extend the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) for another 16 years. Instead, the North American free-trade pact, which still covers most cross-border goods, will be reviewed year by year.

With no new talks planned with the US, Canadian lawmakers are talking up trade opportunities in other markets and weighing other retaliatory measures, including backing away from an order for US fighter jets.

Canada had planned to buy 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s, with 16 already on order. The rest are now on hold.

"When your friend kicks you in the back, one of the first rules is you don't then go and buy $12 billion of fighter jets from that person," British Columbia Premier David Eby said last week.

World.title: EU puts ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox under stricter rules
World.content:
ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox now have over 45 million average monthly users in Europe, making them subject to the Digital Services Act.

The European Commission said on Monday that US-based platforms ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox will now face stricter data protection rules after passing a key user threshold.

Now that all three have over 45 million average monthly users in the European Union, they are now obliged to assess and mitigate potential risks related to illegal content, protection of minors, and users' mental health.

The Digital Services Act (DSA), which came into effect across the bloc in February, has already been applied to companies such as TikTok and Meta.

CharGPT becomes first AI chatbot to face DSA

ChatGPT has now become the first AI chatbot to fall under the law's jurisdiction. Roblox, a user-generated content gaming platform, is now categorized as a Very Large Online Platform (VLOP), as is Reddit.

Owned by OpenAI, ChatGPT is also subject to European AI regulations.

The EU has stepped up its scrunity of tech giants and social media in recent years, including telling TikTok that it must change its addictive design or risk being banned across the bloc.
