World.title: India to receive first Iraqi oil shipment in five months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – India is preparing to receive its first shipment of Iraqi oil in five months, a development reflecting the return of Iraq’s crude oil flows to one of Asia’s largest oil markets, despite ongoing shipping challenges across the Strait of Hormuz.

India’s Bharat Petroleum expects to receive the shipment within the next few days. The tanker carrying Iraqi oil has already passed through the Strait of Hormuz and arrived in Fujairah, UAE, for a ship-to-ship transfer, according to Reuters.

Bharat Petroleum’s Chief Financial Officer, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, said that the company secured a vessel to load the Iraqi shipment and transport it to Fujairah. There, the oil will be transferred from ship to ship before reaching the company’s refineries.

These arrangements reflect the efforts of Asian refiners to find flexible logistical solutions for securing crude oil at a time when transportation cost, insurance, and tanker availability have become crucial factors in determining the viability of purchasing shipments from the Gulf region.

The Indian company typically requires around two million barrels of Iraqi oil per month, making a consistent supply from Baghdad crucial to meeting its refinery’s crude oil needs.

Bharat Petroleum has not disclosed the name of the vessel used to transport the shipment but stated that the ship’s owner agreed to load the crude and proceed to Fujairah for a ship-to-ship transfer.

Iraq is one of the countries most affected by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, given that a significant portion of its oil exports depend on ports located on the Arabian Gulf.

World.title: Iraq exports 21 million barrels of fuel oil through Syria
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s fuel oil exports through Syria have seen a significant increase since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28.

Iraqi oil flows via neighboring Syria are part of alternative routes for the country’s oil shipments to global markets following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Total Iraqi fuel oil exports transported via Syria reached 21.4 million barrels between March and the end of August 2026.

This step is part of Baghdad’s continuous efforts to establish alternate export channels amid shipping disruptions via the Strait of Hormuz, the country’s primary maritime trade artery, which led to unprecedented challenges to the oil industry.

Iraqi fuel oil began flowing overland through Syrian territory after the Iraqi state-owned oil marketing company (SOMO) reached deals to transport approximately 650,000 tons per month (approximately 4.7 million barrels) to be stored at the Baniyas port before being shipped to global markets.

Iraqi fuel oil shipments via Syria increased rapidly between March and the end of August 2026.

Iraq’s fuel oil exports through Syria were 254,000 barrels in March, 686,000 barrels in April, 3.86 million barrels in May, five million barrels in June, 5.65 million barrels in July, and 5.91 million barrels in August.

World.title: Integrity Commission halts 550-dunam land auction in Anbar, saving 19B dinars
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Federal Commission of Integrity announced on Monday, August 31, 2026, that it has successfully halted the fraudulent sale and auction procedures of a prime 550-dunam state-owned real estate parcel in Anbar Governorate, preventing the squandering of over 19.25 billion IQD (approximately $14.7 million) in public funds.

According to an official statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the operation was executed by a field investigation unit from the Commission’s Anbar Investigation Office as part of its ongoing oversight of state-owned properties nationwide.

Field investigators conducted comprehensive on-site audits and cross-referenced documentation across the State Real Estate Department in Anbar, the Urban Planning Directorate, and the City Organization Division at the Ramadi Municipality Directorate:

Location & Unauthorized Sale: The 550-dunam plot is situated within the master plan designated for the future urban expansion of Ramadi. It had been auctioned and sold to an individual buyer without obtaining statutory municipal approvals from the Ramadi Municipality Directorate.

Severe Undervaluation: The official appraisal committee at the Anbar State Real Estate Department had valued the property at just 25.09 million IQD per dunam, resulting in a total sale price of 13.75 billion IQD.

Market Discrepancy: The Commission’s field investigators analyzed land coordinates and comparable market pricing, referencing the General Commission for Taxes’ benchmark guidelines. They determined that the actual market value stands at 60 million IQD per dunam, bringing the true aggregate value to 33.00 billion IQD.

Total Prevented Loss: The fraudulent undervaluation represented a direct financial deficit of 19,250,000,000 IQD against the state treasury.

World.title: Iran, US trade fire in first exchange for a month
World.content:
Tehran – Iran attacked US military targets in the Middle East on Monday in retaliation for American strikes on an island in the Strait of Hormuz, the first exchange of fire for a month in a war that has engulfed the region.

Six months into the conflict, the two sides remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic strait shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.

The United States had signalled a pivot to economic pressure in place of military action, but on Sunday said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the small island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the strategic shipping lane.

“US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz,” the US military’s Central Command wrote on X.

Tehran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of its military, said they responded by striking two US air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage”.

Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.

Iran also claimed it targeted US personnel at an air base in the United Arab Emirates and shot down an American drone over Hormuz.

The UAE responded by saying it had “dealt with” a drone over its waters, but dismissed claims that Al Minhad Air Base had been targeted as “baseless”.

The exchange of fire between the United States and Iran came at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.

In recent weeks, the administration of US President Donald Trump had prioritised “economic warfare” over military action.

But the militaries of the two sides remain vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran having blocked the passage of commercial ships since the war began.

One-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait before the US and Israel triggered the war with strikes on Iran on February 28.

Trump has insisted the US navy has “total control” of the strait and has even called it US territory, with Washington last week announcing it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.

“US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce,” said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for US Central Command.

Iran’s leaders have remained defiant in the face of US pressure, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying Monday that “we are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors”, according to state TV.

Iran’s Guards said their strikes on Jordan were a “response to the US-Zionist aerial aggression”.

The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the US attacks on Larak and justified the Jordan strikes as “legitimate defence”.

– ‘Economic warfare’ –

Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war.

While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming, and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.

The US naval blockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran during a shortfall in domestic production, while the US Treasury has announced expanded sanctions.

The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks — mainly around the Strait of Hormuz — have dimmed prospects for a final peace agreement.

The last US strike on Iran before Sunday came on July 29. Earlier in July, the American military attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights.

Throughout the war, Iran has fought back by striking US facilities and allies in the Gulf region, hitting targets in Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others.

Its closure of Hormuz has caused pain around the world in the form of price hikes and shortages of fertiliser and energy.

Both main crude oil contracts rose at least two percent on Monday.

The war is also unpopular with the US public as midterm elections loom in November.

“Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved,” US Senator Jack Reed said on Friday, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.

World.title: PM Modi-Putin hit the road together again, share car ride after bilateral talks in Bishkek
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday shared a car ride with Russian President Vladimir Putin after their bilateral meeting in Bishkek on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit.

PM Modi and Putin travelled to the opening ceremony of the VI World Nomad Games at Bishkek Arena, following their bilateral meeting.

During the bilateral meeting, PM Modi called for an immediate end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and urged Putin to move from "endless war to the end of war."

PM Modi said that every day of war sets humanity back and that India, the land of Gandhi and Buddha, supports all efforts towards peace and will continue to do so.

"We have been discussing the Ukraine issue. When we met previously, you briefed me in detail on all aspects of the matter. As you know, India supports all efforts towards peace and will continue to do so," PM Modi said.

Not the first time

This was not the first time when PM Modi and Putin shared a car ride. Last year in China's Tianjin, PM Modi and Putin shared a ride in the Russian President's Aurus limousine as they left the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit.

World.title: 'Vishwaguru, not a Mahashakti': RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat highlights India's legacy of refuge, global service in Toronto
World.content:
TORONTO: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (

) Chief

stated that India became a "Vishwaguru" (world teacher) through its selfless service to humanity rather than by acting as a "Mahashakti" (superpower), emphasising that the country's civilisational DNA is rooted in universal friendship, refuge, and respect for diversity.

Addressing the "Hindu Vishwa Bandhu - Embrace the World in Friendship" gathering in Toronto, Bhagwat highlighted India's historical role as a sanctuary for those fleeing persecution and war worldwide.

"One may call Bharat a superpower, but it was not one. It served the world and by its own character, it became 'Vishwaguru', not Mahashakti," he said.

Bhagwat recalled historical and modern examples of India stepping up during international humanitarian crises.

Recalling the plight of Polish refugees during the Second World War, he noted how the Maharaja of Jamnagar offered them refuge and protection until they could safely return home.

"There are so many instances; it is still continuing," Bhagwat said, referring to Bharat's tradition of extending assistance during crises.

Pointing to modern conflict evacuations in the Middle East, he highlighted how Indian military transport aircraft rescued not only Indian citizens but also nationals from seven other countries trapped in the war zone.





"When, some years back in the Middle East war, people were trapped, the military planes of Bharat went there and rescued not only Bharatiya citizens; citizens of seven countries were rescued from there by Bharatiya," he said.

He noted that Muslims, Christians, Jews, and Parsis have historically found peaceful refuge and knowledge in India without fear of persecution.

"Anywhere in the world, if someone was persecuted, he got asylum in Bharat only," Bhagwat said.

The RSS chief contrasted India's historic global outreach with imperial expansionism, stating that Indian civilisation spread knowledge rather than dominance.

"Our ancestors travelled from Mexico to Siberia... They crossed the Himalayas on foot, went to Southeast Asia through small boats, but they conquered no country. They gave knowledge, astronomy, ayurveda, imparted civilisational values... Even today, when an ordinary Bharatiya goes to any country, the people there offer Namaskara," he added.

Underscoring Bharat's civilisational tradition of helping others, the RSS chief said the country never refused assistance when people in distress sought its help and often extended help without being asked.

"This is the tradition. This is the DNA of Bharat," he said.

Defining the essence of Hindu philosophy, Bhagwat clarified that the identity transcends narrow linguistic or religious boundaries.

"When I say Hindu, the word Hindu cannot be defined by any specific language, through any specific worship, or through any living style," he said, adding that Hindus "respect all" and "accept all".

Bhagwat also called for embracing diversity while recognising the underlying unity of humanity.

"We have to serve, accept, respect this diversity because it is an expression of unity. It beautifies it. It is the decoration. We celebrate it," he said.

He said Bharat's ancient ethos recognises diversity as natural while regarding unity as the fundamental reality.

"There have been many castes, many creeds, many languages. Everything is many. Nothing

"Nature, expression of reality, is diverse. Diversity is natural.

Unity is the reality. You have to tackle with natural, keeping in mind reality. That is the ancient ethos of Bharat," he added.

Emphasising the philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, Bhagwat said those who are open-minded and knowledgeable recognise the idea that the entire world is one family.

"Those who are open-minded and knowledgeable embrace the concept of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam--the belief that the entire earth is one family," he said.

He said that while people may differ in their physical appearance, "in essence, we are all one", making service to others a duty.

"Therefore, serving others is our duty. We have gained this wisdom, which brings us enduring happiness and satisfaction," Bhagwat said. (ANI)

World.title: PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
World.content:
From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Narendra Modi's carefully curated bandhgalas, from Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and sunglasses to the Thackerays' colour-coded political imagery, what Indian politicians wear has often been more than a question of personal style.

Their clothes have helped construct identities, signal ideology, project modernity, invoke tradition and increasingly generate the kind of visual moments that social media loves.

So when Rahul Gandhi appeared in a pink shirt and later in a yellow one, the change from his usual white clothing drew attention online. The yellow shirt, along with the line "Smash the patriarchy", became part of the social-media conversation.

The interest was less about the shirt itself and more about how unusual it looked compared with his regular public appearance.

But this is not the first time that a politician's attire has made more headlines than their speech. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's clothes have often drawn attention, from his signature jackets and bandhgalas to the regional outfits he wears during visits across the country. Over the years, they have become a familiar part of his public image.





As designer Gaurav Jai Gupta puts it, "Fashion can communicate before a politician has spoken a single word. Clothing conveys identity, ideology, relatability, authority and even regional or cultural affiliation almost instantly." Politics, he adds, is fundamentally about perception, and "an outfit can become the visual shorthand for an entire political moment.

Indira Gandhi, elected as Prime Minister on January 14th, 1977, adresses to the crowd in the Rae Bareli Lok Sabha constituency (Credit: Magnum Photos)

PM Modi: How his wardrobe became part of his public image

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has taken political dressing into the era of personal branding.

His wardrobe moves easily between traditional Indian clothing and sharply tailored modern silhouettes. The signature kurta, sleeveless jackets and bandhgalas have become instantly recognisable, while his international appearances often combine Indian craftsmanship with global tailoring.

Some of the looks have become headline-makers in their own right.

His wardrobe has since offered plenty of other visual moments.

A burgundy bandhgala during his first overseas trip as prime minister created a polished diplomatic look. A signature khadi kurta during his Bhutan visit emphasised Indian textiles and craftsmanship. In Nepal, saffron attire paired with a rudraksh mala made a strong cultural and religious statement at Pashupatinath Temple.

This habit of dressing for the country he's visiting â or the region of India he's in â is itself a strategy, according to Gupta: "I would definitely consider it a form of fashion diplomacy.

Clothing can be a very subtle way of acknowledging the culture of the country you are visiting while siultaneously representing your own identity." Retaining elements of one's own traditional identity alongside that, he says, "reinforces national representation.

"

His recent looks have been more state-centric. From sporting the gamcha look in Bihar, to a turban in Punjab, and even the traditional mund in Kerala, Modi has worn his "vocals for locals" tag.

Pink, yellow, blue â Rahul's pattern?

For years, Rahul Gandhi's public wardrobe has largely stayed within the safe territory of political dressing â white kurta-pajamas, jackets and understated casual wear. It is a familiar uniform in Indian politics, one that keeps the focus on the politician rather than the clothes.

But the pink and yellow shirts were different.

Bright, instantly noticeable and far removed from the monochrome political wardrobe, they became an unlikely talking point.

Gupta explains why a single garment can take on a life entirely of its own online: "The internet loves symbols that are simple, recognisable and easy to reproduce. A yellow shirt is, in itself, just a yellow shirt. But once social media attaches a narrative to it, the garment can acquire an entirely new meaning.

" The audience, he says, effectively co-authors the outfit's significance â "memes, edits, captions and commentary can transform an ordinary look into a cultural reference point," helped along by the fact that "colour is highly emotional and visually immediate."

Rahul's shade of politics through the years

He did not wear it just anywhere, either. He wore it to the 'Chhatron ki Goonj' programme, where the audience was predominantly Gen Z. But this is not the first time the Leader of Opposition has made news for his fashion. In 2019, Rahul attended a Kerala college event in a t-shirt and jeans, taking a break from his classic white kurta look, with his "You can call me Rahul" reels still going viral.

Likewise, it was not a conincidence that he went with a blue t-shirt, when he held up the red book in his hand and said "Save the Constitution", or a black one to protest outside the Parliament.

It's a pattern. Every Rahul Gandhi's politics has reflected in his preference for colours.

The Thackerays: When colour carries politics

If PM Modi's wardrobe demonstrates the power of personal branding, the Thackerays show how colour and clothing can become political shorthand.

Bal Thackeray initially adopted the shirt-and-trouser look of the urban office worker, appealing to an aspirational Maharashtra audience. Later, as Hindutva became central to his political positioning, orange became a defining element of his public appearance.

Fashion designer Nivedita Saboo, who has dressed several politicians, explains why colour carries this kind of political weight in the first place: "Colour communicates emotion before language does. Saffron can evoke spirituality, sacrifice, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity. White can communicate simplicity, peace, authority or the traditional Gandhian vocabulary. Electric or deep blue has powerful associations with social justice, equality and Ambedkarite politics.

" But, she cautions, "colour is never universal. Its meaning changes with culture, history, political association, fabric, styling and even the person's body language. That's why political dressing is fascinating: you can say something without saying anything."

Uddhav Thackeray developed his own visual identity through simple, brightly coloured sadra-pajamas closely associated with Maharashtrian culture.

Uddhav and Raj Thackeray, whose political styles reflect the Thackeray family's use of colour and cultural imagery

Aaditya Thackeray, meanwhile, represents another generational shift, combining traditional Indian clothing with contemporary fashion.

Three generations. Three styles. And three different ways of speaking to their audiences without saying a word.

Mamata, Kejriwal and the politics of looking 'aam'

Then there are politicians whose biggest fashion statement is that they appear to have made very little effort at all.

Mamata Banerjee's white cotton saree with a blue border and hawai chappals have become almost inseparable from her political identity.

Arvind Kejriwal's muffler achieved a similar status.

The appeal is simple: don't look like a politician; look like the people who vote for you. As Gupta puts it, "politics is about recognition and relatability, not necessarily luxury." A consistent, uncomplicated look, he says, "can become incredibly powerful because people can immediately identify it" â Mamata Banerjee's saree and Kejriwal's muffler "function almost like logos," communicating accessibility in a way an expensive designer wardrobe rarely can.

"In a country like ours, simplicity is more relatable," he says. "In mass politics, that emotional connection can be far more valuable than sartorial sophistication."

The repetition is what makes it powerful. Eventually, the garment becomes a logo.

See the white-and-blue saree, think Mamata. See the muffler, think Kejriwal. See the kurta and jacket, think Modi.

And now, in the age of viral fashion moments, perhaps even a yellow shirt can enter the political visual dictionary.

Arvind Kejriwalâs signature muffler became a recognisable part of his political image

Vijay: Breaking Tamil Nadu's white-shirt, veshti political dress code

When Vijay took oath as Tamil Nadu chief minister, he broke from the traditional white shirt-and-veshti look, arriving instead in a sharply tailored black suit. He has since made black-and-white suits a regular part of his public image.

Addressing the attention around his wardrobe, Vijay said, âMany people have been talking about the new suit that I have been wearing recently. Are we not allowed to wear a coat and suit? Is it meant only for people in positions of authority? There is nothing like that.â

Explaining his choice, he added, âI am not wearing many colours. It is just black and white, like all our hearts. The choice of these colours is to show that I will remain transparent and simple in everything, just like black and white.â

Tamil Nadu CM Vijay in his iconic black and white suit

Indira Gandhi: The saree that became a power statement

Long before politicians had to worry about going viral, Indira Gandhi had already mastered the art of having a recognisable political look.

Her sarees, from Banarasi silk to handlooms and Tanchois, became an important part of her public image.

They projected tradition and authority at the same time, allowing her to appear deeply rooted in Indian culture while commanding political spaces at home and abroad.

The saree wasn't simply a sartorial choice. The way she wore it, with the pallu covering her head from the loose end of the saree, made it distinct.

Indira Gandhi in one of her signature sarees during a public event

Gupta points to exactly this kind of repetition as the foundation of a political fashion identity: "Consistency is the key to creating a fashion identity.

When a politician repeatedly wears a particular silhouette, colour palette, accessory or garment, it becomes part of their visual vocabulary." Indira Gandhi's sarees, he notes, "became inseparable from her public image," much "like branding in fashion or advertising: repetition creates recognition.

" Eventually, he says, "you don't need to see the entire person; a particular silhouette, colour combination or accessory can be enough to trigger recognition."

But he's careful to add a caveat: "successful political style usually feels authentic rather than overly constructed. The strongest personal brands emerge when the clothes reinforce something the politician already represents."

For women in politics especially, clothing has always carried an extra layer of scrutiny. Too traditional, and a leader can be boxed into convention. Too Western, and questions about cultural authenticity can follow.

Moreover, most female political leaders of the time or the ones who preceeded her wore sarees the same way.

Indira's style largely sidestepped that binary. She made traditional Indian clothing look powerful.

Nehru's jacket, Rajiv's sneakers: Political wardrobe evolves

The political fashion story goes back even further.

Jawaharlal Nehru's iconic jacket became so closely associated with him that his name effectively became part of the garment's identity. The jacket was a descendant of the northern Indian achkan, a closed-neck, coat-like garment traditionally associated with Indian nobility.

It was largely when the style was marketed to Western audiences that it took the "Nehru" name, after the prime minister popularised it through his public appearances.

The minimalist look later found fans beyond politics, including the Beatles and Sammy Davis Jr, who reportedly owned more than 200 Nehru jackets.

Jawaharlal Nehru in his signature Nehru jacket, which later became a global fashion symbol

Khadi and handlooms carried an even bigger political history, associated with nationalism, self-reliance and the freedom movement.

Then came Rajiv Gandhi.

Dark sunglasses, sneakers, sleeveless fleece jackets and khadi kurta-pajamas gave him a distinctly more contemporary appearance. His wardrobe reflected the image he projected politically â younger, modern and more comfortable with the technological future.

Rajiv Gandhi sporting a pair of sneakers

In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule.

Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.

Mao & Castro: The outfit of revolutionaries

In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule.

Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.

Mao Zedongâs uniform-like suit became a visual shorthand for his revolutionary politics

Fidel Castro, meanwhile, swapped the traditional military and political imagery for tracksuits later in life. He was famously photographed wearing a red, white and blue Adidas tracksuit while recovering from surgery in 2006. The look soon became part of his public image, with Castro later wearing sportswear from brands including Fila, Puma and Nike.

Fidel Castro in his guerrilla boots during his early political years (left); Castro in a tracksuit in his later years (right)

What would it take to dress for Gen Z?

If a yellow shirt at a college event can trend for days, the question naturally follows: what does it actually take for a politician's wardrobe to land with a generation raised on Instagram and short-form video?

Saboo, who has worked closely with politicians on exactly this brief, is blunt about the trap most of them fall into. "Gen Z has grown up in a visual culture where identity is communicated through what you wear," she says.

"But breaking the dress code simply to look young can backfire. Gen Z is extremely good at detecting what feels manufactured. The clothes have to feel like the person, not like a stylist has dressed them to look young.

" A politician who "wears the traditional kurta beautifully and owns it completely," she argues, can be "far more compelling than somebody wearing sneakers and a T-shirt because someone told them that's what young people like."

For her, the real shift isn't from tradition to trend â it's "from dress code to personal code."

Asked to imagine one outfit that could say "young India" without a single slogan, she describes something quietly hybrid: a relaxed, engineered jacket in a lightweight Indian textile over a tapered trouser, perhaps a modernised kurta with sharper, almost architectural proportions underneath, finished with one unexpected element â an unusual seam, a technical fabric panel, a monogram, a contemporary sneaker.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The palette, she says, would be "sophisticated rather than loud â ivory, charcoal, deep blue or earthy neutrals with one energetic accent." The test, in her words: "It shouldn't look like 'politician trying to be fake and dress young.' It should look like India's next generation has naturally evolved its own version of Indian clothing."

Her advice to politicians boils down to five principles: don't dress younger, dress more authentically; modernise proportions rather than identity; find one recurring signature â a colour, a silhouette, a jacket, a watch â rather than constantly changing the wardrobe; make sure the clothes actually function in a country that "lives fast"; and, above all, stop being afraid of personality. As she puts it, "politics has traditionally rewarded conformity.

Gen Z is attracted to people who appear comfortable in their own skin." Fashion, she concludes, "cannot manufacture relatability. It can only amplify it."

BENGALURU: IISc has set up a not-for-profit company to help build Indiaâs capabilities in quantum computing, a technology expected to play a role in areas ranging from scientific research and industry to computing and communications in the coming years.Called the Foundation for QC Innovation (FQCI), the new Section 8 company will serve as the Quantum Computing Thematic Hub at IISc under the Union Govtâs National Quantum Mission.Itâs one of four thematic hubs set up under the mission and will bring together researchers, academic institutions, industry and startups to develop quantum computing technologies in India.Quantum computers use the principles of quantum physics to process certain kinds of information differently from conventional computers. While the technology is still at an early stage, countries and companies around the world are investing heavily in it because of its potential to solve some problems that are difficult for existing computers.At IISc, the new hub will work across several approaches to building quantum computers, including systems based on light particles, superconducting circuits, semiconductor devices, neutral atoms and trapped ions.It will also work on quantum algorithms.âThe National Quantum Mission provides a unique opportunity to build a strong and globally competitive quantum computing ecosystem in India. Our focus is on bringing together Indiaâs research capabilities, advanced infrastructure, industry and entrepreneurial talent to translate cutting-edge research into indigenous quantum computing technologies and applications,â Shankar Kumar Selvaraja, project director, FQCI and professor, Centre for Nano Science and Engineering at IISc, said.A major part of the initiative will be the creation of shared facilities for making, testing and characterising quantum devices. The aim is to give researchers and companies access to infrastructure that can help move laboratory research towards working technologies.âFQCI will also focus on building the workforce and startup ecosystem required for the sector. Its programmes will support student research and internships, industry-academia collaboration, startup development and knowledge-sharing. The initiative has launched programmes called QC Rise, QC Bridge, QC Leap, QC Accel and QC Quest as part of these efforts,â IISc said.The larger goal, it added, was to reduce dependence on overseas technology by developing quantum computing capabilities within the country.

World.title: Keralam must focus on high-tech industries to reverse migration, says Vice-President
World.content:
Vice-President C.P. Radhakrishnan has said that Keralam must focus on high-tech industries to create jobs and enable reverse migration.

“High-tech industries should come to Keralam as the State has all the natural resources. You should concentrate on that so that migration from Kerala will stop and reverse migration should take place,” he said in his inaugural address at the silver jubilee celebrations of Rajagiri School of Engineering and Technology, Kakkanad, here on Monday.

“In Kerala, land is a scarce commodity. But you have to develop the State with more opportunities. Traditional industry may not be possible because of the land cost,” he said.

He said that education cannot merely be about memorising information or earning a professional certificate. “You cannot simply produce graduates. We have to understand what is required for society and the market,” he said.

Mr. Radhakrishnan said that higher education in the country had witnessed a tremendous expansion during the past 12 years under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He added that new higher education institutions, including 16 Indian Institutes of Information Technology, eight Indian Institutes of Management, seven Indian Institutes of Technology, and 12 All India Institutes of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), among others, had been established since 2014.

“I am sure that Kerala is also going to get one AIIMS in the near future,” he said. The Vice-President urged the youth to “say no to drugs” and to utilise their talents for the betterment of themselves, society, and humanity.

He also inaugurated ‘Confluence 3.0’, an industry-academia summit on ‘India, Impact of AI’ on the occasion.

Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, Union Minister Suresh Gopi, and Minister for Higher Education Roji M. John attended.

World.title: Families of Rayagada railway staff stage protest at SCoR HQ in Vizag
World.content:
Families of railway employees from the erstwhile Waltair division, who are currently stationed in the Rayagada railway division staged a protest in front of the South Coast Railway (SCoR) headquarters in Siripuram on Monday, demanding their immediate repatriation to the Visakhapatnam railway division

The protestors, including women, children, and elderly parents, accused railway authorities of administrative apathy following the contentious division bifurcation.

They raised slogans against the SCoR and the East Coast Railway (ECoR) administrations, and sought an early resolution to their longstanding deployment issues.

The demonstrators noted that employees were under severe mental agony because of the long separation from their families while stationed at Rayagada. They also rains concerns regarding their children’s education and medical care of the elderly, which continues to remain unaddressed.

The Joint Action Forum of the Rayagada Railway Employee Families submitted a memorandum outlining six key demands. One of the key demands was the immediate implementation of Para 9.3 of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) of inviting options and establishing combined seniority lists. Families also pressed for the immediate release of a Joint Procedure Order (JPO) in line with the principal Chief Personnel Officer (PCPO) meeting held on July 24, alongside the protection of service liens and promotion prospects in Visakhapatnam.

Protesters further demanded the revival of the traditional triangular and pentagonal rotation policy, wherein new recruitment batches are assigned directly to Rayagada to balance regional manpower, allowing senior personnel who have served years in the subdivision to return to Visakhapatnam. The forum also called for the immediate revocation of unilateral posting orders issued since June 1, 2026, which disregarded combined seniority lists.

The representatives warned that protests would be intensified unless concrete administrative relief is issued. Representatives urged the Railway Board to intervene directly to safeguard the career progression and welfare of the affected workforce.

World.title: Workshop on International Law held at DSNLU
World.content:
Damodaram Sanjivayya National Law University’s Centre for International Law and Allied Disciplines (CILAD) hosted a one-day international workshop titled “Beyond the Borders 2.0: Careers and Trends in International Law” in Visakhapatnam on Monday.

Vice-Chancellor Prof. D. Surya Prakash Rao delivered the welcome address, setting an academic tone focused on expanding the professional landscape of global jurisprudence.

Prof. R. Venkata Rao of International Law University, Goa, participated as the Chief Guest, while Y. Uma Shankar, Joint Secretary (Legal and Treaties) in the Ministry of External Affairs, served as the Guest of Honour.

Addressing the gathering, Prof. Rao underscored the interplay between the Indian Constitution and international law within developing nations, encouraging students to actively engage with global legal discourse.

Prof. Uma Shankar outlined practical career pathways beyond conventional courtroom practice, citing real-world examples such as diplomacy and extradition.

The dignitaries formally released The Guide for Career in International Law - Volume 2 during the programme.

World.title: Australian varsity invites Singareni to enter exploration of critical minerals
World.content:
HYDERABAD

A delegation from Monash University, Melbourne, Australia, met top executives of the Singareni Collieries Company Ltd (SCCL) and invited the coal mining company to explore opportunities for collaboration in Australia, particularly in the area of unearthing critical mineral resources.

Dean (Engineering) of Monash University Prof. Yiannis Ventikos led the MU delegation and they had a meeting with Chairman and Managing Director of SCCL Buddhaprakash Jyothi, Directors Gowtham Potru (Personnel & Finance), L.V. Suryanarayana (Operations), K. Venkateshwarlu (Projects & Planning) and others.

The delegation stated that Australia is keen to encourage partnerships with international organisations in the critical minerals sector and invited Singareni having extensive experience in mining to explore a mutually beneficial partnership.

They observed that there is a growing global demand for critical minerals and stated that Monash University is prepared to provide technical expertise in advanced technologies, environmentally sustainable mining practices and commercially viable strategic business initiatives in this sector.

Further, they highlighted Monash University’s expertise in research, education, industry collaboration and transforming research outcomes into commercially viable technological solutions. It stated that the university has been working with industries and research institutions across the world in various sectors.

The meeting primarily focused on the growing global importance of critical minerals and the opportunities available in their exploration, extraction, processing and refining as well as the manufacture of value-added products. The Monash University delegation also explained the potential for creating additional value through downstream processing and refining rather than limiting operations to the extraction of raw minerals.

The Singareni officials made a PowerPoint presentation on the company’s activities, including coal mining, thermal and solar power generation and exploration for gold and copper deposits in Karnataka.

World.title: Family of U.S. citizen held on terror charges flags accused’s health, seeks diplomatic help
World.content:
The family of a U.S. citizen, who was arrested by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) along with six Ukrainians on charges of illegally crossing into Myanmar from Mizoram to train armed ethnic groups in weapons handling and drone warfare, has said that U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has raised the issue with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, when the latter was on a visit to Delhi in May.

The family of Mathhew Van Dyke, who was detained at the Kolkata airport on March 11 and later arrested by the NIA, has renewed calls for urgent diplomatic intervention amid concerns over his health and prison conditions.

The External Affairs Ministry is yet to respond to the issue.

Sons of Liberty International, the NGO founded by Mr. Van Dyke, said that the accused reportedly began a liquids-only hunger strike on May 6, which he attempted to end on June 18.

“A humanitarian food application was approved July 21. Matthew Van Dyke has yet to receive approved mosquito nets, and kettle. Matthew is reportedly eating only oatmeal as other purchased foods are not provided to him,” it added.

The family said Mr. Van Dyke was transferred from the NIA headquarters to Tihar Jail in Delhi on April 6 “despite suffering from an injured leg, declining eyesight, and without access to his prescribed medication.”

It said that his mother, Sharon Van Dyke, who is over 80, was only allowed a five-minute emergency call with him months ago.

Advocates Rohit Dandriyal and Rohit Gour applied to the Delhi Court for Mr. Van Dyke’s medical treatment at a private hospital and establishment of proper communication with his family in the U.S.

“However, the Delhi Court denied both application requests on June 1 alleging foreign government communications. Matthew was too weak to stand or walk during a court appearance, and utilises a wheelchair to meet with his attorneys,” the statement added.

Mr. Gour said that Mr. Van Dyke is lodged in a high-security ward in Tihar and his judicial custody has been extended till September 8. “The NIA is yet to file a chargesheet and the specific allegations against Van Dyke are not clear,” he said.

His mother and the family’s spokesperson, Gia Santos, visited Washington in June and July to speak with Congressional offices and the State Department.

Mr. Van Dyke, along with six Ukrainians, has been charged under Section 18 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). Earlier, the NIA had told the court that they had entered India on tourist visas and later travelled to Mizoram allegedly without obtaining the required Protected Area Permit, crossed the border to Myanmar, and were allegedly planning to train anti-India ethnic armed groups there.

The NIA is investigating the case to unearth the alleged conspiracy involving the accused, who are also suspected to have smuggled drones into Myanmar.

According to Section 18 of the UAPA, those attempting to commit terrorist acts can face a jail term of five years or imprisonment for life if convicted.

World.title: Nepal floods: At least 13 people from Karnataka yet to be traced, says CM
World.content:
At least 13 people stranded in Nepal following floods are yet to be traced, while the remaining had been accounted for, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar said on Monday.

“My officials have been in touch with those who have been traced, and some of them have also spoken to the people concerned,” he said.

The State government officials said that Mr. Shivakumar and Deputy Chief Minister and Revenue Minister G. Parameshwara are in constant touch with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) and the Resident Commissioner at Karnataka Bhavan in New Delhi to facilitate the safe return of those from the State.

The Resident Commissioner has constituted dedicated teams to track the situation and coordinate with authorities.

The State government is collating details of stranded and missing persons through a Google Form and the SEOC helpline. The consolidated information is being shared with the Rapid Response Cells of the MEA, Indian Missions in Kathmandu and Beijing, and the Integrated Control Room of the Ministry of Home Affairs to facilitate search, rescue, and repatriation efforts. The Embassy of India in Beijing has also opened two 24-hour helplines in the Tibet Autonomous Region to assist families seeking information about missing persons.

World.title: CIIL will publish 75 books on linguistics: Director
World.content:
Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) Director Basavaraj Kodagunti on Monday announced CIIL’s initiative to prepare around 75 introductory books in linguistics, incorporating greater representation of Indian languages and perspectives.

“Around 15 volumes are expected to focus on Indian grammatical traditions, while other books will incorporate Indian perspectives in areas including phonology, morphology, syntax and semantics,” he said at the inauguration of a two-week orientation programme on Indian Grammatical Traditions at CIIL.

Prof. Kodagunti called upon the younger generation, particularly teachers and researchers, to carry these studies forward and integrate them into their academic work.

He said Indian grammatical traditions cannot be confined to Sanskrit alone. Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Pali, Prakrit and other Indian languages have their own traditions and histories of grammatical analysis. He pointed to the interaction among different linguistic traditions as an important feature of India’s intellectual history.

World.title: NTPC celebrates National Sports Day with events promoting fitness
World.content:
NTPC Simhadri marked National Sports Day from August 28-30 with a three-day celebration promoting community fitness, according to a release on Monday.

Aligned with the Fit India Movement theme “Khelega Bharat, Jeetega Bharat”, events included swimming, throwball, and a closing cyclothon honouring hockey legend Major Dhyan Chand. Head of Project Ayaskanta Jena and senior officials presided over the conclusion event, awarding winners and reinforcing the station’s commitment to an active lifestyle.

World.title: Hague court orders India to uphold Indus Waters Treaty, suspend work on its hydropower project
World.content:
The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) on Monday ordered India to uphold the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) with Pakistan and suspend work on a hydro project in occupied Kashmir.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between India and Pakistan, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year — a move that was followed by a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025.

Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

In its order, the PCA backed Pakistan’s stance, declaring that the IWT between the two countries remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

The Hague-based court issued an award on the status of the IWT “in respect of India’s decision on abeyance” and an order on Pakistan’s application dated March 4 regarding “interim measures” concerning the Ratle hydro-electric plant.

In a press release detailing its ruling, the PCA said it “examined the potential grounds upon which India could suspend or terminate the treaty, including the grounds cited by India in its public statements”.

“In a unanimous decision, the court found that none of these grounds could justify suspension or termination of the treaty.”

It declared that the IWT “remains fully in force, and India must observe its obligations under the treaty, including those relating to the design and operation of its hydro-electric projects on the Western Rivers”.

The IWT allocates the eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India, while the western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — are largely allocated to Pakistan. The 1960 water-sharing agreement has also established mechanisms for data-sharing and dispute resolution.

During the proceedings, Pakistan requested the court to address the “design of certain components of the run-of-river hydro-electric projects that India is permitted by the IWT to construct on the Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab rivers and their tributaries (“western rivers”), before those rivers flow into Pakistan”, the PCA statement said.

The proceedings in the interim measures’ application concerned India’s Kishenganga Hydro-Electric Plant (KHEP) and the Ratle Hydro-Electric Plant (RHEP).

The court noted that the Kishenganga and Ratle plants were “also the subject of proceedings” before a World Bank-appointed neutral expert, who is expected to issue a final decision in July 2027 on whether they were in line with the IWT.

In its order, the PCA unanimously decided to “impose measures prohibiting India from concreting the RHEP dam wall and power intake structure above certain levels until 90 days after the neutral expert’s final decision”.

The court also imposed a reporting measure related to the RHEP Construction Schedule until shortly after the neutral expert’s final decision. It declined to grant two other measures requested by Pakistan.

The PCA noted that the IWT “does not provide for one party to terminate or suspend the operation of the treaty, or for ‘abeyance’”. The IWT provides that it will remain in force unless modified or terminated by India and Pakistan acting together through adoption of a further treaty.

The Court of Arbitration was chaired by Professor Sean D. Murphy of the United States. The other members were Professor Wouter Buytaert of Belgium, Professor Jeffrey P. Minear of the United States, Judge Awn Shawkat Al-Khasawneh of Jordan, and Dr Donald Blackmore of Australia.

Pakistan welcomes findings

Islamabad “took note” of the press release and welcomed the PCA’s finding that India “remains bound by and must observe its obligations under” the IWT, the information ministry said.

It also welcomed the finding regarding the Ratle plant, as well as the measures ordered by the court.

The government “will now be giving careful consideration to the detail of the award and decision, pending their publication, and how these may best assist in finding a pathway back to the parties’ engagement under the treaty”, the statement added.

India, which is officially a member of the intergovernmental court, said it did not recognise the court and “categorically” rejected the verdict.

“This so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions,” India’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

While India did not participate by making written or oral submissions in response to Pakistan’s application, the PCA sought to consider India’s positions on the matters “to the extent they could be discerned from India’s statements and conduct outside of these proceedings (including Indian government communications to Pakistan and to the neutral expert, and public statements made by Indian officials)”.

India has no grounds to suspend IWT

The PCA examined possible grounds for India’s action outside the treaty — ie under customary international law rules — but found that “there is no rule allowing a state to unilaterally terminate or suspend the operation of a treaty based on its ‘sovereignty’”, as argued by India.

The court considered several potential arguments based on India’s statements, but found that they did not justify New Delhi’s actions to suspend the IWT.

It identified three of the “few, highly restricted grounds” upon which a state could unilaterally terminate or suspend the operation of a treaty: material breach of the pact by a party, fundamental change of circumstances, and effect of armed conflict.

On India’s claim that Pakistan had violated the IWT’s “cooperative spirit” by failing to enter into negotiations to modify the treaty, the court found that “no provision of the treaty obliged Pakistan to enter into such” discussions and therefore, this cannot be a material breach of the IWT.

In fact, after examining the correspondence between the two governments, the court said it “found that Pakistan had been willing to discuss with India the issue of treaty modifications”.

On India’s allegations of cross-border terrorism, which New Delhi had cited while unilaterally suspending the IWT last year, the PCA observed that the treaty “does not address terrorism or the use of force and expressly indicates that it governs only” the rights and obligations regarding the Indus waters.

The court said it “did not find evidence that the alleged terrorism had impeded India’s ability to construct its HEPs on the western rivers and instead noted that India has built and is building many such HEPs, including in recent years”.

“Even if India’s allegation was assumed to be true, they would not establish a material breach of the treaty by Pakistan,” it said.

Regarding possible fundamental change of circumstances, the court considered India’s arguments of “(1) demographic changes; (2) the need for clean energy in India; (3) changes in dam infrastructure technology; (4) escalating cross-border terrorist attacks; and (5) the effects of climate change”.

However, in each instance, the court found that the “necessary conditions for invoking a ‘fundamental change of circumstances’ under the law of treaties had not been met”.

The court pointed out that the IWT “was of a type that would remain operational” even during an armed conflict, adding that such a conflict did not exist at present.

Furthermore, the PCA also considered whether India’s conduct could be justified “as a ‘countermeasure’ against an antecedent violation of international law by Pakistan”, but found that the requirements for a lawful countermeasure had not been met.

The court ruled that a “termination or suspension of the operation of the treaty would affect India’s obligations to protect fundamental human rights, would not permit the resumption of India’s obligations under the treaty, and would preclude the operation of dispute settlement provisions under the treaty”.

Timeline of proceedings

Pakistan had initiated the arbitration proceedings regarding the western rivers in August 2016, the PCA press release recalled.

However, in December that year, the World Bank decided to “pause” the process of appointing the chairman of the Court of Arbitration and the neutral expert. This pause was lifted in 2022, following which a neutral expert was appointed.

After India unilaterally held the IWT in abeyance in April 2025, the PCA considered its effect on the court’s competence in a “Supplemental Award on Competence” issued on June 27 that year.

The court held that “India’s decision on the ‘abeyance’ of the treaty cannot limit the competence of the Court over this dispute”. “However, the court did not go further in determining whether the Indus Waters Treaty remained in force,” it added.

On March 4, Pakistan filed an application before the court to “determine the present status of the Treaty in light of India’s decision on ‘abeyance’”.

The PCA noted that India was invited to indicate whether it would participate in the proceedings but received “no response”. The court then directed Pakistan to “file a written memorial further detailing its application and held a hearing at the Peace Palace in The Hague” from April 26 to 28.

Additional input from Reuters

World.title: Tripartite agreement to be called ‘Makkah Defence Alliance’, with first secretary general from Pakistan: Turkish FM Fidan
World.content:
Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Monday said that the tripartite agreement between Ankara, Islamabad and Riyadh will be known as “Makkah Defence Alliance”, with its first secretary general to be from Pakistan.

He made the announcement while addressing a press conference following the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, established under the agreement, held in Istanbul.

Foreign and defence ministers of the three countries, as well as top military officials, attended the meeting in Istanbul’s Ciragan Palace.

Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, and Defence Minister Khawaja Asif represented Pakistan.

In his press conference, Fidan noted that his country hosted the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee on Monday.

He said the meeting was held “in relation to the concrete steps that are going to be taken for the implementation of the agreement” and an exchange of views was held for that purpose.

“As of today, we have started the process of establishing the institutional structure of the alliance,” Fidan said, announcing that the agreement’s official name will be “Makkah Defence Alliance”.

“There is a secretariat that has been established in Riyadh, and the first secretary general will be appointed amongst our Pakistani brothers,” he said.

He said that during the meeting, decisions were taken on “how and when to begin institutionalisation and all our brothers expressed views during the meeting”.

Fidan hoped that decisions taken in the meeting will yield “excellent results”.

“For the future of a secure, stable and prosperous region, this alliance is based on international principles such as respecting the sovereignty of other states, territorial integrity and not intervening in internal affairs,” he said, adding that the alliance was not against any country.

He maintained that the alliance was “open for the partnership and participation of any other country”. However, Fidan stressed that there were “some conditions, rules and standards”, adding that the alliance’s nature was such that it was “expected to expand”.

Stressing the need for institutionalisation of the alliance, he said: “If an ally wants to join, the alliance should be functional in a proper manner by then.”

He added that the alliance did not “eliminate our countries’ responsibilities to other agreements or alliances”. Fidan hoped that with Monday’s meeting, the three countries had demonstrated readiness to take responsibility for the security and stability of the region.

“We will closely cooperate with friendly countries, and we will continue coordinating our efforts,” he said. Fidan also noted that the lack of “alliances and trust” between regional countries had given rise to security problems.

The joint defence pact, signed on August 7, empowers the member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

Inaugural meeting of ‘Makkah Defence Alliance’

The Foreign Office (FO) shared pictures from the tripartite meeting, which was attended by FM Dar, Asif and CDF Munir.

DPM Dar, in a post on X, termed it a “great inaugural meeting”.

According to Anadolu Agency, Fidan, National Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu represented Turkiye at the meeting.

Representing Saudi Arabia, FM Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff General Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili attended the meeting.

Anadolu Agency also shared a video showing the participants seated in a hall, with Fidan seated in the middle. The clip showed the Turkish FM greeting Dar, CDF Munir and others at the venue.

In a statement issued on Sunday, FO said Pakistan’s participation in the meeting signifies its “historic bonds of friendship with the brotherly countries of Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, as well as its desire for lasting regional peace and stability”.

The maiden ministerial meeting under the Makkah pact is being seen as the first step towards establishing a framework for trilateral strategic and defence cooperation.

Bilateral meetings

Ahead of the trilateral pact’s inaugural moot, the signatories held multiple bilateral meetings in Istanbul.

CDF Munir met Turkish National Defence Minister Yaşar Güler ahead of the first meeting under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul.

In a post on the social media platform X, the Turkish Ministry of National Defence shared a video of CDF Munir meeting Güler.

The Turkish minister also held a separate meeting with Asif, with Chief of General Staff General Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu in attendance.

According to Radio Pakistan, Asif and the Turkish leadership agreed to enhance joint defence cooperation in the region.

Meanwhile, Turkiye’s foreign minister met his Saudi counterpart on the margins of the trilateral moot.

Fidan had already held a meeting with Dar on Sunday. Both the deputy premier and the army chief had arrived in Turkiye a day earlier.

After concluding his visit to Istanbul, Dar departed for Bishkek alongside the Turkish foreign and defence ministers, FO said.

He will join Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and the Pakistani delegation for the SCO Council of Heads of State Meeting and the SCO Plus Summit.

World.title: PPP chairman Bilawal refutes reports of his engagement, wedding
World.content:
PPP Chairman Bilawal-Bhutto Zardari, the man at the centre of engagement and wedding rumours, himself refuted the reports on Monday.

“Social media has gotten my baat pakki, engagement and wedding done. I clarify that nothing as such has taken place; neither do I know any Princess Gloria,” the Bhutto scion said in a video statement.

He added, “If any such decision about my life is made, the announcement will come from my family. Till then, focus on the real issues and ignore the social media fuss.”

Bilawal contended that the social media ruckus was made to “distract the public’s attention from the real issues”.

He then turned his attention towards the tragic fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in Islamabad that claimed the lives of 14 infants.

“A minister, who wants to become the Gorbachev of Pakistan and divide our country into 30 pieces, cannot manage one hospital himself,” he claimed, apparently comparing Health Minister Mustafa Kamal to the last leader of the Soviet Union until it dissolved in 1991.

Kamal belongs to the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P), which has been demanding that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh. The PPP, which rules the province, opposes this strongly.

“At a time when a Lahore minister is telling the businessmen of Lahore that make provinces and govern them, at a time when the Sindh Assembly has taken a courageous stance and asserted that such discussions cannot take place on the streets or at business forums,” Bilawal said.

The PPP chief said that any such discussions and decisions must be taken in the Sindh Assembly, noting it was the first province to join Pakistan.

Bilawal’s clarification video comes after reports circulated that the PPP chairman — the son of President Asif Ali Zardari and ex-premier Benazir Bhutto — was preparing to marry into a European family.

The reports claimed that President Asif Ali Zardari had travelled to Liechtenstein — a small sovereign state between Switzerland and Austria — to discuss and set a date for his son’s wedding.

There were also claims that Bilawal’s prospective bride was a former Austrian princess.

On August 27, the Presidency posted on X that Zardari “has proceeded abroad on a private visit”, but did not share any further details.

World.title: PM Shehbaz meets Iranian President Pezeshkian on sidelines of SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Kyrgyzstan on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of State meeting on Monday, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

PM Shehbaz arrived in Bishkek earlier today on a three-day official visit from Aug 31 to Sep 2, at the invitation of President Sadyr Nurgozhoevich Zhaparov to attend the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting.

The leaders of China, Iran, Turkiye, Russia, and India were in Kyrgyzstan for the two-day SCO summit. The regional bloc, which also includes Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus, is celebrating its 25th anniversary.

On the sidelines of the summit, PM Shehbaz and Pezeshkian held a “warm and cordial” meeting, during which they reaffirmed the close and longstanding ties between both countries, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said.

They emphasised the need to further strengthen bilateral relations across all areas of mutual cooperation, in line with decisions taken during the visit of President Pezeshkian to Pakistan in June this year.

The leaders reviewed ongoing efforts aimed at enhancing regional connectivity and people-to-people contacts, as well as exchanged views on the evolving regional situation.

While reaffirming that Pakistan would continue its sincere efforts for regional peacebuilding, PM Shehbaz said that the recent visit of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir to Tehran and his “constructive engagements augured well”, the PMO noted.

The premier stressed the importance of restraint and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region.

He also underscored the need to build on the understandings reached under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the United States and Iran on June 18.

PM Shehbaz noted the MoU “offered the only viable pathway towards enduring peace in the region”.

On his part, President Pezeshkian appreciated Pakistan’s “consistent diplomatic efforts for regional peace and security”, according to PMO.

He also underscored the enduring strength of Pakistan-Iran relations, rooted in centuries of shared history, culture, and faith and reaffirmed Tehran’s strong desire to further deepen cooperation across a wide range of sectors.

The president reiterated the need to forge unity among the Muslim community to deal with contemporary challenges.

PM Shehbaz extended an invitation to President Pezeshkian to undertake an official visit to Pakistan at his earliest convenience.

The Iranian president also invited the prime minister to the forthcoming summit of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) in Tehran in December 2026.

The meeting was attended by Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Special Assistant to PM Tariq Fatemi and Foreign Secretary Ambassador Amna Baloch, PMO said.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other high officials were also present.

PM arrives in Kyrgyzstan

Adylbek Kasymaliev, chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers, welcomed PM Shehbaz upon his arrival at Manas International Airport, the government’s official account on social media platform X stated.

Announcing the premier’s departure, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said he would address the SCO summit and “present Pakistan’s stance on various regional and global issues”.

It added that Minister of Commerce Jam Kamal Khan, Minister of Communications Abdul Aleem Khan, and Minister of Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar were accompanying PM Shehbaz.

During the visit, Pakistan is set to assume the chairmanship of the SCO’s Council of Heads of State for 2026–27, with next year’s CHS summit to be hosted by Islamabad.

Earlier in the day, the Foreign Office had issued a statement on PM Shehbaz’s visit, saying that it would include participation in the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting, as well as bilateral engagements in the Kyrgyz Republic.

“During his stay in Bishkek, the prime minister will participate in the meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State and the SCO Plus Summit,” the statement said.

“The prime minister will also assume Pakistan’s chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026-2027,” it said, adding that he would also hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of the participating countries on the sidelines.

PM Shehbaz will also participate in the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games on Aug 31, the statement said.

It added that on Sept 2, the prime minister would hold bilateral discussions with the Kyrgyz president on the “entire spectrum of Pakistan-Kyrgyzstan relations”.

“The two sides will comprehensively review Pakistan-Kyrgyzstan relations and discuss ways to further deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and investment, energy, regional connectivity, education, tourism, and people-to-people exchanges,” it said.

“The leaders will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest and cooperation at regional and multilateral fora,” it added.

“Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan enjoy warm and fraternal relations, rooted in shared history, faith and cultural affinity, as well as common aspirations for peace, connectivity and prosperity in Central and South Asia,” the FO said.

“The forthcoming visit will provide an important opportunity to consolidate the momentum generated by recent high-level exchanges, translate political goodwill into enhanced practical cooperation, and further strengthen the enduring partnership between Pakistan and the Kyrgyz Republic,” the statement concluded.

Deputy PM Ishaq Dar will join the Pakistani delegation in Bishkek for the SCO Council of Heads of State Meeting and the SCO Plus Summit, FO said in a separate update.

Dar will accompany PM Shehbaz during his engagements in Bishkek, including bilateral discussions with President Sadyr Zhaparov on 2 September on Pakistan–Kyrgyzstan relations and ways to further strengthen cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

World.title: Lionel Messi says retiring from international football
World.content:
Lionel Messi said on Monday he is retiring from international football after leading Argentina to a second successive World Cup final in July.

Following the death of his father Jorge in August, Messi had said he had “serious doubts” about continuing to play football of any sort for “much longer”.

“It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul, but I understand that it is the right time,” Messi, 39, wrote on Instagram.

In the post, the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner notes that he wrote these words two days after Argentina’s defeat to Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final on July 19.

“After what happened with my father, I am more convinced than ever,” he added.

Messi swore that he “always gave everything” to his fans and “not just during these last few years when we won everything, but before that as well”.

“I always fought and gave my all for this shirt, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football,” he wrote.

“There isn’t much time left, and chapters are gradually coming to a close, and this is one that hurts me a lot,” Messi added, expressing his love for the Argentine national team.

“I gave everything I had; I have nothing more left to give. And besides, there are some very talented young players coming through who deserve to be there.”

The football icon expressed gratitude to his fans for their support over the past two decades, as well as his family, coaches and teammates.

“Now I’ll be one of you, always cheering and supporting from the outside (in good times and bad, even more so),” he added, addressing his fans.

“I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you, together with my teammates, moments we could only have dreamed of. It was crazy to have lived it all with you. I love you!”

Messi led Argentina to World Cup glory by winning the 2022 final against France in a penalty shootout in Qatar. His contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.

World.title: Court hands Hindu woman to family after alleged forced conversion and marriage
World.content:
LAHORE: A 21-year-old Hindu woman from Sanghar district in Sindh, who was allegedly lured into a relationship and persuaded to convert to Islam by a man from Gujranwala in Punjab, was handed back into her family’s custody after a judicial magistrate on Monday rejected a police request to shift her to a shelter home.

The woman went missing from her hometown. Sanghar police registered an FIR on the complaint of her brother.

The complainant alleged that CCTV footage from a camera installed at their residence showed some unidentified persons forcibly taking his sister, along with valuables and mobile phones, during the night between August 23 and 24.

Her family alleged that she was lured away and taken to Gujranwala, where she was pressured to convert to Islam and marry a local man, who was already married.

Officials from the Sindh Home Department informed their counterparts in Punjab about the FIR and sought assistance in recovering the woman.

Acting on the information, Eminabad police in Gujranwala recovered the woman and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday.

During the proceedings, the investigating officer also filed an application requesting the magistrate to send the woman to Darul Aman for “safe custody”, claiming that she was unwilling to go with her parents.

However, her lawyers opposed the police request, telling the court that she was, in fact, willing to return to her parents’ home with her real brother, who was present in court.

They said the woman also wanted to record her statement.

The magistrate ordered that the woman’s statement be recorded directly.

In her statement, given on oath, she said she wished to go with her brother to her parents’ home in of her own free will and consent.

She added that she faced no threat to her life and was under no pressure while recording her statement.

In his order, the magistrate ruled that, in view of the woman’s recorded statement, the police request to send her to Darul Aman “is hereby turned down”.

The magistrate allowed her to go with her brother, entrusting him with her safe custody and transportation back to her parents’ home in Sanghar.

Personnel from Sanghar police station in Sindh were also present in court.

World.title: Mir Raza murder case: Post-mortem report rules findings 'inconsistent' with suicide
World.content:
KARACHI: The final report of the second post-mortem for the Mir Raza Ali murder case on Monday termed its findings “inconsistent” with suicide as the manner of his death.

Ali, a 25-year-old Karachi-based businessman, was found dead with a gunshot wound in Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he was reported missing on July 28. The case has been a controversial one, as police had initially built the case around the possibility that he died by suicide, but questions were later raised by post-mortem findings.

The report, issued by the office of the police surgeon of Karachi, said that the Exhumation Board was of the unanimous opinion that the death was caused by a gunshot wound to the back.

“Death occurred due to cardiac rupture consequent to perforating firearm injury of the chest,” the report stated, adding that the entry wound was on the posterior thorax (back) and the exit wound on the anterior thorax (front of the chest).

“The findings are inconsistent with suicide as the manner of death,” it confirmed.

A meeting of the exhumation board on Monday was convened by Karachi’s Police Surgeon Dr. Summaiya Syed and comprised six other members: Prof. Dr. Naseem Ahmed of Dow Medical College; Dr. Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University; Additional Police Surgeon Dr. Sirichand; Aamir Hasan Khan of the Citizens Police Liaison Committee; Dr. Muhammad Yaseen from the administrative office of the police surgeon; and Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre’s Medico-Legal Officers Dr. Daniyal Mirza and Dr. Kamran Khan.

The post-mortem report provided a summary of the provisional exhumation report issued earlier this month. It also cited a forensic report confirming Ali to be the biological son of Mir Hussain Ali and Marium Hussain, based on DNA analysis.

Additionally, it detailed the findings of reports received from the Industrial Analytical Centre of the Husein Ebrahim Jamal Research Institute of Chemistry, a research institute managed by the University of Karachi, regarding the examination of several articles of evidence retrieved in the case.

Tests performed included a Gas-Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) for four articles submitted on Aug 6 and a Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) for the fifth article, a shirt. The shirt was also physically examined and Wet Chemistry applied for acid detection, the report said.

The physical examination of the shirt found a “perforation” on the back of approximately 6.99mm in diameter, and a “corresponding larger defect” of approximately 35.37mm in diameter on the front. Traces of acid were also detected on the shirt, which were identified by the analytical centre as hydrochloric acid (HCl), while barium and lead were also detected around the defects — in higher relative concentration around the back defect than the front one.

Additionally, the GC-MS analysis detected traces of bupivacaine — an “amide-type local anaesthetic” — in the victim’s blood.

Thirteen articles were also submitted on Aug 10 for examination, with GC-MS analysis performed on nine. SEM-EDS analysis was performed on swabs taken from the victim’s chest wound, back wound and skin of both hands.

This analysis found “no traces of sedative, psychotropic, narcotic or poisonous substances” in the other nine articles, but found traces of gunshot residue in the swabs, the report noted.

An official statement issued by the office of Sindh’s Inspector General of Police on Monday said that a high level inquiry team was continuing its inquiry into the case. The statement noted that the final report was being shared with the public keeping in view the requirements of public interest and furthering the probe in light of the final report.

SHC reserves order on family’s plea seeking JIT

Separately, the Sindh High Court (SHC) reserved its verdict on a plea seeking the formation of a joint investigation team (JIT) in the case.
