World.title: Kazakhstan Has Begun Structural Shift Toward Non-Resource Economy, Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has entered a new investment cycle that is beginning to change not only the volume but also the structure of capital entering the economy, according to the country’s leading financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov.

While the country remains dependent on extractive industries, growing investment in manufacturing, processing and high-technology production suggests that the long-discussed shift toward a more diversified economy is beginning to take shape.

“We can already confidently speak about the beginning of a structural shift. It is still too early to say that we are moving away from the resource-based model, but the figures show that the state is now moving toward a non-resource model not just in words, but in practice,” Rysmambetov said in a comment to The Astana Times.

From investment growth to structural change

The change is visible in investment data. Between 2019 and 2025, investment in fixed capital in Kazakhstan increased from 12.6 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) to 23.5 trillion tenge (US$51 billion), while investment in manufacturing tripled from 1 trillion (US$2.2 billion) to 3 trillion tenge (US$6.5 billion). The sector’s share of total investment rose from 8.1% to 12.7%, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Aug. 31.

Foreign investment is also diversifying. Gross foreign direct investment reached $20.5 billion in 2025, up 14.4%. Investment in manufacturing increased by 47.4%, or $1.4 billion, while investment in mining fell by 47%, or $3 billion. The changing composition suggests Kazakhstan is attracting more capital into activities beyond raw-material extraction.

This trend is supported by the growing pipeline of industrial projects. The Kazakh Invest portfolio currently includes 215 projects worth $78.6 billion, with more than 88,000 jobs expected to be created. Of these, 93 projects worth $32.2 billion are already being implemented, while 122 projects worth $46.4 billion remain under development.

A new system for turning capital into projects

The government is seeking to reinforce this shift through a new investment-support system. Since 2025, a three-level investment attraction model has been operating, with regions identifying priority projects and targeting investors. Fast Track mechanisms, investment headquarters and a “prosecutorial filter” are intended to reduce administrative barriers, while the National Digital Investment Platform provides monitoring and coordination.

Investment agreements are another part of the framework. Since the mechanism was introduced in 2021, 66 agreements worth more than 17.8 trillion tenge (US$38.6 billion) have been concluded. In 2025 alone, 30 agreements worth nearly 11.2 trillion tenge (US$24.3 billion) were signed. By August, another 25 agreements worth approximately 4.4 trillion tenge (US$9.5 billion) had been concluded.

The approach reflects a broader shift in investment policy: attracting capital is increasingly being linked to specific economic needs, including import substitution, exports, localization and the development of domestic supply chains.

The real test is what happens after investment

The quality of this investment, however, will ultimately matter more than the headline figures, Rysmambetov said. In his view, the next test is whether new factories generate exports, domestic value added, higher productivity and better-paid jobs.

“Investments should not simply increase gross output, but also increase labour productivity and real wages,” he said.

This distinction matters as Kazakhstan expands projects in pharmaceuticals, agricultural processing, food production and digital infrastructure. New pharmaceutical plants are expected to localize production of hundreds of medicines, while projects by international companies in agriculture and food processing are designed to create demand for domestic suppliers.

Large-scale projects such as Dalian Hesheng Holdings’ $739 million wheat-processing complex, Fufeng Group’s $340 million corn-processing plant and Tiryaki Agro’s approximately $320 million agro-industrial complex illustrate the move toward deeper processing. Rather than exporting agricultural commodities with limited processing, these projects aim to produce starches, gluten, amino acids, protein isolates and other higher-value products.

Beyond factories: building domestic technological capacity

A similar logic is emerging in digital infrastructure. The planned Data Center Valley near Ekibastuz is being developed as a major computing and artificial intelligence hub, with investment potentially reaching $30 billion and energy capacity expanding from 300 megawatts to 1 gigawatt. In June, Kazakhstan signed a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird and NVIDIA covering AI and digital infrastructure.

For Rysmambetov, however, industrial diversification must be accompanied by stronger domestic technological capacity. He pointed to limited spending on research and development and underused laboratories at universities and enterprises as areas requiring greater attention.

“Industry often relies on ready-made engineering solutions from abroad instead of developing them internally,” he said, arguing that Kazakhstan needs greater investment in R&D, industrial analytics and applied research.

From foreign capital to domestic value

The international dimension is equally important. Kazakhstan’s ability to attract capital from the UAE, Qatar, Singapore, China, the United States and European countries gives the country access not only to financing but also to technology, markets and supply chains. The challenge is to ensure that foreign investment creates lasting links with domestic businesses rather than operating as isolated production facilities.

The emerging investment cycle therefore represents a transition rather than a completed transformation. Manufacturing’s growing share, rising non-resource investment, and the expansion of processing industries provide evidence that Kazakhstan’s economic structure is changing.

The decisive indicators over the next several years will be whether these projects reach operation, increase exports, deepen domestic value chains, raise productivity and stimulate innovation.

“The transformation has begun. But to replace the economic model, we still need some time – three to five years,” Rysmambetov said.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: First Korea–Central Asia Summit Marks New Phase in Seoul’s Eurasian Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — South Korea is moving to place its nearly two-decade engagement with Central Asia on a presidential footing, bringing the region’s five leaders to Seoul in September for an inaugural summit expected to focus on critical-mineral supply chains, energy infrastructure and artificial intelligence, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea Jung Ki-Hong said in an interview with The Astana Times, his first interview since formally assuming the post.

The gathering, scheduled for Sept. 16-17 in Seoul, will elevate a diplomatic mechanism launched at the deputy minister level in 2007 into a leaders’ platform, a shift the ambassador described as more consequential than any single agreement expected from the summit.

“I think the formation of this multilateral forum at the presidential level itself is the most important outcome,” said Jung, who presented credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Aug. 19.

Jung said the leaders are expected to discuss cooperation on critical minerals and energy infrastructure, the resilience of supply chains, artificial intelligence and digital transformation, as well as cultural and people-to-people ties.

“This is not going to be just a one-time event,” he added.

Untapped potential

Kazakhstan is South Korea’s largest trading partner and investment destination in Central Asia, but considerable potential remains untapped, Ambassador Jung said.

According to the Ministry of Trade and Integration, bilateral trade reached $3.17 billion in 2025, up 1.4% from the previous year. In the first six months of this year, trade reached $1.3 billion, while Kazakhstan’s exports to South Korea increased 17.2% to $510 million. In 20 years, South Korea’s gross investment in Kazakhstan surpassed $10 billion.

Ambassador Jung identified three particularly promising areas: critical minerals, artificial intelligence, and power generation and the transition to cleaner energy.

The 21st century is about critical minerals

“Critical minerals are not just mineral resources, they are geopolitical resources,” he added, echoing a recent assessment by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

“They say the 20th century is about oil and gas, but the 21st century is about critical minerals,” Jung said. Semiconductors, batteries, renewable-energy systems and AI infrastructure all depend on these materials, he added, making Kazakhstan’s resource base increasingly important to South Korean industry.

Jung emphasized the two economies bring complementary strengths. Kazakhstan possesses substantial critical-mineral resources in deposits, concentrates and mine tailings, while South Korea has advanced processing technologies, industrial capacity and demand as an end user.

Cooperation on critical minerals is beginning to show progress. On Aug. 5, Kazakh and South Korean institutions met at Satbayev University in Almaty to finalize arrangements for a joint research center focused on rare and rare-earth metals. The initiative brings together the Korea Institute of Industrial Technology, or KITECH, and Korea National Institute of Rare Metals, known as KORAM, with Satbayev University’s Institute of Metallurgy and Ore Beneficiation.

According to Ambassador Jung, the initiative followed two years of feasibility work supported by the two governments. The center is intended to assess Kazakhstan’s mineral resources and identify technologies that could extract and process rare metals from ores, concentrates and industrial waste.

Jung said South Korea wanted the partnership to move beyond research and development toward business partnerships and commercially viable processing projects.

“We want a business-to-business matchmaking in the critical mineral sector.”

Jung said he had raised the proposed transition toward commercial cooperation during talks with Kazakhstan’s Minister of Industry and Construction Yersain Nagaspayev on Aug. 21. The two sides would need to match South Korean processing technologies with specific Kazakh deposits and determine whether potential projects could be scaled to commercially viable production, he said. If major Kazakh mining companies, including Tau-Ken Samruk and Eurasian Resources Group, identify common interests with South Korean industrial companies, Jung said, they could potentially establish processing facilities in Kazakhstan to produce intermediate materials or higher-value finished products.

AI ‘revolution’ is underway

AI offers another area for closer cooperation, Jung said, describing South Korea as one of the few countries outside the United States and China with advanced homegrown AI capabilities. Kazakhstan, meanwhile, has positioned itself as a regional leader in the sector.

“I think we have a huge room to help each other, exchange data and exchange our technologies together,” he said.

Jung noted energy cooperation would become increasingly important. Expansion of AI and data-center infrastructure would sharply increase electricity demand, creating further opportunities for cooperation in power generation. He pointed to South Korea’s experience in gas-fired generation and nuclear energy, including small modular reactors.

That cooperation is already visible in Kazakhstan’s power sector, where South Korean companies have taken on major generation projects. Doosan Enerbility completed the 310-megawatt Karabatan combined-cycle gas power plant in the Atyrau Region in 2020 and is now the engineering, procurement and construction contractor for a 1,000-megawatt power plant in the Turkistan Region.

Cooperation is also expanding into nuclear energy. During talks in Astana on June 8, Kazakh and South Korean officials discussed a proposed memorandum covering small modular reactors, workforce training and scientific and technical cooperation. The officials said Kazakhstan was interested in drawing on South Korean expertise in reactor technology and nuclear safety.

What Korean companies want to see in Kazakhstan

Nearly 800 companies with South Korean participation operate in Kazakhstan. Yet Jung cautioned that commercial interest alone would not be enough to unlock a new wave of South Korean investment. Large energy projects carry substantial financial risks, he said, while the experience of some earlier Korean investors in Kazakhstan has made companies more cautious.

He contrasted South Korean companies’ approach to risk with that of larger American and Chinese competitors.

“I met many Korean entrepreneurs and companies who have already invested here in this country,” he said. “If you want to get more profit, you have to take the risk as well. But Korea is not the U.S. and not China, so they [companies] are very much worried about the risk factor. If the Kazakh government or the big companies can share this risk factor together with the Korean investor, I think it would encourage Korean companies to further invest.”

Rebuilding confidence, Jung said, would require projects that demonstrate that long-term investment in Kazakhstan can succeed.

“We need to create more success stories of Korean investment here in this country. (…) We need fresh investment and new success stories between our two countries. That’s our hope,” he added.

Kazakhstan’s flagship project

Jung pointed to Alatau City as both an opportunity for deeper cooperation and a test of whether the two countries can turn political ambition into commercially viable projects.

Senior Kazakh officials were in Seoul in October presenting opportunities stemming from Kazakhstan’s flagship project. In December, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Industry and Construction, the Alatau City Authority and Korea Overseas Infrastructure and Urban Development Corporation (KIND) signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a framework for cooperation on Alatau Smart City. KIND, a state-backed corporation, has worked on urban and infrastructure projects in South Korea and abroad, including in Vietnam and Indonesia.

“They are eyeing this Alatau City project with great interest, but with great prudence. They are now undertaking pre-feasibility study,” said the ambassador.

Jung expects Alatau City to feature in talks between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev during their meeting in Seoul in September.

“We will see what the future holds,” he added.

“We found the Alatau City project fascinating, but it is also true that it entails huge risk as well. When I arrived in Kazakhstan, the first thing that I did was to go there. I made a field trip to Alatau City,” said Jung.

There, the ambassador also visited K-Park, a Korean cultural and business complex now under construction, as well as sites planned for urban air mobility infrastructure and a new science and technology university modeled on South Korea’s Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or KAIST.

“If all these important projects are realized in the future, it is an ideal scenario,” he added.

Educational opportunities

Beyond investment and technology, Jung said South Korea’s cultural appeal among young Kazakhs had created demand for deeper educational and professional ties. South Korea remains a popular higher-education destination for Kazakh citizens, with more than 1,500 students enrolled at Korean universities as of April 2024.

Dozens of universities and secondary schools across Kazakhstan also offer Korean-language instruction, he said, while the Korean Cultural Center in Astana and the Korean Education Center in Almaty provide language courses and cultural programs.

“I feel a huge demand for and great interest in Korean culture among the Kazakh young generation. (…) You can make the most of the diverse programs that Korean institutions can offer you, so I very much encourage the Kazakh young generation to think seriously about learning Korean language,” he said.

According to the ambassador, tangible progress has also been made on the proposed Qazaqstan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or QAIST. A feasibility study for the planned KAIST branch campus in Alatau City was completed and presented in Astana in July. The university is modeled on the experience of KAIST, Korea’s leading research university, established in 1971.

Jung said the September summit will also advance Kazakhstan’s admission to South Korea’s Employment Permit System, or EPS. South Korea designated Kazakhstan as the system’s 18th labor-sending country on Aug. 14, with the first Kazakh workers expected to arrive in 2028.

The program provides a regulated pathway for foreign workers to take jobs in South Korean industries facing labor shortages, such as manufacturing, construction, agriculture and fisheries. Kazakhstan’s participation would expand opportunities for its citizens to work legally in South Korea, acquire professional experience and receive formal labor protections.

Jung also pointed to direct air links as another factor bringing the two countries closer. Nonstop flights connect Seoul with both Astana and Almaty, placing the cities within roughly six to seven hours of one another.

A sense of familiarity

When asked what had made him feel most connected to Kazakhstan in the two months since he arrived in the country, Jung pointed first to a sense of cultural familiarity. During a diplomatic career spanning more than 33 years, he has served primarily in Europe and the United States, as well as Argentina. Kazakhstan is his first posting in Central Asia.

“Frankly speaking, I feel very much comfortable living and working in this country because people are quite similar to me. Sometimes I found many Kazakh people more similar than the Koreans in Seoul,” he said smiling.

That connection is reinforced by Kazakhstan’s community of more than 120,000 ethnic Koreans, known as Koryo-saram. In 2027, Kazakhstan will mark 90 years since Soviet authorities forcibly relocated Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia.

“We have a very strong bridge that connects our two countries already,” said Jung.

World.title: Sixth World Nomad Games Kick Off in Kyrgyz Republic
World.content:
ASTANA, BISHKEK – Following the fifth World Nomad Games (WNG) in Kazakhstan, the country has handed over the hosting baton to the Kyrgyz Republic, which holds the sixth edition Aug. 31-Sept. 6. The six-day international celebration of traditional nomadic sports to open tonight, will bring together over 100 countries, more than 2,000 representatives of sports, cultural and academic delegations.

Launched in 2014, the WNG are the world’s only multisport competition dedicated entirely to traditional sports of nomadic peoples. Held every two years, the games aim to preserve and promote the cultural heritage of the steppe. Many of the disciplines are rooted in skills traditionally essential to life on the steppe, including wrestling, bone throwing, falconry, archery and horse racing.

The idea for the WNG originated in the Kyrgyz Republic, which hosted the first three editions in Cholpon-Ata.

In 2014, the Games brought together 583 athletes from 19 countries competing in 10 sports. In 2016, participation grew to 1,200 athletes from 62 countries across 26 sports. By 2018, around 2,000 athletes from 82 countries competed in 37 sports. The games were held in Iznik, Türkiye, in 2022, attracting more than 3,000 athletes from 102 countries across 13 sports.

In 2024, Kazakhstan hosted the fifth edition, with around 2,500 athletes from 89 countries competing in 21 sports. Kazakhstan sent the largest delegation, with 195 athletes, followed by the Kyrgyz Republic with 172 and Russia with 144. Wrestling was the largest discipline at the games, attracting 266 competitors.

Horses at the heart of the games

This year’s program is built around three main areas: sports, culture and science. The sporting program features traditional ethnic sports, national games and competitions practiced by peoples worldwide.

Some of the most anticipated events will take place around Lake Issyk-Kul. At the hippodrome in Cholpon-Ata, riders will compete in events that draw on centuries-old traditions of speed, agility and horsemanship. Horse racing will have a particularly prominent place in the program. Events include alaman baige, a long-distance race in which endurance and the ability to manage a horse’s strength are crucial.

The cultural program will feature festivals and an ethnovillage, where regions of the Kyrgyz Republic will showcase living traditions through crafts, music, dance, customs, rituals and national cuisine.

Kazakhstan is also preparing for the games, with a qualifying championship in zhorga zharys, a traditional pacing-horse race, recently held at the Central Hippodrome in Almaty, reported the capital’s akimat (city administration) on Aug.20.

Riders from Astana took first and second place after completing a 9-kilometer course.

One of the notable performances came from a 13-year-old female jockey who recently joined the team. Despite her young age, she delivered a strong performance in one of her first competitions and won a silver medal.

Aliya Toktassynova, a coach and champion rider, said the competition was particularly important because it served as a qualifying event for the upcoming WNG.

Volunteering adds a new dimension to the games

Volunteers play a key role in organizing and hosting the WNG, supporting visitors and participants and helping maintain order at sporting and cultural venues.

Around 3,000 volunteers are taking part in this year’s games, including international volunteers. Kazakhstan is also represented by a delegation selected through a competitive process.

The head of the Kazakh delegation Asiya Sarbayeva from the Mangystau Region, said that she had long wanted to take part in the WNG because of their atmosphere and cultural significance.

According to her, the games bring together professional athletes worldwide to showcase their strength and skills while allowing participants and visitors to experience traditional nomadic culture firsthand.

“Holding such a large-scale event is crucial for our culture, so I wanted to contribute in some way. I especially want to see the golden eagle hunting and tayak tartysh competitions. After all, reading in a book and seeing the ancient art of our nomadic ancestors in person are two different things,” Sarbayeva told The Astana Times.

For 73-year-old volunteer Galiya Nurutdinova from Kazan, Russia, these games are far from her first experience with the event.

She attended the WNG in 2016 and 2018 in Cholpon-Ata and volunteered at the 2024 Games in Astana. This year, she has returned to Cholpon-Ata.

“The WNG are not standard sporting competitions. They are extraordinary, emotional and captivating. In addition to witnessing unique sports that are rarely seen outside their regions of origin, you can take part in master classes, try traditional crafts and taste authentic nomadic cuisine,” Nurutdinova told The Astana Times.

She noted the atmosphere of ethnic sports is different from that of conventional sporting competitions held in stadiums and sports complexes.

“It really draws you in. You have to see it for yourself. It is difficult to describe,” she said.

Nurutdinova has volunteered at various world championships and Olympic events, however, she said the WNG hold a special place for her because of their cultural dimension.

“We are united by our shared nomadic heritage. These Games bring people from around the world together while introducing them to the history and traditions of nomadic peoples. They also help revive, preserve and promote the heritage of nomadic civilizations worldwide,” she said.

She also highlighted the games as an opportunity to meet people from various regions and countries.

“During the WNG in Astana, I met the silver volunteers, volunteers like me who are older and retired. Recently, I also came to Astana as a volunteer for the World Future Games and met friends I had made during the Nomad Games. Events like these bring people together,” Nurutdinova said.

World.title: Rybakina Begins US Open Campaign With World No. 1 Ranking in Sight
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has moved to No. 1 in the WTA live rankings as the US Open women’s singles main draw gets underway in New York, putting her within reach of becoming the first Kazakh player to top the official world rankings.

Rybakina currently leads the live standings with 7,911 points. Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus is second with 6,585, followed by American Jessica Pegula with 6,555 and Coco Gauff with 6,474. The official WTA rankings, however, still have Sabalenka at No. 1 with 8,575 points and Rybakina at No. 2.

The difference reflects points being recalculated during the US Open. Rybakina is defending only 230 points from last year’s tournament, while Sabalenka, the reigning champion, is defending 1,990 points.

A clear path to No. 1

According to the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA), Rybakina has the clearest route to the top ranking. She can become No. 1 without winning a match if Sabalenka, Pegula and Gauff do not win the title. If Rybakina reaches the semifinals, she will secure the No. 1 ranking regardless of the other results.

For Sabalenka to remain No. 1, she must win the US Open and have Rybakina lose before the semifinals. Pegula and Gauff also need to win the title and hope Rybakina exits before the semifinals.

The scenario adds significance to a tournament in which Sabalenka is seeking a third consecutive US Open title.

Rybakina focused on health

Despite the ranking implications, Rybakina said she is trying not to focus on the calculations, particularly after her recent injury.

“I don’t check the ranking exactly, the point situation. The most important [thing is to] try to stay healthy, play match at a time,” she said ahead of the tournament.

The 27-year-old sustained an ankle injury during her Cincinnati quarterfinal against Iga Swiatek on Aug. 20 and retired from the match. She has since returned to training and expressed confidence in her recovery ahead of the US Open.

Rybakina is scheduled to face 17-year-old U.S. Thea Frodin in the first round.

A symbol of Kazakhstan’s tennis growth

Rybakina’s potential breakthrough also comes as Kazakhstan’s tennis infrastructure and development system continue to expand.

In a 2025 interview with The Astana Times, Kazakhstan Tennis Federation Executive Director Dave Miley said the country had made tennis increasingly accessible beyond Almaty, with tennis centers, tournaments and junior programs developing across the country.

Speaking about Rybakina and another Kazakh tennis star, Alexander Bublik, Miley said: “Rybakina and Bublik have been very important for Kazakh tennis.” He added that when Kazakhstan’s leading players compete in the Davis Cup or Billie Jean King Cup, they spend time with juniors, helping inspire the next generation.

For Rybakina, the immediate task is simpler: win her opening match and take the tournament one round at a time.

The US Open, the final Grand Slam of the 2026 season, runs through Sept. 13 in New York.

World.title: Kazakhstan, CERN Advance Framework for Kazakh Scientists’ Participation in Research
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research and a leading global center for particle physics, are advancing a new mechanism that will enable Kazakh scientists to participate in CERN research experiments and scientific internships.

This was discussed at a meeting between acting Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek and CERN Director-General Mark Thomson, reported the ministry’s press service on Aug. 31.

The officials discussed next steps to expand scientific and technological cooperation, focusing on high-energy physics, fundamental science and training highly qualified scientific and engineering personnel.

Kazakhstan and CERN’s partnership is based on an international cooperation agreement signed in 2018. A draft protocol to the agreement has been developed to provide a practical framework for Kazakh scientists’ participation in CERN’s scientific experiments and research programs.

The proposed mechanism will allow Kazakh researchers to undertake scientific internships and participate in CERN research through the Bolashak International Scholarship Center’s Scientific Internships program.

The initiative is expected to strengthen the expertise of Kazakh specialists, expand international research cooperation and provide new opportunities for domestic scientists to work alongside leading researchers at one of the world’s major scientific centers.

The initiative also aligns with Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to connect its universities and researchers with global scientific networks. In a 2025 interview with The Astana Times, Nurbek said international and Kazakh academics were increasingly working together on joint research projects, international grant competitions and the development of new laboratories, helping strengthen the country’s access to global research networks.

“President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has set the task of training domestic engineering and technical personnel in the peaceful use of nuclear energy, taking into account the prospects for Kazakhstan’s nuclear industry,” Nurbek said.

He noted that Kazakhstan is transforming its scientific ecosystem and introducing a new model of science management focused on applying research results and their contribution to the economy.

Nurbek also highlighted Kazakhstan’s expanding international partnerships in science and higher education, including cooperation under the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation program.

“Against this backdrop, cooperation with CERN is of particular importance,” he said.

The officials reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the partnership, noting its potential to advance fundamental science, develop scientific and engineering expertise and expand opportunities for Kazakh researchers.

World.title: Kazakhstan Steps Up Gulf Diplomacy Amid Hormuz Shipping Risks
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan intensified diplomatic engagement in the Gulf last week as Iran and Oman moved to restore safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Arman Issagaliyev held talks in Oman and the United Arab Emirates and attended an emergency session of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Jeddah on Aug. 27.

Kazakhstan-Oman cooperation

Issagaliyev met Oman’s First Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Khalifa Al-Harthy. The officials discussed bilateral relations, regional and international topics, high-level visits and preparations for the second round of political consultations between the two foreign ministries in Astana.

Issagaliyev also met First Deputy Chairman of the Oman Investment Authority Mulham Al-Jarf to discuss joint projects and expand business ties, the Foreign Ministry’s press service reported.

Particular attention was paid to the development of transport and logistics cooperation, including the potential use of Oman’s port infrastructure to expand access for Kazakh products to the markets of the Gulf countries and the Indian Ocean.

Kazakhstan-UAE strategic ties

In Abu Dhabi, Issagaliyev met UAE officials to discuss political, trade, investment and consular cooperation. The officials also discussed Kazakhstan’s initiative to establish an International Organization for Water Resources and preparations for the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December.

OIC emergency session

In Jeddah, Issagaliyev attended the OIC’s 23rd Extraordinary Session on Palestine. Kazakhstan called for a political settlement and reaffirmed support for humanitarian assistance and Gaza’s reconstruction, as well as an independent Palestinian state within the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. The session adopted a resolution on Palestine and elected a new OIC Secretary-General.

World.title: Karin Elected Vice President as Bektenov Stays on as Prime Minister
World.content:
ASTANA – Erlan Karin was elected vice president of Kazakhstan on Aug. 31, while the Kurultai also backed Olzhas Bektenov to remain as prime minister, filling two of the country’s most senior posts as the new unicameral parliament began its work. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev nominated both candidates during a meeting with the leaders of political party factions in Kurultai on Aug. 31.

Speaking at the meeting, President Tokayev described Karin as an experienced public servant with extensive knowledge of state governance, reported Akorda.

“He has worked in the system of public administration for many years. One can say that he is a person of broad outlook, with rich experience and a true patriot,” Tokayev said.

The President also highlighted Karin’s understanding of Kazakhstan’s strategic priorities and long-term development agenda.

“Therefore, I consider Erlan Karin worthy of this position. I ask the Kurultai to support this candidacy,” Tokayev said.

Subsequently, 141 members of Kurultai out of 145 voted in favour of Karin’s candidacy. Under the Constitution, the vice president may not serve as a lawmaker or belong to a political party, and would assume presidential powers if the head of state leaves office before the end of the presidential term.

Karin graduated from Zhubanov University in Aktobe in 1996 with a degree in history and geography. He began his career in academia as a university lecturer before moving into political analysis, research and public service.

He later held several senior positions in public administration, including director of the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, aide to the President, state secretary and state counselor. On June 30, he was appointed first deputy head of the Presidential Administration.

During the same meeting, Tokayev nominated Olzhas Bektenov to remain as prime minister. Under the Constitution, the President must consult with the leaders of political party factions represented in the Kurultai before submitting a nominee.

The Kurultai backed Bektenov’s nomination by 137 votes.

Bektenov has served as the country’s prime minister since 2024.

The consultations were attended by the leaders of the factions of the Adilet party, Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party, Respublica party, Aq Jol Democratic Party and the National Social Democratic Party.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan in Hot Seat: Japarov Hosts 25-Year SCO Milestone
World.content:
On Sept. 1, leaders from ten nations will gather in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz Republic, for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s heads of state. This year’s gathering marks the organization’s 25th anniversary, and its quiet evolution into one of the most consequential forces in Eurasia in a shifting, increasingly precarious world order.

President Sadyr Japarov of Kyrgyzstan, host and chairman, has chosen a motto that says as much about ambition as nostalgia: 25 Years of the SCO: Together Towards Sustainable Peace, Development, and Prosperity. It is both a tribute to the past and conveys a commitment to the future.

The roll call in Bishkek will include Belarus’s Alexander Lukashenko, China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian, Kazakhstan’s Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Tajikistan’s Emomali Rahmon, Uzbekistan’s Shavkat Mirziyoyev, alongside Japarov as host. Ten heads of state, representing close to half the world’s population, will sit at one table in the Kyrgyz Republic. A decade ago, few Westerners had ever heard of the country and fewer could have located it on a map. That in itself is part of the story.

SCO Plus

The SCO Plus meetings widens the summit’s list of attendees beyond the organization’s 10 full members, bringing in two observer states (Afghanistan, Mongolia) and 15 dialogue partners spanning the Caucasus, West Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia (Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Cambodia, Egypt, Kuwait, Laos, the Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Türkiye and the UAE).

Last year’s summit was the largest SCO gathering on record, drawing dozens of national leaders as well as the UN Secretary General and other international organization heads. Twenty-seven countries in all now orbit the organization in some capacity with more expected. The SCO has been a concern for the United States.

Japarov’s Summit to Win — or Lose

Hosting the summit lends Kyrgyzstan added prestige and visibility on the world stage. Yet beyond the chairmanship, President Japarov’s core focus remains raising living standards at home, ensuring economic stability, and elevating Bishkek’s diplomatic standing, particularly with an anticipated UN Security Council seat in 2027.

As SCO host, he is expected to draw on Kyrgyzstan’s reputation as the Switzerland of Central Asia, steering part of the agenda toward ecological issues, mountain ecosystems, and glacier preservation—themes that will also feature prominently at the 2026 World Nomad Games this September.

A clear subtext is that Japarov does not want Bishkek hijacked by outside noise, whether that means great-power theatrics, last-minute diplomatic ambushes, or the kind of external meddling that has derailed other multilateral gatherings in recent memory.

What Cholpon-Ata Already Told Us

Last July in Cholpon-Ata, SCO foreign ministers approved the adoption of the SCO’s thematic statements, including one on cooperation in the field of energy security.

Security dominates the agenda: terrorism, extremism, separatism, cybercrime, and organized crime. Counter-narcotics gets separate treatment, with a proposed SCO-wide focus on continuing the World Without Drugs campaign.

Alongside economic integration efforts such as trade corridors, digital connectivity, the operationalization of the SCO Development Bank, there’s quieter discussion of internal reform, building on a 2025 decision to modernize how the now ten-member SCO functions. Maintaining open trade routes, reliable trade flows, diverse currency settlement options, and continued infrastructure development will remain core priorities, regardless of the state of the international economic order.

The Multipolar undercurrent

Beneath the discussion of security and economic integration runs a deeper thread. The SCO has increasingly cast itself as an inclusive Eurasia-centric structure aligned with a multipolar vision, one that offers dialogue and diplomacy as a proposed counterweight to unipolarity and a bloc mentality. Whether or not one buys this framing entirely, it is the organization’s own stated strategic logic: win-win cooperation over zero-sum competition, joint work over a go-it-alone approach.

In this sense, the expected 2026 Bishkek SCO Declaration will not be much different from the declarations issued in 2025 at Tianjin and in 2024 at Astana.

West Asia and currencies loom over everything

West Asia will loom over this year’s summit. President Pezeshkian is expected to arrive in Bishkek as Iran’s relations with Washington over the Strait of Hormuz remain deadlocked; this is set against tensions across the globe causing additional havoc in energy, trade and capital markets.

India’s Modi and Pakistan’s Sharif will sit at the same table. Though the Taliban are expected to be absent, tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan will still weigh heavily on the SCO talks.

Payment system reform and currency diversification will also figure prominently, as over reliance on dollar-based clearing has left some members exposed to sanctions and monetary shocks.

A quarter-century test

To be sure, twenty-five years after its birth in Shanghai, the SCO has grown into something that can claim a seat at the table where global geopolitics are discussed—like it or not. The summit will not untangle West Asia’s troubles, nor eliminate Eurasia’s geoeconomic rivalries. But, despite their differences, ten states, along with observers and dialogue partners, will unite behind achieving this political objective set forth in last year’s Tianjn SCO Declaration: “Member States reaffirm that Central Asia is the core of the SCO and support the efforts of Central Asian states to ensure peace, security and stability in their countries and in the region as a whole.”

Should Japarov get his way, the summit’s takeaway won’t be rhetoric or crisis diplomacy, but a definite reminder that dialogue still pays off, and that, with pragmatism and cool headedness, a road map for action can be hammered out.

As the SCO turns 25 on Sept. 1, its greatest test may be whether countries can find common ground, not only across economic and political divides, but across civilizations. Twenty-five years on, that would be no small achievement but a signal accomplishment in itself.

The author is Javier M. Piedra, a financial consultant, specialist in international development and former deputy assistant administrator for South and Central Asia at USAID.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: 1,795 applicants in Georgia to get second chance to enrol
World.content:
University admissions in Georgia in 2026

A total of 1,795 applicants in Georgia who passed the minimum threshold in the Unified National Examinations but failed to secure a place at a university will be given a second chance to enrol.

This year, the number of applicants who passed the minimum threshold but were unable to gain admission to a university increased 2.5 times compared with the previous year.

Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the decision, saying it had been made as a one-off exception this year because it is the first year of the higher education reform introduced by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Mikanadze said that registration for vacant places at public and private higher and vocational education institutions would open in the first half of September for applicants who had not previously secured a university place.

“As we have embarked on nationwide higher education reform, and this year is something of a transitional period, we are making an exception. Only this year, at the initiative of Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, we are giving 1,795 applicants who passed the minimum competency threshold in the Unified National Examinations the opportunity for so-called second-round admission,” Mikanadze said.

The Georgian government has radically changed the higher education system. Under the new reform, admission to public universities is organised around strict specialisation, with specific academic fields assigned to individual cities and universities.

The authorities say the measures are aimed at aligning the education system with labour market needs and concentrating resources. However, the changes have already raised questions about academic freedom, regional development and university autonomy.

More on the higher education reform can be found here.

World.title: Salaries rise 7% while house prices climb 12.4%: Is it worth buying home in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Buying a home in Azerbaijan

The average price of a 65-square-metre flat in Baku is now around 178,000 manats (about $105,000). Someone earning the country’s average monthly salary of 1,174 manats (about $690) would have to save their entire income for 12 and a half years to afford it. But once the cost of food, rent, transport and other everyday expenses is taken into account, this calculation is purely theoretical.

According to an August review by the Central Bank, house prices rose by 8.6% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. Prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%, while those on the secondary market rose by 8.6%. Rents increased by 7.4%. Over the same period, average nominal wages rose by 7%.

Wage growth is failing to keep pace with house prices

In Azerbaijan, the average nominal wage rose by 7% over the year, or about 77 manats (around $45), reaching 1,174.4 manats. At the same time, prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%. This means new homes became 5.4 percentage points more expensive than the rate at which average wages increased.

The gap shows that housing affordability for potential buyers has not improved. The rise in wages increased a worker’s annual pre-tax income by around 920 manats (about $541). Meanwhile, a 12.4% increase in house prices means that a flat costing 170,000–180,000 manats would have become roughly 19,000–20,000 manats (about $11,200–11,700) more expensive over the year.

It should also be noted that 1,174 manats is the average nominal wage across the economy as a whole. The figure is calculated before taxes and social contributions and does not reflect the actual income of most workers.

How many years would it take to buy a 65-square-metre flat?

The m2map platform, which analysed more than 82,000 active listings in August, estimated the median asking price in Baku at 2,735 manats (about $1,609) per square metre. At that price, a 65-square-metre flat would cost 177,775 manats.

According to July data from the Azerbaijan Chamber of Appraisers, the median price per square metre for newly built homes was 2,812.5 manats (about $1,655), compared with 2,616.7 manats (about $1,540) on the secondary market. This puts the price of a flat of this size at roughly 170,000 to 183,000 manats (about $100,000–108,000), depending on the segment.

At the national average monthly wage of 1,174.4 manats, 177,775 manats is slightly more than 12 and a half years of a worker’s total earnings. Using Baku’s average wage of 1,487 manats (about $875), the period falls to around 10 years. But this is only a theoretical calculation, assuming a person spends none of their salary on anything else. In reality, someone on an average income would need considerably longer to save the full price of a flat.

If a buyer can save 20% of their salary, it would take around 50 years to accumulate the full cost of the property. To save the down payment required under a standard mortgage, which in this case would be around 28,000 manats (about $16,500), would take almost eight years.

The average wage also does not reflect the incomes of all workers. According to data from the State Statistics Committee, during the first five months of the year, average monthly wages were 763 manats (about $449) in retail, 825 manats (about $485) in education, and 800 manats (about $470.50) in tourism and catering. For workers in these sectors, a mid-range flat in Baku is equivalent to around 18–19 years of their combined earnings.

Does a mortgage make housing more affordable – or more expensive?

The maximum amount available under a standard mortgage from the Mortgage and Credit Guarantee Fund is 150,000 manats (about $88,235), with a loan term of up to 25 years, an annual interest rate of 8% and a minimum down payment of 15%. However, 85% of the 177,775-manat price of the flat exceeds the loan limit, meaning the buyer would have to provide at least 27,775 manats from their own funds.

If the remaining 150,000 manats were borrowed for 25 years at 8% interest, the monthly payment would be around 1,158 manats (about $681.20). Over the full term, the borrower would repay more than 347,000 manats (about $204,000) to the bank. Including the down payment, the total cost would exceed 375,000 manats (about $220,600). Insurance, property valuation, notary fees and other associated costs are not included.

A monthly payment of 1,158 manats is almost equal to the average salary across the country and represents 78% of the average salary in Baku. Under the Fund’s rules, mortgage payments must not exceed 70% of borrowers’ combined income after tax. This means that a Baku resident earning a single average salary would find it practically impossible to service such a mortgage alone.

In a household where two people earn the average Baku salary, the monthly mortgage payment would account for 39% of their combined nominal income. After tax, the share would exceed 40%. According to OECD and Eurostat methodology, housing costs exceeding 40% of disposable income are considered an excessive housing burden.

Under the subsidised mortgage scheme, the annual interest rate is 4%, the loan term can be up to 30 years, and the maximum loan amount is 100,000 manats (about $58,820). Although the monthly payment would be around 477 manats (about $280.60), buying a 65-square-metre flat at Baku’s average price would require around 78,000 manats (about $45,882) in the buyer’s own funds. The lower interest rate therefore does not solve the main problem for families without substantial savings.

Is renting cheaper?

The median advertised rent in Baku is 11 manats (about $6.50) per square metre per month. Renting a 65-square-metre flat would therefore cost around 715 manats (about $420.60) a month – 443 manats (about $260.60) less than the monthly payment on a standard mortgage. However, this still amounts to around 48% of the average salary in Baku, excluding utility bills.

If an investor bought such a flat for 178,000 manats and rented it out for 715 manats a month, the gross annual rental yield would be around 4.8%. After accounting for maintenance, periods when the property is vacant and other associated costs, the actual return would be even lower. Buying a flat with a mortgage and then renting it out therefore generally does not allow the owner to cover the full cost through rental income alone. The model may make sense primarily for investors with substantial capital who are betting on further increases in property prices.

What is driving prices higher?

The Chamber of Appraisers attributes the rise in new-build prices to strong demand in the mid-to-upper and premium segments, the availability of mortgage financing and the perception of housing as an investment asset. The Chamber’s land price index also points to rising prices and limited supply in premium areas. This may put additional pressure on the cost of newly built homes.

At the same time, according to the State Statistics Committee, investment in residential construction fell by 2.7% in real terms in the first half of the year. These figures strengthen the suggestion that demand, growing faster than household incomes, is running up against limited supply.

State-backed mortgages make housing more affordable for some families: in the first half of the year, 2,242 families received mortgage loans worth a total of 226.3 million manats (about $133.1 million). Since 2019, just over 10,000 families have used the rent-to-own scheme. However, it remains unclear whether these programmes are large enough to curb the overall rise in property prices.

Buying a home in Baku today is therefore more affordable for a household with two stable official incomes, substantial savings for a down payment or another property that can be sold than for someone living on a single average salary. Those who qualify for subsidised mortgages and have tens of thousands of manats in savings are also in a stronger position.

For everyone else, the choice is essentially between increasingly expensive rent and taking on long-term, substantial debt.

Buying a home in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Occupation is off’: Russian state media RIA Novosti on Georgian PM Kobakhidze’s remarks
World.content:
RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

Russia’s state-run news agency RIA Novosti has responded to remarks by Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, saying that Tbilisi had decided to reassess the history of its relations with Moscow.

The article, published on 24 August 2026 under the headline “Occupation is off”: Another country refuses to consider Russia an enemy, focused on Kobakhidze’s remarks about the Treaty of Georgievsk.

Background

On 18 August 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that Georgia’s decision to sign the Treaty of Georgievsk had been a “civilisational choice”.

His main argument was that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation. According to Kobakhidze, Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose to align itself with Orthodox Russia.

Kobakhidze argued that the decision was not only justified but also “the only correct and only possible” choice at the time. He said Russia honoured the terms of the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end, and almost 20 years passed between the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country effectively survived.”

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement between the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and the Russian Empire, signed on 24 July 1783. Under the treaty, King Erekle II accepted the protection of Russian Empress Catherine II, while Russia pledged to defend the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and preserve its territorial integrity. The treaty formally preserved the internal independence of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and did not declare it part of the Russian Empire. However, in 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and incorporated it into its territory.

What RIA Novosti says in its article

The Russian state-run news agency says Kobakhidze presented Georgia’s decision to accept the Russian Empire’s protection as the only way for the Georgian people to survive Ottoman and Persian aggression.

The article quotes the views of several political experts, including Nino Skvortsova, whom the agency describes as a “Tbilisi-based political analyst”.

According to Skvortsova, Kobakhidze’s focus on the reign of Erekle II serves not only to reinterpret history but also to justify the government’s current policies.

“Kobakhidze is trying to place Erekle II back in his historical context. For him, the king is important as a ruler forced to choose between major powers while his country’s existence was under threat,” the expert says.

In her view, this approach allows parallels to be drawn with the current policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party:

“Modern Georgia is also caught in competition between major powers, while the authorities justify their actions by the need to preserve peace, sovereignty, traditional identity and freedom of foreign policy manoeuvre.”

RIA Novosti also quotes another expert, Artur Ataev, who says that Georgian Dream is trying to raise a new generation free from old stereotypes. Ataev argues that the opposition, in turn, wants Georgia to follow the example of Ukraine, the Baltic states and other former Soviet republics.

“Today, this is one of the main topics of debate in Georgian society. There are even calls to recognise the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia,” Ataev says.

He argues that Georgian society and the political elite are gradually changing, but that the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is unlikely in the near future.

“After all, most Georgians still see Russia as an occupier,” the expert concludes.

RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

World.title: Saturday March in Tbilisi: growing emigration. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Abkhaz blogger who spoke of ‘shared future’: Who was late Daur Buava?
World.content:
Abkhaz blogger found dead in Georgia

Young Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava has been found dead in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi. According to neighbours, they raised the alarm after Buava had not been seen for several days. Emergency services called to his rented flat found his body inside.

The cause of his death has not yet been established, and an initial examination of the body found no signs of violence. Georgia’s Interior Ministry has opened an investigation under the article covering “incitement to suicide”.

Who was Daur Buava?

Daur Buava, 32, was an Abkhaz blogger who attracted public attention for his open and unconventional views on Georgian-Abkhaz relations. On social media, particularly TikTok, he regularly posted videos advocating peaceful coexistence, dialogue and the rebuilding of trust between Georgians and Abkhaz.

Buava was born in Abkhazia in 1994. The Georgian-Abkhaz war had ended a year before he was born, meaning his understanding of the conflict was largely shaped by what he had been told by those around him. In 2021, Buava travelled to Tbilisi in an attempt to examine that version of events for himself.

“Later, I realised that it was the truth as seen by only one side. I learned the other side’s truth here,” he told Georgian media outlet Netgazeti that same year.

Within months, Buava had become one of the most recognisable Abkhaz bloggers on TikTok. His videos focused primarily on relations between Georgians and Abkhaz, the war, peace and Abkhazia’s future. He had tens of thousands of followers, including young people in Abkhazia.

Buava’s public activities were not confined to social media. He gradually became one of the few Abkhaz voices openly advocating dialogue with Georgians. It was this position that made him a target of persecution in Abkhazia.

Meeting the “enemy”

Buava said that before travelling to Tbilisi, his views of Georgia had been based largely on the information he received in Abkhazia.

One of the reasons he decided to visit Georgia was a TikTok livestream in which Georgians and Abkhaz called each other enemies and exchanged insults. For Buava, this became another reason to see for himself the place he had been taught since childhood to regard as hostile.

He said that in both societies there was a small group of people fuelling hatred, while most people wanted to communicate with one another.

Daur Buava

Persecution in Abkhazia

Buava’s activities did not receive unequivocal support in Abkhazia from the outset. In late 2021, he said that many people criticised his presence and activities in Tbilisi, although he also received messages of support from Abkhazia. Over time, however, criticism was followed by threats.

According to Buava, his supporters also faced pressure. He said that people who posted positive comments during his livestreams were identified and, in some cases, people even went to their homes. Buava also said that several of his supporters had been beaten.

In June 2022, Abkhazia’s de facto security service opened a criminal case against Buava on charges of “high treason”.

The agency said that videos posted by Buava on TikTok contained appeals that undermined Abkhazia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity, state security and defence capabilities”. It also accused him of promoting the idea of Abkhazia existing as an autonomous republic within Georgia.

The case against Buava was opened in absentia. He remained in Tbilisi and no longer planned to return to Abkhazia.

‘Amra’ and idea of shared future

In Tbilisi, Buava and his Georgian friend Mikheil Kvatashidze founded the Amra youth movement. The name means “Sun” in Abkhaz. The organisation aimed to create opportunities for young Georgians and Abkhaz to communicate with one another.

In December 2022, Buava obtained Georgian citizenship, which he said was granted under a simplified procedure. This became another source of criticism against him within Abkhaz society.

In 2023, Buava was invited to the European Parliament, where he spoke about relations between young Georgians and Abkhaz, the free exchange of information and overcoming the conflict.

“We must move forward and build a shared future,” he said.

At the European Parliament, Buava also addressed Russia’s role. In his view, Moscow had contributed to the escalation of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict and was continuing to obstruct dialogue between Georgians and Abkhaz.

That same year, Buava opposed the adoption of the so-called “apartments law” in Abkhazia, saying he did not want Russians to buy property and settle in Abkhazia in large numbers. He regarded the main threat to Abkhazia as not the restoration of relations with Georgians, but the loss of its own demographic and cultural identity.

World.title: Georgian president pardons nine activists, one may face deportation to Russia
World.content:
Georgian president pardons nine activists

On the occasion of the Orthodox feast of Mariamoba (the Dormition of the Mother of God), Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned 226 prisoners. They included nine people detained during various protests. Georgian civil society groups and several organisations consider them political prisoners.

According to pro-government media, those pardoned include Denis Kulanin, a Russian citizen who, according to his lawyer, faces possible deportation.

World.title: Moscow posters: Are radical nationalists acting independently of Kremlin in Azerbaijan row?
World.content:
Protest at Azerbaijani embassy in Russia

On 27 August, at a time when independent political protests have become rare in Russia, a group of radical nationalists staged a protest outside Azerbaijan‘s diplomatic mission in Moscow. Participants put up three posters, filmed the action and posted the video on the group’s Telegram channel, which has tens of thousands of subscribers.

Azərbaycanın Rusiya səfirliyinin qonaq evi qarşısında naməlum şəxslər tərəfindən Azərbaycan əleyhinə təxribatın videosu pic.twitter.com/3CkEXuYacp — Unikal.az (@UnikalOrgPortal) August 27, 2026

Although the protest was small, it raises a question: can radical nationalists in Russia, where public expressions of opposition are tightly restricted, intervene in relations between Baku and Moscow without the Kremlin’s knowledge?

There is no clear answer so far. The issue is not whether the Kremlin learned about the protest after the event, but what boundaries the authorities set for the activities of such groups.

There is no evidence that the protest was organised at the request of the Russian authorities. However, the fact that the same group has now targeted Azerbaijan for a second time, coupled with the authorities’ differing treatment of public expressions of political views, raises questions about whether such groups may receive preferential treatment.

What accusations appeared on the three posters?

According to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry, the posters were placed not outside the main embassy building but in front of its guest house. The protest was covered by the Telegram channel Direct Action Z, which describes itself as an information resource of Eduard Limonov’s Other Russia party.

The posters accused Azerbaijan’s State Security Service of torture and President Ilham Aliyev of covering it up. They also carried the slogans “Russian blood is on your hands” and “Hands off Russian citizens”.

In a statement, the organisers portrayed the detention of eight Russian nationals in Azerbaijan, criminal proceedings against Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev, Baku’s position on Ukraine and the deaths of Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh in 2023 as manifestations of a single “anti-Russian policy”. They also accused the Azerbaijani diaspora of running “shadow businesses”.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the incident as an “unacceptable provocation” and said it could be a continuation of what it alleges is a campaign against Azerbaijan by a number of Russian media outlets. Baku called on Moscow to investigate the incident and ensure the security of its diplomatic mission.

Azərbaycan Respublikasının Rusiya Federasiyasındakı Səfirliyinin qonaq evi qarşısında təxribatla bağlı açıqlama



⬇️⬇️⬇️https://t.co/YPLnFLJ4Mx



Statement on the provocation in front of the Guest House of the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Russian Federation… pic.twitter.com/D9TwDicyqr — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 27, 2026

Same group staged protest exactly one year ago

One detail that makes it difficult to dismiss the incident as a random street protest is the date. On 27 August 2025, three members of the same movement staged a protest outside the Azerbaijani consulate in St Petersburg. They were detained by police.

The accusations made at the time differed from those voiced now. The protesters opposed Baku’s alliance with Ankara, its support for Ukraine and Azerbaijan’s competition with Russia on the energy market. In the following months, individual pickets were also held outside the consulate under the slogan “Russophobia is a disease”.

The fact that the second protest took place exactly a year later gives the impression that it may be a continuation of the earlier campaign. However, the organisers did not say whether the date had been chosen deliberately.

Close to Kremlin or opposed to it?

The Other Russia of E. V. Limonov is an unregistered political organisation founded by former members of the National Bolshevik Party, which a Russian court designated as extremist and banned in 2007. Its ideology combines Russian nationalism, “Soviet nostalgia” and imperialist ideas.

Its members support Russia’s war against Ukraine, and some have fought on the Russian side. The movement’s Interbrigades unit has operated in Donbas since 2014. In this respect, the group’s foreign policy rhetoric does not contradict the Kremlin’s broader line.

However, this does not mean the organisation is directly controlled by the Kremlin. National Bolshevik activists have also protested against the Central Bank, Roskomnadzor and other state bodies. In October 2025, four members of the movement were detained during a protest outside the Central Bank. In February 2026, activists from the organisation placed a lock on the door of Roskomnadzor’s Moscow office before leaving the scene.

On 18 August, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that statements by Knyazev, Uralov and Chadayev did not reflect Moscow’s position towards Azerbaijan. In their latest statement on Azerbaijan, the National Bolsheviks, in turn, accused the Foreign Ministry of failing to defend the three men. The group claimed that the state was putting the interests of “foreign entities” above those of Russian citizens.

In other words, the protest was directed not only against Baku but also against Moscow’s own policy, which the organisers regard as “not tough enough”.

Question of preferential treatment

National Bolshevik activists themselves are also periodically detained and given administrative jail terms. It would therefore be an oversimplification to portray them as an untouchable group carrying out the Kremlin’s orders.

On the other hand, it is clear that political protests in Russia are not treated equally. According to the latest available data from OVD-Info, more than 20,000 detentions for expressing anti-war views were recorded between February 2022 and July 2025. At the same time, groups that support the war in Ukraine but call on the authorities to take a tougher line have been able to hold public events, raise donations and operate actively on social media.

The Counter Extremism Project, which researches extremist movements, describes the relationship between the Kremlin and the National Bolsheviks as an “uneasy alliance”: the group criticises the authorities and its members are periodically detained, but its activities in Ukraine and pro-war campaigning are generally treated with considerably greater tolerance.

This pattern does not prove that the protest outside Azerbaijan’s diplomatic mission was organised at the state’s behest. However, it once again raises the question of which protests the authorities immediately suppress and which they allow to proceed without intervention.

Defending rights or exerting ethnic pressure?

The situation of the Russian nationals detained in Azerbaijan continues to raise questions that remain unanswered. In footage released after their detention, some appeared to have visible signs of violence on their faces. There have also been reports that the psychological condition of convicted Russian national Dmitry Fedorov has deteriorated and that he has stopped recognising his relatives.

However, the National Bolsheviks’ statement goes beyond defending the rights of individual detainees. It combines human rights concerns with rhetoric about “Russian blood”, criticism of Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine and accusations directed at the Azerbaijani diaspora as a whole.

World.title: Why is Russian tourist boom in Abkhazia giving way to falling demand? Video from Pitsunda
World.content:
Russian tourists in Abkhazia

Pitsunda is perhaps the most popular tourist destination in Abkhazia. The town receives around 20–25% of all incoming tourist traffic, thanks to the high-rise Pitsunda Resort complex and its private accommodation sector.

The overwhelming majority of tourists visiting Abkhazia come from Russia, meaning the success or failure of the tourist season largely depends on the situation there.

Even before international sanctions were imposed on Russia following the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, Abkhazia received around 1.2–1.5 million tourists per season, with Pitsunda already operating at the limits of its ageing accommodation capacity.

At the time, Abkhazia was marketed as a budget alternative to neighbouring Russia’s Sochi. Infrastructure problems — including water and electricity shortages and ageing utility networks — existed even then, but were viewed more tolerantly because of the low cost of holidays.

After the start of the war in Ukraine, Abkhazia saw an unprecedented influx of Russian tourists. A record 1.88 million people visited in 2025.

Demand increased as many countries introduced restrictions affecting Russian citizens.

But since the start of the 2026 season, demand for holidays in Abkhazia has fallen noticeably, by 15–20%.

Experts cite several main reasons:

Increased competition. Inflation has pushed prices in Abkhazia to levels comparable with holidays in Turkey, Egypt and cheaper European destinations.

Legal and logistical barriers. In particular, border-crossing rules for children under 14 are creating significant difficulties.

● Infrastructure problems, including electricity and water outages at the height of the tourist season.

● Price dumping by major Russian tour operators, which is driving small local businesses out of the market.

● The threat to Pitsunda’s relict pine grove from uncontrolled construction.

● A general mismatch between the quality of service provided and the prices being charged.

What Abkhazia’s tourism market looks like

The private sector and guest houses account for 65–70% of the market, including small hotels, flats in apartment blocks and private homes in the villages of Ldzaa and Alahadzy. Most tourists choose these types of accommodation.

Large hotels, boarding houses and Soviet-era resorts, including the high-rise buildings of the Pitsunda Resort complex, as well as sanatoriums and newer mid-sized hotels, account for 30–35% of the market. However, they attract the lion’s share of the most lucrative tourists — those who book organised tours and package holidays.

Positive developments over the past couple of years include the partial modernisation of old Soviet-era resort buildings, the opening of modern boutique hotels in Ldzaa and the digitalisation of services, with a shift towards online booking and cashless payments.

Private accommodation sector reluctant to pay taxes

The main economic problem is that an estimated 60–70% of private accommodation providers have operated in the shadow economy for years, without paying full taxes into the local budget.

In recent years, the authorities have sought to tighten oversight by introducing a patent-based tax system for the self-employed and mandatory classification of accommodation providers. However, these measures have been slow to take hold.

World.title: Azerbaijan to host 4th International Conference on Missing Persons
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. The 4th International Conference on Missing Persons will be held in Azerbaijan as part of the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons.

This was announced by the State Commission on Prisoners of War, Missing Persons, and Hostages.

The main theme of this conference will be “Strengthening Trust and Developing Effective Mechanisms and Solutions in Addressing the Issue of Missing Persons.”

“One of the main focuses of the current discussions will be building and strengthening trust between the parties. Experience shows that real progress in determining the fate of missing persons is impossible without cooperation, transparency, and the timely provision of accurate information.

In this regard, special attention will be paid to providing complete information about missing persons, including available data on the locations of mass and individual graves, as well as to discussing opportunities for joint humanitarian efforts by the parties to the conflict to search for, locate, and identify missing persons.”

The information notes that the conference aims not only to facilitate discussions but also to promote the development of practical and sustainable mechanisms that build trust and cooperation, ensure families’ right to know the truth, facilitate the exchange of information, and expand the use of modern forensic, DNA, and technological capabilities.

“Representatives of states, international organizations, experts, families, and other stakeholders will gather once again in Baku to discuss ways to translate humanitarian cooperation into concrete results. For thousands of families, the uncertainty has lasted far too long. Trust begins with information. Cooperation must lead to answers,” the statement reads.

World.title: Tajikistan, UN discuss water, climate initiatives and sustainable development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. Tajikistan and the UN discussed the country’s international initiatives on water, glaciers, climate change and sustainable development.

This was announced by the press service of the Tajik President, following the meeting between President Emomali Rahmon and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).

According to the information, during the meeting, Emomali Rahmon expressed appreciation to the UN Secretary-General for his congratulatory message on the adoption of the resolution proclaiming the “Decade of Strengthening Peace for Future Generations” and for the UN’s continued support for Tajikistan’s international initiatives.

The Tajik president emphasized that achieving the goals of the decade would contribute to further strengthening peace and stability internationally.

For his part, Antonio Guterres highlighted Tajikistan’s role in addressing global water-related challenges and promoting the international agenda on glaciers.

"Thanks to Tajikistan, the issue of water resources has become one of the central topics of international discussions. In addition, Tajikistan plays a leading role in promoting the international agenda on glaciers," Antonio Guterres said.

The UN secretary-general also reaffirmed the organization’s support for Tajikistan’s initiatives and its readiness to assist the country in its development efforts.

Emomali Rahmon, in turn, said Tajikistan fully supports the UN leadership’s efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals through 2030, restore trust, resolve conflicts and disputes, address the consequences of climate change, prevent biodiversity loss and improve the socio-economic situation of countries.

The sides also discussed the role of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Emomali Rahmon noted that Tajikistan had taken these objectives into account when presenting a draft resolution on the role of artificial intelligence in creating new opportunities for sustainable development in Central Asia.

Climate change, the rapid melting of glaciers, depletion of water resources and the growing risk of natural disasters were identified as major challenges facing the international community.

In this context, Emomali Rahmon highlighted Tajikistan’s efforts to strengthen international cooperation in the water and climate sectors within the framework of the Dushanbe Water Process.

The Tajik president also referred to the planned UN Water Conference in Dushanbe in 2028 and proposed establishing a “Dushanbe Water Framework Program” as a strategic mechanism for guiding international cooperation in the water sector.

The sides also exchanged views on other regional and international issues of mutual interest.
