World.title: ‘The time has come’: Argentine great Lionel Messi retires from international football
World.content:
Lionel Messi has ended his career as a player for the Argentine national team at 39 years old, after nearly two decades representing the national side.

Messi, who played in six World Cups, won the tournament in Qatar in 2022 and led Argentina to the final in 2026 losing to Spain.

“It was a decision that hurt – and still hurts deep down – but I understand that the time has come,” the 39-year-old posted on Instagram. “I swear to you that I always gave it my all – not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football.”

Messi explained that he wrote his retirement letter on July 21 – two days after losing the World Cup final – but waited to publish it because his father was facing health issues that eventually claimed his life.

World.title: Buckley ‘rapt’ fellow Collingwood icon Pendlebury is moving out of the Magpie nest
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Buckley ‘rapt’ fellow Collingwood icon Pendlebury is moving out of the Magpie nest Scott Spits September 1, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nathan Buckley says he is rapt about Scott Pendlebury’s late-career shift from Collingwood to Gold Coast, declaring that by making such a move now the AFL’s games record holder will be “super ready” for his next AFL career step. Collingwood great Buckley – who coached Pendlebury between 2012 and 2021, a large portion of which Pendlebury was Pies captain – said the 442-game AFL veteran would have made the best decision “based on all the available evidence”. Pendlebury has decided to accept a four-year contract from the Suns, which will include two years as a player and two as a coach. There are options for that deal to be modified if Pendlebury cannot see out the term on the field. He will be 40 by the end of the two-year playing contract. Loading “He’s not going to be a player forever, and this is the perfect lead-in to whatever aspirations he has beyond that,” Buckley said on Fox Footy’s On The Couch on Monday night.



“I’m rapt to see him move out of Collingwood, go to another environment, learn more there, and be super ready to take whatever the next steps are.” Pendlebury’s management and Collingwood boss Craig Kelly are in discussions for the dual premiership player and five-time Copeland Trophy winner to be paraded at a Magpies home game early next season at a time that also suits his new club. The Pies will also pay tribute to him at their best-and-fairest function. Collingwood captain Scott Pendlebury and coach Nathan Buckley talk tactics in 2021. Getty Images Buckley backed Pendlebury’s decision to reveal his decision on Saturday morning – after their season ended with a wildcard final loss to the Western Bulldogs. Collingwood supporters farewelled fellow club great Steele Sidebottom, but they – and Pendlebury’s teammates – were left in the dark about his move. “He was commiserating with his teammates after the siren,” Buckley said. “I guarantee you none of them would have been aware of what was going on at that point because you do hold your counsel until the appropriate time, and the appropriate time was on the Saturday morning.”



Buckley said Pendlebury would continue to be an on-field asset for Gold Coast coach Damien Hardwick. “I’ve got no doubt that it looked like he was sore as the year went on,” he said. “But what’s to say that that wasn’t a response to the colder months? “He has structured up that Collingwood side and pulled them together and been the on-field coach and Craig McRae’s proxy on-field when it’s required.

World.title: In limbo, ‘in pieces’: State of Andrews statue revealed as Carroll confesses $60,000 spent
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD In limbo, ‘in pieces’: State of Andrews statue revealed as Carroll confesses $60,000 spent Fiona Byrne and Christine Lacy Updated September 1, 2026 — 12:02am ,first published 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What to do with a problem like a Daniel Andrews statue that no one wants any more after you’ve spent $60,000 on it? It turns out the now-cancelled plan to erect a statue of Andrews has so far led to that amount being paid on a contract worth $134,000. Premier Ben Carroll has axed the statue of former premier Daniel Andrews. Joe Armao Premier Ben Carroll revealed the figure on ABC Radio Melbourne late on Monday afternoon. “Half of the contract has been paid, which is around $60,000, and the design work had commenced,” Carroll said, before blaming former premier Jeff Kennett for the statue stuff-up.



“This was a Liberal Party policy under Jeff Kennett of doing statues of premiers. I believe our statues, particularly on the Labor side of politics, are hospitals and schools.” He added that having future taxpayer-funded statues of former premiers didn’t pass the pub test. The Daniel Andrews statue had been commissioned by Jacinta Allan in March. Chris Hopkins When Carroll pulled the pin on the divisive project at the weekend, he told reporters he had no idea how advanced the construction of the taxpayer-funded Andrews statue was, so CBD did some digging and discovered design work had started and some casts had been made. The early stages of the dumped statue project are apparently sitting in pieces in a Fitzroy foundry. CBD has been told by people unauthorised to speak publicly that instructions are yet to be received on the next move for the unloved proposed work of art.



Whether the early design work amounts to a full Dan or is simply a collection of proposed appendages with other bits still to be moulded is unclear. Even the identity of the sculptor remains unclear. The statue was commissioned by then-premier Jacinta Allan back in March, and when news of its dumping broke, Kennett suggested the statue be recast in honour of US singer Dolly Parton, who died last week. Nice idea. Shadow federal treasurer Tim Wilson even joined the conversation, telling Nine’s Today show there was serious risk that if the statue did see the light of day it could become a public urinal. Carroll said that while the Dan plan would be scrapped, the contract to build a statue would not be cancelled and an independent panel would come up with an alternative subject for it. The make-up of that panel is still to be revealed. Carroll’s decision to axe the Dan monument is part of his move to clean up the PR mess he inherited when he took the reins of the government. Keep swinging that axe, Ben.



Payne rides into ‘mum mode’ When Michelle Payne marked last November a decade since her history-making victory in the 2015 Melbourne Cup, she described it as the closing of an extraordinary chapter. Michelle Payne is expecting her first child. Alex Coppel/Supplied Now, she is writing a new chapter as she prepares to start a family. Payne, 40, is five months pregnant with her first child, with partner Gabriel Ribeiro. “I felt like I did everything I could in achieving my goal of winning the Melbourne Cup, and as the first female to ride the winner I wanted to give back to racing and to women and sport,” Payne told CBD.



“That was something I felt was important to do. Then [after the 10-year anniversary] it was time to focus on myself and my own dreams, and everything has fitted into place. “It is super-duper exciting. I’m feeling so excited and scared because it’s a whole new chapter that is just so foreign to me, even though I’ve been around lots of sisters that have had children and my brother, Patrick. Payne is making big changes in her life 10 years on from her victory in the Melbourne Cup. Alex Coppel/Supplied “I’m definitely not taking it lightly, but it is just really exciting at the same time because it is a real privilege to fall pregnant naturally.” Payne, who grew up in the public eye as part of the thoroughbred racing Payne family – she was one of 10 children, eight of whom became jockeys – and had her life story told in the Rachel Griffiths-directed film Ride Like A Girl, said having a family had been a long-held goal.



“Right from when I was a little girl it was winning the Melbourne Cup and having a family of my own; they were certainly at the top of my list,” she said. Related Article Good Weekend Michelle Payne’s rise to the top was swift – then came stalkers, the agony and the heartbreak With Payne’s baby due in January, Ribeiro’s mother recently visited from Brazil. “She could not be any more excited or supportive,” said Payne, who is working with DrinkWise to urge women to avoid alcohol during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. “It is great to have the support of a great partner and his family. We are over the moon.”



In further change, Payne has placed her thoroughbred training property at Ballarat on the market. “If the right buyer comes along, that would be fantastic, but if not, it is a great property and investment to have,” she said. For now, Payne is in “mum mode” and is “just totally focused on giving this little person the best start to life that they can have”. ‘Franchise’ move by top comic There were some slick moves by funny guy Anthony “Lehmo” Lehmann on Saturday night, and not just on the dance floor, when he managed to be virtually in two places at once.



Lehmann was a celebrity guest at the My Room charity ball at Crown Palladium but disappeared from his table just after entree, only to return as mains were plated. In the intervening time he bolted to the NGV to do a stand-up set at the Brainwave charity gala. Anthony “Lehmo” Lehmann Getty Images Social media revealed his double dip. CBD is not having a crack. We’re just impressed at the multitasking on show. And he got good laughs at the Brainwave event.



“I’ve franchised myself out,” Lehmann quipped when CBD checked in on his Saturday dinner circuit sprint. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter Shane Wright September 1, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Property values are falling in almost every suburb in the country, with $40,000 wiped from the median value of the nation’s homes through winter as high interest rates, the federal government’s budget tax changes and low levels of affordability crunch the entire market. Figures released by Cotality show the value of 93 per cent of all properties in capital city suburbs fell during winter, double the proportion that had gone backwards during autumn, creating an economic problem for the Reserve Bank and a political issue for the Albanese government. Across the nation’s capital cities, dwelling values dropped by 1.1 per cent in August to be down by 3.7 per cent over the past three months. The median value slipped to $990,394 compared to the $1.03 million recorded at the start of winter. Regional values are also falling, down by 0.4 per cent last month to be 1.2 per cent lower through the quarter.



The downturn is being driven by Sydney, where dwelling values dropped by 1.4 per cent in August to be down by a nation-leading 4.7 per cent through winter. The city’s median house value dropped by 1.8 per cent last month, taking it below $1.5 million for the first time in more than a year. Related Article Property prices In a slump: Warning house prices won’t rebound until 2028 Values fell in every capital city bar Darwin, easing by 1.1 per cent in Melbourne and Canberra, 1 per cent in Brisbane, 0.8 per cent in Adelaide and Perth and by 0.2 per cent in Hobart. Sydney and Melbourne values are down by 4.6 per cent and 4.7 per cent respectively from August last year. By contrast, values are still 15.6 per cent higher in Perth, by 14.6 per cent in Darwin and 10.8 per cent in Brisbane. The nation’s property slowdown accelerated after Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions in the May budget.



The government has said its changes are aimed at improving housing affordability for young Australians. Despite the drop in values this year, every city bar Melbourne is still up on where it was five years ago while values in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth are more than double their 2016 levels. But it has faced an increasingly strident political attack over the fallout from the tax changes, with the Coalition accusing the government of trying to “destroy” the wealth of Australians held in their homes. House values across the nation have fallen through winter. Joe Armao House values, particularly among the most expensive properties, are falling fastest and are down by 3.3 per cent so far this year. By contrast, the values of units and apartments have slipped by 1.8 per cent through 2026. Cotality’s research director Tim Lawless said values had now fallen for five consecutive months to sit 3.6 per cent below their peak in March.



He said demand across the entire market was falling while the number of homes up for sale was 24 per cent up on the same point last year. “What started as a more concentrated easing across higher-value segments has now become a much

more generalised softening, with the vast majority of capital city suburbs recording some level of decline,” he said. “The shift in selling conditions means buyers are generally facing less competition, while vendors are having to be more realistic on price as stock levels rise and days on market extend.” Property prices started to slow in February when the Reserve Bank delivered the first of three interest rate hikes so far this year. Markets believe the bank will push the cash rate to 4.6 per cent by November to deal with high inflation.



The bank’s efforts to curb inflation have been challenged by the fallout from the war against Iran, with oil prices pushing up above the $US90 a barrel on Monday. The International Energy Agency warned global oil supply was likely to be down 4.3 million barrels a day this year with current inventories being drawn down “at a rapid pace”. Figures released on Monday by the country’s prudential regulator showed growth in the value of investor mortgages held by the Commonwealth, Westpac, NAB and Westpac banks slowed through July in further confirmation that the budget changes have pushed many investors out of the property market. Cotality’s Tim Lawless says the spring real estate market is likely to be tough for those looking to sell. Janie Barrett Lawless noted that at the start of the slowdown in the market, values for low-priced homes – dominated by first home buyers – had held up. But even this sector was now in decline, with the situation not likely to improve through the spring selling season. “Premium markets are still generally recording weaker conditions, but lower-priced housing is becoming less insulated as affordability pressures and softer demand weigh more evenly across the market,” he said.



Related Article Population Australia’s big squeeze: How 6 million people went into a handful of areas “Even though values have already moved lower, the combination of sticky inflation, the prospect of higher rates and ongoing pressure on household budgets suggests demand is likely to remain subdued through spring.” There are signs the rental market is easing, despite it remaining historically tight. The rental vacancy rate eased to 1.9 per cent, its highest level since January last year. Asking rents, however, have climbed by 5.7 per cent over the past 12 months. They are now 39 per cent, or about $200 a week, up over the past five years. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Opposition goes loco with $1.7 billion transport pitch
World.content:
A new fleet of hybrid trains that can run on suburban and country tracks would finally deliver a long-promised boost to rail services for people living in Melbourne’s booming west under a $1.7 billion public transport pitch to be announced by the Coalition. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson will on Tuesday promise that bi-mode trains similar to those already in use in NSW and South Australia would bring commuters living along the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines onto a metropolitan system years before Labor’s promised electrification of those lines. A bi-mode train being tested in New South Wales. Jenper The revised western rail plan, which comes eight years after the Andrews government pledged to electrify outer-suburban lines in Melbourne’s fastest-growing population corridor, promises to deliver 25 new trains within the next term of parliament. Bi-mode trains, which have been used for a decade in Europe, access overhead power lines while on suburban tracks and switch to a secondary diesel or battery-powered source of energy when on country tracks.



Labor’s electrification program, which was promised at both the 2018 and 2022 state elections, has been delayed until after a new station is built at Sunshine, and suburban, country and freight services are separated at the major rail junction. The $4 billion station works are not due to be completed until 2030. The Carroll government will open an upgraded Melton Station on Tuesday. Wilson said that while a Coalition government would remain committed to electrifying the two lines, hybrid trains would deliver better services more quickly to suburbs where peak-hour commuters are being left stranded on platforms because of jam-packed trains. “Labor has twice promised and twice failed to deliver the modern train services communities across Melton and Wyndham Vale deserve,” she said. “Our plan will deliver metro-quality train services to Melbourne’s west sooner – meaning more trains, more seats and greater capacity.” The opposition’s public transport pitch, aimed at frustrated voters in Melbourne’s west, reflects a dramatically altered political contest leading up to the November state election, with both the Coalition and One Nation targeting some of Labor’s “dead red” seats. The Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates that since the 2016 census, the Melton local government area has swelled from 135,000 to 231,000 people while the City of Wyndham’s population has grown from 217,000 to 348,000.



That is a combined increase of 227,000 people over 10 years. Editor's pick Exclusive

Public transport The secret rail plan to tackle ‘crush’ hour in Melbourne’s north and west Victorian Department of Transport data shows that between 2019 and 2024, passenger numbers at eight stations on the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines – which currently carry diesel-powered V/Line trains – surged by 26 per cent. In 2025, The Age revealed the government had obtained a secret report warning of “crush” conditions at railway stations across Melbourne’s fast-growing northern and western suburbs – circumstances where trains are forced to leave passengers behind on a station platform – unless the rail system was overhauled. The document supported electrifying the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines, and said commuters could be left waiting on platforms if action wasn’t taken within the next five to 10 years.



This is already a regular rush-hour occurrence at stations such as Tarneit, which was opened in 2015. It sits on the Wyndham Vale line, which is serviced by V/Line trains running from Geelong to Melbourne. Opposition public transport spokesman Matthew Guy said the new rolling stock would enable the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines to access suburban tracks after Sunshine and run through either the City Loop or Metro Tunnel, and allow more services to be run along the lines. Suburban trains, because of their standing room, can also take more passengers than a V/Line train of comparable length. Guy said the “crush” capacity of a six-car VLocity train was 444 passengers, but a six-car suburban train could squeeze in 1300 people. “Suburban passengers should be on suburban trains,” Guy said. “We don’t think that Melton and Wyndham line commuters can wait a decade for suburban trains.



“It is much faster, much cheaper and a realistic answer to the problem of getting suburban trains to the western suburbs.” Guy said hybrid trains would also reduce the air pollution at the busy Southern Cross station, which becomes thick with diesel fumes when too many country trains are idling at the platforms. V/Line trains idling at Southern Cross Station. Luis Enrique Ascui The opposition has also promised to establish an independent Public Transport Victoria board to improve governance of rail and bus services. In 2025, Victorian transport tsar Jeroen Weimar, who left his role as secretary last week, told the West of Melbourne Summit that the Melton line would be electrified after the $4.1 billion untangling of the track around Sunshine station and rebuild of nearby stations was completed in 2030.



Weimar said the government was exploring the use of battery-powered trains to deliver capacity improvements on the Wyndham Vale line, which would follow the Sunshine and Melton upgrades. The Victorian and Commonwealth governments have together committed $152 million to develop its plan to electrify Melton and Wyndham Vale lines. Two sources with knowledge of the plan said the full cost had been estimated at a staggering $8 billion. Editor's pick Suburban Rail Loop How Allan, ministers decided to hide public transport levy in secret talks Rail Futures Institute president John Hearsch said bi-mode trains would be more expensive than VLocity models, the latest model rolled out by V/Line. “It is technically possible and happening in other places, but … ultimately, the operating costs will be higher than a straight electric train,” he said.



“The advantages of it over the existing trains are pretty small.” Hearsch said the bigger issue was that there wasn’t enough track space between Sunshine and the CBD to fit all the services needed to give Melton and Wyndham Vale frequencies comparable to other suburban lines. Transport experts believe the proposed Melbourne Metro 2, another underground rail line to compliment the Metro Tunnel line, could solve this problem by creating a cross-city route that would serve as a second rail corridor connecting the western suburbs to the city. Hearsch said the institute believed in the short term that batteries should replace the auxiliary engines on VLocity trains, which would reduce pollution at Southern Cross Station. World.title: The Perth suburbs where home values are starting to drop
World.content:
PropertyNewsProperty market The Perth suburbs where home values are starting to drop Indigo Lemay-Conway September 1, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New data has laid bare the impact of a national housing downturn, with home values in Perth dropping by 3.2 per cent over the last quarter, according to Cotality. The research group’s latest Home Value Index, released on Tuesday, revealed Beaconsfield, Jane Brook and Southern River topped the list of suburbs that saw the greatest property value drops from May to August. However, real estate agents say the data doesn’t reflect the situation they see on the ground. Cotality executive research director Tim Lawless said this was the fourth month that property values had slowly declined.



“In the last five years, we’ve seen housing values across Perth up about 80 per cent, and if you include the last six years, they’ve more than doubled,” Lawless said. “So I think this was inevitable, despite the fact that there were some headwinds from higher interest rates, and low sentiment, and a sharp pullback in investments, this downturn was inevitable.” Cotality bases its WA market research on Landgate data, which helps determine the group’s Home Value Index. The index measures the movements in the value of Australian housing markets using a methodology combining transacted sale prices, as well as land area, geographical location, and the number of bedrooms and bathrooms in a property. Lawless said the property value drops reported in WA were “pretty broad-based” and not suburb-specific.



“We’re seeing the majority of Perth suburbs are declining in value now,” he said. “So there’s a broad-based pattern where we’re seeing housing values trending lower. Across Perth, 97 per cent of suburbs were down in value over the past three months. “But when you look at that list, there’s a whole bunch of different suburbs in here, and some are quite expensive. “Beaconsfield’s got a median dwelling value of $1.4 million, Swanbourne has a median of $2.6 million, and getting down to some of the more affordable areas, [there are suburbs] around Kwinana, or getting out to Gosnells.”



The 3 per cent of suburbs in Perth that resisted the property value drops were concentrated in more affluent regions of the city. Related Article WA residential property This WA mining town is one of Australia’s fastest-growing property markets “The areas where we’re actually seeing values rising, they do seem to have a predominance of the fairly expensive markets,” Lawless said. “So you’ve got Dalkeith, for example, a 3.4 per cent rise over the past three months, as well as Peppermint Grove – they’re two of Perth’s most expensive markets.” Lawless said these suburbs tended to be more resilient to property trends.



“There really does seem to be a theme in this list where if you went back, say 12 months ago, a lot of these really high-end suburbs were generally in the middle to lower end of the pack in terms of the rate of growth,” he said. “But it does seem like they are a lot more insulated or resilient to value falls as the market moves through this downturn, which probably speaks to simply the fact that I think home owners or prospective buyers at that ultra-high end of the market are probably less sensitive to things like affordability challenges and changes in interest rates.” Coming in at number six on the list for suburbs that saw property values fall was Hilton, on the outskirts of Fremantle, where the Cotality index reported a 5.3 per cent reduction in values over the last three months. But C&CO Real Estate director Lauri Curtain, whose office sits in the heart of the suburbs, said there had been no sign of prices declining.



“To hear [there was a] 5 per cent is actually amazing. We had a property that we listed a few weeks ago at 2A Howson Street, and the price guide was offers from $1.15 million, and it’s now in an unconditional pending settlement for $1.235 million,” she said. Related Article Exclusive

Schools How Perth’s most in-demand schools impact nearby property prices “Then I sold 12A Collick Street which was asking $1.15 million, and I sold it for $1.15 million. “So in our office, we certainly haven’t had any properties selling below the price guide.” Curtain said the recorded value drop could be linked to agents overpricing their homes and having to reduce to the more standard pricing for a property of its value.



“If something comes on, and it’s overpriced, buyers are going to look past that property and wait for something else to come on, because there’s more stock coming on,” she said. White House Property Partners advisor Connie Handcock also said prices haven’t been impacted at her agency, which is based in East Fremantle. “The market has calmed down, there’s no doubt. However, the prices haven’t really been impacted greatly, it’s just they’re taking longer to sell,” she said. “Instead of selling on the first weekend, we may have to open it maybe three, four weekends before we get a result that’s acceptable to the seller.



“If there has been a shift, it’s very slight and personally, I think they were probably a little inflated because of the frenzy initially, so they’ve calmed down and probably come back to where they should be.” Related Article Property prices Two suburbs dominate the top 10 list of Perth’s most expensive streets Ray White property consultant Marisa Rifici said she had not noticed a reduction in property prices in Beaconsfield either, but acknowledged prices across Perth did seem to be heading in a downward trajectory. “I think we’ve still got a shortage of homes, but I haven’t necessarily noticed that the prices have dropped dramatically in Beaconsfield,” she said. “We’re definitely not seeing the fear of missing out, which we were seeing earlier on in the year too.”



Lawless said it looked like it could be the beginning of a downturn in property prices in WA. “I think this is early days for this housing downturn, including Perth,” he said. “Normally markets do have some momentum, so the fact that we’ve only entered this downturn over the past four months, I think probably suggests, at least on a historical level, we probably have some way to go.”

World.title: ‘The homes we build twice’: Repair bill for climate disasters climbing faster than inflation
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeClimate crisis ‘The homes we build twice’: Repair bill for climate disasters climbing faster than inflation Caitlin Fitzsimmons August 31, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Solving the housing shortage faces an overlooked competitor – the $11.3 billion spent rebuilding and repairing homes damaged by extreme weather over the past 4½ years. The Insurance Council of Australia describes them as “the homes we build twice”, noting they suck up the resources needed to build new homes without increasing housing supply. Sheep grazing near a bushfire in Longwood East, in north-east Victoria, in January. Jason South In 2025 alone, declared catastrophes damaged 145,392 homes nationwide – almost as many as the 172,657 new homes completed that year, the council’s annual Insurance Catastrophe Resilience Report said. Between January 2022 and June 2026, insurers received 409,094 claims relating to declared catastrophes and significant weather events at a total insured cost of $11.3 billion.



Insurance Council chief executive Andrew Hall said every insurance claim drew on the same builders, trades and materials needed to deliver new housing, while growing demand for AI data centre construction and the 2032 Olympic Games would add further demand to an already stretched sector. “Australia will not tackle the housing shortage while disasters keep pushing existing homes back into the repair queue, which is why resilience investment must be a core part of the government’s national housing strategy,” Hall said. The cost of building is climbing faster than inflation, with the report noting that the sharpest increases occurred in the materials and trades most relied upon after disasters. Cotality’s Cordell Construction Cost Index, which measures the cost to construct a home rather than its market value, rose 30 per cent in the five years to March 2026. The consumer price index rose 24 per cent over the same period.



Natural disasters such as storms have increased demand for building. Louie Douvis The cost of roof tiles increased 77 per cent in five years – more than three times CPI – the Cotality figures suggest. Windows, plaster, plywood, copper piping, structural steel, cement and concrete climbed between 37 and 48 per cent. The rising costs of roof, window and plaster products – elements commonly damaged by hail, storms and cyclones – were among the largest increases. Labour costs followed a similar trend, with roofers and glaziers recording the most significant wage growth. The cost to build is higher in remote and regional areas, with Alice Springs in the Northern Territory and Broome in Western Australia among the most expensive in the country. In NSW, the cost to build a home in Broken Hill has risen from $395,000 to $555,000, a 40.51 per cent increase in five years. In Wodonga, in Victoria, it’s a 43.01 per cent increase, from $379,000 to $542,000. Scott Hawkins, managing director for Australasia at global reinsurance company Munich RE, said the rising costs were connected to global supply chain disruptions.



“In Australia, we’re largely a net importer of a lot of the goods that go into construction, and therefore we could be more exposed than someone who does that themselves locally,” Hawkins said. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster “I wouldn’t see that as an Australian-only topic. If we see what’s happened in the world in the last few years with supply chain disruptions, inflation globally has been at elevated levels. All of those things flow through to construction costs, and also the labour costs that go with that.” The Insurance Council is calling on governments to reform state taxes and levies that increase the cost of insurance, establish a Flood Defence Fund at a cost of $30.15 billion over 10 years to protect the most at-risk communities, strengthen the federal government’s Disaster Ready Fund, and prevent development of homes in high-risk locations. Since 2019, the peak body for the insurance industry has declared 29 extreme weather events, totalling $20.7 billion, from more than 760,720 home and building claims.



In the 2025-26 financial year alone, there were $3.98 billion in losses incurred across 147,552 claims. The most expensive insurance event was severe storms and hail in Queensland and NSW over eight days in November 2025, which exceeded $2.2 billion in damage spread across 95,692 claims – an average of $23,252 a claim. The Victorian bushfires in January 2026 resulted in smaller losses for the industry but bigger individual claims, with $599 million in insured losses across 4852 claims, or $123,378 on average per claim. Insured losses from events declared by the Insurance Council since 2019 Three bushfire events – $2.58 billion from 22,451 claims

One cyclone – $374.2 million from 6696 claims

Sixteen floods – $11.47 billion from 486,109 claims

Three storms – $2.62 billion from 119,670 claims

Five hail events – $3.51 billion from 108,573 claims

One earthquake – $90.7 million from 17,221 claims Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Crown alleges minor traffic accident led to murder as Lok Fung Lorrence Li trial begins
World.content:
How does a minor traffic accident lead to double murder?

That is what Crown prosecutors have put forward as their version of events in the trial of Lok Fung Lorrence Li.

Li is accused of murdering Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong at their Ellerslie home in November 2023.

In the High Court at Auckland on Monday, Li entered guilty pleas through an interpreter to manslaughter, while pleading not guilty to murdering the couple.

Li also pleaded not guilty to a charge of conspiring to murder another person, who has name suppression.

He had been charged alongside another man, Shu Man Poon, who jurors were told earlier admitted to his role in the murder.

Poon was expected to give evidence later in Li's trial.

Prosecutor Harrison Bell gave jurors the Crown's account of the night of the murder.

Kwok, who was a theatre nurse at Auckland's North Shore Hospital, had arrived home from work late the night before the murder.

Two hours later, the Crown said Li along with Poon arrived in a car with a stolen license plate, went into the home, and attacked Kwok.

Kwok was shot with an air gun, and stabbed four times in the chest and once in the neck, killing him, Bell said.

Mei Han Chong who was also in the home was killed by blunt force trauma to the head, before being taken out to Greenhithe on the city's North Shore, where her body was dumped, the Crown submitted.

"What possessed these men to act in such a violent way, killing two people?" Bell asked.

"The Crown says the answer begins with Mr Li."

Bell said about 11 months earlier, Li and Kwok had been involved in a traffic accident.

Li was told by Kwok's insurance that he was at fault, and the issue was taken to the Disputes Tribunal.

"The Crown says as a result of that grievance and having received the Kwok's home address from disclosure received from the Disputes Tribunal proceedings, Mr Li decided to go to the Kwok's address, intending to kill them, and he enlisted the assistance of Mr Poon in doing so," Bell said.

Bell explained that Kwok was found by his son, who was expecting a visit from his parents in Hamilton.

"He entered the house, saw his father lying on the floor with the smell of death, as he describes it," Bell said.

The trial was also expected to go through a conspiracy between Poon and Li to murder another person, going so far as to travel to her property and spray paint over the security cameras, before being interrupted by a vehicle on the street, Bell said.

Li had received an email from the Disputes Tribunal earlier that same day, with the Kwok's address attached, he said.

"Mr Li's murderous plan shifted at that point from [the person] to the Kwok's, or to Mr Kwok and anyone else they might encounter in his house," the Crown submitted.

It was the Crown's case that Li was not a bystander in the murder, but in fact the instigator of the murders.

"It might be suggested to you that this was all Mr Poon and that Mr Li did not knowingly participate in making the plan or assist in any way with the killings of the Kwoks as alleged by the Crown," Bell said.

"The evidence, once you've heard it all, you may agree, does not support that proposition."

The Crown could not say which of the two men dealt the fatal blows to the Kwok's, but did not need to, Bell said.

One of Li's defence lawyer, Rosemary Thomson, told jurors what happened to the Kwok's was a tragedy, that should never have happened.

"There is nothing that I'm going to say in my opening or indeed the defence is going to say throughout the trial which should in any way suggest otherwise," she said.

She pointed the jury to Li's guilty plea of manslaughter.

"Mr Li has taken responsibility for his actions and accepts that he played a role."

Thomson said Li did not have the necessary intention to commit the murders.

"The trial will therefore proceed on the basis that it will be a matter for you whether the Crown can establish a murderous intent."

Thomson urged jurors to keep an open mind.

"All trials have two sides," she said.

"As judges, you need to keep an open mind until you have heard all of the evidence and the legal directions from Her Honour.

"It is only then you can start reaching some conclusions."

The trial is set to hear from its first witnesses on Tuesday.

Manslaughter within murder

Li had entered guilty pleas on Monday morning to manslaughter for both of the victims, despite not having those charges read out in the courtroom.

Justice Jane Anderson explained to the jury that every murder charge included within it a charge of manslaughter.

She said murder had three elements, the killing of one person by another, that the killing was done by an unlawful act, and intent.

"Not all homicides are blame worthy," she said.

"However, the criminal law intervenes when a homicide is caused by an unlawful act."

World.title: Meet the Northland farmer turned baby blanket knitter
World.content:
Meet Dargaville's prolific baby blanket knitter Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A retired Northland farmer has found fulfilment by knitting hundreds of woollen blankets for premature babies.

Mike Gilligan, of Dargaville, said he had so far knitted about 600 of the colourful, pint-sized blankets, with 47 delivered to Whangārei Hospital's Special Care Baby Unit this year alone.

The 76-year-old was first taught to knit by his wife, Edith, when they were newly married.

She was expecting their first child and he'd been put out of action by a horse kick that dislocated his knee.

"It was obvious that within a few weeks one or other of us was going to end up in a mental asylum, so Edith taught me to knit. Then through the years I knitted my own jerseys and jerseys for the boys."

Edith and Mike Gilligan with one of his bigger blankets, knitted for a granddaughter. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

However, Mike's hobby really took off once he retired.

Until then he'd been too busy working on dairy and kumara farms, plus the job left his hands ingrained with grime.

He started by knitting tiny cardigans for premature babies.

"But one of the nurses very politely said to me, 'Oh, we have old ladies that knit really beautiful cardigans', and I didn't do patterns very well. She said, 'What we need is blankets', so I've been doing it ever since."

These days Mike is the cornerstone of the Dargaville Craft Group that meets at the Gilligans' home twice a week to knit for various causes.

Mike Gilligan gets started on yet another baby blanket. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

He was not fazed by jibes that knitting was a women's pastime, or by being the only male in the group.

"They just accept me as I am. I'm the sort of person you take me as you see me or don't bother to take me at all."

Mike said he rarely met the families who were given his blankets, but he sometimes received thank-you letters.

"But I don't do it for thanks. I do it because I love doing it. The wife and I can just sit here and do our knitting together. I haven't got any other sort of interests other than sneaking off fishing with my son occasionally," he said.

Edith and Mike Gilligan in their happy place. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

He sometimes tried his hand at other items, such as gloves.

"I went up to visit a mate of mine in the old folks' home one day and his hands were cold. Old people don't like their fingers being covered so I came home and I knitted him a pair of fingerless gloves and took them to him the next day," Mike said.

"The lady sitting beside him said, 'Why is he so special? Why can't I have one?' Long story short, 59 pairs of gloves later, everybody in the rest home had them."

He had also raffled off a fire engine-themed blanket and donated the proceeds to Dargaville's volunteer fire brigade.

Mike said he had been contacted by people who wanted to buy his blankets but he had refused.

"As soon as you start selling things it becomes a chore. I'm not interested in chores and I'm not interested in making money out of it. I just do it for the pure enjoyment of doing it."

While Mike did the bulk of the knitting in the Gilligan household, the blankets were very much a team effort.

Edith's role was to take her husband's ideas, photos or images from the internet, and convert them into knitting 'graphs', using software designed for making cross-stitch patterns.

Edith Gilligan works on a knitting pattern based on a photo of a Dargaville fire truck. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

She said the aim was to find an image that would appeal to very small children, then simplify it and reduce the number of colours to make it knittable.

Edith said knitting kept them both sane.

"He was used to working flat out all day every day on the farms, so this keeps him occupied and keeps him out of my hair. And he enjoys it."

Dargaville fire chief Jason Campbell said the brigade first met Mike when he donated the proceeds of a blanket raffle.

"Since then he's given us another blanket with a fire truck on it to auction off," he said.

"What he does for the hospital, knitting blankets for the neonatal unit, is outstanding. It's good for the community to have people like Mike in it."

Farm themes feature frequently on Mike Gilligan's baby blankets, a nod to his former profession. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Whangārei Hospital clinical nurse manager Jules Dewhurst said the unit was "incredibly grateful" for the baby blankets donated by Gilligan and his knitting group.

They added warmth and comfort to the unit and featured cartoon characters, farm animals and colourful designs.

"Each blanket brings its own unique personality, something that parents absolutely love during what can be a challenging time," she said.

"They're also the perfect fit for our bassinets, making them both practical and special. These handmade blankets are treasured by our families and help create a sense of care and connection for our tiniest patients."

Mike said he had no plans to put down his knitting needles.

World.title: Most young people 'following their noses' to find work, not dodging student loans, economist says
World.content:
Young people who left New Zealand in recent times might have been forced to do so by the employment market, economists say, rather than deliberately choosing to take their skills offshore.

National announced at the weekend it would cut the repayment rate for New Zealand-based student loan borrowers from 12 percent of their income to 10 percent from April next year.

The repayments become compulsory once someone earns more than $24,128 a year.

But overseas borrowers will face stiffer penalties.

Finance Minister Nicola Willis said it was not fair that graduates could take their skills offshore after receiving a heavily subsidised tertiary education, and not repay their loans.

Interest is applied to student loans when someone is out of the country for more than six months.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

National said it would add 1 percent to the interest rate, taking it to 6.6 percent at the current rate, with tiered penalties for sustained default, on top of existing late payment interest.

They would also have to clear their student loan before accessing KiwiSaver and there would be tighter arrest settings for serious and sustained defaults.

Overseas borrowers account for 93 percent of student loan debt and only about 30 percent meet their repayment obligations in a typical year, compared to 95 percent of borrowers within New Zealand.

The total number of New Zealand-based student loan borrowers increased by 0.8 percent in the year to March, and the number of overseas-based borrowers lifted 0.3 percent.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said it was a challenging job market for young people.

"You have to find a job where you can find one. Youth unemployment is very high right now… you could understand that people that are in that part of the labour force, they're probably just following their noses in terms of where the opportunities are. And it tends to be overseas as much as within New Zealand."

He said it was prudent for the government to try to have student loans repaid more quickly from people who were overseas, when there was a higher default rate among them.

But he said it might be seen as unfair to increase their interest rate.

He said higher repayments for student loans were unlikely to be the deciding factor for anyone weighing up whether to move. "I think they're much more driven by changes in the labour market status in New Zealand versus overseas."

'Fewer New Zealanders appear to be leaving'

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said many of the people who had left New Zealand in recent years may have done so in search of work.

But he said there were some signs that things were changing.

The number of New Zealand citizens arriving back in New Zealand permanently had increased 6.1 percent over the past year, to just over 26,000.

The number of citizen departures had fallen 2.7 percent to nearly 38,000.

"Previously, there was a well-trodden path for young Kiwis to head to the UK on a Youth Mobility Scheme visa. The visa, available for 18-35-year-olds, allows Kiwis to live and work in the UK, and is often used for lawyers and various others to provide both new work experiences and easy access to Europe and beyond, as a working OE.

"It would seem that such interest in moving to the UK from NZ has reduced. UK entry clearance visas, including the Youth Mobility Scheme, from New Zealand have dropped to their lowest outside of the Covid-19 pandemic in 20 years."

He said that was probably due to a change in the UK labour market, where unemployment has also increased.

"More challenging job conditions seem to be making Kiwis considering a shift to the other side of the world question whether they'll find a role. It's one thing to earn London money and pay London costs - it's quite another to pay London costs while you battle it out with so many others for the roles available."

The trans-Tasman flow had also stabilised.

"Migration decisions are ultimately about relative opportunities, and for much of the last few years New Zealanders have had plenty of reasons to look offshore," Olsen said.

"Higher wages, stronger labour markets, and different lifestyle opportunities have encouraged a sizeable number of Kiwis to head overseas, particularly to Australia. But those comparisons are becoming less clear-cut. Job markets in the UK and Australia have softened, Australian housing remains expensive, and higher interest rates add further pressure to household finances across the Tasman.

"New Zealand's own economic challenges haven't disappeared, and there is still a substantial net outflow of Kiwis. But as conditions elsewhere become more difficult, fewer New Zealanders appear to be leaving and more are coming home. For anyone contemplating whether opportunities might be better overseas, the latest trends provide a useful reminder: apparently, the grass isn't always greener."

'Kicking the can down the road'

But National was just "kicking a can down the road" with its promised changes to student loan debt, according to a tax lawyer.

David Ananth said reducing the compulsory repayment rate was not enough of a reward to stop newly qualified students leaving the country without paying their debt off.

Ananth negotiates on behalf of some people overseas to get IRD to reduce the penalties his clients have incurred for not paying.

He told Checkpoint he dealt with people who left this country 15-20 years ago on a daily basis, and the government's changes were not going to do much in practical terms.

He said they were leaving the country for a large variety of reasons, including for health and family reasons, not just employment.

It would be more effective to increase the threshold before any deductions were made from just over $24,000 to more like $30,000, said Ananth.

"That would have a bit more of a positive impact."

He said most of the debts he dealt with were in the $100,000 to $150,000 range.

"That's a normal day for me, the highest I've gone is more than half a million dollars."

World.title: AI in business: 'How can we do things completely differently now?'
World.content:
Lack of skill and fear of job losses are slowing down businesses using artificial intelligence (AI) to transform their operations, a technology consultancy says.

Datacom surveyed more than 200 business leaders in organisations of more than 100 employees and found 91 percent were using AI.

But only four percent were using it to transform their core operations.

Most companies using AI according to snapshot Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Datacom director of AI Lou Compagnone told Checkpoint she was not surprised at the precautionary approach.

"Organisations are going gung ho on adoption but not thinking strategically about AI and the impact on people and processes in their organisation," she said.

Nearly two-thirds of respondents thought New Zealand should introduce specific AI legislation and controls.

The survey also found 74 percent said they would support a body like Australia's Office of AI to manage the development of mandatory standards.

Compagnone said businesses were adopting AI, but not adapting it to the organisation.

"How can we do things completely differently now, because of AI?"

She said organisations needed to make sure workers had the skills they needed to use AI - and dedicated AI leaders needed to be appointed, rather than AI management tacked on to other roles.

World.title: Sailors to make Cook Islands stopover after 53 years
World.content:
Veterans return to Pacific over 50 years after observing nuclear testing Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

It is a trip more than 50 years in the making.

Two New Zealand frigates were sent to the Pacific to observe and protest French nuclear testing at Mururoa Atoll in 1973, exposing 500 sailors to radiation.

One of the frigates - the HMNZS Canterbury - was invited to Rarotonga on the way back, but the ship's captain decided to head home.

Nineteen veterans who witnessed the tests are now finally heading to the Cook Islands for one last tour of duty together.

A nuclear explosion at Mururoa atoll in 1971, France stopped atmospheric testing in the Pacific in 1974. Photo credit:AFP AFP

'It was like a desert up there'

Prime Minister Norman Kirk farewelled HMNZS Otago before it headed to the Pacific to bear witness to the atmospheric testing.

HMNZS Canterbury was redirected from Honolulu for the same reason and in late July 1973 its crew saw a French test, from about 30 kilometres away.

Ant Kennedy - who turned 20 during the trip - remembers the sound.

Ant Kennedy got married before the Canterbury headed to the Pacific. Supplied

"I got up there just as the cloud was melting away, as it were, but apparently it wasn't quite as well formed as the Otago explosion," he told RNZ from his home in Whataroa on the West Coast.

"And I thought perhaps something might have gone wrong with the test.""

Like many, he did not appreciate the risks of what they were exposed to.

"At the time, the thing that stood out for me was it was a bit like a desert up there.

"There was no birds. Usually you'll see some sort of fish life, but there was none, so it was a really bleak place.

"I often thought afterwards, 'There's a reason for that. There's some reason for there being no bird life or sea life around it'."

Christchurch man Paddy Long - now known for his steel guitar playing - was also among the crew who viewed the test from the Canterbury's helicopter deck.

"We didn't actually have much in the way of protection at all for the whole trip, other than a little, what they called, a dosimeter,

"This was, in essence, a little blue plastic disk with a little litmus paper in it pinned to my shorts and, supposedly, if that was to change colour we should all get below deck fairly quickly."

Radiation alarm turned off

Radio mechanic Steve Aldridge was aware of the risks of radiation and said the Canterbury itself offered its crew protection, if warnings were acted on.

He remembers one occasion where they were not.

"We were having a BBQ on the flight deck - 44-gallon drums cut in half that they could BBQ on and a few beers, and a few rums.

"I got called to the bridge because an alarm was going off. It was a radiation alarm."

But there was no concern from his superiors, Aldridge said.

Paddy Long during the 1973 deployment. Supplied

"I said to the officer watch, 'I think you should clear the upper deck'. And he said, 'I'll make decisions like that. Just stop that noise. I can't hear myself think.'

"I said, 'Well, sir, to stop it, I'm going to have to disconnect the battery and disconnect the power supply to it. You'd better give me a direct order because I don't think I should do that'."

He received the order.

Aldridge - who lives in Auckland - thinks that given the timing, the Canterbury was sailing through fallout from the test the Otago witnessed.

The trip has had consequences for many down the years, including Long, who have battled cancers.

"I have had quite a long history with skin cancers. But, a lot of people have had a lot worse than that. So I can probably say I'm one of the lucky ones," Long said.

"I've just had another round of having a few bits and pieces surgically removed, but it's a constant maintenance thing with me. Other than that, I've been pretty good."

Aldridge said a high proportion of his children, with different partners, had autism or related conditions, leading him to think he was the common thread, and the reason was the radiation.

Veterans' health is covered by the government, but that was not the case for their children and grandchildren.

Kennedy is co-president of the Mururoa Nuclear Veterans Group, which is battling for change there.

Still going strong

For him, the trip away in 1973 has extra special memories from the Canterbury's time in Honolulu.

"Well, I got married. Yeah, against some advice, but we're still married today, so it was a good decision."

It was a whirlwind romance for Kennedy and his wife Stasia. Now, she will accompany him on the six-night visit to Rarotonga leaving on Tuesday.

Kennedy said that had come about because some former sailors have decided to take up the 1973 invitation to visit from then-Cook Islands Prime Minister Sir Albert Henry.

Although, Aldridge remembers the Canterbury maybe was not that welcome, saying while the trip was intended, the Cook Islands decided the vessel was radioactive.

"Otago came back and had a ticker-tape parade. We came back to some stale sandwiches the politicians were all eating in the overseas terminal."

This year's visit includes a presentation to the Cook Islands RSA as a thanks for the country's support in 1973.

It is a trip Long says he can not miss.

"Surprisingly, it'll be my first trip to Rarotonga. I've been to just about every other Pacific Island imaginable, so that'll be nice.

"It'll be all a new experience for me in the travelling department. We've got a bit of fishing organised and plus that night at the RSA will be quite memorable, I'm sure.

"Other than that, it'll be about enjoying some warm weather and having a few cold beers with my mates. It'll be great."

Long may also get a chance to reminisce on the time he appeared on Radio New Zealand back home, instead of government minister Fraser Colman.

Colman would spent a large part of his day giving interviews from around the world and it was Long's job to organise the connections.

One night Colman was not feeling great, so disappeared early, leaving Long to put on his best impression to unsuspecting listeners back home.

"I was pretty good at doing accents. Incidentally, when I got out of the navy, I ended up working for Radio New Zealand in Christchurch for about 16 years, but as a network engineer, rather than an announcing job."

France conducted almost 200 nuclear tests in the area between 1966 and 1996. About a quarter of these were atmospheric.

World.title: Hawke's Bay community makes big effort to restore native A'Deane's Bush
World.content:
Rural Hawke's Bay community working hard to restore native bush Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A small community in rural Hawke's Bay is working hard to restore a large area of precious native bush that's home to one of New Zealand's largest Totara trees, a colony of threatened long tail bats and a rare native mistletoe.

A'Deane's Bush is the best remaining example of the original podocarp forest of the Ruataniwha Plains. Conservation powerhouse Kay Griffiths is the driving force behind the restoration project, which is funded by local landowners John and Jay Benton.

"The aim of 'Friends of A'Deane's Bush' has always been to have a bush where the fauna and flora that's characteristic of this kind of lowland podocarp forest that's acutely threatened - that those plants and animals that belong in there are flourishing," said Griffiths.

The Totara tree in A'Deanes Bush is one of New Zealand's largest and thought to be over 600 years old, standing at over 33 metres tall with a girth of 8.8 metres. Alexa Cook/RNZ

A'Deane's Bush was once part of the massive Ashcott Station and cattle grazed around the edges of the bush. In the 1980's the farm owner threatened to chop the bush down and convert it into more grazing, but was luckily persuaded to sell it to the Department of Conservation instead.

Then 18 years ago the Benton's and Kay Griffiths joined forces with DOC and signed a management agreement to restore the area.

"Ours was the very first one to go across the minister's desk, and now it's become the norm.

"It's successful because we have ongoing funding from John and Jay Benton. We don't have to go looking for extra funding every five minutes, which is very time consuming," said Griffiths.

A small community in rural Hawke's Bay is working hard to restore a large area of precious native bush. Alexa Cook/RNZ

Over the years the group, along with others in the community, have cleared large areas of blackberry and put thousands of plants in the ground.

At 40 hectares in size, A'Deane's is much larger than other pockets of protected bush in the area, and is a special habitat for various creatures and critters.

"It's only these big bits of bush that hold the key to biodiversity. So we've got a colony of long tailed bats that utilise this area for maternity roosting and breeding. 80 percent of their roosts are in this bit of bush and then 20 percent of them are in the 2000 hectares around.

"That just shows you why the 40 hectares is actually so important. It means that we can focus our pest control in this area knowing we are protecting about 80 percent of the roosts," said Griffiths.

The surrounding land is owned by the White family, and Larry White said protecting the bush is a priority.

"A lot of the pest control happens on our land around here, there are traps set everywhere. Without that buffer zone around it the pests are going to come up," he said.

Jane and Larry White own the surrounding land and are part of 'Friends of A'Deane's Bush'. Alexa Cook/RNZ

About 500 to 700 plants are planted each year during community planting days, and by students from Sherwood School.

"The idea is to just increase the habitat. The local school is heavily involved, they've got a shade house and they grow plants. The kids come down and do two or three plantings a year.

"Some of those kids are here today, they've grown up planting and know exactly what they are doing because they've been doing it since they were five - it's so cool," said Griffiths.

Seven-year-old Lottie White is an expert planter, having learnt through Sherwood School planting days since she was five. Alexa Cook/RNZ

This is something local DOC ranger Claire Grant is also thrilled about.

"These community days of bringing people together to do this mahi is really important to keep people engaged and interested and connected with their environments and with nature for the long term," said Grant.

Hawke's Bay DOC Ranger Claire Grant. Alexa Cook/RNZ

Others at the community planting day have travelled from further afield, such as 86-year-old Teresa Hurst from Hastings.

"I've worked on the land all my life. I've been at Forest and Bird for 26 years and I've been volunteering for DOC for 26 years.

"I just love nature and helping out," she said.

Teresa Hurst travelled nearly an hour to help with the A'Deane's Bush community planting day Alexa Cook/RNZ

The Flynn family from Maraekākaho were there too, making the most of the sunny Sunday weather.

"This is actually our first time doing this as a family so it's really exciting. Seersha is working towards her Duke of Edinburgh so this is what we're doing to tick away at our community hours for that," said Jayme Flynn.

Seersha, Brent and Jayme Flynn enjoying a family day out planting natives. Alexa Cook/RNZ

The group, 'Friends of A'Deane's Bush', has recently become an incorporated society to give the project longevity and the ability to source funding in future from other places.

"You just have to keep going and that can often be overlooked as well because it's very easy to start something, but to keep going for 18 years and keep having the enthusiasm and keep having this amazing number of people turning up to help us is pretty cool," said Griffiths.

A promising sign that the bush is flourishing, are the insects that Griffiths has found using 'insect tree wraps' to see what is living there.

Kay Griffiths from the Conservation Company is the powerhouse behind the A'Deane's Bush restoration project. Alexa Cook/RNZ

"We go around and check them and have a look at the different kinds of insects that are in them and we have things like peripatus that are in there, which is a velvet worm.. that's a sign that our pest control is working really well because they are very vulnerable to predation, particularly from rats."

Griffiths has also shown the Sherwood School students how to use light traps, which tells them what insects are in the middle of the forest versus out in the nearby farmland.

"Out in the open paddock you get thousands of the same kind because we've got a monoculture there, but in here you get lots and lots of different species, but not very many of them, that's the diversity.

"Then in the middle you get a real mix of the two. So we really are changing the diversity by doing these sorts of plantings... and that's all food that bats eat," she said.

World.title: Snow closes highway in South Island, power restored to most in Hawke's Bay
World.content:
Heavy snow closed roads and highways in the South Island on Monday while strong winds buffeted Hawke's Bay in the north, leaving hundreds without electricity and fire crews battling vegetation fires.

Dunedin hit with snow flurries and icy temperatures Checkpoint Download MP3 2m

State Highway 1 between Dunedin and Waitati (north of Dunedin) was closed due to snow on Tuesday morning but it had reopened by mid-afternoon with travellers still urged to take extra care on the route.

Earlier in the day roading crews were out helping people who were stuck in cars on SH1.

Driver Amy Turoa said she was heading south on State Highway 1 when traffic came to a standstill for about 30 minutes.

"It's probably the heaviest snow I've been in, it just came down so fast," she said.

Turoa said when things started slowly moving again she could see dozens of cars stuck in the opposite direction and a truck and trailer that had slid into a ditch.

"The snow plow came through maybe three times and now we're just following all the other trucks. We've probably passed maybe 40 cars waiting," she said.

Snow at Flagstaff, Dunedin. Tess Brunton / RNZ

Although SH1 has now reopened, SH87 from Outram to Middlemarch, in Otago, is set to remain closed overnight because of snow.

SH94 Te Anau to Milford Sound was expected to remain open overnight, but with snow forecast to continue throughout the day, disruptions and temporary closures were possible while snow clearing machinery is working.

The snow wasn't bad news for everyone though, one Dunedin dogwalker said his dogs loved a snow day.

In the South Island, MetService has issued road snowfall warnings for Lewis, Arthur's, Porters and Lindis Pass, as well as Crown Range Road, Milford Road and Dunedin to Waitati Highway and they are set to expire between 6pm and 11pm on Monday.

There is also a snowfall warning for the Desert Road in the North Island from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday and it says around 1cm could accumulate above 800 metres.

MetService forecasts that snow could lower to near sea level in Dunedin and Clutha on Monday night.

"Keep an eye on the snow level in your local forecast if you're planning to drive, especially in Dunedin and Clutha Monday evening, and keep up with any updates on road conditions from NZTA Waka Kotahi and local council or emergency management," MetService meteorologist Ethan Walton-Jones advised.

Snow in Dunedin's Halfway Bush. Vyshak Mohan / SUPPLIED

Strong winds cut power, fan fires in Hawke's Bay

Meteorologists said strong winds around Hawke's Bay were forecast to last until Monday evening.

An orange strong wind watch for for Hawke's Bay south of Hastings and the Tararua district is in place until 7pm.

Severe gale westerlies gusting 120km/h were expected in exposed places.

Firefighters tackle vegetation fires in Hawke's Bay. Hawke's Bay - Fire and Emergency

Earlier on Monday hundreds of homes in Hawke's Bay were without power due to the weather, but that had reduced to less than 100 Unison customers by Monday afternoon.

At one stage fire crews were struggling with four vegetation fires in the region that were being fanned by the high winds.

Twenty-two trucks were working across two of the fires earlier on Monday and then called in extra personnel and appliances to deal with another two fires.

By Monday afternoon, the service said two fires on Swamp Road in Ongaonga had been extinguished after tree stumps and slash caught fire.

Fires at Argyll Road and White Road have been extinguished except for one on Argyll Road that's still being monitored.

Fire crews have handed a fire at Maharakeke Road back to the landowner for monitoring.

World.title: Mike's Metres: Canterbury cancer survivor skiing to fundraise $58k for others in treatment
World.content:
Blood cancer suvivor raising money for other patients through skiing Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

A Canterbury based skier has only just recovered from his blood cancer but is already hitting the slopes to raise money for others travelling for treatment.

A few years ago Mike Wilwert was diagnosed with blood cancer and spent almost a year at Ranui House, which provides free and subsidised accommodation for families travelling to Christchurch for medical treatment.

Wilwert, who was living in Methven at the time, said Ranui House had become even more than a "home away from home".

"It gave me a chance to heal while I was going through my chemo treatments... but also it gave my wife a sense of calm and serenity in this maddening world of treatments and not being about to go home."

Having spent 17 seasons as a ski instructor at Mt Hutt and 30 more seasons in Utah's Park City, Wilwert decided to use his passion for skiing and raise donations for a place that helped him in a time of need.

Mike Wilwert spent 17 seasons as a ski instructor at Mt Hutt. SUPPLIED

So, he started Mike's Metres, were every metre he skis will benefit families staying at Ranui House.

His goal is to complete 100,000 vertical metres and raise $58,140, which is how much it would have cost to stay at Ranui House for the ten months he spent there.

He thinks it would take him about 20 more days to complete the challenge.

What makes Wilwert's goal even more impressive is that he's still undergoing treatment to keep the cancer in remission and his kidneys from failing.

"My health is doing quite well considering I have bone marrow cancer and kidney failure. I do my kidney treatment three to four times a week and I still take maintenance drugs to help keep the cancer in remission."

He said he was at about 80 percent of where he was before and felt that this was now the "new norm".

Mike Wilwert spent more than ten months at Ranui House with his wife Kate by his side. SUPPLIED

He still has to travel to Christchurch for dialysis treatment, but now that he lives in Rolleston the trip is easier.

Before being diagnosed and while living in Methven he was skiing five to seven times a week but now with his location and treatments he is on the slopes three or four times on a good week and about twice on a bad week.

"It's always great to give back ... its giving other families a chance to experience Ranui House if they go through these really bad, horrible situations."

World.title: Cats claim they are not distracted by concussion controversy
World.content:
Geelong midfielder Tom Atkins is adamant the club's concussion saga has not been a distraction for the players as they prepare for Friday night's elimination final against Carlton at the MCG.

The Cats were last week fined $140,000 for failing to officially inform the AFL about the concussion waiver in Jake Kolodjashnij's contract.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

The penalty is $100,000 plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

Asked on Monday whether he or another player had a discussion around a similar concussion agreement, Atkins said: "No."

"Our focus has been performing on the weekends and we just wanted to make sure Kola [Kolodjashnij] was all right as teammates and as friends," Atkins said.

Voss assesses Blues' finals hopes Michael Voss speaks about the Blues' chances in the finals following their stunning turnaround.

"That's probably the extent of the detail that we looked into it as players."

Atkins said it was "awesome" to have Kolodjashnij around the club, now the finals had arrived.

"Obviously we'd love him to be back playing and back in training, but hopefully that can get itself sorted soon," Atkins said.

"But just having him in the rooms and seeing him smiling again is good."

AAP

World.title: Ex-Carlton coach Voss gives assessment of Blues' finals hopes
World.content:
Michael Voss has stopped short of declaring Carlton a genuine premiership threat but sees no reason his former team cannot make a deep run in the finals.

The Blues are riding a wave of momentum under Josh Fraser, who has engineered a remarkable turnaround since taking the coaching reins when Voss stepped down in May.

Fraser has won 11 of 14 matches at the helm, capped off by the come-from-behind victory over Melbourne in last week's wildcard encounter.

The staggering run has optimistic Carlton fans daring to dream of a first premiership since 1995, ahead of an elimination final against Geelong at the MCG on Friday night.

But with another three wins required in sudden-death matches just to reach the grand final, Voss said a drought-breaking flag was most likely beyond the Blues this year.

"It's very hard, isn't it? Percentages say that's a tough gig," Voss said.

"But they're certainly playing a high level of football if you look over the course of the last 10 or 11 weeks.

"They're the equal-form team of the competition, so there should be no reason that they can't look at every game and say that it's winnable."

The Blues ended the Demons' season last Saturday night. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Voss fell on his sword at Carlton after a 1-8 (win-loss record) start to the season and is determined to look forward rather than back at what might have been.

He said Fraser was "doing a great job" as coach and results showed "the right decision has been made" in appointing the former Collingwood ruck as Blues coach.

Voss lauded captain Patrick Cripps and leaders of the playing group for their efforts in turning Carlton's season around.

"One of my last messages with the leaders was: 'It's over to you and how do you make this a really player-led group?'" Voss said.

"They've clearly done that and more numbers are coming with them, so the heavy lifting isn't just on a few.

"You've got a lot of people responding and there's some pretty incredible human beings amongst that group.

"I'm just really pleased that they're getting the rewards that they've obviously been working really hard for."

Voss says Carlton in a better place than when he took charge Michael Voss has struck a defiant tone after leaving Carlton, insistent the AFL club is in better shape than when he started as coach.

Carlton has won three of its past four meetings with Geelong, with Voss noting extra attention on key Cats duo Tom Stewart and Gryan Miers had served them well.

Voss said the Blues' work in the contested areas of the game would hold them in good stead.

"Where Geelong are underestimated quite a fair bit is their contested game," he said.

"They're not so much dominant when it comes to stoppages, but they are post-stoppage.

"Carlton can do that blindfolded and they showed that again on the weekend against Melbourne.

"When the whips were cracking they really ramped that part of the game up.

"Because they match up really well against that, they actually put themselves in a really good position to win games."

AAP

World.title: Knight's prop cops season-ending ban after send-off
World.content:
Jacob Saifiti's NRL season is all but over after the Newcastle prop was handed a four-game suspension for a high tackle on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii.

Saifiti was sent off in the first half of Sunday's 46-32 defeat in Auckland and was handed a grade two reckless high tackle charge by the NRL's match review committee on Monday morning.

The Knights have a bye for the final round of the regular season, meaning Saifiti's ban will only kick in for their first finals game.

Newcastle — currently sitting seventh — will play an elimination final in week one but even if they were to upset the odds and qualify for the grand final, the Fijian prop would still be on the sidelines.

Saifiti's only hope of playing in the NRL again this season hinges on the prop contesting the charge at the judiciary on Tuesday in a bid to reduce his punishment.

Should the front-rower fight the suspension and lose his appeal, he will have another week added to his four-game ban.

Elsewhere, Cronulla prop Tom Hazelton is set to miss Cronulla's final regular season game against Melbourne after being cited for a hip-drop tackle on Ronald Volkman.

Hazelton was sin-binned by referee Ashley Klein late in Sunday's loss to Parramatta but will serve a one-game ban with an early guilty plea and be free to return for week one of the finals series.

AAP

World.title: Indigenous numbers in the AFL are down, but there's talent in the Top End
World.content:
A couple of years ago Hawthorn's Kaitlyn Ashmore, a Dja Dja Wurrung woman, spent some time in Alice Springs.

She was immediately taken by the gift for footy so many kids had up there, but knew the pathways for development were limited.

"I've been out to the communities … the talent up there is incredible," Ashmore said on the eve of the AFLW's Indigenous Round.

"But it's just getting them down here, or getting them in a program, and then keeping them in there and making them feel culturally safe."

Loading Instagram content

She was in the Red Centre in support of the Dreamtime Academy, an initiative founded by AFLW player Lulu Pullar along with fellow First Nations players Courtney Hodder, a Badimaya and Whadjuk woman, and Ally Anderson, a Ghungalu and Wakka Wakka woman.

There are 22 Indigenous players listed across the AFLW competition, down from 26 in 2023. In the men's competition the number has dropped from 87 in 2020 to 62 this season.

Ashmore said that was why the Indigenous Round was so important.

"It's honestly representation," she said.

"If we keep doing that, and celebrating Indigenous people, culture and stories like that, then hopefully we can get some more girls that want to join us."

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

On Sunday night more than 4,000 people packed out the stands at Marrara Stadium to watch Richmond beat Essendon in the Dreamtime match.

Among the spectators were diehard Tigers and Bombers fans and some who had never seen an AFL game before.

Last year the marquee Indigenous Round match was on a Friday night in Darwin and attracted almost 6,000 people.
