Tech.title: ATM Flaws Reveal Key Weaknesses in the Software Supply Chain
Tech.content:
For the past five years, security researcher Matt Burch has immersed himself in the esoteric and high-stakes world of ATM security, in which small software flaws can sometimes expose cold, hard cash. As Burch has bored deeper into the computers powering these digital lock boxes—and continued to find vulnerabilities in key digital security systems—he has started working to raise the alarm, not just about overlooked ATM flaws, but about how that same software used in other industries can introduce weaknesses in an array of critical systems.

At the Black Hat and Defcon security conferences in Las Vegas this month, Burch presented findings about nine vulnerabilities that have been fixed in disk encryption and pre-boot authentication software called CryptoPro Secure Disk. The flaws could have been exploited to bypass CryptoPro's integrity checks and gain full access to encrypted devices.

Made by the German software firm CryptWare, CryptoPro is marketed to ATM makers and is used in some ATMs, including as part of Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Suite. But CryptoPro is also sold as a security solution for other embedded-device makers, as well as big organizations using Microsoft Windows, underscoring the supply chain challenge of addressing bugs when software is widely implemented in numerous industries.

“ATMs are what brought me down this path, but I think there may be an even higher impact of these findings beyond that,” Burch says. “From the perspective of ATMs and the financial network, there are a lot of layers, and I think as a result of that, things just get implemented a certain way and then there’s limited technical insight—bugs can get overlooked or they don’t get addressed.”

CryptWare managing director Uwe Saame tells WIRED that the company patched the nine bugs in two phases with CryptoPro version 7.7.2 in early November and 7.7.3 in early December. Burch says the company was prompt and collaborative throughout his disclosure process and he validated that the patches actually fix the vulnerabilities he found. While CryptoPro does not seem to publicly release update notes, Burch says he believes that the company distributed information about the patches to its customers.

Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson Michael Jacobsen tells WIRED in a statement that only two of the nine vulnerabilities are relevant to Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Hard Disk Encryption, the system where the ATM maker uses CryptoPro software. Jacobsen says that Diebold Nixdorf issued fixes related to those two bugs in December, but that they could not have been exploited on their own to compromise a Diebold Nixdorf ATM.

In ATMs, embedded devices, and enterprise security more broadly, the challenge of the software supply chain comes from all of the steps to actually apply fixes in the world. As in this case, a developer has to release a patch, then companies that implement the product in their own software need to develop a tailored fix, and then customers need to actually hear about and install that patch—which can be difficult for systems that are running in the field or can't easily be paused and updated.

Speaking generally about this challenge, Jacobsen, the Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson, says that “when a security issue is identified, Diebold Nixdorf assesses the impact, identifies affected products and configurations, and develops any needed updates through our product security and engineering processes. We then notify impacted customers and provide updates through standard software distribution channels, including the Global Security Portal where applicable. For deployed ATMs, updates are coordinated with each customer based on their operating model, service agreements, and change-management processes.”

Security researchers have warned for decades about the danger of relying on “security through obscurity” by trying to hide software from view or keep it locked away. And, as a result of this work, internet-of-things manufacturers and those in critical industries like the financial sector and medical device manufacturing have made some progress on transparency and promoting patch adoption. But Burch points out that as AI systems make it easier to evaluate software and find vulnerabilities—even for researchers or attackers who don't have granular expertise in a given area—it is more pressing than ever to shed light on niche security products.

“AI really blows away the obscurity model,” Burch says. “You don’t need to fully understand how something works anymore to move forward and potentially have a big impact.”

Tech.title: Google Maps Now Shows ‘Lake America’ Instead of Lake Ontario
Tech.content:
Lake Ontario is no more on Google Maps in the US. Google changed the name of the easternmost of the Great Lakes to “Lake America” late Saturday, days after President Donald Trump ordered its rebranding in official government databases.

Trump issued the executive order on Thursday as part of an ongoing feud over tariffs with Canada, whose province of Ontario borders the lake. It followed a similar order he issued in January 2025 to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America as part of a fight with the US trading partner to the south.

Google, Apple, Microsoft, and other maps providers adopted the Gulf of America naming as soon as the US Department of the Interior updated its records, which came a couple of weeks after Trump’s order. So it was no surprise that when those records—which are used to determine names on roadway signs and in government literature—reflected Lake America, digital maps from Google also quickly took on the new name.

Apple Maps and Bing Maps have not yet reflected the change but are expected to. In fact, the map for the federal government’s Geographic Names Information System database, which informs these changes, still showed Lake Ontario as of Sunday morning, with a note that the maps are “in the process of being updated to reflect this name change.”

While Google and other private organizations that provide maps are not bound by law to use official names, they generally follow government databases like GNIS. The location names a user sees depends on their own geography.

“People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in an unsigned statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.”

Trump’s efforts to rewrite maps have generated considerable public debate in open-source mapping communities such as OpenStreetMap, whose technology is used by companies such as Uber and Lyft. Ultimately, OpenStreetMap recognizes both the US and foreign names and gives organizations using its maps the choice over which to show.

One map provider that has so far declined to make the change is MapQuest, which said in a social media post in response to Trump’s order, “We’re not changing it.”

Tech.title: Best Mesh Wi-Fi Systems (2026): I Tested Them All
Tech.content:
Asus ZenWifi BD5 Outdoor for $180: While I listed the cheaper TP-Link Deco BE25 as my top outdoor pick, you should always choose a node that is compatible with your existing mesh system. If you are running an Asus setup, the BD5 Outdoor is the way to go. It features dual-band Wi-Fi 7, an IP65 weather-resistant rating, and two 2.5-Gbps PoE ports—allowing you to power the unit and run a wired backhaul over a single Ethernet cable. Thanks to AiMesh support, it integrated flawlessly with the three different Asus systems I tested it with, and it will easily blanket your backyard in strong Wi-Fi.

TP-Link Deco BE67 (2-Pack) for $500: This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh is a little cheaper than our top pick but offers similar performance. The setup was a little glitchy for me. Each unit has one 10-Gbps Ethernet port, one 2.5-Gbps port, a Gigabit port, and a USB 3.0 port. Performance was consistently impressive throughout my home, with some of the fastest speeds I have recorded at close and medium range. The BE67 falls between the BE63 and the flagship BE85, and might be the sweet spot in TP-Link’s lineup. The Deco BE68 is the same system as the BE67, but exclusive to Best Buy.

Netgear Orbi 370 Series Photograph: Simon Hill

Netgear Orbi 370 Series (3-Pack) for $350: While it is great that manufacturers offer budget-friendly options, dual-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh routers are a tough sell. Not only do you miss out on the 6-GHz band, but the 5-GHz band must be shared between your devices and the wireless backhaul traffic connecting the nodes. In my thick-walled Victorian home, this resulted in terrible performance for anything connected to a satellite node. Even after extensive tinkering with the Orbi 370, I struggled to get more than 15 Mbps from a node despite having a 1 Gbps internet connection. While it is an affordable system that offers the same easy setup as our top pick, there are simply too many caveats for me to fully recommend it.

TP-Link Deco BE25 (3-Pack) for $300: Almost everything I just said about the Orbi 370 Series applies to the dual-band Wi-Fi 7 Deco BE25. But, this mesh is cheaper, the units are smaller and disc-shaped, and they’re all identical, with two 2.5 Gbps each. Speed and range on the 5-GHz band were better with Netgear’s 370 Series, but the opposite was true on the 2.4-GHz band.

Netgear Orbi 870 (3-Pack) for $1,300: This tri-band mesh from Netgear is a step up on the 770 Series above, adding a 10-Gbps WAN/LAN port and doubling the bandwidth on the 5- and 6-GHz bands. My experience with the 870 Series was flawless. The setup was straightforward, performance was top-notch on every band and at various distances, and this mesh system was near the top of the table in all my tests. It also proved extremely stable and had no trouble covering my entire home and garden. The only reason the 870 doesn’t appear above is that the 770 is likely enough for most folks, but if your internet connection is faster than 2.5 Gbps, this is what I recommend.

Asus ZenWiFi BT8 Photograph: Simon Hill

Asus ZenWiFi BT8 (3-Pack) for $850: Based on its mostly stellar speed and range, the tri-band BT8 is a Wi-Fi 7 mesh worth considering. Sadly, the highs were hamstrung by inconsistent performance and perplexing intermittent lag, which made testing the BT8 a frustrating roller-coaster experience. A step down from the BT10 but still more than fast enough for most homes with 2.5-Gbps or slower internet connections, the BT8 was a breeze to install, offered impressive speeds across all three bands, and delivered excellent range. Consider the subscription-free parental controls and security software, and the BT8 looks like a real contender. While the release firmware was poor, this system is now consistently stable, and Asus has started to offer tempting discounts.

TP-Link Deco BE85 (2-Pack) for $800: The Deco BE85 was TP-Link's first Wi-Fi 7 mesh. As the flagship, it offers unrivaled performance, with double the bandwidth of the more affordable BE63 listed above. Each router boasts four auto-sensing WAN/LAN Ethernet ports, two 10-Gbps ports (one is an SFP combo), two 2.5-Gbps ports, and a USB 3.0 port. It delivered wide coverage and excellent performance in my tests, but unless you have a very fast multi-gig internet connection and loads of Wi-Fi 7 devices, it will be overkill for your home.

Tech.title: Why the Hottest New Wearables Want to Be Ignored
Tech.content:
There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable. You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.

They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series, the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg. One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good.

I have reviewed wearables since they went mainstream the first time around with the early waves of Fitbits from 2009 and onward. In some ways this new generation of trackers feels like a callback to those days. Back when I used the Fitbit Ultra, a 2011 tracker that clipped to your jeans, I paid so little attention to it that two days passed before I realized I’d lost it somewhere on the streets of Zagreb, Croatia. While, like many, I fell for the sub-Tamagotchi little cartoon faces of the 2012 Fitbit Zip’s screen, it—like a Fitbit Air—wasn't something you were meant to pay attention to more than a couple times a day, max.

Over the last few years, though, I’ve spent most days referring to a Garmin, Samsung, Fitbit, Coros—the list goes on—dozens or hundreds of times a day. WhatsApp messages and emails buzz on their little screens and my wrist reflexively raises to see what’s up. When I wear a Garmin watch, I’m also lulled into the rhythm of checking evening and morning “reports,” and pathologically looking at my sleep score as soon as I wake up. And let’s not even get into the move alerts, an eye-rolling nag wearables have had for years now.

What Wearables Have Become

Part of the sell-in of new-breed wearables is that they're, in some ways, the antithesis of what other watches have grown into. Fitness watches are more smartwatch-like than ever. OLED screens are near-ubiquitous even in health trackers; hardcore running wearables let you communicate with AI assistants. And this is all even though smartwatches have never really fulfilled the original promise of a life-changing app or feature beyond what people used the first Apple Watch for back in 2015: not much.

Sure, Apple Watches may have saved a life or two, but that’s not necessarily what you’re buying them for. I waited years to report on smartwatch apps that would change things and instead saw entire wearable app ecosystems wither like neglected houseplants. Screen-free wearables want to hit “reset” on the entire category.

The most interesting factor isn't that bands like the Fitbit Air exist now, but why this is all happening now, in 2026. These wearables are largely a case of design subtraction. They are much like a normal fitness tracker—heart rate sensor, battery, accelerometer, Bluetooth transmitter, and whatever other sensors are packed in on a per-case basis—with the display excised.

Tech.title: The Best Label Makers (2026): Brother, Niimbot, Dymo
Tech.content:
There’s not a whole bunch more the average person could want in a handheld label maker other than what the PT-n25bt offers, particularly at such an approachable price. With this device, even a label-making newbie should have no issue making a custom tag in less than a minute. After clicking the tape cartridge into place, simply close the back of the machine, power it on, and type directly onto the standard QWERTY keyboard. Press print, and then use the on-device cutting mechanism to get a clean, straight edge every time. If you’re not in a huge rush, you can putter around with three font options, seven font styles (think: bold, underline, italic), 15 text frames, and hundreds of symbols. The LCD screen lets you preview any edits you make to your label, minimizing unintended surprises you get when it, say, spits out a thick border design you really hate.

For even more design flexibility, you can opt for the Brother Design&Print 2 companion app that’s available on iOS and Android devices. It connects via Bluetooth and provides dozens of templates geared toward specific purposes, like gift tags, file folders, or food containers. You can also design your own custom label on the app without using a template. If you go this route, you’ll have way more font, frame, and design options at your disposal than if you design directly on the app.

The labels themselves offer a level of customization. Because the tape cartridges are available in 17 colors, you can choose to make your labels look all your own, particularly if you opt for a less-common color, like black print on green tape. The labels also hold up to the conditions. Brother markets its durability-minded laminated BTag label tapes—specifically for its P-touch line of label makers—as being water-, temperature-, and fade-resistant, along with microwave-, dishwasher-, and freezer-resistant. In my few weeks of testing, these claims held up.

For all of its wins, there are a few drawbacks of the PT-n25bt: It runs on a whopping six AAA batteries that aren’t included in the box. You can also power it with an AC adapter, but you have to buy that separately for $26. You’re also limited to labels that are 12 millimeters wide (roughly half an inch), so you’ll need to stack labels if you’re looking for a bigger visual.

Tech.title: Google Maps Relabels Lake Ontario After Trump’s Executive Order
Tech.content:
Google on Saturday changed its Maps software to comply with President Donald Trump’s order designating Lake Ontario as Lake America.

In a blog post, Google explained that the renaming — which is already in effect — would only appear to users in the US. “Those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” the company said.

So far, Apple Maps, Microsoft’s Bing Maps and MapQuest have not made the change. CNET has reached out to Microsoft and Apple for comment. Neither company has stated publicly how soon it might change its maps to show Lake America.

It may feel like a familiar situation: It’s the Gulf of America all over again.

Last year, Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico as part of an executive order. Now, in the middle of a trade war with Canada, he’s going back to the same playbook by issuing an order to rename Lake Ontario.

As happened last year, this is likely to affect how the region is labeled on Apple Maps and Bing Maps in addition to Google’s revision. It took several weeks, but eventually all three ended up labeling the gulf differently based on the change in the Geographic Names Information System, the US government’s national naming standard.

One holdout was MapQuest, which already said it will not change the name of Lake Ontario in its software. In a cheeky post on X, the company said, “We’re not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure,” inviting people to craft their own personalized names. It was accompanied by a screenshot showing “Lake Are We Doing This Again?”

We're not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure: https://t.co/E2I0Ezd57W



(tag us so we can see your work 🙂) pic.twitter.com/x8lIAMt6ab — MapQuest (@MapQuest) August 27, 2026

In an email to CNET on Friday, a White House spokesperson did not answer questions about MapQuest’s post or how soon the administration expects tech companies to comply.

“As the President said yesterday, the majority of the great lake’s volume sits in United States territory,” Assistant Press Secretary Allison Schuster said. “Thanks to President Trump’s bold action, its name will now reflect its place in America and her heritage.”

One key difference

As the website Tech Times points out, one big difference between renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario is that the US-Canada border runs through the lake. That means there are additional technology considerations even if the map apps go through with the change. For instance, it could require the name to change on the fly if someone is traveling across the border.

Apple, Google and Microsoft are under no obligation to display the new name to customers in Canada.

Another wrinkle is that it could affect mnemonics. As part of the Great Lakes, Lake Ontario is remembered by students as part of the shorthand “HOMES.” As New York Gov. Kathy Hochul pointed out in her criticisms of Trump’s order, the new acronym could be “SHAME.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford blasted the naming change after introducing a new sign on the Canada side of the lake that reads, “Lake Ontario Now and Always.” The premier compared the Trump order to a Saturday Night Live sketch, telling the ABC News show This Week, “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”

Tech.title: Smart Glasses Are Recording in Public. These Apps Can Detect When They’re Nearby
Tech.content:
Smart glasses have a detection problem: Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses and similar products from other manufacturers can record video continuously without producing any obvious tell beyond a small LED indicator that’s easy to miss, cover or simply ignore.

A new category of mobile apps is trying to address that and respond to the mounting public backlash by scanning for the Bluetooth signals smart glasses emit while powered on and alerting users when a recording-capable device is detected nearby. Zuckoff is among the most visible of these apps, and its premise is straightforward: use the wireless signals the glasses can’t hide to warn the people who might be in their frame.

Broad concerns over privacy have led to a technical battle. On one side, hardware modifiers are tweaking wearable cameras to make them even harder to spot, often by disabling LED indicators. On the other, developers and privacy-focused coders are launching counter tech to give you a heads-up when a hidden camera walks into the room.

One of those developers has already gained traction with a free Apple iOS app called Zuckoff, a digital detection tool to spot nearby Ray-Ban Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles or similar hardware.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Sniffing out smart glasses

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

What drove Szydlowski to actively develop a software detector was seeing social media videos of people wearing smart glasses who recorded pranks or harassed women with pickup lines. None of the targets seemed aware that their content would appear online, which made Szydlowski angry. “There was not even a blur involved to try to censor them, to give them some sort of feeling of privacy,” he said. “These days, everybody feels entitled to post everything.”

App developer Pawel Szydlowski said he developed his app, Zuckoff, to help address people’s privacy concerns about smart glasses. Pawel Szydlowski

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Smart glasses detected… now what?

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

Unlike with smartphones, where it’s easier to tell when someone is recording or taking photos, “smart glasses shift the burden of privacy entirely onto the person being photographed,” Ananthakrishnan said.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

Privacy-conscious smart glasses?

That surveillance anxiety may prompt some hardware-makers to release alternative versions of smart glasses that entirely avoid potential privacy violations.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker. Scott Stein/CNET

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

The future of smart glasses detectors

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Zuckoff’s Szydlowski said it’s possible a company could shrink the kind of 5G technology to fit in smart glasses, making them less dependent on phones and Bluetooth, but that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. If Meta or Snap deliberately updated their hardware to hide from detection apps and disable smart glasses’ digital footprint, it would further undercut any claim of privacy accountability.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

Tech.title: I Started Wearing a Pebble Watch Again: Time 2 Took Me Back to the 2010s in the Best Way
Tech.content:
Twelve years ago, I was traveling to the UK in the summer with my wife and then-tiny kids. And on my wrist was a Pebble watch.

I still go overseas each summer to visit my in-laws, but my kids are taller than me now and my beard is grayer. But this year, I had the chance to put a new Pebble Time 2 on my wrist for a while during the trip, and it brought back a lot of the old smartwatch feelings from the 2010s. Now that I’m back home, it has found its way onto my wrist again. That surprised me, because Pebble’s comeback is remarkably well done. It also turns out that smartwatches haven’t changed all that much over the past 12 years — or have they?

The $225 Pebble Time 2 is part of a new wave of Pebble watches that includes a round model arriving in about a month. But it isn’t like the Pebbles of old. It’s a nicer piece of hardware, done up to look and feel retro. In that sense, nostalgia may be playing tricks on my memory. The Time 2 has a backlit color screen and buttons on both sides to control the interface, but it also has a touchscreen (which old Pebbles never had). It also offers optical heart-rate tracking and basic step and fitness features. More importantly, you can download a vast selection of classic Pebble apps and watch faces for free.

A new Pebble mobile app syncs the watch up, and it’s refreshingly clean and easy to use. I got on my feet fast via an iPhone and was able to load up watch faces and apps quickly, too.

Hello, Kirby. And there I was at a church fete, eating scones and jam!

Scott Stein/CNET

Goofy watch faces are back, baby

Watch faces were the best thing about the earlier versions of the Pebble — and they still are. There are plenty of clever, weird, janky, useful and downright ugly Pebble faces to try, many of which play fast and loose with copyright. (I found Kirby and Sonic watch faces; please let them stay.)

The Pebble displays the weather, counts steps, automatically tracks walks and sleep, and quickly syncs notifications. It’s all very functional, but I miss some of the Apple Watch’s finesse. Simple tasks such as muting notifications or silencing vibrations require more taps and fiddling on the Pebble. It’s swim-friendly, and its silicone band fits snugly. I like the clean steel case: It gives me a bit of Pebble Time Steel throwback feelings.

The Pebble has stopwatch and timer features, but while grilling one evening, I missed the voice-activated timer I frequently use on my Apple Watch.

Thank goodness I didn’t miss my mom’s daily Wordle score share while at a garden party.

Scott Stein/CNET

I also oddly missed making payments with my wrist, something I started doing by default on vacation — and everywhere else in my life — via Apple Pay. Sure, I could pay with my phone or wallet, but I missed having the Apple Watch as my easy go-to.

But I really got a kick out of the Pebble’s massive collection of watch faces again. I searched for “Adventure Time” and found a whole bunch of fan-made faces. Jake was smiling on my wrist seconds later. Then I found a tarot watch face with cards showing numbers, followed by one with a wrist-activated cubic time layout and another with a cool minimalist dial. And then I found some watch games. It’s all here, just an app search away. All the developers ask is that you perhaps make a donation later, if you feel like it.

The Pebble Time 2’s automatic fitness tracking actually works!

Scott Stein/CNET

Surprisingly functional, delightfully quirky

I love the indie spirit of it all, and suddenly it all flooded back to me: This is what the world of smartwatches was once like. Before Google, before Apple. Before Fitbit acquired Pebble and Google acquired Fitbit and buried Pebble deep in the belly of nested tech giants.

Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky’s little labor of love — a rescue mission to bring the Pebble back — really works. And now that I’m home in New Jersey, I’m enjoying wearing it around the house. As I write this, my wrist is buzzing with Signal notifications, and I find myself wondering: Where exactly is my Apple Watch? Did I leave it upstairs to charge?

The battery on this Pebble lasts almost a month, depending on how often the backlight comes on or heart-rate tracking kicks in. I got a few weeks from my first charge, so I’m unlikely to need the little charging dongle very often. It plugs into a USB-C cable and snaps magnetically onto the Pebble. I just hope I don’t lose it.

Sausage shopping at Tescos, Kingsbridge. Scott Stein/CNET

Whatever I miss, I love this battery life

And as long as I don’t care about voice-activated timers — I manually set a one-minute timer for my coffee today, and it was fine — or Apple Pay, there’s not much else I’ll miss. (The Pebble Time 2 does have a microphone, but it isn’t used for core features and doesn’t seem to work with messages or anything else on the iPhone.)

In exchange, I get these fun watch faces that make me smile, and I’m getting a kick out of having a Pebble on my wrist again. But most of all, I really, really love barely having to charge it.

With battery life this good, it’s easy to wear it to sleep. Scott Stein/CNET

I don’t think I’ll wear the Pebble Time 2 all the time … or will I? I admire its battery life a ton, along with its fun approach to watch faces. In the 13-plus years since the first Pebble, neither the Apple Watch nor Google’s Wear OS watches, for that matter, have done it better.

What’s a watch for? Sure, the future is full of ever more advanced, sensor-studded wearables, from watches to rings. Add the ways watches now work with earbuds and upcoming smart glasses, and it’s a lot. Then there are AI agents doing increasingly interconnected things, while finger gestures, voice commands and near-field taps turn these devices into keys, payment hubs and health monitors. But — deep breath — The Pebble Time 2 has turned back the clock and reminded me that watches can just be watches, too. I don’t know whether it will become my everyday watch, but right now, I’m really enjoying the comeback.

Tech.title: What Is Grok? Everything to Know About Elon Musk’s AI Tool
Tech.content:
Elon Musk isn’t one to sit out a tech trend. In November 2023, he launched Grok, an AI chatbot created by his artificial intelligence startup, xAI. Musk, who co-founded OpenAI before departing in 2018, created Grok to compete with ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google’s Gemini. But he gave it a sarcastic twist and direct access to X (formerly Twitter), the social platform he purchased in October 2022.

Initially, Grok was available exclusively to paying X subscribers. It has since expanded far beyond X and is now available through grok.com, standalone iOS and Android apps and in qualifying Tesla vehicles.

What started as an irreverent chatbot now includes advanced reasoning models, voice conversations, image and video generation, coding tools, workplace integrations and autonomous AI agents.

Since its launch, it has transitioned through several upgrades. The latest model is Grok 4.6, released in August and designed for long-running agent tasks, coding and complex knowledge work. This model is available in Cursor and Grok Build. Grok 4.5, released a month earlier, is also available directly through Grok on the web, X and mobile apps to everyone.

The background story

Grok was developed by xAI, an AI startup founded by Musk in July 2023. The company’s stated mission is “to understand the universe,” and it maintains close ties with Musk’s other ventures, including X, Tesla and Neuralink.

Its corporate structure has since changed. SpaceX acquired xAI in February, bringing Musk’s AI company and Grok under the SpaceXAI umbrella.

Grok’s attitude was originally inspired by The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, with Musk promising a chatbot that answers with wit, humor and attitude. SpaceXAI now describes Grok as a “truth-seeking AI assistant” that combines chat, search, reasoning and content creation in one place.

On its website, SpaceXAI emphasizes that Grok aims to provide accurate information, though its edgy, less-moderated approach with a “rebellious streak” sometimes blurs the line between useful and controversial.

This unfiltered so-called free speech style has led to backlash, with Grok being known to occasionally generate biased or offensive content (more on that later). And, like all the other AI chatbots, it warns you that it may hallucinate.

Its defining feature is its real-time integration with X, which means it can pull from trending posts, user conversations and breaking news in addition to standard web sources. The company says it may use your X data and interactions with Grok for model training and fine-tuning, and to personalize your Grok experience. But you can opt out using your X settings.

What can Grok do?

Similar to most AI chatbots, Grok can answer questions, summarize articles, write emails, explain complex topics, translate text, brainstorm ideas and help with coding. It supports more than 30 languages and can analyze uploaded files, PDFs, images, screenshots and diagrams.

If you’re on X and see a post you want more info about, you can ask Grok directly in the comments section, though a response isn’t guaranteed.

Grok/Screenshot by CNET

The dedicated Ask Grok button is limited to Premium and Premium Plus subscribers. To reply, Grok uses context from X and web sources and sometimes answers in a casual, humorous or sarcastic tone similar to Musk’s own posts.

Meta AI is similarly integrated across its socials, but Grok’s direct connection to X gives it access to public posts, conversations and trending topics as they unfold. That real-time connection to X remains one of Grok’s distinguishing features, but it’s no longer the only thing setting it apart.

Grok’s image tools have expanded considerably since its early Aurora image model. Grok Imagine now generates and edits images as well as video. Imagine Image 2.0, released in August, improves instruction following, typography and layout while allowing you to edit existing images. Grok Imagine Video 1.5 can turn images into video while generating motion, sound effects, ambiance and speech in different languages. People have been extensively playing with those features on X .

1- You can have Grok speak in your language; he speaks perfectly with the right accent.

(here in french)

2- You can build a long scene in 1080p by taking the last frame of an animation to start another animation. It's easy with Grok (Right-click on the animation and copy the… pic.twitter.com/g6NzTKqu4G — Déborah (@dvorahfr) August 19, 2026

Grok also supports voice conversations. The company has expanded Grok Voice with more natural speech and a growing library of multilingual voices.

You can now connect outside apps and services with Grok. It has integrations for Google Workspace as well as Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, allowing you to work with documents, spreadsheets, presentations and email without leaving those apps.

Skills is another neat feature. It lets you teach it how to handle specific tasks. You can create one by describing what you want Grok to do, then reuse or share it. Skills can be used for work, such as creating documents, presentations, spreadsheets and PDFs, though the feature is currently limited to SuperGrok Heavy subscribers.

Grok/Screenshot by CNET

For developers, SpaceXAI has also expanded Grok into agentic coding. Grok Build runs from your terminal and can work across codebases, execute longer tasks and coordinate multiple agents. You can use it to create websites, games, apps and interactive dashboards.

In August, SpaceXAI autonomous workplace agent Grok Bot launched. It’s SpaceXAI’s version of similar AI work agents like Claude Cowork, ChatGPT Work, Gemini Spark and Perplexity Computer. These tools can keep working after you close your laptop and return when it needs your approval.

Instead of only answering prompts, Grok Bot gets its own cloud computer and can work across websites, apps, inboxes and files to complete multi-step jobs. This service is currently in beta.

Grok Bot isn’t SpaceXAI’s first move into AI agents. DeepSearch, introduced with Grok 3, already used agentic behavior to search for information and compile reports. But Grok Bot pushes much further into autonomous work.

Another capability with Grok is enhanced cultural fluency. Grok is adept at interpreting memes, internet slang and humor.

Grok models and pricing

When Grok 4 arrived in July 2025, Musk claimed its capabilities exceeded those of humans in academia.

“Grok 4 is postgrad-level in everything,” Musk claimed. “At least with respect to academic questions, Grok 4 is better than a PhD level in every subject. No exceptions.”

John Licato, assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of South Florida, says these claims are absolutely misleading, however.

“‘PhD-level’ is being thrown around as a marketing term with no real rigorous benchmarks behind it,” Licato tells CNET. “It also completely misunderstands what PhDs actually do.”

SpaceXAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for clarification or comment.

SpaceXAI has continued developing the Grok 4 family. Grok 4.5 came out in July 2026, followed by Grok 4.6 in August. The newer versions are built for more demanding tasks such as coding, agentic work and longer, more complex requests.

Grok offers a free plan with limited usage. SuperGrok costs $30 per month and provides higher usage limits, access to Grok 4.5, connectors and image and video generation. The company also offers SuperGrok Lite, Plus and Heavy tiers, alongside Business and Enterprise plans.

You can access Grok through paid X subscriptions, though features and limits vary between plans.

Grok’s controversies and safety concerns

While ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude tend to be neutral or overly polite, Grok is intentionally informal. Some responses are laced with sarcasm or off-color jokes, which might appeal to Musk’s fans but could turn off people expecting a neutral assistant. Sometimes Grok is helpful, sometimes it’s snarky and sometimes it just goes too far.

SpaceXAI pitches this as an advantage — a bot that isn’t afraid to “tell you the truth,” even if it’s controversial. However, that approach got Grok in hot water in July 2025 with a series of later-deleted antisemitic posts on X. SpaceXAI removed the posts and said it was working to improve safeguards against hate speech.

Grok’s real-time access to X is both a strength and a risk, since the platform is known for hosting unmoderated or misleading content. Because of its reliance on X, Grok may amplify misinformation or reflect the platform’s user biases more unless it checks those claims against stronger sources.

Licato agrees that this is concerning and adds that he’s not convinced the leadership behind Grok is doing anything to ensure responsible use of its technology.

“Grok is marketed as more of a truth-teller than its competitors, and this is leading to a lot of people believing that it is somehow more reliable,” Licato says. “But I do not see any good evidence that this is actually true, and I worry that, since so much of the public does not know how easy it is to get LLMs to spout false information, they may just be aiding in the spreading of mis- and disinformation.”

In late 2025 and early 2026, Grok’s image tools were used to create sexualized and nonconsensual manipulated images of real people. Reports estimate that Grok generated millions of nonconsensual sexualized deepfakes on X within a span of days. The backlash prompted an EU investigation into SpaceXAI. Apple also reportedly threatened to remove Grok from the App Store unless the company added stronger safeguards.

Teenage girls later sued SpaceXAI, alleging Grok had been used to create and spread AI-generated child sexual abuse images of them. And the legal scrutiny continued in August, when SpaceXAI challenged a new Minnesota law targeting AI “nudification” tools, arguing parts of the law violate the First Amendment.

Michael Berthold, CEO and co-founder of AI analytics company Knime, tells me he’s concerned about the broader implications of AI chatbots rewriting or summarizing knowledge.

“The worry I have, and I see it with my own kids, is how the next generation will be learning things,” Berthold says. “There will be so much content that’s not going to be consumed in the original anymore, but in some sort of AI-rewritten, summarized form.

“Something can be lost, either accidentally or intentionally. We already see AI systems from different countries reflecting slightly different preferences.”

What’s next for Grok?

Grok is no longer confined to X or easily described as Musk’s sarcastic alternative to ChatGPT. With its capabilities expanding quickly, it could eventually be integrated into future versions of Optimus, Tesla’s humanoid robot, as well as Musk’s other projects.

Grok is carving out a unique space in the AI arms race, especially with its provocative digital personality. We’ll see whether SpaceXAI can keep that distinct identity as Grok takes on more serious work and a bigger role across Musk’s ecosystem.

Tech.title: How to Disable Apple Intelligence Features You’re Not Actually Using
Tech.content:
If Apple’s AI features aren’t part of your workflow, turning them off frees up storage and background resources in a few steps. Jeff Carlson/CNET

Apple Intelligence arrived with iOS 26 turned on by default, which means it’s been running on eligible iPhones and Macs whether their owners engage with it or not. For users who don’t use Writing Tools, have no interest in Image Playground and find notification summaries more disruptive than useful, the features are occupying storage and background resources for no practical benefit. Turning them off, either individually or all at once, takes a few taps in Settings and doesn’t affect any core iPhone functionality. Here’s how to do it on iPhone, iPad and Mac.

See also: Did a well-meaning friend send you a message about Apple Intelligence possibly reading your private information? I explain what’s actually going on.

Why turn off Apple Intelligence in the first place?

Since the first Apple Intelligence features rolled out in iOS 18.1, some people have opted out of the new technology. Tools such as Image Playground, Genmoji and message summaries can use up to 7GB of your device’s internal storage — a sizable chunk, especially if you tend to run against the upper limit of its free space.

Even if storage is not an issue, you just may not be interested in Apple’s set of AI features. A recent CNET survey finds that just 19% of US smartphone owners are choosing to upgrade their devices to take advantage of new AI features. And a recent ZDNET/Aberdeen survey reveals that the majority of US adults say they will not use most AI features, and just 8% would consider paying extra for them. Some AI features are more welcome than others, with 58% of respondents saying using AI for photo editing would be valuable.

Or, honestly, you may not want to deal with features that are creating inaccurate summaries or that can be replicated without Apple Intelligence.

The trainer killed someone? Nelson Aguilar/CNET

(Earlier iOS 18 updates re-enabled Apple Intelligence automatically even if you had turned it off, but as of iOS 18.4, the setting is honored.)

Is Apple Intelligence really ready to be on by default?

I’m not an AI crank — I appreciate features such as notification summaries and the Clean Up tool in the Photos app. And yet, Apple Intelligence is also a work in progress, an evolving set of features that Apple is heavily hyping while gradually developing. I wouldn’t hold it against you if you wanted to not be distracted or feel like you’re doing Apple’s testing for them (that’s what the developer and public betas are for).

Remember that Apple Intelligence works only on the iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, iPhone 17E, iPhone 16, iPhone 16E, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro or M-series Macs and iPads, plus the newest iPad mini.

How to see the amount of storage Apple Intelligence is using

If you’re concerned about the storage requirements of Apple Intelligence, you can find out how much the system is using by going to Settings > General > iPhone (or iPad) Storage > iOS (or iPadOS).

See how much space Apple Intelligence is using in Settings. Screenshots by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Note that even after turning off Apple Intelligence, that storage still shows up in the iOS Storage list. However, I was able to confirm that if the phone’s storage fills up and the system needs that now-inactive space, iOS reclaims what it needs.

How to turn off Apple Intelligence entirely (iPhone, iPad and Mac)

Open Settings (iPhone or iPad) or System Settings (Mac) and choose Apple Intelligence & Siri. Then turn off the Apple Intelligence option. Confirm your choice in the dialog that appears by tapping Turn Off Apple Intelligence.

Turn off Apple Intelligence entirely with one switch. Screenshots by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Here’s what you lose:

(Curiously, the Clean Up tool in Photos sticks around even when Apple Intelligence is turned off, perhaps because the first time you use it the app downloads resources for it and holds onto them.)

How to turn off individual Apple Intelligence features

Maybe you’re finding some Apple Intelligence features helpful while others are annoying (or just highly amusing). You can turn off specific features in the settings for apps to which they apply.

For example, to disable text summaries in Messages notifications, go to Settings > Apps > Messages and switch off the Summarize Messages option.

Turn off Messages summaries while still using other Apple Intelligence features. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Some features are not as app-specific. Writing Tools, which use Apple Intelligence to proof or rewrite text, appear as an option when you select text, regardless of the app. To turn that off, you need to disable Apple Intelligence system-wide.

Also note that nearly every app includes an Apple Intelligence & Siri option in Settings, with a Learn from this App option (turned on by default). That applies just to whether Apple Intelligence and Siri can monitor how you use it to make suggestions; it doesn’t affect any particular Apple Intelligence features. (Did someone forward you a social media post saying that Apple Intelligence is stealing your private data? That’s not what’s happening.)

How to turn off Apple Intelligence features in Screen Time settings

Another option for restricting what Apple Intelligence can do is buried in the Screen Time settings. Screen Time is designed to control which apps and features can run on another device, such as the iPhone used by a child in your household. But it’s also helpful for tracking how much time you’re spending on the device and, in this case, turning off some components of Apple Intelligence.

Open the Settings app and go to Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions. Turn on the Content & Privacy Restrictions option if it’s not already enabled. If this is the first time you’re flipping this switch, don’t worry — everything is allowed by default. Tap Intelligence & Siri. Tap on the following three features and decide whether to allow or don’t allow their use: Image Creation (such as Image Playground and Genmoji), Writing Tools and the ChatGPT Extension (which uses ChatGPT to process requests that are beyond the built-in Apple Intelligence capabilities).

Turn off selected Apple Intelligence features in the Screen Time settings. Screenshots by Jeff Carlson/CNET

If you haven’t upgraded to iOS 26 yet, make a good backup first. Then be sure to check out the hidden features you should try right now.

Tech.title: Just How Water-Resistant Is Apple’s iPhone? I Tested It in My Swimming Pool
Tech.content:
There’s nothing I love more than testing a tech company’s claims. I used to host a CNET YouTube series called Breaking Point, where I got to do what most people try to avoid: torture their tech. That meant purposely dropping thousands of dollars’ worth of phones on the ground, dunking them in water and pushing them to their limits.

So when Apple released its first water-resistant iPhone in 2016, I thought, “Game on!”

It’s hard to imagine now, but before the iPhone 7, a splash of water could make your Apple phone useless. Its IP67 rating means it can withstand 30 minutes in 1 meter of water (about 3 feet). To test it, I took the iPhone 7 for a “swim” in the pool at my old San Francisco apartment building, along with then CNET senior editor Sean Hollister, and filmed the whole thing.

We ended up testing it beyond its limits and didn’t exactly follow all the care instructions. Spoiler alert: The iPhone mostly survived, but it did come away with a battle scar or two.

At the time, I was blissfully unaware that just because a phone is fine after being underwater doesn’t mean it escaped damage. Chlorinated pool water and ocean saltwater can slowly corrode the materials inside a phone, even after it’s dried out. That wouldn’t kill a phone right away, but it would shorten its lifespan. Water damage (intentional or not) will void Apple’s warranty.

Looking back at this 10-year-old video of Hollister and me throwing an iPhone 7 into a pool is ironic. Instead of taking my phone on more water-related adventures, safe in the knowledge that my tech should be fine, I’m careful with my iPhone around water. Less fun, yes, but more informed.

Watch my full Did the iPhone 7 Survive Our Water Test? video down below.

Tech.title: The Free Tech Recycling Guide That Finally Gets the Job Done in One Afternoon
Tech.content:
Old laptops, desktop towers and printers can all be recycled for free through major retailers and manufacturer take-back programs. Here’s how to use them. Johner Royalty Free/Getty Images

The old laptop hasn’t moved in two years. The printer stopped working in 2023 and has been on the floor next to the desk ever since. There’s a desktop tower somewhere in the garage that predates the current administration. All of it needs to go, and the fact that it’s still there usually comes down to the same sticking point: Nobody is quite sure how to get rid of electronics responsibly, what it costs and what to do about the data first. The answers, it turns out, are simpler than the delay suggests, and the whole process, from factory reset to final drop-off, typically takes less than an afternoon.

Major retailers such as Best Buy and Staples have become drop-off hubs for digital junk. You can walk into a store with a dead PC or a clunky old scanner and hand it over for free, regardless of where you bought it. Some of these places will even give you a discount on new gear or a trade-in credit just for helping them reclaim the heavy metals and plastics that don’t belong in a landfill. It’s the easiest way to recover your storage space without feeling like a jerk for tossing electronics in the trash.

The only real “work” on your end is making sure you aren’t handing over your entire life history along with the hardware. Before you dump a device, you need to do a legitimate data wipe — not just drag files to the trash can. A 10-minute factory reset or a dedicated drive-scrubbing tool ensures your old tax returns and saved passwords don’t become someone else’s property. Stop acting like you’re going to “fix” that laptop from 2015 and let a professional recycler break it down for parts instead.

What to do before you recycle your old computer

Wherever you take or mail in your items to be recycled, you’ll want to protect your data by removing it as best you can. One way to do this is to perform a factory reset on your computer. Our guide walks you through the process.

Where to recycle your old printers and computers

Some retail stores will accept computers and printers for recycling, but it’s not always a free service. Policies vary by company.

Apple

You can recycle your old Apple computers, monitors and peripherals, such as printers, for free at an Apple store, but there’s a costly catch. According to the Apple Free Recycling program, you must purchase a qualifying Apple computer or monitor to receive this service. Need another option? A third-party company called Gazelle buys old MacBooks to recycle them. After accepting Gazelle’s offer, you print a prepaid label or request a prepaid box and ship the machine to them.



Best Buy

Best Buy generally accepts up to three household items per household per day to be recycled for free, including desktop computers and printers, as well as other items ranging from e-readers to vacuum cleaners. While three is the limit for most items, there’s a higher limit for laptops — Best Buy will take five of those per household per day. Note that rules for dropping off monitors vary by state, and it’s not always free to do so. Best Buy also offers a mail-in recycling service for select items, but that’s also not free. A small box that holds up to 6 pounds costs $23, while a large box (up to 15 pounds) costs $30. One CNET editor recently lugged in an old, nonworking tube TV-VCR combo for e-cycling, and was happy to pay $30 to be rid of it.

Office Depot

Office Depot and OfficeMax merged in 2013. The retailers offer a tech trade-in program both in-store and online, where you may be able to get a store gift card in exchange for your old computers and printers. If the device has no trade-in value, the company will recycle it for free. Office Depot also sells e-waste recycling boxes that you can fill with electronics to be recycled and then drop off at the stores, but they aren’t free. The small boxes cost $8.39 and hold up to 20 pounds, the medium ones cost $18.29 and hold up to 40 pounds, and the large boxes cost $28 and hold up to 60 pounds.

Staples

You can bring your old desktop computers, laptops, printers and more to the Staples checkout counter to be recycled for free, even if they weren’t purchased there. According to a Staples rep, the retailer also has a free at-home battery recycling box, which has led customers to recycle thousands of batteries per week, up from an earlier average of 50 per week. Here’s a list of everything that can be recycled at Staples.

Where to find electronics recycling centers

If you don’t live near a major retailer or would rather take your computers and printers to a recycling center, you can locate places near you by using search tools provided by Earth911 and the Consumer Technology Association.

Earth911

Use the recycling center search function on Earth911 to find recycling centers near your ZIP code that accept laptops, desktops and printers. Note that the results may also turn up places that accept mobile phones and not computers or printers, so you may have to do a little filtering.

Greener Gadgets

Consult the Consumer Technology Association’s Greener Gadgets Recycle Locator to find local recycling centers in your area that will take old items. The search function also allows you to filter the results to separately hunt for places that take computers versus printers.

Tech.title: China’s Robot Olympics Keep Getting Wilder
Tech.content:
It’s that time of year again when humanoid robots of all shapes, sizes and specialties converge in Beijing to see just how far this technology has come, and how far it still has to go.

Robots bested human world records in the standing high jump, 400-meter sprint and even the 100-meter sprint held by Usain Bolt.

The humanoids also took their fair share of punishment, taking spectacular falls on the track, in kickboxing, and on the dance floor. To see all the wildest highlights, check out the video in this article.
